Name the module `W4Od18m9p6t4`.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home door lock network issues digital keys to household devices. Membership of the household is managed by epoch-numbered reconfiguration: an epoch counter advances whenever the household is rebuilt, and only a device that knows the current epoch may issue a key. Every key carries the epoch it was issued under. Separately, the household's key allowance — how many keys may be outstanding at once — is changed at runtime by the account owner, and it can be set below the number of keys already outstanding.

The system behaves as follows. Reconfigure advances the epoch counter and, in the same step, revokes every outstanding key, because a key issued under the previous household is exactly what a re-keyed home must not honour. SyncAll is the household broadcast: whenever at least one device is behind, every device is brought up to the current epoch in one step. Grant issues a key: a device that knows the current epoch may hand out a key that is not already outstanding, provided the number of keys outstanding is below the current allowance, and the key is stamped with the current epoch. Revoke takes a named outstanding key back. SetAllowance changes the key allowance to any new value without touching the epoch, which is how the allowance can end up below the number of keys already outstanding. TrimKeys handles exactly that case: while the number of outstanding keys is above the allowance, one outstanding key is revoked, and it keeps happening until the household is back inside its allowance.

Two things must hold together here. No key may outlive the household it was cut for, and an allowance that has been lowered must actually come into force rather than being a number nobody honours.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every outstanding key is stamped with the current household epoch.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Whenever more keys are outstanding than the allowance permits, the household eventually comes back within its allowance.
===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

    /\ allowance \in 0 .. MaxAllowance
    /\ granted \subseteq Keys
    /\ keyEpoch \in [Keys -> 0 .. MaxEpoch]
    /\ known \in [Devices -> 0 .. MaxEpoch]

    /\ allowance = MaxAllowance
    /\ granted = {}
    /\ keyEpoch = [k \in Keys |-> 0]

    /\ epoch < MaxEpoch

    /\ granted' = {}

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A car-wash conveyor line allocates numbered conveyor slots to wash jobs, and a slot is only bound to a job after a two-phase commit across the bay controllers. The coordinator runs one attempt at a time, and every attempt carries a round number taken from a counter that advances with each new attempt. Votes come back over a link that reorders freely, so a vote cast for an earlier attempt can turn up during a later one; each vote therefore carries the round number it was cast for, and a vote whose round does not match the attempt in progress is thrown away rather than counted. Both the conveyor's own slot map and each job's record of the slot it holds are kept, and they must agree.

The system behaves as follows. Propose opens an attempt when none is in progress: the round counter advances, and the attempt records a job that currently holds no slot together with a slot the conveyor map shows as free. CastVote puts one bay controller's vote for the attempt in progress onto the link, stamped with that attempt's round number, provided a vote from that controller for that round is not already in flight. CountVote takes any vote off the link in any order; it joins the tally only if its round number matches the attempt in progress, and is otherwise discarded. CommitAttempt binds the slot when every bay controller's vote has been counted and the conveyor map still shows the slot as free: the map records the job and the job's record gains the slot, and the attempt closes with an empty tally. AbortAttempt closes the attempt without binding anything when the conveyor map no longer shows the slot as free, which is how a race for the same slot is resolved. FinishJob releases a job's slot, clearing it from the job's record and from the conveyor map together.

Two jobs on one slot is the collision the whole protocol exists to prevent, and it shows up the instant a job's record of the slot it holds disagrees with the conveyor's slot map.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every slot a job records as its own is recorded by the conveyor map as belonging to that same job.

Votes == Bays \X Rounds

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A bank's interbank settlement batch writes into a single settlement ledger, and the ledger is a critical resource: exactly one member bank may be writing to it at a time. The right to write is not taken, it is granted, and it is granted only by a two-phase commit round in which every member bank votes. Member banks can be slow without being failed: a bank may drop into a lagging state where it is still up and still part of the membership but is not answering votes for the moment, and it comes back on its own.

The system behaves as follows. OpenRound starts a commit round when no round is in flight and the write right is not currently granted, naming the bank that wants it and starting with an empty tally. CastVote records the vote of a member bank that is not lagging and has not yet voted in this round. ToggleSlow flips a bank between the responsive state and the lagging state, which is what makes a round stall without anybody having failed. CommitGrant closes a round in which every member bank has voted, handing the write right to the bank the round named. AbortRound abandons a round that has not yet collected every vote, clearing the tally and leaving the write right ungranted, which is how the batch escapes a round stalled behind a lagging bank. EnterLedger puts the bank holding the write right into the ledger, provided nobody is in there. LeaveLedger takes the bank out of the ledger and gives the write right back up in the same step, so a bank cannot step out and step back in without winning another round.

Because the write right is surrendered together with leaving the ledger, and a new round cannot even open while the right is granted, the only bank that can ever be inside the ledger is the one the last successful round named.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Any bank writing to the settlement ledger is the bank currently holding the write right.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A bank writing to the settlement ledger always eventually leaves it.
===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

A power-grid load shedder decides which feeders to drop during an emergency by quorum voting among the control-room operators. Only operators who hold a current certification may vote, and certification is granted and withdrawn while the grid is running. A privileged system-operator override also exists, which can drop a feeder without any ballot at all, and the override budget is finite.

The system behaves as follows. Certify adds an operator to the set of currently certified operators. Decertify withdraws an operator's certification and, in the same step, strikes that operator's vote from any ballot in progress, because a vote cast by someone who is no longer certified must not be allowed to stand and be counted. OpenBallot starts a ballot on a feeder that is not already shed, when no ballot is in progress, with an empty set of voters. Vote records a currently certified operator's vote on the ballot in progress; no operator votes twice in the same ballot. ShedByQuorum drops the feeder under ballot once a strict majority of the currently certified operators have voted, clearing the ballot and the voters. AdminShed is the privileged path: the system operator drops any feeder outright, spending one unit of override budget and touching no ballot. Restore brings a shed feeder back into service.

The point of striking votes on decertification is that the quorum is measured against the operators certified right now; if a stale vote could linger on a ballot, a feeder could be dropped on the authority of somebody the control room has already stood down.

Conflict is the losing side of a race: a service whose recorded version no longer matches the claim's current version drops the claim and goes idle without paying anything. The right to open the safe is granted by dispatch as a message, and dispatch messages travel over a radio link that reorders and delays them freely. The hoist is a critical resource: at most one suite may be on it, because two suites drawing from it at once mixes their instrument trays. A privileged charge-nurse override exists that can hand the token directly to a named suite out of ring order, for emergencies, and its budget is finite.

The system behaves as follows. RequestHoist moves an idle suite into the queued state, meaning it wants the hoist. GrabHoist moves the suite holding the token from queued into the using state, which is the state of actually being on the hoist. FinishHoist moves a suite from using back to idle. A car-wash conveyor line keeps its wash programs in one shared configuration pool, and two independent scheduling instances edit that pool. There is no lock: edits use optimistic locking with retry against the pool's version number, and the pool admits one edit session at a time. An edit may only be opened by an operator whose badge is currently valid, and badges are revoked and reinstated while the line is running, which is how an operator becomes stale mid-edit.

OpenEdit starts a session when the pool has no session open, recording the instance running it, the operator who authorised it, and the pool version that operator read; the operator's badge must be valid at that moment. RevokeBadge withdraws an operator's badge and, in the same step, tears down any edit session that operator authorised, because a session carrying a withdrawn badge must not be allowed to sit there and later commit. ReinstateBadge gives a badge back. ExternalBump models the other instance landing a change into the shared pool: the pool version advances, which silently invalidates the version any open session read. Retry re-bases an open session whose recorded version has fallen behind, taking the current version and spending one unit of the session's retry allowance. AbortEdit tears a session down when its recorded version no longer matches, or when the pool version can no longer advance.

A university course-registration system is fronted by two independent registration instances that share one pool of course seats. Seats are only filled by a two-phase commit across the departmental approvers, and the pool admits one commit round at a time. An elevator bank in a skyscraper lets technicians into the machine room, which is a critical resource: only one technician may be in there, because the brake test they run there acts on the whole bank. Entry is protected by a two-level lock hierarchy — a technician must first hold the single bank lock, and only then may it take the lock on an individual car. A technician can crash silently, stopping work with no notice while still holding everything it has taken, so the building system carries a watchdog that can force the whole hierarchy open.

The system behaves as follows. AcquireBank gives an uncrashed technician the bank lock when it is free, starting a fresh session in which no car has yet been used and the machine room has not yet been visited. AcquireCar gives the technician holding the bank lock the lock on a free car, provided that car has not already been used and given back during this session. ReleaseCar gives back a car lock the technician holds and records that car as used for the rest of the session. EnterRoom puts the technician holding the bank lock into the machine room, provided the room is empty and the room has not already been visited during this session. LeaveRoom takes the technician out of the machine room and marks the room as visited for the rest of the session. ReleaseBank gives back the bank lock, and requires that the technician holds no car locks and that the machine room is empty. Crash silently disables a technician, after which it can acquire, release, enter and leave nothing. ForceRelease is the watchdog: when the bank lock is held by a technician that has crashed, it tears the whole hierarchy down at once — the bank lock and every car lock are released and the machine room is cleared.

Because the room can only be entered by the bank-lock holder and the bank lock cannot be handed on while the room is occupied, at most one technician is ever in the machine room; the watchdog is what stops a crashed holder from making that "at most one" mean "exactly one, forever".

A wildfire drone surveillance swarm maintains one shared fire-perimeter record. LandUpdate is the compare-and-swap: a drone whose held read still matches the record's version extends the perimeter by its amount, the version advances, a revision-log entry pairing the superseded version with the extension is written, and the drone's read is cleared. A hospital operating-room scheduler keeps a master theatre schedule that is edited under a lease. A node takes the lease, makes its change against the version it read, and commits; the lease carries a countdown, and when the countdown runs out the lease is taken back whether or not the holder ever committed. Every committed change advances the schedule's version by one and writes the committing node into the authorship record for the version it superseded. A privileged duty-manager override can seize the lease from whoever holds it.

The system behaves as follows. TakeLease gives a node the lease when it is free, starting the countdown at its full value and recording the version the node read as its base. Commit applies a change: the node holding the lease, whose recorded base still matches the schedule's version and whose countdown has not run out, advances the version by one and writes itself into the authorship record for the version it just superseded; the lease is given up in the same step. Rebase lets the holder whose base has fallen behind pick up the current version and try again without giving up the lease. Tick advances the clock, decrementing the countdown while it is above zero. ExpireLease takes the lease back once the countdown has reached zero, discarding whatever the holder was working on. SeizeLease is the privileged path: the duty manager takes the lease away from its current holder outright, leaving it free.

An update is lost when a version is superseded without anybody being recorded as its author, or when the authorship record claims a version that the schedule has not actually passed. Because commit does both things in one step and no other step touches either, the authorship record and the version counter are two views of the same history.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A held lease on the master schedule is always eventually free again.

Allocate gives a feeder an additional block of import capacity, and requires the total load afterwards to stay within the rated import; the feeder's countdown is restarted at its full value. ShedBlock takes a block of capacity back off a feeder that holds at least that much, lowering the total load. Tick advances the clock, decrementing every feeder's countdown that is still above zero. ExpireLeases fires whenever at least one feeder has run its countdown to zero while still holding capacity, and returns everything held by every such feeder in one step, lowering the total load accordingly. EmergencyRedispatch is the privileged path: the control room drops every feeder's allocation to nothing and gives one named feeder a block within the rated import, spending one unit of override budget; because it clears the board first, the emergency block is always inside the rating.

A bank's interbank settlement batch runs on a cluster of settlement servers with leader election and failover. Only the leader of the current term may post to the batch. Election messages travel over a link that reorders and delays freely, so a vote cast in an earlier term can arrive in the middle of a later one; every vote message therefore carries the term it was cast for, and a vote whose term does not match the term now running is thrown away rather than counted.

Campaign starts a new term: the term counter advances, the leadership of the new term begins vacant, the tally is emptied, and the campaigning server puts its own vote for the new term onto the link. SendVote puts one server's vote for the current term onto the link, provided that server does not already have a vote for that term in flight and has not already been counted. CountVote takes any vote message off the link, in any order: it joins the tally only if the term it carries is the term now running, and is otherwise consumed and discarded. TakeLeadership makes a server that has been counted the leader of the current term, provided a strict majority has been counted and the term has no leader yet. PostBatch lets the leader of the current term post an entry into the settlement batch. StepDown vacates the leadership of the current term.

The tally is what authorises a leader, so the tally must never contain anything but votes cast for the term actually running; a vote that drifted in from an earlier term would let a server claim a majority it never had, and post to the batch on stale authority.

A car-wash conveyor line finishes cars with a hot-wax coat drawn from a single drum. Applying the wax is irreversible — the coat is on, it cannot be taken off, and a second coat would draw a second measure out of the drum. Several finishing bays work the line at once and none of them locks anything: they use optimistic locking with retry against each car's record version. A bay reads a car and the version it is at, and its application only goes ahead if that version is still current; every application advances the car's version, as does an independent revision of the car's record. A privileged shift-manager override can wax a car outright without reading anything, and its budget is finite.

The system behaves as follows. ReadCar has an idle bay pick up a car that has not been waxed, recording the car and the version it saw. ApplyWax is the irreversible act: the bay applies the coat when the version it recorded still matches the car's current version, the drum has at least one measure left, and the car's version can still advance; the car joins the waxed set, one measure leaves the drum, the car's version advances and the bay goes idle. Conflict is the losing side of a race: a bay whose recorded version no longer matches drops the car and goes idle without applying anything. ReviseCar amends a car's record independently, advancing its version and thereby invalidating any read a bay is holding on it. ManagerWax is the privileged path: an unwaxed car whose version can still advance is waxed outright, one measure leaves the drum, the car's version advances and one unit of override budget is spent.

The drum is the audit trail. It started full, and exactly one measure leaves it for each car that joins the waxed set. A smart-home installation has several door-lock controllers wired to one shared unlock channel -- the single low-voltage line that actually throws the deadbolts. Only one controller may be driving that line at a time; two controllers driving it together brown out the bus and leave bolts half-thrown. The hub decides who is allowed to drive it, and it does so by publishing a numbered configuration: each new configuration carries the next epoch number and names exactly one controller as the epoch's designated driver, or names nobody at all while the installer is mid-change.

Controllers learn about new configurations lazily, one epoch at a time, over the same slow mesh that carries battery reports. A controller may only take the channel if it is the controller the current configuration names and it has actually caught up to the current epoch -- a controller that still believes an older configuration is in force must not touch the line, even if it was the driver under that older configuration. Whenever the hub publishes a new configuration it first cuts power to the channel, so nobody is left driving the line across an epoch boundary.

Controllers can also die silently: no error, no last message, just an entry that stops answering. A controller that has died may still be recorded as holding the channel, and the hub cannot wait for it to give the line back politely, so the hub is allowed to revoke the channel from a holder it has marked dead. A healthy holder gives the line back on its own once its bolt sequence finishes. A controller that has died can come back: the installation's nightly power cycle brings a dead unit back onto the mesh, still believing whatever epoch it last learned, and a unit can die again afterwards. The actions of the system are: the hub publishing a new numbered configuration, a controller catching up one epoch, the named driver taking the channel, a healthy holder releasing the channel, the hub revoking the channel from a dead holder, a controller dying silently, and a dead controller coming back on a power cycle.

A car-wash conveyor has several wash bays and a handful of attendants working the line. Each bay has a ticket record -- what package the car bought, which extras were added at the arch, whether the wax pass ran. Attendants edit those tickets from a shared terminal, and the shop protects them with two levels of lock taken in a fixed order: first the coarse line lock, which only one attendant can hold at a time and which covers the whole conveyor, then the fine lock on the particular bay whose ticket is being edited. An edit starts by taking the line lock and then the bay lock, at which point the attendant copies down the bay ticket's current revision number as the basis for its edit. Committing writes the edited ticket back, advances that bay's revision number, drops the bay lock and the line lock together, and lets the next attendant in. A commit is only meaningful if the revision the attendant copied down is still the revision the bay is on -- an edit computed against a revision that has since moved on would silently throw away whatever moved it.

Attendants can walk off. The failure is silent: no handover, no shout down the line, the attendant simply stops and the locks they were holding stay held. A car-wash conveyor draws its soap from a bonded store of detergent concentrate. The store is measured in sealed units, and the number of units on the site is fixed for the day: nothing is delivered mid-shift and nothing may be poured away. Units leave the store only on a lease to one of the two wash bays. A lease covers a whole number of units and comes with a countdown; while the countdown is running the units sit in that bay's day tank, still on the books as leased rather than as store stock.

A bay draws down its lease one unit at a time as cars go through, and each unit drawn is logged as consumed. When a lease's countdown reaches zero the lease ends: whatever units are still sitting in that bay's day tank are pumped back to the store and the bay's lease goes to nothing. A bay may only take out a new lease once its previous lease has ended, and a lease can only be granted for units the store actually has.

Bays fail silently. A bay's controller can stop answering with no alarm and no partial-drain report; the units already in its day tank are stranded there and are still leased to that bay, which is exactly why the countdown is on the lease and not on the bay. When the lease expires the stranded units come back to the store whether or not the bay is answering, and a failed bay is eventually power-cycled back onto the line.

An operator runs a network of vending machines that all draw change from one bonded coin float held in a central register. The number of coins in the whole system is fixed between route visits: coins move around but none appear and none vanish. A print shop's job spooler lets operators edit the ticket attached to a queued job -- stock, sides, finishing, due time. To edit a ticket an operator takes a lease on that job. A lease names one operator and carries a countdown; leases are not renewed, so every lease runs out on its own. While an operator holds a live lease on a job it may stage an edit, which means noting the job ticket's current version number and holding the edited ticket ready to write.

Committing a staged edit writes the ticket and advances that job's version number. What must never happen is a staged edit that is still considered writable while resting on a version the job has already moved past, because writing it would silently undo whatever moved the version. The spooler therefore ties staging to the lease: when a lease's countdown reaches zero, the lease ends and any edit staged against that job under that lease is thrown away in the same motion. The shift supervisor has an override. A supervisor can seize the lease on any job at any time -- a rush order, a press about to go idle -- taking ownership away from whoever held it and setting a fresh countdown. Seizing throws away whatever edit was staged against that job by the previous holder, for exactly the same reason expiry does. The shop limits how many seizures a shift may contain, so the override cannot be used to hold a job open indefinitely.

A box may also change its own settings locally, but only between rounds, and only while it has no vote outstanding. Every write that lands records the version it was computed against and moves the section to the next version, which means the recorded bases form an unbroken chain: the change in force on a section was always computed against the version immediately before the one the section is on now. A lost update would show up as a break in that chain -- a change in force whose recorded base is two or more versions back, meaning something in between was written and then silently overwritten.

Sections stop accepting writes once they reach the registrar's version ceiling for the term; a worker holding an attempt against a section that has hit the ceiling abandons the attempt rather than retrying forever.

Workers crash silently. A worker simply stops, and the attempt it was holding stops with it -- there is no rollback to do, because an attempt that never landed changed nothing. The scheduler notices workers that have gone quiet, clears whatever attempt they were holding and puts them back in the pool.

Dropping the trip is not something you undo from the control room: the train stops where it stops, a supervisor walks the tunnel, and the service pattern is rewritten for the rest of the day. Authority moves between interlocking controllers by numbered reconfiguration. Each reconfiguration advances the epoch and records, against that epoch number, which controller holds authority in it. The record for an epoch is written once, when the epoch begins, and the whole history of who held authority in which epoch is what the incident investigators read afterwards.

A busy airport allocates departure slots on its runways from several controller positions at once. There is no lock on a runway. A controller opens a claim against a runway and notes the sequence number that runway's movement list was on when the claim was opened. Committing the claim only works if the list is still on that sequence number; otherwise another position got a movement in first, and the controller re-reads and works from the new number.

Every runway has a hard movement ceiling, set by the noise abatement agreement and the arrestor-bed inspection schedule. The ceiling is not a soft target: exceeding it is a reportable event, and no path through the tower's software may put more movements on a runway than the ceiling allows. Movements come off the list again when an aircraft actually rolls, which frees room under the ceiling.

The duty supervisor has an override for the cases the optimistic path handles badly -- a medevac, a fuel emergency, a diversion that has to go now. Using the override forces a movement onto a runway without waiting for a claim's sequence number to line up. What the override does not do is lift the ceiling: a forced movement still has to fit under it, because the ceiling is the one number the tower cannot argue with. The supervisor is allowed a limited number of overrides per shift, logged and reviewed afterwards.

A controller holding a claim against a runway that has reached its ceiling gives the claim up rather than spinning on it, and comes back when a movement has rolled. The same applies when the runway's movement list has run to the end of the shift's sequence book: there is no number left to commit against, so the claim is given up.

A hospital's operating-room scheduler is written around a single compare-and-swap register. The register holds the count of rooms currently booked together with a generation number, and every scheduler terminal that wants to book or cancel does the same thing: read the generation, work out the change, then swap. The swap only takes if the generation is still the one that was read; otherwise another terminal got in first and the attempt is dropped, to be started again from a fresh read.

How many rooms can be booked at once is not a property of the building. It is a property of who is on shift: an operating room without an anaesthetist and a scrub team is not a room, it is a cupboard with a table in it. The staffing office therefore sets the number of staffed rooms during the day as people clock on and off, and that number is the ceiling on booked rooms. The ceiling moves both ways, but the staffing office may never set it below the number of rooms already booked -- a booked room has a patient consented, premedicated and often already in the anaesthetic bay, and there is no mechanism in the scheduler to un-book somebody because a nurse went home. Lowering staffing therefore waits for cases to finish.

A booking attempt whose swap takes adds a booked room, but only if the booking would still be under the staffed ceiling at the moment the swap lands, which is what stops a stale attempt from booking into a ceiling that has come down since it was read. A cancellation attempt whose swap takes removes a booked room. Every swap that takes, in either direction, advances the generation.

The actions of the system are: a terminal starting an attempt and reading the generation, a booking swap taking and adding a booked room under the ceiling, a cancellation swap taking and removing a booked room, an attempt being dropped because the generation has moved since it was read, or because the register has run out its generation book for the day, or because there is nothing left for it to do -- a booking attempt with the ceiling already reached, or a cancellation attempt with nothing booked --, and the staffing office setting the number of staffed rooms to any value not below the number already booked.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of booked rooms never exceeds the number of staffed rooms, and no outstanding attempt was read against a generation ahead of the register's current one.

The overnight interbank settlement batch is driven by one member bank at a time. The banks elect a batch leader, and the election stamps a term number on the winner. Only the bank that is both the current leader and has itself caught up to the current term number may post settlement legs into the batch; every other bank is either not the leader or is running on a term that has already been superseded, and in either case its postings would be junk that the clearing house cannot reconcile.

Leaders fail. When the batch leader falls over, the seat is empty, that bank is marked down, and whatever posting run it had open is stopped where it stands. A new election fills the seat and advances the term, up to the highest term the batch register can record for one night; a bank that is marked down cannot win an election until the operations desk brings it back up. Banks that are not the leader learn about term advances lazily off the settlement bus, which is why a bank can be sitting on a stale term without knowing it.

The central bank's duty officer has an override. On a night when the elections are thrashing and the window is closing, the duty officer installs a leader directly: the named bank takes the seat, the term advances, that bank is brought level with the new term, and every posting run in progress anywhere is stopped. The override is rationed -- a fixed number per night, each one written into the morning report.

The actions of the system are: electing a leader for the batch and advancing the term, the leader failing and leaving the seat empty with its posting run stopped, a non-leader bank learning the current term off the settlement bus, the current leader opening a posting run, a bank closing its posting run, the duty officer installing a leader directly and stopping every posting run, and the operations desk bringing a downed bank back up.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every bank with a posting run open holds the batch leader's seat and has caught up to the current term number.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A bank that has a posting run open eventually has no posting run open.

A container terminal moves boxes between three places: the ship's cells, the quay stack alongside the crane, and the yard block inland. A box is always in exactly one of those three places -- the terminal's whole accounting rests on it, because a box that is on the books in two places is a box that will be looked for in the wrong one, and a box on the books in none of them is a box that has been lost.

No single planner may order a move. The terminal runs three planning systems -- the stowage planner, the yard planner and the crane scheduler -- and a move only goes ahead once a strict majority of them have approved that particular box's move. Approvals accumulate against the box: a planner adds its approval, and when the majority is there the move is executed and the box's approvals are cleared, because the next move has to be approved on its own merits. Approvals can also be cleared without a move, which is what happens when the planning cycle rolls over and the planners re-plan from the berth schedule.

The moves themselves are the ordinary sequence of a discharge and a re-stow: a box comes off the ship onto the quay stack, a box goes from the quay stack into the yard block, and a box comes back out of the yard block onto the quay stack for a later loading.

The terminal superintendent has an override. When the crane is about to go idle and the planners have not converged, the superintendent forces a box off the quay stack into the yard block without waiting for a majority. The override is rationed and each use is logged; what it does not do is invent or destroy a box, because the box still goes from exactly one place to exactly one other.

The actions of the system are: a planner approving a box's move, a box moving from the ship to the quay stack on a majority, a box moving from the quay stack to the yard block on a majority, a box moving from the yard block back to the quay stack on a majority, the superintendent forcing a box from the quay stack to the yard block without a majority, and the planners clearing a box's accumulated approvals at a planning cycle rollover.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The boxes on the ship, the boxes on the quay stack and the boxes in the yard block partition the whole set of boxes, so no box is ever in two of those places and none is in fewer than one.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An approach control facility hands landing clearances out of a shared pool. The pool has a hard size: the number of aircraft that may be inside the final approach corridor at once, fixed by the separation minima and the runway occupancy time. Each approach sector takes a lease when it wants to run an aircraft down the corridor, and a lease occupies one place in the pool for as long as it is live. The facility also works to a fixed issue budget: only so many leases may be granted in one watch, after which the corridor is closed out and the next watch starts a fresh book.

Every lease carries a countdown, wound to the full lease duration when it is granted. The countdown runs down step by step. When it reaches its last step the lease expires: the lease is torn down and its place in the pool is handed back in the same motion. A sector that has finished early can also give its lease back before the countdown runs out, which frees the place immediately. What must never happen is a lease that is live with no countdown left on it, because that is a place in the pool that nothing will ever hand back.

Sectors fail silently. A sector position can lose its data feed and stop working the corridor without any indication to the facility -- no alarm, no handover, and no early release of the lease it is holding. This is exactly the case the lease countdown exists for: the failed sector's place comes back when the lease expires, whether or not anybody at that position is still alive to notice. A silently failed sector is eventually brought back onto the position by the watch supervisor.

Because places only leave the pool when a lease is granted and only return when a lease is torn down or given back, the number of live leases never exceeds the size of the pool, and the corridor never holds more aircraft than the separation minima allow.

The actions of the system are: granting a sector a lease while the pool has a free place and the watch's issue budget has not run out, a live lease's countdown running down one step, a lease expiring on its last step and handing its place back, a sector giving its lease back early, a sector failing silently, and the watch supervisor bringing a failed sector back onto position.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of live leases never exceeds the size of the clearance pool, and no live lease has a countdown of zero left on it.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A sector that holds a live lease eventually holds none, because every countdown runs out even when the sector has silently failed.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A whole-home security installation coordinates its battery-powered door locks over a single shared pool of wireless time slots. Two coordinators run side by side and independently -- the ground-floor coordinator and the upstairs coordinator -- and both draw from that one pool; nothing outside the two of them hands out slots. A lock can only transmit in a slot that has been assigned to the coordinator responsible for it, so a slot that is handed to both coordinators at once produces two radios talking over each other and a door whose state is reported wrongly.

The installation is reconfigured from time to time (a lock is added, the mesh is re-surveyed), and reconfiguration is numbered: the hub advances a network epoch counter. Each coordinator learns about the new epoch on its own schedule and records the epoch it has adopted. A coordinator may only assign a slot while the epoch it has adopted is the current network epoch; a coordinator that has fallen behind is frozen out of the pool until it catches up. Every slot handed out is stamped with the epoch it was handed out in.

When a reconfiguration happens, every slot currently assigned to any coordinator is pulled out of that coordinator's assignment set and parked in an orphan holding area. Orphaned slots do not go straight back into the free pool: a slot returns to the pool only once every coordinator has adopted an epoch strictly later than the stamp the slot carries, which is the point at which no coordinator can still believe it holds that slot.

The full set of actions is: Assign, in which a coordinator whose adopted epoch equals the current network epoch takes a slot out of the free pool, adds it to its own assignment set, and stamps it with the current epoch; Release, in which a coordinator gives a slot it holds back to the free pool; Reconfigure, in which the hub advances the network epoch by one (up to a configured maximum) and moves every assigned slot from every coordinator into the orphan area; Adopt, in which a coordinator that is behind the network epoch catches up to it; and Recycle, in which an orphaned slot whose stamp is strictly older than every coordinator's adopted epoch is returned to the free pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The free pool, the orphan area and the two coordinators' assignment sets always partition the slot space -- every slot sits in exactly one of them -- so no slot is ever allocated to two coordinators at once or advertised as free while it is still held.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A hospital pharmacy runs several dispensing stations that all write into one shared dispense record for a patient: the set of prescription items that have actually been handed out. The record is the legal document, and the danger being modelled is not two people touching the cabinet at once -- it is an update disappearing. A station reads the record, works out what it wants to add, and writes back the whole record it believes in; if it writes back a picture it took before a colleague's item landed, that colleague's item is silently erased and a patient's chart says a drug was never dispensed when it was.

The stations sit in a ring and a single work token circulates around it. A station may only write the record back while the token is with it. Passing the token is unconditional -- it moves on whether or not the station it is leaving did anything -- so no station can hold up the ring.

A station is allowed to be slow but never to drop out: it can go quiet for a while (a pharmacist walks away from the terminal) and later come back. While a station is quiet it neither takes a fresh picture of the record nor writes anything back, but it stays in the ring and the token keeps passing through it, and whatever picture and staged items it had are still there when it returns.

The write-back is guarded: a station may only write the record back if the picture it holds is still exactly the record as it stands right now. If someone else has written in the meantime, the station's picture is out of date and it must take a fresh one, which discards nothing it has staged but re-bases it.

The full set of actions is: Snapshot, in which an active station replaces its picture with the record as it currently stands; Prepare, in which an active station stages a prescription item that is not in its own picture; WriteBack, in which the station holding the token, if it is active, has staged items, and holds a picture equal to the current record, replaces the record with its picture plus its staged items, clears its staged items, and re-bases its picture on the new record; PassToken, in which the token moves to the next station in the ring; GoQuiet, in which an active station becomes quiet; and ComeBack, in which a quiet station becomes active again.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Everything any station has ever seen in the shared record is still in the shared record -- the union of all the stations' pictures is always a subset of the record itself -- so no station's write-back ever erases an item another station had already observed.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

ASSUME RingSize \in Nat \ {0}

Stations == 0 .. RingSize - 1

VARIABLES record, picture, staged, token, active

vars == <<record, picture, staged, token, active>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ record \in SUBSET Items
    /\ picture \in [Stations -> SUBSET Items]
    /\ staged \in [Stations -> SUBSET Items]
    /\ token \in Stations
    /\ active \in [Stations -> BOOLEAN]

Init ==
    /\ record = {}
    /\ picture = [s \in Stations |-> {}]
    /\ staged = [s \in Stations |-> {}]
    /\ token = 0
    /\ active = [s \in Stations |-> TRUE]

Seen == UNION {picture[s] : s \in Stations}

\* Taking a fresh picture is the only way a station learns what is recorded.
Snapshot(s) ==
    /\ active[s]
    /\ picture' = [picture EXCEPT ![s] = record]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, staged, token, active>>

Prepare(s, i) ==
    /\ active[s]
    /\ i \notin picture[s]
    /\ i \notin staged[s]
    /\ staged' = [staged EXCEPT ![s] = @ \cup {i}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, picture, token, active>>

\* Read-modify-write: the station writes back its own picture plus its
\* staged items, so it may only do so while that picture is still current.
WriteBack(s) ==

    /\ active[s]
    /\ staged[s] # {}
    /\ picture[s] = record
    /\ record' = picture[s] \cup staged[s]
    /\ picture' = [picture EXCEPT ![s] = record']
    /\ staged' = [staged EXCEPT ![s] = {}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<token, active>>

PassToken ==
    /\ token' = (token + 1) % RingSize
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, picture, staged, active>>

    /\ active[s]
    /\ active' = [active EXCEPT ![s] = FALSE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, picture, staged, token>>

    /\ ~active[s]
    /\ active' = [active EXCEPT ![s] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, picture, staged, token>>

    \/ \E s \in Stations : WriteBack(s)
    \/ PassToken

<|start|>user<|message|>Write a TLA+ specification that implements EXACTLY the system described below, and a TLC .cfg to model-check it. The system's safety property described in the NL text must be captured as a real, non-trivial INVARIANT (not `Inv == TRUE`) in the .cfg.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A wildfire surveillance swarm keeps one shared perimeter map: the set of sectors currently confirmed to be burning. Two mission consoles run side by side and independently -- the incident-command console and the aviation console -- and both write into that single map. Neither is subordinate to the other and there is no lock to take.

Instead the map carries a revision number and every write is optimistic. A console starts a cycle by reading the map: it copies the map into its own draft and remembers the revision number it read at. It then folds in whatever its drones have reported, adding sectors to its draft one at a time. When it tries to publish, the write is a compare-and-set: it goes through only if the map's revision number is still the one the console read at. Publishing installs the console's draft as the new map and advances the revision number by one.

Because the two consoles are independent, either can be beaten to the punch. A console may also abandon a cycle at any point and go back to reading -- that is the retry arm of the scheme, and it is what a console does when its compare-and-set is no longer going to succeed. Abandoning throws the draft away; the console must re-read the map and re-fold its observations onto the fresher picture. Reading is what re-bases the draft on reality, and it is precisely why a stale draft can never be published: publishing requires the revision number to be untouched since the read.

The revision number runs up to a configured bound and does not wrap, so a console never mistakes an old revision for the current one.

The full set of actions is: Read, in which a console in the reading phase copies the current map into its draft, records the current revision number, and moves to the publishing phase; Extend, in which a console in the publishing phase folds one further sector into its draft; Publish, in which a console in the publishing phase whose recorded revision number still equals the map's revision number installs its draft as the new map, advances the revision number, and returns to the reading phase; and Abandon, in which a console in the publishing phase gives up on its draft and returns to the reading phase without changing the map.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No console can ever erase a sector another console has already published -- any console whose recorded revision number is still the map's current revision number holds a draft that contains the whole current map, so the draft it is entitled to publish is an extension of the map and never a rollback of it.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: The optimistic retry scheme never livelocks -- the map's revision number eventually reaches its bound, so it is impossible for both consoles to spin forever reading and abandoning without any of their publishes ever landing.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

---- MODULE W4Od14m0p1t2 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Consoles, Sectors, MaxRevision

ASSUME MaxRevision \in Nat \ {0}

Phases == {"reading", "publishing"}

VARIABLES map, revision, readAt, draft, phase

vars == <<map, revision, readAt, draft, phase>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ map \in SUBSET Sectors
    /\ revision \in 0 .. MaxRevision
    /\ readAt \in [Consoles -> 0 .. MaxRevision]
    /\ draft \in [Consoles -> SUBSET Sectors]
    /\ phase \in [Consoles -> Phases]

Init ==
    /\ map = {}
    /\ revision = 0
    /\ readAt = [c \in Consoles |-> 0]
    /\ draft = [c \in Consoles |-> {}]
    /\ phase = [c \in Consoles |-> "reading"]

\* Reading is what re-bases a draft on reality; it is the only way a console
\* learns the map, and it records the revision the compare-and-set will test.
Read(c) ==
    /\ phase[c] = "reading"
    /\ draft' = [draft EXCEPT ![c] = map]
    /\ readAt' = [readAt EXCEPT ![c] = revision]
    /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![c] = "publishing"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<map, revision>>

Extend(c, s) ==
    /\ phase[c] = "publishing"
    /\ s \notin draft[c]
    /\ draft' = [draft EXCEPT ![c] = @ \cup {s}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<map, revision, readAt, phase>>

\* The compare-and-set: it lands only if nobody else published meanwhile.
Publish(c) ==
    /\ phase[c] = "publishing"
    /\ readAt[c] = revision
    /\ revision < MaxRevision
    /\ map' = draft[c]
    /\ revision' = revision + 1
    /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![c] = "reading"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<readAt, draft>>

Abandon(c) ==
    /\ phase[c] = "publishing"
    /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![c] = "reading"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<map, revision, readAt, draft>>

Next ==
    \/ \E c \in Consoles : Read(c)
    \/ \E c \in Consoles, s \in Sectors : Extend(c, s)
    \/ \E c \in Consoles : Publish(c)
    \/ \E c \in Consoles : Abandon(c)

\* Reading is always available, so weak fairness suffices for it; publishing
\* comes and goes as the other console wins races, so it needs strong fairness.
Spec ==
    /\ Init
    /\ [][Next]_vars
    /\ WF_vars(\E c \in Consoles : Read(c))
    /\ SF_vars(\E c \in Consoles : Publish(c))

\* A draft that is still entitled to publish covers the whole current map,
\* so installing it extends the map instead of rolling part of it back.
NoStaleDraftCanErase ==
    \A c \in Consoles : readAt[c] = revision => map \subseteq draft[c]

\* Optimistic retry cannot livelock: the revision counter always gets home.
RevisionAdvances == <>(revision = MaxRevision)

====

What they share is one pool of game servers, and a server running a ranked match is a server that cannot run a casual one.

Each matchmaker keeps its own waiting queue, and each queue is bounded. When a queue is at its bound the matchmaker applies backpressure: it simply refuses to take another ticket until a match starts and a place frees up. The bound is what stops a queue growing without limit during an outage and then dumping thousands of stale tickets onto the pool when the outage clears.

Tickets are only as good as the session they were minted in. A token stamped with an older epoch is stale, and a stale token is not a player the matchmakers may act on. Rotating the epoch therefore empties both waiting queues in the same motion, because everything sitting in them was admitted on the strength of a token that no longer means anything. A player whose token has gone stale refreshes it against the current epoch and can then queue again.

The one thing neither matchmaker can check for itself is whether the other has already taken a player, so the studio enforces it at the point of admission: a player is only admitted to a queue if they are in neither queue at that moment.

A wildfire surveillance swarm carries one satellite uplink between all of its drones. The uplink is a single radio: two drones keying it at the same time produce a collision that costs the ground station the whole pass, so exactly one drone may be transmitting at any instant, and only the drone that currently holds the uplink may transmit at all.

Imagery comes off the sensors faster than the uplink can carry it, so each drone buffers frames into a bounded outbound queue. When a drone's queue is full it applies backpressure and stops accepting frames from its own sensor rather than overwriting what is already buffered -- a dropped frame in the middle of a burn perimeter is worse than a gap at the end of it. A drone with nothing buffered has no reason to want the uplink; a drone with frames buffered asks for it and waits its turn.

Holding the uplink is a three-step affair: a waiting drone is granted the uplink, keys the transmitter and starts sending, and then stops sending and gives the uplink back when its buffer has drained enough. The grant is what makes the exclusion work: a drone that has not been granted the uplink never keys the transmitter.

The incident commander can preempt. When a spotter drone has line of sight on a new head of fire, the commander takes the uplink away from whoever has it -- stopping that drone's transmission in the same motion -- and gives it to the drone that matters. Preemption is rationed for the flight, because every preemption is a truncated frame somebody has to re-fly.

A blood bank's inventory records are posted to by technicians working without any lock on the record. A technician opens a posting against a unit record, notes the revision the record was on, and writes only if the record is still on that revision; if it has moved, the technician re-reads and works from the new revision instead.

Every technician's competency is certified to a particular point on the bank's audit clock, and the clock advances as the day's audit windows close. A technician whose certification point is behind the clock is out of certification and may not post to anything. The bank is strict about this because a posting made by an uncertified technician has to be backed out by hand and every unit it touched has to be re-tested. When the clock advances past a technician's certification point, any posting that technician had open is closed out in the same motion -- the posting cannot be allowed to sit there and land later. Technicians re-certify against the register and can then post again.

Technicians here are slow, not broken. A technician is interrupted by a cross-match, a phone call from theatre, a courier at the door; a posting can sit open across several clock advances while the record underneath it moves on. That is what the re-read is for, and it is why the certification check has to be made again at the moment of writing rather than only when the posting was opened.

Unit records stop accepting postings once they reach the revision ceiling the bank keeps for a single audit day; a technician holding a posting against a record at the ceiling closes it out rather than re-reading forever.

The gangs elect a leader and the election stamps a shift number on the winner, up to the highest number the berth log can carry for one shift. Gangs are slow, not absent. A gang that has taken on a piece of work stays on it for a while -- lashing rods do not come off quickly, and there is no way to hurry a gang that is mid-set. ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A hospital books its operating rooms through a single compare-and-swap register that carries a generation number. Requests to book a named room do not reach the register directly: they are posted onto the theatre message bus by the surgical units, and the bus reorders freely. A request that a unit posted first can be processed last, and there is no way for a unit to know where in the order its request will land.

Every posted request carries the room it names and the generation the register was on when the unit posted it. Applying a request is the compare-and-swap: it only takes if the register is still on the generation the request carries, and applying it books the named room and advances the generation. Advancing the generation is what invalidates every other request still sitting on the bus -- their carried generations no longer match, so they are stale and get dropped rather than applied. A unit whose request was dropped posts a fresh one.

The hospital will not staff more than a fixed number of rooms at once, so a request that arrives while that number is already booked is dropped rather than applied, and the unit tries again after a case finishes. Because a request is only ever posted against a room that is free at the moment of posting, and because applying one request makes every other outstanding request stale, no request that is still applicable can be pointing at a room that is already booked.

Cases finishing is a separate ledger operation, not a compare-and-swap: a booked room is released and becomes free again without touching the generation, because releasing a room can only make an outstanding request easier to satisfy, never harder.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No more rooms are booked than the hospital staffs, and no request that is still applicable names a room that is already booked.

The opening auction on a stock exchange collects resting orders at a set of price levels, and every level has a hard depth limit -- the number of orders the matching engine will hold at that price before it refuses more. The limit counts orders already resting at the level and orders that have been submitted for it but have not been written in yet, because a submitted order is depth that is coming.

Member sessions reach the book through two levels of lock, taken in a fixed order. A session first takes the book lock, which the whole auction shares and which only one session can hold. Only then may it take the lock on the particular price level it wants to work, and only then may it submit an order for that level. Releasing gives up the level lock and the book lock together. The ordering is not decoration: sessions that grabbed level locks directly used to deadlock against each other across two levels during the pre-open.

Submitted orders do not reach the book immediately. They go onto the entry bus, which reorders freely: an order submitted for one level can be written into the book long after one submitted later for another level, and the engine writes whatever is at the front of whichever queue it services next. That is why the depth limit has to count the orders still on the bus -- checking only what is resting would let a session submit into a level that is about to fill up from the bus.

Orders are also cancelled off levels, which frees depth outright and does not go through the bus at all.

The actions of the system are: a session taking the book lock, a session that holds the book lock taking a free price level's lock, a session submitting an order for the level it holds while that level's resting orders and bussed orders together are under the depth limit, the engine writing one bussed order into the level it was submitted for, a resting order being cancelled off a level, and a session releasing its level lock and the book lock together.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every price level, the orders resting at it plus the orders still on the entry bus for it never together exceed that level's depth limit.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An airport baggage router has a disposal chute for bags that have gone through the whole unclaimed-baggage process and are to be destroyed. Sending a bag down that chute is irreversible: there is no path back, and a bag that goes down it twice is a bag whose paperwork says one thing and whose count says another. Each bag may therefore be sent down the chute at most once.

The router does not lock bag records. An operator opens a disposal request against a bag and notes the status version that bag's record was on. The request then goes onto the router's control bus, and the bus reorders freely -- a request raised early can be acted on last, and there is no ordering between the requests of different operators at all. Acting on a request is only allowed if the bag's status version is still the one the request noted; anything else has happened to that bag since, and the request is stale and is dropped rather than acted on.

Every event that touches a bag's record advances its status version: a disposal, a re-scan when the bag turns up on a different belt, and an owner claim being registered. Advancing the version is exactly what makes every other request outstanding against that bag stale, and it is the mechanism that stops two operators both disposing of the same bag: whichever request is acted on first advances the version and invalidates the rest.

Bags stop accepting record events once they reach the version ceiling the router keeps for one operating day; an operator holding a request against a bag at the ceiling drops it rather than retrying.

The actions of the system are: an operator opening a disposal request against a bag and noting its status version, an operator acting on a request whose noted version still matches and sending that bag down the chute, an operator dropping a request whose noted version no longer matches, an operator dropping a request against a bag that has reached the day's version ceiling, a bag being re-scanned onto a different belt, and an owner claim being registered against a bag, which marks it claimed and puts it permanently out of reach of the chute.

The two lines are run by separate teams on separate schedules and neither knows what the other is doing; what they share is the one vault. The quantity that matters here is countable physical stock -- ampoules -- and the whole point of the paperwork around a controlled drug is that the count never drifts. An ampoule is at any moment in exactly one place: still in the vault, on the trolley in transit to a line, sitting in a line's local drawer, or already administered to a patient.

Access to the vault is arbitrated by a work token that circulates around the lines in a fixed ring. Only the line currently holding the token may draw stock out of the vault. The token moves on unconditionally, so neither line can monopolise the vault and neither can stall the other.

Everything downstream of the vault draw is local to a line and needs no token: the trolley arriving at a line, a drawer ampoule being administered, and a drawer ampoule being walked back and returned to the vault all happen on the line's own initiative. The full set of actions is: Draw, in which the line currently holding the token takes one ampoule out of the vault and onto its trolley, provided the vault is not empty; Deliver, in which one ampoule on a line's trolley arrives in that line's drawer; Administer, in which one ampoule in a line's drawer is given to a patient and leaves circulation; Return, in which one ampoule in a line's drawer is walked back and put into the vault; and PassToken, in which the work token moves to the next line in the ring.

Spending the permit consumes it: the permit does not go back into the pool and there is no way to manufacture another, which is what makes the release irreversible and unrepeatable.     /\ authorisedBy = [s \in Sections |-> NoOne]

A team may only wheel a patient in while the token is with it and the theatre has been turned over and is clean. Once a team is in the theatre, the token stays with that team: it cannot be passed on while its holder is operating or still closing up. Only when the holder is back to waiting or idle does the token move on to the next team in the ring.

Teams are allowed to be slow but are never allowed to disappear. A team that is running slow -- a difficult case, a trainee list -- simply takes longer in the theatre: it must clock a longer minimum time before it can close. It does not fail, does not have to be timed out, and the token is never wrenched away from it. A team's pace is set while it is idle and holds for the case it then takes on.

Turnover matters: when a team closes, the theatre is left dirty, and it is only clean again after that same team's turnover completes and the team goes back to idle. Nobody can enter a dirty theatre.

ASSUME SlowMinimum <= LongestCase

Teams == 0 .. RingSize - 1
Stages == {"idle", "waiting", "operating", "closing"}

vars == <<stage, theatre, clock, slow, token>>

    /\ theatre \in {"clean", "in-use", "dirty"}
    /\ clock \in [Teams -> 0 .. LongestCase]
    /\ slow \in [Teams -> BOOLEAN]
    /\ token \in Teams

    /\ theatre = "clean"
    /\ clock = [t \in Teams |-> 0]
    /\ slow = [t \in Teams |-> FALSE]
    /\ token = 0

Operating == {t \in Teams : stage[t] = "operating"}

\* A slow team owes a longer minimum in the room; it is never timed out.
MinimumFor(t) == IF slow[t] THEN SlowMinimum ELSE 1

Request(t) ==
    /\ stage[t] = "idle"
    /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![t] = "waiting"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<theatre, clock, slow, token>>

SetPace(t, fast) ==
    /\ stage[t] = "idle"
    /\ slow' = [slow EXCEPT ![t] = fast]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<stage, theatre, clock, token>>

Enter(t) ==

    /\ stage[t] = "waiting"
    /\ theatre = "clean"
    /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![t] = "operating"]
    /\ theatre' = "in-use"
    /\ clock' = [clock EXCEPT ![t] = 0]

    /\ clock[t] < LongestCase

    /\ clock[t] >= MinimumFor(t)
    /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![t] = "closing"]
    /\ theatre' = "dirty"
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, slow, token>>

    /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![t] = "idle"]
    /\ theatre' = "clean"
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, slow, token>>

A university runs course registration on a small set of registration servers that all front the same seat ledger for a course. Editing that ledger is the critical section: exactly one server may be inside it at a time, because the ledger is read-modify-written and two servers inside it at once oversell the course.

There is no lock service. Instead a server that wants the ledger canvasses the faculty registrars for backing. Each registrar has one vote and may hold it uncommitted or commit it to one canvassing server. A registrar may not switch its vote directly: it must first retract, and it is not allowed to retract a vote from a server that is currently inside the ledger -- backing is held for the duration of the edit, which is what stops a server losing its mandate mid-edit. A server may enter the ledger on the strength of a strict majority of the registrars backing it, and only while no other server is inside.

Registration also has a privileged path. The registrar's office can assert an administrative override naming one server. While an override is standing, the quorum path is closed to everybody: no server can enter on votes, and only the named server may enter, and it may enter straight from idle with no canvassing and no votes at all. Every entry records the basis it was granted on -- admin or quorum -- and that record is cleared when the server steps out. The office cannot withdraw an override until the server it names has actually got inside the ledger, and it cannot name a new server while one override is still standing.

The full set of actions is: Canvass, in which an idle server starts canvassing; Cast, in which an uncommitted registrar commits its vote to a canvassing server; Retract, in which a registrar takes back a vote from a server that is not currently inside the ledger; Enter, in which a server enters the empty ledger, either because it is the server named by a standing override, recording its basis as admin, or because no override is standing, it is canvassing and it has a strict majority of registrars behind it, recording its basis as quorum; Adjust, in which the server inside the ledger changes the seat count by one within the configured range; Leave, in which the server inside the ledger steps out, goes idle and forgets the basis it entered on; Override, in which the registrar's office names a server while no override stands and that server is not already inside; and Clear, in which the office withdraws an override whose named server has got inside.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Never more than one server is inside the seat ledger, and whoever is inside is there legitimately -- the set of servers inside the ledger is a subset of the servers that either entered on an admin basis or still hold a strict majority of the registrars behind them.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: An administrative override is always honoured -- whenever the registrar's office names a server, that server eventually gets inside the seat ledger, no matter who is inside when the override is asserted and no matter how the registrars have voted.

    /\ stage \in [Servers -> Stages]

    /\ stage = [s \in Servers |-> "idle"]
    /\ override = NoServer
    /\ seats = 0
    /\ basis = [s \in Servers |-> "none"]

Backers(s) == {r \in Registrars : vote[r] = s}

Legitimate == {s \in Servers : basis[s] = "admin" \/ HasMandate(s)}

          /\ HasMandate(s)
          /\ basis' = [basis EXCEPT ![s] = "quorum"]
    /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![s] = "editing"]

    \/ \E r \in Registrars : Retract(r)

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A skyscraper's elevator bank dispatches hall calls to a small number of cars. A hall call is raised at a floor and sits in a pool of unassigned calls until the dispatcher hands it to a car. Each car has a work queue of calls it has accepted, and that queue is deliberately small: a car that has accepted more stops than it can plausibly run within its service window gives every passenger on it a bad ride, so the dispatcher will not hand a car a call once its queue is at its bound. That refusal is the backpressure -- the call simply stays in the unassigned pool until some car has room, and there is no path that pushes work into a full queue.

A car takes calls off the front of its own queue one at a time. It can only pick up the next call once it has finished the one it is running, and finishing a call means arriving at that floor and letting the call go. A hall call is in exactly one place at any moment: unassigned, sitting in one car's queue, or being run by one car.

The building also has a privileged path: the fire panel. The fire service can designate a floor, and that designation does not join a queue and is not subject to backpressure at all. A designated floor is taken directly by a car, which drops whatever call it was running back into the unassigned pool to do it, and the designated floor is struck out of every car's queue at the same moment so it does not remain queued behind the car that is already running it. Only one designation can stand at a time, and the panel cannot be reset until some car is actually running the designated floor, so a designation cannot be quietly dropped.

The full set of actions is: Call, in which a floor that is nowhere in the system raises a hall call into the unassigned pool; Assign, in which the dispatcher moves an unassigned call onto the back of a car's queue, allowed only while that queue is below its bound; Dispatch, in which a car with an empty running slot takes the call at the front of its queue and starts running it; Arrive, in which a car finishes the call it is running and empties its running slot; Designate, in which the fire panel designates a floor while no designation stands; Preempt, in which a car takes the designated floor directly into its running slot, strikes that floor out of every car's queue so it is not left queued as well, and returns whatever it was running to the unassigned pool, allowed only while no car is already running that floor; and Reset, in which the fire panel clears a designation that some car is now running.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No car's queue ever exceeds its configured bound, and no hall call is ever both sitting in the unassigned pool and queued at a car, so the bound really is a bound on outstanding accepted work and cannot be evaded by double-counting a call.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every fire-panel designation is eventually run -- once the panel designates a floor, some car eventually has that floor in its running slot, regardless of how full the car queues are and regardless of what that car was running at the time.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A regional power grid runs a load shedder that puts feeders into rotating outage slots. There is one slot book for the whole region and a slot in it is a physical rotation window: putting two feeders into the same window sheds twice the load that was planned for it and can collapse the very thing the shedding was meant to protect.

Only one control node acts as the shedding leader at a time. Leadership is carried by a term number: starting a new term raises the term and installs whoever started it as leader, and every control node separately records the highest term it has heard about. A node only acts as leader while the term it has heard about is the current term. This is what handles a leader that is running slow: a node that has fallen behind is still there, still nominally the leader of an older term, and is perfectly capable of trying to act -- it is simply not allowed to, because the term it knows is no longer the current one. Nothing has to declare it dead and nothing has to time it out.

Placing a feeder is two steps rather than one, because the promise to a feeder and the booking of the slot are made by different parts of the system. The leader first promises a feeder a slot -- recording, against that feeder, the slot it will get -- and only afterwards books that slot in the region's slot book. Between those two steps the promise is outstanding: the feeder holds a claim on a slot the book has not yet written down. The leader will not promise a slot that any feeder already claims.

Failover leaves outstanding promises behind, so a leader for the current term can also cancel a promise that was never booked, and can release a feeder whose slot was booked, returning the slot to the book unbooked.

The full set of actions is: StartTerm, in which a control node raises the term, becomes leader, and records the new term as the one it knows; Learn, in which a node behind the current term catches up to it; Promise, in which the current leader gives an unplaced feeder a slot that is unbooked and that no feeder already claims; Book, in which the current leader writes into the slot book the booking for a feeder whose promised slot is still unbooked; Cancel, in which the current leader withdraws a promise that was never booked, leaving the feeder unplaced; and Release, in which the current leader takes a booked feeder back out, unbooking its slot and leaving the feeder unplaced.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A slot is never allocated twice -- every feeder that claims a slot finds that slot either booked to itself or not booked at all, and never booked to some other feeder, so no two feeders can end up sharing one rotation window.

\* a slow node is still alive and still tries, and this is what stops it.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A wildfire surveillance swarm feeds observation commands from its drones into a single ground-station work queue, and the ground station executes them one at a time. The swarm is re-keyed periodically: a re-key raises the swarm's authorisation epoch, and every drone must separately pick up a fresh credential stamped with the new epoch before it counts as authorised again. A drone that has not picked up a fresh credential is stale -- it is still flying and still capable of submitting, it simply no longer speaks for the swarm.

Submissions go through backpressure. The queue has a capacity and a drone whose credential is current may only submit while the queue is below it; there is no other path into the queue. That capacity is not fixed. The ground station raises and lowers it at runtime as radio conditions change, but it will never lower it below the number of commands already sitting in the queue, so shrinking capacity throttles new work rather than silently dropping accepted work.

Every queued command carries the epoch it was submitted under. The ground station only ever executes a command from the front of the queue whose stamped epoch is the current one; a command at the front stamped with an older epoch is thrown away unexecuted rather than run. Re-keying is only allowed while the ground station has nothing in execution, so the swarm quiesces before its authority changes and no command can be left running across an epoch boundary.

The full set of actions is: ReKey, in which the swarm's authorisation epoch is raised while nothing is in execution; Recredential, in which a drone behind the current epoch picks up a fresh credential; Submit, in which a drone whose credential is current appends a command stamped with the current epoch to the queue, allowed only while the queue is below its capacity; Resize, in which the ground station sets a new capacity that is not below the number of commands already queued; Dispatch, in which the ground station, with nothing in execution, takes the command at the front of the queue into execution provided its stamp is the current epoch; Discard, in which the command at the front of the queue is thrown away unexecuted because its stamp is not the current epoch; and Complete, in which the ground station finishes whatever it has in execution.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The ground station never acts for a stale or unauthorised participant -- whenever a command is in execution, it was stamped with the epoch that is still current and the drone that submitted it still holds a credential for that same current epoch.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Nothing in execution ever hangs -- once the ground station takes a drone's command into execution, it eventually finishes it and returns to having nothing in execution.

    /\ credential = [d \in Drones |-> 0]
    /\ queue = << >>

\* be left running across an epoch boundary.
ReKey ==
    /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
    /\ running = NoDrone
    /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<credential, queue, capacity, running, runStamp>>

Recredential(d) ==
    /\ credential[d] < epoch
    /\ credential' = [credential EXCEPT ![d] = epoch]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, queue, capacity, running, runStamp>>

    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, credential, capacity, running, runStamp>>

    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, credential, queue, capacity, runStamp>>
