A clearing bank runs its end-of-day interbank settlement as a batch of payment instructions drawn against one liquidity pool at the central bank. Two settlement engines work the batch side by side. They were built by different teams for different corridors and share nothing except that one pool of central-bank liquidity and the batch itself.

Settling an instruction is irreversible: the funds leave, the counterparty is credited, and there is no unwind inside the batch. The permanent record of what happened is the settlement journal, an append-only list of instructions in the order they were settled. Everything else in the system is working state and can be rolled back; the journal cannot.

Access to the batch is arbitrated by a window token that passes around the engines in a ring. Only the engine holding the token may claim an instruction out of the queued state; once claimed, the instruction belongs to that engine and the engine can work it without the token. An engine may give a claim back, returning the instruction to queued for either engine to pick up later. Settling requires the engine to hold the claim and requires the liquidity pool to have the funds; the settlement takes the funds out of the pool, moves the instruction to settled, drops the claim, and appends the instruction to the journal in the same step. Nothing ever moves an instruction back out of settled, and nothing appends to the journal except a settlement.

The pool is topped up during the window from incoming receipts, which is what lets a batch settle more than the opening balance, and is the only thing that puts liquidity back.

The full set of actions is: Claim, in which the engine holding the token takes a queued instruction and becomes its claimant; Unclaim, in which an engine gives back an instruction it has claimed, returning it to queued; Settle, in which an engine settles an instruction it has claimed, provided the pool has the funds, deducting the funds, marking the instruction settled, dropping the claim and appending the instruction to the journal; Fund, in which a receipt tops the liquidity pool up by one, up to its ceiling; and PassToken, in which the window token moves to the other engine.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending operator restocks its machines through route planners who take out short leases on individual machines. A lease names the machine, the planner who holds it, and the wall-clock time it runs out. Only the current leaseholder may open a machine and restock it, and the point of the expiry is that a planner who wanders off does not have to be detected or declared dead: the lease simply lapses and the machine becomes available again.

The service clock advances in ticks up to the end of the service window. A tick is also the moment leases are swept: every lease whose expiry time has been reached is torn down, and any restock in progress under such a lease is abandoned at the same instant. That is what makes the expiry real -- a planner cannot be left holding an open machine on a lease that has run out, because the tick that runs the lease out is the tick that ends the restock. A planner may renew a lease it still holds before it lapses, and may hand a lease back early provided it is not currently inside that machine. New leases cannot be taken out once the window has reached its end.

The route itself changes size while all this is going on: machines are added to the route and taken off it as sites open and close. A machine can only be taken off the route while nobody holds a lease on it, so the route can shrink underneath the planners without ever stranding one inside a machine that is no longer there.

The full set of actions is: Acquire, in which a planner takes an unleased machine that is on the route, before the window has ended, and gets a lease running to the lease term from now or the end of the window, whichever is sooner; Renew, in which a planner pushes out the expiry of a lease it still holds; Handback, in which a planner gives up a lease it holds on a machine it is not currently inside; Begin, in which a planner not already inside a machine opens one it holds an unexpired lease on and that is still on the route; Finish, in which a planner closes up the machine it is inside; Tick, in which the service clock advances by one, tearing down every lease that has reached its expiry and abandoning any restock running under one; Add, in which a machine is put on the route; and Remove, in which an unleased machine is taken off the route.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No planner ever acts under a stale or borrowed authority -- whenever a planner is inside a machine, that machine is on the route, its lease is held by that same planner, and that lease has not yet reached its expiry.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: No machine stays leased forever -- once a lease is taken out on a machine, that machine eventually becomes unleased again, whether the planner hands it back or the clock runs the lease out.

A container terminal works its yard with gantry cranes. The yard is divided into blocks, each block is striped into ground slots, and every slot holds at most one box. Two boxes booked into the same ground slot is the failure being ruled out here: the second lift arrives to find the slot taken, the box goes down somewhere unrecorded, and the terminal loses it.

There are two records that have to agree. The yard plan records, for each container, the slot it is sited in. The ground record records, for each slot, the box standing on it. These are written by the same crane in the same movement, but they are separate records, and the terminal's whole idea of where anything is depends on them being exact inverses of one another.

Cranes coordinate through two levels of lock. The coarse level is the block: a crane takes a block before it can touch anything in it. The fine level is the individual slot, and a slot's lock can only be taken by a crane that already holds the lock on the block that slot currently belongs to. Only the holder of a slot's lock may put a box down on it or lift a box off it. Locks come off in the reverse order: a crane cannot give a block back while it still holds a slot lock inside that block.

The yard is re-striped while work goes on -- blocks are re-drawn and a slot can be moved from one block to another as the terminal reshapes capacity for a different ship. A slot can only be re-homed while nobody holds its lock and nothing is standing on it, so re-striping never moves a slot out from under a crane that is working it or a box that is sitting on it.

The full set of actions is: TakeBlock, in which a crane takes an unheld block; TakeSlot, in which a crane holding the block a slot currently belongs to takes that slot's unheld lock; Place, in which the crane holding a slot's lock puts a container that is not sited anywhere onto that empty slot, writing both the yard plan entry and the ground record in the one movement; Lift, in which the crane holding a slot's lock takes the box off it, clearing both records in the one movement; DropSlot, in which a crane gives back a slot lock it holds; DropBlock, in which a crane gives back a block it holds, provided it holds no slot lock inside that block; and Restripe, in which an unlocked, empty slot is moved into a different block.

A wildfire drone swarm carries out a coordinated retardant drop over a single ridge. Each drone carries exactly one load, and releasing it is irreversible: the load is gone, the ridge is covered, and a second release by the same drone is not a mistake that can be corrected -- there is nothing left to release. A partial drop is worse than none, so the swarm agrees the drop with a two-phase commit before anybody opens a hopper.

The live fleet changes while the swarm is airborne: drones come on station and go off station for fuel throughout the sortie, and that churn is not tied to the transaction. What the transaction runs against is a sealed cohort -- the snapshot of the fleet taken at the moment the drop is prepared. Sealing happens once. After it, drones joining or leaving the live fleet change nothing about who is party to this drop, and there is no second preparation.

Each drone in the sealed cohort votes once, yes or no. If every drone in the cohort has voted yes, the coordinator commits. If any drone in the cohort has voted no, the coordinator aborts. The decision is taken once and nothing takes it back: there is no path from committed to aborted or the other way round, because the drop it authorises cannot be undone.

Only after a commit does a drone open its hopper, and only a drone that is in the sealed cohort and voted yes may do so. Releasing moves the drone's load out of its bay for good; a drone with no load has nothing further to release.

The full set of actions is: Join, in which a drone comes on station and joins the live fleet; Leave, in which a drone goes off station and leaves the live fleet; Prepare, in which the coordinator seals the current live fleet as the cohort for this drop, provided nothing has been sealed yet and the fleet is not empty; Vote, in which a drone in the sealed cohort that has not yet voted casts a yes or a no, before any decision is taken; Commit, in which the coordinator decides to commit because every drone in the sealed cohort voted yes; Abort, in which the coordinator decides to abort because some drone in the sealed cohort voted no; and Release, in which a loaded drone of the sealed cohort that voted yes opens its hopper after a commit, moving its load out of its bay for good.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A print shop runs two production sites that both draw from one shared finishing line. The finishing line can have only so many jobs in flight at once -- it is a physical pool of binding capacity, and pushing more than it holds jams it. The two sites are otherwise independent operations with their own presses, their own queues and their own operators; the finishing pool is the only thing they share, and neither can see the other's floor.

Because neither site can see the other, admission to the pool is not something either site decides for itself. One of the two spoolers acts as the admitting leader, and leadership is carried by a term number that goes up whenever a spooler takes over. Every spooler records the highest term it has heard of, and only a spooler whose recorded term is the current one is acting as leader.

The leader admits jobs against its own running count of how much of the pool is committed. That count is a belief, not the truth: it is the leader's own ledger, and a spooler that has just taken over is holding whatever ledger it happened to have from before, which may be wildly out of date. So a new leader must resynchronise before it admits anything -- it reads the true amount of work in flight across both sites into its ledger and records the term it did so in. Only a leader that has resynchronised in the current term may admit. A leader may also resynchronise again at any point where its ledger has drifted away from the truth, which is what lets it recover the capacity that finished work gave back. This is the whole safety argument for the shared pool: a leader admits against a ledger it knows is current, and increments that ledger as it admits, so it can never hand out more of the pool than the pool has.

Jobs finishing reduce the work in flight but do not touch anybody's ledger, so a leader's ledger drifts upward of the truth over time. That drift is in the safe direction -- it makes the leader more conservative, not less -- and resynchronising is what pulls it back.

The full set of actions is: TakeOver, in which a spooler raises the term, becomes leader, and records the new term as the one it has heard of; Learn, in which a spooler behind the current term catches up to it; Resync, in which the current leader, either because it has not resynchronised in this term or because its ledger no longer matches the truth, reads the true total work in flight into its ledger and records that it has resynchronised in the current term; Admit, in which the current leader, having resynchronised in this term and holding a ledger below the pool's bound, puts one more job in flight at one of the sites and raises its ledger by one; and Finish, in which a job in flight at a site completes and leaves the pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total work in flight across both sites never exceeds the finishing pool's bound, however leadership changes hands and however stale a spooler's ledger has become.

A car wash runs a conveyor line past a ring of treatment bays -- pre-soak, foam, rinse -- each with its own actuator. Only one bay may run its actuator at a time, and which one is decided by a control token that circulates the ring. The token visits every position on the ring in order, including positions whose bay is currently out of service; those simply pass it straight on.

The line runs in cycles. Each time the conveyor recycles, the cycle number goes up and every bay's authorisation ticket becomes stale. A bay must be reissued a ticket for the current cycle before it may actuate again: an actuator firing on a ticket from the previous cycle sprays the wrong chemical at the wrong car, and a bay that has simply not caught up is exactly the kind of participant that must not be allowed to act. The conveyor will not recycle while any actuator is running, and the token will not move on while the bay holding it is running, so nothing is ever left running under an authority that has moved on beneath it.

Bays go out of service and come back while the line runs -- a bay is taken offline for a blocked nozzle and brought back when it is cleared -- so the number of bays actually working the line changes as the line runs. A bay can only be taken out of service while its actuator is idle.

The full set of actions is: PassToken, in which the control token moves to the next position on the ring, allowed only while the bay currently holding it is not running its actuator; Recycle, in which the conveyor's cycle number goes up, allowed only while no actuator is running, which makes every bay's ticket stale; Reissue, in which a bay behind the current cycle is issued a ticket for it; Actuate, in which a bay that holds the token, is in service, and holds a ticket for the current cycle starts its actuator; Finish, in which a running actuator stops; TakeOffline, in which an in-service bay with an idle actuator is taken out of service; and BringOnline, in which an out-of-service bay is brought back.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: The control token never comes to rest -- whichever position holds it, it eventually moves off that position, so no bay can wedge the ring by holding the token and running its actuator forever.

A competitive game's matchmaker runs lobbies that players sit in before a ranked match. Launching a lobby is irreversible: the match is created on the ranked ladder, everyone on the roster has the result counted against their rating, and there is no un-launching it. A lobby launches at most once, and what it launched with is fixed at that instant.

A lobby launches on the strength of its own members. Each seated player may mark themselves ready or take that back, and a lobby may launch when a strict majority of the players seated in it are ready. There is also a moderator path: a moderator can force-start an open lobby, and a forced lobby may launch regardless of how few of its players are ready. Force-starting is a decision about an open lobby only -- a moderator can set it and take it back while the lobby is open, and once a lobby has launched neither is possible any more.

Launching freezes two things into the lobby's permanent record: the roster, meaning exactly the players seated in it at that instant, and the ready roll, meaning which of those players were marked ready. That record is what an appeal is judged against, and no later action touches it. A lobby that has not launched has no record at all.

The lobby itself carries on afterwards as a post-match room: players who were not on the roster can sit down in it and players can get up and leave, but none of that changes the roster or the ready roll that were frozen at launch.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A public library runs reservations against a shared availability register. A patron with a hold checks what is available, and the register carries a version number that moves every time a copy is actually handed over. Handing a copy over is the irreversible step here: the hold is consumed, the copy is transferred out of the reservation system for good, and there is no path that gives a patron their hold back or takes a transferred copy back into the pool of things a hold can be filled from. A patron whose hold has been filled is finished and is not filled a second time.

Because several patrons check availability at the same time and any of them may be beaten to a copy, the register is not locked. A patron checks and remembers the version they checked at. When the transfer is attempted it is a compare-and-set: it only goes through if the register's version is still the one the patron checked at. If it is not -- because somebody else's transfer moved it -- the patron goes back to browsing and checks again. Backing out is only for that case: a patron whose remembered version is still current does not abandon its attempt, it waits for a copy, and it is only additionally allowed to back out once the register has reached its bound and can move no further.

The collection itself changes size while all of this is going on: copies are acquired into the collection and withdrawn from it as the branch rebalances its shelves. Acquiring is unrestricted, but the branch will not withdraw stock while any patron has an attempt in flight, so the shelves are never rebalanced out from under someone who is mid-transfer.

There are two records of a filled hold and they are written in the same step: the patron's own status turns to filled, and the copy's record names the patron it went to. The library's entire reconciliation depends on those two never disagreeing.

The full set of actions is: Check, in which a browsing patron reads the register's current version, remembers it, and moves to attempting; Transfer, in which an attempting patron whose remembered version still matches the register's version takes an unissued copy that is in the collection, marking that copy as issued to them and their own status as filled, and moving the register's version on by one; Retry, in which an attempting patron whose remembered version no longer matches the register, or whose register has reached its bound, goes back to browsing without changing anything; Acquire, in which a copy that is not in the collection is added to it; and Withdraw, in which a copy that is in the collection is taken out of it, allowed only while no patron has an attempt in flight.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The two records of a filled hold never disagree -- the set of patrons whose status is filled is exactly the set of patrons that some copy's record names -- so no hold is marked filled without a copy going out and no copy goes out without the hold it filled being marked.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: The optimistic scheme always eventually makes a transfer -- some patron's hold is eventually filled, however the collection is rebalanced and however many attempts are beaten and retried along the way.

A game's matchmaker fills team slots for a ranked match. Each slot takes exactly one player, and a slot that ends up allocated to two players is the failure being ruled out: two clients both think they own the same position, both load in, and the match is unplayable.

There is no single authority that hands out slots. A set of matchmaking shards votes. Each shard may cast at most one vote per slot, naming the player it thinks should have that slot, and it can never take that vote back or change it. A slot is won by a player once a strict majority of all the shards -- counted over every shard there is, not over the ones that happen to be responding -- have named that player for it. Because every shard votes at most once per slot, two different players cannot both hold a majority for the same slot, and that is the entire argument that a slot is never allocated twice.

A shard can fail silently. It simply stops voting: nothing announces it, nothing detects it, and the rest of the system has no way to distinguish a shard that has crashed from one that is merely slow. Because the majority is counted against the full set of shards rather than the responding ones, a silent failure can only ever prevent a slot from being won, never cause it to be won by two players. A failed shard may come back later, and votes it cast before it failed still stand.

Once a slot has been won it is committed to its winner, and after that no further votes may be cast for it. A committed slot is then loaded into the match. A player already committed to some slot is not a candidate for any other, so votes naming an already-placed player are not cast.

A vending operator's cash is physical coin, and the audit that matters at the end of a shift is that the coin adds up. The shift starts with every coin sitting as float inside the machines' hoppers. An airport's runway allocator hands out runways to approach controllers as leases. A lease names the runway, the controller holding it, and the allocation generation it was cut in. The allocator works in generations: it winds the current generation up, hands out leases against it, and when it starts a new generation every lease cut in an older one is dead.

A controller can fail silently. Its position goes dark with no alarm, no handover and no way for the allocator to tell it apart from a controller that is simply quiet. Nothing in the system detects the failure. What recovers the runway is the generation, not a detector: a lease cut in a superseded generation can be reaped by anyone, and the runway goes back into the pool. A controller that has gone dark may also come back up later.

Issuing a clearance onto a runway is the act that must never be done on stale authority. A controller may only issue one if it is up, holds the lease on that runway, that lease was cut in the generation currently running, and it has not already issued a clearance in this generation. A clearance already issued survives its controller going dark -- the aircraft is on the approach and the clearance stands -- so what the safety condition demands is that the clearance was authorised when it was issued and that the authority behind it has not been superseded since.

That is why the allocator will not wind the generation on while any clearance is still being worked: winding it on is precisely what would make a live clearance stale. The pattern has to empty first.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: The pattern always empties -- whenever there is a clearance in progress, there is eventually a moment with no clearance in progress at all, so the allocator can never be blocked forever from winding the generation on.

A warehouse keeps a shared pick manifest: for each bin, how many units have been picked out of it this wave. Leadership is carried by a term number. A controller takes over by winding the term up and installing itself, so leadership and term change together and there is never a term with two leaders. Every staged update records the term it was staged in.

A controller can fail silently. It stops, nothing announces it, and in particular a staged update it had in flight is simply left dangling: nobody rolls it back and nobody knows it is there. A vending network is re-planogrammed by a team of planners working against the machines' column registers. Each product column has a register naming the planner that currently owns it, together with a stamp that moves every time the register changes. Owning the register is not the same as having the column on your own worksheet. A planner writes the column onto its own worksheet as a separate step after the register grants it, and the discipline that makes the whole thing safe is the order things come off in: a planner takes the column off its worksheet first, and only then hands the register back. A planner may set the product for a column that is on its worksheet, or clear it back to having no product set. Columns themselves come and go while the planners work: a machine is reconfigured and a column is installed or retired. The stamp on a register is bounded; once a column's stamp is at its ceiling the register can no longer be swapped either way. A vending operator books restock deliveries into numbered dock slots at each site. Two dispatch desks share the booking book, and a work token circulates between them in a ring: only the desk holding the token may change a booking. The site itself does not hold the book -- it learns about bookings from notices the desks send it.

The link to the site reorders. Notices are not delivered in the order they were sent: a notice sent first can arrive after one sent later, and the site has no way to tell from the notice itself how recent it is other than by what the notice carries. That is why every notice carries the sequence number the desks stamped it with. The desks keep a per-slot sequence that goes up on every change they make, and the notice carries the number the change was made at.

The site keeps, per slot, the booking it currently believes and the highest sequence number it has applied. A notice is applied only if its sequence number is higher than the highest the site has applied for that slot; a notice whose number is not higher is dropped unapplied, because it is describing a state of the slot that has already been superseded. This is the entire defence against reordering: a stale notice arriving late cannot reinstate an old booking and leave the site believing a dock slot is held by an order that the desks have since moved elsewhere.

A desk will not book an order into a slot if that order is already booked into another slot, and will not book into a slot that is already booked.

The full set of actions is: Book, in which the desk holding the token books an unbooked order into an unbooked slot, moves that slot's sequence on by one and puts a notice carrying the new sequence into flight; Cancel, in which the desk holding the token clears a booked slot, moves that slot's sequence on by one and puts a notice carrying the new sequence into flight; Apply, in which a notice in flight whose sequence is higher than the highest the site has applied for that slot is applied, setting the site's belief about the slot and its highest applied sequence, and leaving flight; Discard, in which a notice in flight whose sequence is not higher than the highest applied for that slot leaves flight unapplied; and PassToken, in which the work token moves to the other desk.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A dock slot is never held by two different orders across the two books -- the site is never ahead of the desks on any slot's sequence, and any slot on which the site has caught up to the desks' sequence is a slot the site and the desks agree the owner of.

A container terminal discharges boxes out of the yard through a single gate lane. Discharging a box is irreversible: the box leaves the terminal's custody, goes onto the permanent discharge manifest, and there is no action anywhere that brings it back into the yard or takes it off the manifest. A box is discharged at most once because once it is gone it is no longer in the yard to be staged again.

The gate lane is a bounded work queue and the bound is the backpressure: a box can only be staged into the lane while the lane is below its bound, so a busy gate simply refuses new work and boxes wait in the yard. A staged box that is not currently at the gate and is not the manager's designated box can be pulled back to the yard to make room. From the lane a box moves to the gate itself, which handles one box at a time, and from the gate it is discharged.

Normally a box may only be staged once customs has cleared it, and customs can revoke a clearance again at any time. The terminal manager has a privileged path around this: the manager can designate one box -- a reefer running out of power, a box a ship is waiting on -- and a designated box may be staged whether or not customs has cleared it. While a designation is standing it also takes priority absolutely: no other box may be staged into the lane and no other box may be moved onto the gate, so the lane drains and the gate frees up in front of the designated box. The manager cannot lift a designation until the box it names has actually been discharged, and cannot designate a second box while one designation stands.

The full set of actions is: Clear, in which customs clears a box; Revoke, in which customs takes a clearance back off a box; Stage, in which a box in the yard that is either customs-cleared or the designated box moves into the lane, allowed only while the lane is below its bound and only if no other box is designated; Unstage, in which a box in the lane that is not at the gate and is not the designated box is pulled back to the yard; ToGate, in which a box in the lane moves onto the free gate, allowed only if no other box is designated; Discharge, in which the box at the gate leaves the terminal for good, going onto the permanent discharge manifest and freeing the gate; Designate, in which the manager designates a box in the yard while no designation stands; and Lift, in which the manager lifts a designation whose box has been discharged.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A designation is always carried out -- once the manager designates a box, that box is eventually discharged, however full the lane is when the designation is made and whether or not customs ever clears it.

A hospital's theatre scheduling desks all edit one day list -- which session runs in which theatre. ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A warehouse robot fleet writes to one shared task board. There is no lock on the board: a robot reads the board's version, works out its change, and commits with a compare-and-set that only lands if the version has not moved. If it has moved, the robot's attempt is dead and it abandons it and starts again.

Authority to write is separate from the optimism. The fleet is re-keyed periodically -- the shift changes, the site's key rotates -- and a re-key moves the fleet's authorisation epoch. A robot has to pick up a credential for the current epoch before it may start an attempt, and every attempt records the epoch it was started in. An attempt started in a superseded epoch is dead the same way a beaten compare-and-set is dead: it is abandoned, not committed. A re-key is only taken while no attempt is in flight, so no attempt is ever half-run across an epoch boundary.

A robot can fail silently: it stops, nothing announces it, and an attempt it had in flight simply stays in flight with nobody working it. There is no detector and no timeout. What makes that safe is that a dangling attempt is still subject to both checks when anybody looks at it: it is only committable while its recorded version is still the board's version and its recorded epoch is still the fleet's epoch, and the robot itself must still hold a credential for that epoch. A robot that stopped may come back later with its attempt and its credential as it left them.

The full set of actions is: ReKey, in which the fleet's authorisation epoch moves on by one, allowed only while no attempt is in flight; Recredential, in which a robot that is up and behind the current epoch picks up a credential for it; Begin, in which a robot that is up, holds a current credential and has no attempt in flight starts one, recording the board's current version and the current epoch; Commit, in which a robot that is up, holds a current credential and an attempt in flight whose recorded version and epoch are both still current, moves the board's version on by one and ends its attempt; Abandon, in which an attempt in flight whose recorded version or epoch is no longer current is ended without committing; Fail, in which a robot that is up stops silently, leaving any attempt in flight exactly as it was; and Return, in which a robot that stopped comes back up.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Nothing stale or unauthorised can be committed -- every attempt that is still committable, meaning its recorded version and epoch are both the current ones, belongs to a robot that still holds a credential for the current epoch.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: The optimistic scheme never livelocks -- the task board's version always eventually reaches its ceiling, so the fleet cannot spin forever beginning and abandoning attempts without any of them landing, however the robots fail and return.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

A car wash runs one conveyor line. Two things about it are hard limits. The line itself holds only so many cars at once -- put another car on a full line and the last one comes off the end before it is finished. Separately, the water plant only supports so many cars being actively washed at the same time; cars beyond that sit on the line waiting their turn under the arches.

Admission to the line is decided by whichever supervisor terminal is currently the leader. Leadership is carried by a term number: a terminal takes over by winding the term up and installing itself, and every terminal separately records the highest term it has heard of. A terminal only acts as leader while the term it has heard of is the current one, so a terminal that has been superseded, or that has not caught up, cannot admit anybody.

The site manager has a privileged path. With the manager override standing, a car can be put onto the line without any leader involved at all -- no term, no leadership, no terminal. What the override does not do, and this is the point, is touch either capacity: the manager's car goes onto the line only if the line has room, exactly like everybody else's. The override is a way around the leadership, not around the plant.

A car on the line may be started under the arches while the water plant has room, and stops washing when it is done. A car only comes off the end of the line once it has stopped washing.

<|start|>user<|message|>Write a TLA+ specification that implements EXACTLY the system described below, and a TLC .cfg to model-check it. The system's safety property described in the NL text must be captured as a real, non-trivial INVARIANT (not `Inv == TRUE`) in the .cfg.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending operator restocks its machines from a van that works a fixed round. A work token marks where the van currently is, and it moves from position to position around the round. Each machine's shelf has a hard capacity: physically only so many units fit, and pushing another one in jams the mechanism.

The depot's picture of a shelf is not the shelf. What the depot holds is a reading, taken by the van when it was last at that machine. Between visits the reading goes out of date in both directions: customers buy units out of the shelf, and the site's own franchisee tops the shelf up locally from a cupboard without telling the depot. The franchisee can see the shelf so it never overfills, but the depot cannot, and a reading that is lower than the shelf really is is exactly what would make the van push a unit into a machine that is already full.

That is why the van will not restock on an out-of-date reading. It restocks only a machine whose reading is currently equal to the shelf -- in practice, the machine it is standing at and has just read. Reading is something the van does where it is: it takes a fresh reading of whatever machine the token is at, which is what makes a stale reading a temporary condition rather than a permanent one. A machine whose reading has gone stale is not broken and nothing gives up on it; it is simply behind until the van gets to it.

The van carries a bounded load, and reloads at the depot up to that bound.

The full set of actions is: PassToken, in which the work token moves to the next position on the round; Read, in which the van takes a fresh reading of the machine the token is at, bringing the depot's reading for it into line with the shelf; Sell, in which a customer takes a unit out of a machine's shelf; TopUp, in which the site's franchisee puts a unit into a machine's shelf locally, allowed only while that shelf is below its capacity; Restock, in which the van puts a unit from its load into the shelf of a machine whose reading is equal to its shelf and whose shelf is below its capacity, bringing the reading along with it; and Reload, in which the van takes on one more unit at the depot, up to its load bound.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No shelf is ever over its capacity -- there is never a machine holding more units than the shelf physically takes, however far the depot's readings have drifted from the shelves they describe.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A stale reading is always temporary -- whenever the depot's reading for the machine the token is at disagrees with that machine's shelf, it eventually agrees with it again.

A regional airport runs runway allocation from two independent allocator instances -- the "alpha" tower complex on the north side and the "beta" complex on the south side. Each instance was commissioned separately and keeps its own local record of which runways it believes it has been granted, but both instances draw from the same physical pool of runways, and both must go through the same shared set of ground-radar stations to obtain a runway.

Each allocator controller is idle, voting, or holding. An idle controller may propose a runway from the shared pool, entering the voting phase with that runway as its target. A radar station that has not yet pledged itself to anyone may grant its vote to a controller that is currently voting; each station holds at most one outstanding pledge. A voting controller that has collected the pledges of every radar station commits: it moves to the holding phase, is recorded as the owner of its target runway, and the runway is added to its own instance's local claim record. A voting controller that observes any station pledged to a different controller aborts: it returns to idle, releases whatever pledges it had collected, and clears its target. A holding controller may release: it returns to idle, the runway's owner record is cleared, the runway is dropped from its instance's claim record, and all of its pledges are returned to the pool of free stations.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A national clearing house settles interbank payments in batches. Each batch is a bundle of payment instructions of some declared size, and the settlement window that the clearing house holds open can carry only a bounded number of instruction units at any one time. Batches are agreed by a two-phase commit across the member banks: a batch is only settled if every member bank has pledged to it.

A batch sits idle until the clearing house proposes it with a declared size, at which point it enters the voting phase with no pledges. A member bank may pledge to a voting batch, but only when that bank is responsive (at most one bank is unresponsive at any moment), only when it has no outstanding pledge to some other voting batch, and only when the batch's declared size still fits in the free part of the settlement window as the bank sees it. A voting batch that has collected pledges from every member bank commits, and its units are added to the window's load. A voting batch that some bank refuses -- because that bank's pledge is already outstanding to another voting batch, or because the batch no longer fits the free window -- is aborted, and its pledges are returned. A committed batch is later settled, at which point its units leave the window. Settled and aborted are final: the clearing house never recycles a batch identifier within a session. Independently, a member bank may become slow and stop answering, and a slow bank may become responsive again; banks here are slow but never failed, so a slow bank always comes back.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The settlement window's load never exceeds the clearing house's declared window capacity.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every batch that enters the voting phase is eventually decided, reaching the committed, settled, or aborted state.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

---- MODULE W4Od3m2p4t3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Members, Batches, Capacity, MaxSize, NoBank

\* load is the number of instruction units occupying the settlement window;
\* pledged[b] is the set of member banks that have promised to settle b.
VARIABLES status, size, pledged, load, slow

vars == << status, size, pledged, load, slow >>

Decided == {"committed", "settled", "aborted"}

TypeOK ==
    /\ status \in [Batches -> {"idle", "voting"} \cup Decided]
    /\ size \in [Batches -> 0..MaxSize]
    /\ pledged \in [Batches -> SUBSET Members]
    /\ load \in 0..(Capacity + MaxSize)
    /\ slow \in Members \cup {NoBank}

Init ==
    /\ status = [b \in Batches |-> "idle"]
    /\ size = [b \in Batches |-> 0]
    /\ pledged = [b \in Batches |-> {}]
    /\ load = 0
    /\ slow = NoBank

Elsewhere(m, b) == \E o \in Batches : o # b /\ status[o] = "voting" /\ m \in pledged[o]

Propose(b, n) ==
    /\ status[b] = "idle"
    /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![b] = "voting"]
    /\ size' = [size EXCEPT ![b] = n]
    /\ pledged' = [pledged EXCEPT ![b] = {}]
    /\ UNCHANGED << load, slow >>

\* A bank holds at most one outstanding pledge, so at most one batch can be
\* unanimous at a time and the fit test taken at pledge time stays sound.
Pledge(b, m) ==
    /\ status[b] = "voting"
    /\ m # slow
    /\ m \notin pledged[b]
    /\ ~Elsewhere(m, b)
    /\ load + size[b] <= Capacity
    /\ pledged' = [pledged EXCEPT ![b] = @ \cup {m}]
    /\ UNCHANGED << status, size, load, slow >>

Commit(b) ==
    /\ status[b] = "voting"
    /\ \A m \in Members : m \in pledged[b]
    /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![b] = "committed"]
    /\ load' = load + size[b]
    /\ UNCHANGED << size, pledged, slow >>

Refuse(b) ==
    /\ status[b] = "voting"
    /\ \/ \E m \in Members : Elsewhere(m, b)
       \/ load + size[b] > Capacity
    /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![b] = "aborted"]
    /\ pledged' = [pledged EXCEPT ![b] = {}]
    /\ UNCHANGED << size, load, slow >>

Settle(b) ==
    /\ status[b] = "committed"
    /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![b] = "settled"]
    /\ load' = load - size[b]
    /\ pledged' = [pledged EXCEPT ![b] = {}]
    /\ UNCHANGED << size, slow >>

\* At most one member bank is unresponsive at a time, and it is slow rather
\* than failed, so it is always eventually heard from again.
Delay(m) == /\ slow = NoBank /\ slow' = m /\ UNCHANGED << status, size, pledged, load >>
Resume    == /\ slow # NoBank /\ slow' = NoBank /\ UNCHANGED << status, size, pledged, load >>

Next ==
    \/ \E b \in Batches, n \in 1..MaxSize : Propose(b, n)
    \/ \E b \in Batches, m \in Members : Pledge(b, m)
    \/ \E b \in Batches : Commit(b) \/ Refuse(b) \/ Settle(b)
    \/ (\E m \in Members : Delay(m)) \/ Resume

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
    /\ WF_vars(\E b \in Batches : Commit(b))
    /\ WF_vars(\E b \in Batches : Refuse(b))
    /\ WF_vars(\E b \in Batches : Settle(b))
    /\ SF_vars(\E b \in Batches, m \in Members : Pledge(b, m))
    /\ WF_vars(Resume)

WindowWithinCapacity == load <= Capacity

EveryVotingBatchDecided ==
    \A b \in Batches : (status[b] = "voting") ~> (status[b] \in Decided)

====

INVARIANT WindowWithinCapacity

PROPERTY EveryVotingBatchDecided

A container terminal keeps a single stowage plan for the crane yard: a record listing which crane moves have been accepted for the current shift. The terminal is operated by two independently commissioned yard-management instances, the north gantry office and the south gantry office, whose planners share that one plan record. Because neither office will wait on the other, updates are applied optimistically: a planner reads the plan, decides on a move, and writes back only if the plan has not changed underneath it.

A planner with no snapshot in hand reads the record, taking both its version stamp and a copy of its accepted-move set. A planner holding a snapshot but no chosen move picks a crane move from the shared move pool. A planner holding a snapshot and a chosen move commits if the record's version stamp still matches the stamp it read: the record's accepted-move set becomes the planner's snapshot plus its chosen move, the version stamp advances, and the planner's snapshot and choice are cleared. A planner whose snapshot version no longer matches the record retries: it discards its snapshot and its chosen move and will read again. A planner may also simply drop its chosen move while keeping its snapshot, so it can choose differently.

The yard supervisor separately records every move that has ever been accepted into the plan, which is how a dropped move would be noticed at shift handover.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every crane move that has ever been accepted into the stowage plan is still present in the plan's accepted-move set, so no office's commit ever silently discards another office's move.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS North, South, Moves, MaxVersion, NoMove, NoVersion

Planners == North \cup South

\* snapVer/snapSet are the optimistic snapshot each planner is holding;
\* accepted is the supervisor's handover record of every move ever admitted.
VARIABLES version, plan, snapVer, snapSet, choice, accepted

vars == << version, plan, snapVer, snapSet, choice, accepted >>

TypeOK ==
    /\ version \in 0..MaxVersion
    /\ plan \in SUBSET Moves
    /\ snapVer \in [Planners -> (0..MaxVersion) \cup {NoVersion}]
    /\ snapSet \in [Planners -> SUBSET Moves]
    /\ choice \in [Planners -> Moves \cup {NoMove}]
    /\ accepted \in SUBSET Moves

Init ==
    /\ version = 0
    /\ plan = {}
    /\ snapVer = [p \in Planners |-> NoVersion]
    /\ snapSet = [p \in Planners |-> {}]
    /\ choice = [p \in Planners |-> NoMove]
    /\ accepted = {}

ReadPlan(p) ==
    /\ snapVer[p] = NoVersion
    /\ snapVer' = [snapVer EXCEPT ![p] = version]
    /\ snapSet' = [snapSet EXCEPT ![p] = plan]
    /\ UNCHANGED << version, plan, choice, accepted >>

Choose(p, mv) ==
    /\ snapVer[p] # NoVersion
    /\ choice[p] = NoMove
    /\ choice' = [choice EXCEPT ![p] = mv]
    /\ UNCHANGED << version, plan, snapVer, snapSet, accepted >>

\* The version test is the whole of the concurrency control: a planner writes
\* its own snapshot back, so a commit on a stale stamp would erase the moves
\* that landed in between.
Commit(p) ==
    /\ snapVer[p] = version
    /\ choice[p] # NoMove
    /\ version < MaxVersion
    /\ plan' = snapSet[p] \cup {choice[p]}
    /\ accepted' = accepted \cup {choice[p]}
    /\ version' = version + 1
    /\ snapVer' = [snapVer EXCEPT ![p] = NoVersion]
    /\ snapSet' = [snapSet EXCEPT ![p] = {}]
    /\ choice' = [choice EXCEPT ![p] = NoMove]

Retry(p) ==
    /\ snapVer[p] # NoVersion
    /\ snapVer[p] # version
    /\ snapVer' = [snapVer EXCEPT ![p] = NoVersion]
    /\ snapSet' = [snapSet EXCEPT ![p] = {}]
    /\ choice' = [choice EXCEPT ![p] = NoMove]
    /\ UNCHANGED << version, plan, accepted >>

DropChoice(p) ==
    /\ choice[p] # NoMove
    /\ choice' = [choice EXCEPT ![p] = NoMove]
    /\ UNCHANGED << version, plan, snapVer, snapSet, accepted >>

Next ==
    \/ \E p \in Planners : ReadPlan(p) \/ Commit(p) \/ Retry(p) \/ DropChoice(p)
    \/ \E p \in Planners, mv \in Moves : Choose(p, mv)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* No accepted move is ever lost from the plan, whichever office committed it.
NoLostCraneMove == accepted \subseteq plan

A skyscraper's elevator bank is driven by a group controller that periodically reconfigures itself -- when a car is taken out for maintenance or a new dispatch profile is loaded, the controller advances its configuration epoch. Every car carries the epoch it last registered under, and the controller will only let a car act on the bank's behalf while that car's epoch matches the controller's current one. Cars are slow rather than failed: a car may stop responding for a while, but it always answers eventually.

A hall call at a floor may be raised if it is not already waiting, assigned, or completed. A car whose registered epoch matches the controller's and that is currently free may take a waiting hall call, which removes the call from the waiting set. A car holding a call whose registered epoch still matches the controller's may serve the call, completing it and freeing the car. The controller may reconfigure while it has epochs left in its commissioning schedule: the epoch advances, and every in-flight assignment is dropped back into the waiting set, because no car is registered under the new epoch yet. A car whose registered epoch is behind the controller's may re-register, adopting the current epoch. A car may also become the one unresponsive car in the bank, and the unresponsive car may start answering again; a car that is not answering neither takes calls nor re-registers.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A car never holds an assigned hall call unless the epoch it registered under is the group controller's current epoch, so no stale car ever acts on the bank's behalf.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every hall call that is raised is eventually completed.

vars == << epoch, carEpoch, held, waiting, done, mute >>

TypeOK ==

    /\ carEpoch \in [Cars -> 0..MaxEpoch]
    /\ held \in [Cars -> Calls \cup {NoCall}]
    /\ waiting \in SUBSET Calls
    /\ done \in SUBSET Calls
    /\ mute \in Cars \cup {NoCar}

Init ==
    /\ epoch = 0
    /\ carEpoch = [c \in Cars |-> 0]
    /\ held = [c \in Cars |-> NoCall]
    /\ waiting = {}
    /\ done = {}
    /\ mute = NoCar

Assigned(k) == \E c \in Cars : held[c] = k

Raise(k) ==
    /\ k \notin waiting /\ k \notin done /\ ~Assigned(k)
    /\ waiting' = waiting \cup {k}
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, carEpoch, held, done, mute >>

Take(c, k) ==
    /\ carEpoch[c] = epoch
    /\ c # mute
    /\ held[c] = NoCall
    /\ k \in waiting
    /\ held' = [held EXCEPT ![c] = k]
    /\ waiting' = waiting \ {k}
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, carEpoch, done, mute >>

Serve(c) ==
    /\ held[c] # NoCall
    /\ carEpoch[c] = epoch
    /\ done' = done \cup {held[c]}
    /\ held' = [held EXCEPT ![c] = NoCall]
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, carEpoch, waiting, mute >>

\* Reconfiguration invalidates every car at once, so in-flight assignments
\* must go back to the waiting set rather than ride out the epoch change.
Reconfigure ==
    /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
    /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
    /\ waiting' = waiting \cup {k \in Calls : Assigned(k)}
    /\ held' = [c \in Cars |-> NoCall]
    /\ UNCHANGED << carEpoch, done, mute >>

Register(c) ==
    /\ carEpoch[c] # epoch
    /\ c # mute
    /\ carEpoch' = [carEpoch EXCEPT ![c] = epoch]
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, held, waiting, done, mute >>

GoMute(c) == /\ mute = NoCar /\ mute' = c /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, carEpoch, held, waiting, done >>
Answer    == /\ mute # NoCar /\ mute' = NoCar /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, carEpoch, held, waiting, done >>

\* still fire only finitely often.

    /\ SF_vars(\E c \in Cars : Serve(c))
    /\ SF_vars(\E c \in Cars : Register(c))
    /\ WF_vars(Answer)

NoStaleCarHoldsCall ==
    \A c \in Cars : held[c] # NoCall => carEpoch[c] = epoch

EveryCallCompleted ==
    \A k \in Calls : (k \in waiting) ~> (k \in done)

A subway line is divided into signalling blocks. Every train is either berthed in exactly one block or running between blocks, and the line's signalling controller keeps a manifest: a per-block count of berthed trains plus a count of trains currently running. The controller is periodically reconfigured -- a track possession, a timetable change -- and each reconfiguration advances its signalling epoch. A block will only accept an arriving train once it has resynchronised to the controller's current epoch. The controller itself can crash silently: it simply stops reconfiguring, and nobody is told, but the epoch it last broadcast is still latched in the trackside equipment, so blocks can still resynchronise to it.

A berthed train may depart: it leaves its block, the manifest count for that block is decremented, and the running count is incremented. A train that is running may arrive into any block that has resynchronised to the current epoch: the manifest count for that block is incremented and the running count is decremented. The controller may reconfigure while it is alive and has possessions left in its schedule, advancing the epoch. A block whose latched epoch is behind the controller's may resynchronise to it. The controller may crash, after which it never reconfigures again.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The manifest's per-block berthed counts plus its running count always sum to exactly the number of trains on the line, so the signalling manifest never creates or loses a train.

vars == << pos, berthed, running, epoch, blockEpoch, dead >>

RECURSIVE Tally(_)
Tally(S) ==

    ELSE LET b == CHOOSE x \in S : TRUE IN berthed[b] + Tally(S \ {b})

Fleet == Cardinality(Trains)

TypeOK ==

    /\ running \in 0..Fleet

    /\ epoch = 0
    /\ blockEpoch = [b \in Blocks |-> 0]

\* A block only takes a train once it carries the epoch the controller last

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A regional power grid runs an automatic load-shedding scheme. A dispatcher maintains, for the current scheme configuration, the list of feeder relays it authorises to shed load. The scheme is reconfigured whenever the network topology changes -- a line is switched out, a generator is redispatched -- and each reconfiguration advances the scheme's epoch and voids every authorisation issued under the previous one. Each relay carries the epoch it last synchronised to. Relays are slow rather than failed: at most one relay at a time is out of contact, and it always comes back.

The dispatcher may authorise a relay, adding it to the current authorisation list. The dispatcher may withdraw a relay's authorisation, but only while that relay is in contact, and withdrawing also commands the relay to restore whatever load it is shedding. A relay that is in contact, is synchronised to the current epoch, and is on the authorisation list may begin shedding load. The dispatcher may reconfigure the scheme while it has reconfigurations left in its schedule: the epoch advances and the authorisation list is emptied. A relay that is in contact and whose synchronised epoch is behind the scheme's may resynchronise; on resynchronising it adopts the current epoch and, if it is not on the current authorisation list, it restores the load it was shedding. Finally, the one relay in contact may drop out of contact, and a relay out of contact may return.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A relay that has synchronised to the scheme's current epoch is never shedding load unless the dispatcher's current authorisation list contains it.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Relays, MaxEpoch, NoRelay

\* authorised is the dispatcher's list for the CURRENT epoch only; relayEpoch
\* records how far behind the scheme each relay has fallen.
VARIABLES epoch, relayEpoch, authorised, shedding, offline

vars == << epoch, relayEpoch, authorised, shedding, offline >>

TypeOK ==
    /\ epoch \in 0..MaxEpoch
    /\ relayEpoch \in [Relays -> 0..MaxEpoch]
    /\ authorised \in SUBSET Relays
    /\ shedding \in SUBSET Relays
    /\ offline \in Relays \cup {NoRelay}

Init ==
    /\ epoch = 0
    /\ relayEpoch = [r \in Relays |-> 0]
    /\ authorised = {}
    /\ shedding = {}
    /\ offline = NoRelay

Authorise(r) ==
    /\ r \notin authorised
    /\ authorised' = authorised \cup {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, relayEpoch, shedding, offline >>

\* Withdrawal reaches the relay in the same telemetry cycle, so it can only be
\* issued to a relay that is actually in contact.
Withdraw(r) ==
    /\ r \in authorised
    /\ r # offline
    /\ authorised' = authorised \ {r}
    /\ shedding' = shedding \ {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, relayEpoch, offline >>

Shed(r) ==
    /\ r # offline
    /\ relayEpoch[r] = epoch
    /\ r \in authorised
    /\ r \notin shedding
    /\ shedding' = shedding \cup {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, relayEpoch, authorised, offline >>

Reconfigure ==
    /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
    /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
    /\ authorised' = {}
    /\ UNCHANGED << relayEpoch, shedding, offline >>

\* Catching up is also when a relay learns its authorisation was voided, so
\* resynchronising has to restore load the relay is no longer entitled to shed.
Resync(r) ==

    /\ relayEpoch[r] # epoch
    /\ relayEpoch' = [relayEpoch EXCEPT ![r] = epoch]
    /\ shedding' = IF r \in authorised THEN shedding ELSE shedding \ {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, authorised, offline >>

DropOut(r) == /\ offline = NoRelay /\ offline' = r /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, relayEpoch, authorised, shedding >>
Return     == /\ offline # NoRelay /\ offline' = NoRelay /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, relayEpoch, authorised, shedding >>

Next ==
    \/ \E r \in Relays : Authorise(r) \/ Withdraw(r) \/ Shed(r) \/ Resync(r) \/ DropOut(r)
    \/ Reconfigure \/ Return

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

SyncedRelaysShedOnlyIfAuthorised ==
    \A r \in Relays : (r \in shedding /\ relayEpoch[r] = epoch) => r \in authorised

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A clearing house keeps one shared settlement record: the set of payment instructions accepted for the current session. Several settlement nodes maintain that record, and the service runs in numbered configurations -- every time the record is written, or the operations desk reconfigures the service, the configuration epoch advances. A node works from a private working copy stamped with the epoch it read, and a node may only write the record back while its stamp is still the service's current epoch. The desk also re-provisions the session's carrying capacity at runtime, raising or lowering the number of instructions the record may hold, though never below what the record already holds.

A node whose working copy is stamped with something other than the current epoch re-reads: it copies the record and takes the current epoch as its stamp. A node whose stamp is current may post an instruction that is not yet accepted, provided the record it would write -- its working copy plus that instruction -- still fits the session's capacity; posting replaces the shared record with that set, marks the instruction accepted in the clearing house's audit trail, and advances the epoch, which by construction leaves every node's working copy stale, including its own. The operations desk may reconfigure the service without posting anything, which also advances the epoch. The desk may re-provision the capacity to any different value that is at least the size of the current record.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Any settlement node whose working copy is stamped with the service's current epoch holds every instruction the audit trail has ever accepted, so no node can write the record back in a form that drops an accepted instruction.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every settlement node whose working copy has gone stale eventually holds a working copy stamped with the current epoch again.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

---- MODULE W4Od3m9p1t4 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Nodes, Instructions, MaxEpoch, MaxCapacity, NoStamp

\* record is the shared settlement record; accepted is the clearing house's
\* audit trail of every instruction ever posted into it.
VARIABLES epoch, record, accepted, copy, stamp, capacity

vars == << epoch, record, accepted, copy, stamp, capacity >>

TypeOK ==
    /\ epoch \in 0..MaxEpoch
    /\ record \in SUBSET Instructions
    /\ accepted \in SUBSET Instructions
    /\ copy \in [Nodes -> SUBSET Instructions]
    /\ stamp \in [Nodes -> (0..MaxEpoch) \cup {NoStamp}]
    /\ capacity \in 0..MaxCapacity

Init ==
    /\ epoch = 0
    /\ record = {}
    /\ accepted = {}
    /\ copy = [n \in Nodes |-> {}]
    /\ stamp = [n \in Nodes |-> NoStamp]
    /\ capacity = 1

ReRead(n) ==
    /\ stamp[n] # epoch
    /\ copy' = [copy EXCEPT ![n] = record]
    /\ stamp' = [stamp EXCEPT ![n] = epoch]
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, record, accepted, capacity >>

\* Posting advances the epoch, so every working copy in the service -- the
\* writer's included -- is stale the instant the record changes.
Post(n, x) ==
    /\ stamp[n] = epoch
    /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
    /\ x \notin accepted
    /\ Cardinality(copy[n] \cup {x}) <= capacity
    /\ record' = copy[n] \cup {x}
    /\ accepted' = accepted \cup {x}
    /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED << copy, stamp, capacity >>

Reconfigure ==
    /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
    /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED << record, accepted, copy, stamp, capacity >>

\* Capacity moves at runtime but never below what is already carried.
Reprovision(c) ==
    /\ c # capacity
    /\ c >= Cardinality(record)
    /\ capacity' = c
    /\ UNCHANGED << epoch, record, accepted, copy, stamp >>

Next ==
    \/ \E n \in Nodes : ReRead(n)
    \/ \E n \in Nodes, x \in Instructions : Post(n, x)
    \/ \E c \in 0..MaxCapacity : Reprovision(c)
    \/ Reconfigure

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
    /\ \A n \in Nodes :
        /\ TRUE
        /\ WF_vars(ReRead(n))

CurrentCopiesCarryEveryAcceptedInstruction ==
    \A n \in Nodes : stamp[n] = epoch => accepted \subseteq copy[n]

EveryStaleCopyRefreshes ==
    \A n \in Nodes : (stamp[n] # epoch) ~> (stamp[n] = epoch)

====

A university runs course registration on a hold-and-confirm scheme. Each course has a fixed seat cap. A student who wants a course first takes a hold on a seat; the hold is a lease that carries a countdown and lapses if the student does not confirm in time. A seat that is under an unexpired hold counts against the cap exactly as a confirmed enrolment does, because the registrar will not oversell a room. The registrar's office additionally has a bounded number of privileged overrides it may spend during a registration period.

A student with no hold outstanding may take a hold on a course they are not already enrolled in, provided the course's confirmed enrolments plus its outstanding holds are strictly below its cap; the hold starts with a full lease countdown. A student holding a lease that has not run down may confirm, which turns the hold into a confirmed enrolment. The registration clock may tick while at least one live lease is outstanding, running down the countdown on every outstanding hold. A student whose lease has run to zero loses the hold. The registrar may revoke any outstanding hold immediately, spending one override. The registrar may also directly enrol a student who has no hold outstanding into a course they are not in, again spending one override, and again only while that course's enrolments plus holds are strictly below its cap. A confirmed student may drop the course.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every course, its confirmed enrolments plus its outstanding seat holds never exceed that course's seat cap.

EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Students, Courses, Cap, LeaseTicks, MaxOverrides, NoCourse

\* A live hold occupies a seat just as a confirmed enrolment does, so both
\* sides of the sum below have to be counted against the cap.
VARIABLES enrolled, hold, ttl, overrides

vars == << enrolled, hold, ttl, overrides >>

Occupancy(c) ==
    Cardinality(enrolled[c]) + Cardinality({s \in Students : hold[s] = c})

TypeOK ==
    /\ enrolled \in [Courses -> SUBSET Students]
    /\ hold \in [Students -> Courses \cup {NoCourse}]
    /\ ttl \in [Students -> 0..LeaseTicks]
    /\ overrides \in 0..MaxOverrides

Init ==
    /\ enrolled = [c \in Courses |-> {}]
    /\ hold = [s \in Students |-> NoCourse]
    /\ ttl = [s \in Students |-> 0]
    /\ overrides = 0

TakeHold(s, c) ==
    /\ hold[s] = NoCourse
    /\ s \notin enrolled[c]
    /\ Occupancy(c) < Cap
    /\ hold' = [hold EXCEPT ![s] = c]
    /\ ttl' = [ttl EXCEPT ![s] = LeaseTicks]
    /\ UNCHANGED << enrolled, overrides >>

Confirm(s) ==
    /\ hold[s] # NoCourse
    /\ ttl[s] > 0
    /\ enrolled' = [enrolled EXCEPT ![hold[s]] = @ \cup {s}]
    /\ hold' = [hold EXCEPT ![s] = NoCourse]
    /\ ttl' = [ttl EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED << overrides >>

\* The clock runs down every live lease at once.
Tick ==
    /\ \E s \in Students : hold[s] # NoCourse /\ ttl[s] > 0
    /\ ttl' = [s \in Students |->
                 IF hold[s] # NoCourse /\ ttl[s] > 0 THEN ttl[s] - 1 ELSE ttl[s]]
    /\ UNCHANGED << enrolled, hold, overrides >>

Lapse(s) ==
    /\ hold[s] # NoCourse
    /\ ttl[s] = 0
    /\ hold' = [hold EXCEPT ![s] = NoCourse]
    /\ UNCHANGED << enrolled, ttl, overrides >>

Revoke(s) ==
    /\ hold[s] # NoCourse
    /\ overrides < MaxOverrides
    /\ hold' = [hold EXCEPT ![s] = NoCourse]
    /\ ttl' = [ttl EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
    /\ overrides' = overrides + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED << enrolled >>

\* The registrar's override skips the lease but not the seat cap.
ForceEnrol(s, c) ==
    /\ hold[s] = NoCourse
    /\ s \notin enrolled[c]
    /\ overrides < MaxOverrides
    /\ Occupancy(c) < Cap
    /\ enrolled' = [enrolled EXCEPT ![c] = @ \cup {s}]
    /\ overrides' = overrides + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED << hold, ttl >>

Drop(s, c) ==
    /\ s \in enrolled[c]
    /\ enrolled' = [enrolled EXCEPT ![c] = @ \ {s}]
    /\ UNCHANGED << hold, ttl, overrides >>

Next ==
    \/ \E s \in Students, c \in Courses : TakeHold(s, c) \/ ForceEnrol(s, c) \/ Drop(s, c)
    \/ \E s \in Students : Confirm(s) \/ Lapse(s) \/ Revoke(s)
    \/ Tick

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

SeatCapNeverOversold == \A c \in Courses : Occupancy(c) <= Cap

====

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An airport baggage router decides, for each bag, which make-up chute it will be sent to. A chute holds only so many bags before the handlers must clear it, so the router will not commit a bag to a chute that is already at its limit -- and a bag that has been committed to a chute but is still travelling counts against that chute just as a bag already sitting in it does. Each routing decision is agreed by a two-phase commit across the sector controllers that own the belts along the way. One sector controller may crash silently: it stops answering, and the router is never told, so the router can only recover by timing the bag out.

A queued bag may be proposed to a chute, provided that chute's bags already delivered plus the bags already travelling to it are below its limit; the bag then enters the voting phase with no sector pledges. A sector controller that has not crashed may pledge to a voting bag it has not yet pledged to. A voting bag that has collected pledges from every sector controller is committed and travels to its chute. The router may time out a voting bag at any point, rejecting it and returning its pledges, which is the only way a bag stuck behind a crashed controller is ever cleared. A bag that has arrived at its chute is later cleared by the handlers, freeing its place. A cleared or rejected bag may be re-queued for another attempt. At most one sector controller ever crashes, and it does so silently.

vars == << status, chute, pledged, crashed >>

\* A bag that is still voting has already booked its place in the chute, so
\* both the travelling and the delivered bags count against the limit.
Occupancy(ch) ==
    Cardinality({b \in Bags : chute[b] = ch /\ status[b] \in {"voting", "delivered"}})

TypeOK ==
    /\ status \in [Bags -> {"queued", "voting", "delivered", "cleared", "rejected"}]
    /\ chute \in [Bags -> Chutes \cup {NoChute}]
    /\ pledged \in [Bags -> SUBSET Sectors]
    /\ crashed \in Sectors \cup {NoSector}

Init ==
    /\ status = [b \in Bags |-> "queued"]
    /\ chute = [b \in Bags |-> NoChute]
    /\ pledged = [b \in Bags |-> {}]

Propose(b, ch) ==
    /\ status[b] = "queued"
    /\ Occupancy(ch) < ChuteLimit
    /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![b] = "voting"]
    /\ chute' = [chute EXCEPT ![b] = ch]
    /\ pledged' = [pledged EXCEPT ![b] = {}]
    /\ UNCHANGED << crashed >>

Pledge(s, b) ==
    /\ status[b] = "voting"
    /\ s # crashed
    /\ s \notin pledged[b]
    /\ pledged' = [pledged EXCEPT ![b] = @ \cup {s}]
    /\ UNCHANGED << status, chute, crashed >>

Commit(b) ==
    /\ status[b] = "voting"
    /\ \A s \in Sectors : s \in pledged[b]
    /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![b] = "delivered"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << chute, pledged, crashed >>

\* quiet without saying so; it also gives the chute place back.
TimeOut(b) ==

    /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![b] = "rejected"]
    /\ chute' = [chute EXCEPT ![b] = NoChute]
    /\ pledged' = [pledged EXCEPT ![b] = {}]

    /\ status' = [status EXCEPT ![b] = "cleared"]

    /\ UNCHANGED << pledged, crashed >>

    /\ pledged' = [pledged EXCEPT ![b] = {}]
    /\ UNCHANGED << chute, crashed >>

    /\ crashed' = s
    /\ UNCHANGED << status, chute, pledged >>

    \/ \E s \in Sectors, b \in Bags : Pledge(s, b)
    \/ \E b \in Bags : Commit(b) \/ TimeOut(b) \/ Clear(b) \/ Requeue(b)
    \/ \E s \in Sectors : Crash(s)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

    /\ fine \in [Bins -> Techs \cup {NoTech}]

    /\ Cardinality(permits) < allowance
    /\ permits' = permits \cup {t}
    /\ UNCHANGED << coarse, fine, allowance >>

TakeCabinet(t, c) ==
    /\ t \in permits
    /\ coarse[c] = NoTech
    /\ coarse' = [coarse EXCEPT ![c] = t]
    /\ UNCHANGED << fine, allowance, permits >>

    /\ fine[b] = NoTech

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An airport baggage router hands each bag one make-up slot, and it decides which by putting the question to a set of allocator replicas. Each replica will name at most one bag per slot -- once a replica has named a bag for a slot, that is its answer for that slot for the rest of the session. A bag is awarded a slot only when a strict majority of the replicas' answers for that slot, as actually received by the router, name that bag. The replicas' answers travel over the terminal's message fabric, which promises nothing about ordering: answers become visible to the router in any order at all.

A queued bag may be put forward, entering the seeking state. A replica that has not yet answered for a slot may name any seeking bag for that slot. Any answer a replica has given but the router has not yet received may become visible to the router, in whatever order. A seeking bag may be awarded a slot when the answers the router has received for that slot give that bag a strict majority of the replicas and no other bag already holds that slot. A seeking bag is turned away when, for every slot, either the slot is already awarded to another bag or the answers already fixed by the replicas make a majority for this bag impossible. ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
Two settlement engines, commissioned years apart by different vendors, share one interbank instruction log. The log is an append-only sequence, and ownership of it rotates: the scheme runs in numbered configurations, and each handover advances the configuration number and moves ownership of the log from the engine that has it to the other one. Only the engine that currently owns the log may take instructions in or append them. When an engine takes an instruction in it is staged, not yet in the log; when it appends the instruction the settlement desk acknowledges the position at which the instruction landed, and that acknowledgement is what a member bank is later shown. The log is only so long: a session's log has a fixed maximum length, and there are more instructions in circulation than places in it.

The owning engine may take in an instruction that is not staged anywhere and has never been acknowledged. The owning engine may append an instruction it has staged, provided the log is not yet at its maximum length: the instruction goes on the end, the desk acknowledges it at that position, and it stops being staged. Either engine may discard an instruction it has staged, which puts it back into circulation unacknowledged. The scheme may hand the log over while it has handovers left in its schedule: the configuration number advances and the other engine becomes the owner, while anything staged stays staged with the engine that took it.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every instruction the settlement desk has acknowledged still sits in the shared log at exactly the position it was acknowledged at.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every instruction that is staged by an engine eventually stops being staged, whether by being appended or by being discarded.

\* or 0 if u has never been acknowledged.

vars == << log, ackAt, owner, config, staged >>

Staged(u) == \E e \in Engines : u \in staged[e]

TypeOK ==
    /\ log \in Seq(Instructions)
    /\ Len(log) <= MaxLen
    /\ ackAt \in [Instructions -> 0..MaxLen]
    /\ owner \in Engines
    /\ config \in 0..MaxHandovers
    /\ staged \in [Engines -> SUBSET Instructions]

Init ==
    /\ log = << >>
    /\ ackAt = [u \in Instructions |-> 0]
    /\ owner = CHOOSE e \in Engines : TRUE
    /\ config = 0
    /\ staged = [e \in Engines |-> {}]

TakeIn(e, u) ==
    /\ e = owner
    /\ ~Staged(u)
    /\ ackAt[u] = 0
    /\ staged' = [staged EXCEPT ![e] = @ \cup {u}]
    /\ UNCHANGED << log, ackAt, owner, config >>

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A container terminal has one quay crane rail that gangs must have to themselves while they work it. Access is arbitrated by a single compare-and-swap register in the terminal's control system: the register either reads free or names the gang that owns the rail. A gang first reads the register, then swaps its own name in if what it read is still what the register says. Gangs here are slow rather than failed -- at most one gang at a time may stall between its read and its swap, and it always comes back -- which is exactly why the swap has to re-check what the read saw.

A gang that is not stalled and holds no read may read the register, remembering the value it saw. A gang that is not stalled, read the register as free, and finds the register still free may swap its own name in, taking ownership. A gang whose remembered value no longer matches the register discards its read and will read again. A gang named by the register may mount the rail and begin working it. A gang on the rail may dismount. A gang named by the register that is not on the rail may release the register back to free, clearing its read. A gang that is not stalled may stall, and the stalled gang may come back.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A gang is never on the quay crane rail unless the compare-and-swap register names that gang, so the rail is worked by at most one gang at a time.

vars == << reg, seen, onRail, stalled >>

TypeOK ==

    /\ seen \in [Gangs -> Gangs \cup {Free, NoRead}]
    /\ onRail \in SUBSET Gangs
    /\ stalled \in Gangs \cup {NoGang}

Init ==
    /\ reg = Free
    /\ seen = [g \in Gangs |-> NoRead]
    /\ onRail = {}
    /\ stalled = NoGang

ReadReg(g) ==
    /\ g # stalled
    /\ seen[g] = NoRead
    /\ seen' = [seen EXCEPT ![g] = reg]
    /\ UNCHANGED << reg, onRail, stalled >>

\* The compare half of compare-and-swap: a gang that stalled across a change
\* of the register cannot claim the rail on the strength of a stale read.
Swap(g) ==
    /\ g # stalled
    /\ seen[g] = Free
    /\ reg = Free
    /\ reg' = g
    /\ seen' = [seen EXCEPT ![g] = NoRead]
    /\ UNCHANGED << onRail, stalled >>

FailedSwap(g) ==
    /\ seen[g] # NoRead
    /\ seen[g] # reg
    /\ seen' = [seen EXCEPT ![g] = NoRead]

ReleaseReg(g) ==

Resume  == /\ stalled # NoGang /\ stalled' = NoGang /\ UNCHANGED << reg, seen, onRail >>

A wildfire air operation flies retardant drones. Dropping a load on a target is irreversible: once a target has been treated the load is gone and the operation records the strike. The tasking system therefore keeps an arming register listing the targets that still hold an unspent release authority, and a drone can only release on a target that is still in that register. The swarm's tasking is reconfigured as the fire moves -- each reconfiguration advances the tasking epoch and cancels every drone's current assignment, since assignments made under the old profile no longer describe the fire. Drones carry the epoch they last synchronised to. Wind matters too: a drone will not release above a wind reading over its release limit. The incident commander holds a privileged override for the cases where none of that can be waited out.

A drone synchronised to the current epoch and carrying no assignment may be assigned a target that is still in the arming register. A drone carrying an assignment, synchronised to the current epoch, may release on its target when the wind reading is at or below the release limit and the target is still armed: the target leaves the arming register, the strike is recorded, and the assignment is cleared. The incident commander may order an override release by a drone carrying an assignment whose target is still armed, regardless of that drone's epoch and regardless of the wind. The tasking system may reconfigure while it has profiles left in its schedule, advancing the epoch and cancelling every assignment. A drone whose epoch is behind may resynchronise. A drone may have its assignment cancelled. The wind reading may change to any other value at any time.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The arming register always holds exactly those targets that have not been struck, so no target is ever released on twice.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every target still holding a release authority is eventually struck.
