===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A stock exchange opening auction hands out matching slots to orders. The auction keeps two
views of the slot board: a free list of the slots still available, and a per-slot record of
which order occupies it. The right to hand out a slot travels the matching members as a
numbered token, and a member may hand out a slot only while the token number it is holding is
the ring's current number; the token may be passed to the next member or the one past it, and
when the numbering runs out the ring is re-formed with a member seated at the first number.

The market supervisor holds a privileged override and may hand out a slot without the token
at all, a bounded number of times per auction. The override skips the ring but not the slot
board: the supervisor still has to take the slot off the free list and record its occupant,
exactly as a member would.

The auction behaves as follows. A member holding the ring's current token number may fill a
free slot with an order that does not already occupy a slot, which takes the slot off the
free list and records the order against it. The supervisor may do the same without holding
the token, spending one of the auction's overrides. An occupied slot may be released, which
clears its occupant and puts it back on the free list. A member holding the current token
number may pass the token to the next member or the one past it, taking the next number. When
the numbering is spent, a member may re-form the ring, restarting the numbering with itself
seated and every other member holding nothing.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A slot is on the free list exactly when it has no occupant recorded against
it, so a slot can never be handed out twice nor stranded off the free list unfilled.

CONSTANTS Members, RingSize, Slots, Orders, MaxToken, MaxOverrides, NoOrder

\* The token goes to the next seat or the one past it, so a quiet member does not
\* hold the whole auction up.
Onward(m, k) == ((m + k - 1) % RingSize) + 1

VARIABLES occupant, freeList, token, seat, overrides

vars == <<occupant, freeList, token, seat, overrides>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ occupant \in [Slots -> {NoOrder} \cup Orders]
    /\ freeList \in SUBSET Slots
    /\ token \in 1..MaxToken
    /\ seat \in [Members -> 0..MaxToken]
    /\ overrides \in 0..MaxOverrides

Init ==
    /\ occupant = [s \in Slots |-> NoOrder]
    /\ freeList = Slots
    /\ token = 1
    /\ seat = [m \in Members |-> IF m = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0]
    /\ overrides = 0

Unplaced(o) == \A s \in Slots : occupant[s] # o

\* Both views move together: off the free list and onto the slot record.
Award(s, o) ==
    /\ s \in freeList
    /\ Unplaced(o)
    /\ occupant' = [occupant EXCEPT ![s] = o]
    /\ freeList' = freeList \ {s}

Fill(m, s, o) ==
    /\ seat[m] = token
    /\ Award(s, o)
    /\ UNCHANGED <<token, seat, overrides>>

Override(s, o) ==
    /\ overrides < MaxOverrides
    /\ Award(s, o)
    /\ overrides' = overrides + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<token, seat>>

Release(s) ==
    /\ occupant[s] # NoOrder
    /\ occupant' = [occupant EXCEPT ![s] = NoOrder]
    /\ freeList' = freeList \cup {s}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<token, seat, overrides>>

Pass(m, k) ==
    /\ seat[m] = token
    /\ token < MaxToken
    /\ token' = token + 1
    /\ seat' = [seat EXCEPT ![m] = 0, ![Onward(m, k)] = token + 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<occupant, freeList, overrides>>

ReForm(m) ==
    /\ token = MaxToken
    /\ token' = 1
    /\ seat' = [x \in Members |-> IF x = m THEN 1 ELSE 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<occupant, freeList, overrides>>

Next ==
    \/ \E m \in Members, s \in Slots, o \in Orders : Fill(m, s, o)
    \/ \E s \in Slots, o \in Orders : Override(s, o)
    \/ \E s \in Slots : Release(s)
    \/ \E m \in Members, k \in 1..2 : Pass(m, k)
    \/ \E m \in Members : ReForm(m)

A multiplayer game lobby matchmaker moves players between a region-wide free pool and its
lobbies. The roster of players is fixed: a player is always accounted for in exactly one of
three places -- waiting in the free pool, drawn into a lobby's holding area, or seated in a
lobby -- and the matchmaker must never mislay one between them.

Moving players is protected by a two-level lock. A matchmaker node first takes the region
lock, which is coarse and held by one node at a time, and uses it to take the fine lock on a
single lobby; taking the lobby lock hands the region lock back. Only the holder of a lobby's
fine lock may draw players into that lobby's holding area or seat them from it.

A matchmaker node can crash silently, so the rest cannot tell a dead node from a slow one and
its locks have to be reclaimed. Reclaiming a lobby lock from a crashed node also empties that
lobby's holding area back into the free pool, because players drawn but never seated would
otherwise be stranded in a holding area nobody holds the lock to.

The matchmaker behaves as follows. A live node may take the free region lock. A node holding
the region lock may take the fine lock on an unlocked lobby, which hands the region lock back.
A node holding a lobby's fine lock may draw a player out of the free pool into that lobby's
holding area while the pool is not empty. It may seat a player from that holding area while
the holding area is not empty and the lobby is below its seat limit. It may release the lobby
lock once the holding area is empty. Any node may crash silently, so long as not every node
has crashed, and a crashed node may later come back. A lobby lock held by a crashed node may be
reclaimed, which empties that lobby's holding area back into the free pool. The region lock
held by a crashed node may likewise be reclaimed. A seated player may leave, returning to the
free pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The free pool, the lobby holding areas and the lobby seats always account
between them for exactly the fixed roster of players, so no player is ever created or lost.

A print shop job spooler assigns jobs to presses. A press has a fixed capacity counting
everything it is committed to: jobs holding a reservation on it and jobs actually mounted on
it together may never exceed that capacity. A reservation is a lease with a deadline on the
shop clock; when the deadline passes the reservation is swept away and the capacity it was
holding comes back.

Reservation offers reach the presses out of order and can be arbitrarily late, so an offer may
arrive after its own deadline has already passed, or after the press it names has filled up,
or after the job it names has been placed somewhere else. An offer is taken up only if its
deadline is still ahead of the clock, its job is not already reserved or mounted anywhere, and
the press it names is below capacity; any offer failing those tests is turned away. The
spooler keeps only a bounded number of offers in circulation at a time.

The spooler behaves as follows. The spooler may put an offer into circulation naming a job, a
press and a deadline, so long as the circulation limit is not reached. A circulating offer that
passes all three tests is taken up, reserving that press for that job until the offer's
deadline. A circulating offer that fails any of them is turned away. A job holding a
reservation whose deadline is still ahead may be mounted on that press, which converts the
reservation into a mounting without changing what the press is committed to. A mounted job may
be finished and taken off. A reservation whose deadline has passed may be swept away. The clock
may tick. When the clock has run out and no reservations are standing, the shop may start a
fresh session, returning the clock to the start and clearing every offer in circulation.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every press, the jobs holding a reservation on it together with the jobs
mounted on it never number more than the press's capacity.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every reservation whose deadline has passed is eventually swept off the
press holding it.

Usable(o) == o.until > clock /\ ~Placed(o.job) /\ Committed(o.press) < Capacity

    /\ Usable(o)
    /\ reserved' = [reserved EXCEPT ![o.press] = @ \cup {o.job}]
    /\ deadline' = [deadline EXCEPT ![o.job] = o.until]
    /\ circulating' = circulating \ {o}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, mounted>>

TurnAway(o) ==

    /\ ~Usable(o)
    /\ circulating' = circulating \ {o}

\* Mounting converts a reservation into a mounting, so the press's commitment is
\* unchanged by it.
Mount(j, p) ==

    /\ deadline[j] > clock

TakeOff(j, p) ==
    /\ j \in mounted[p]
    /\ mounted' = [mounted EXCEPT ![p] = @ \ {j}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, reserved, deadline, circulating>>

Sweep(j, p) ==
    /\ j \in reserved[p]
    /\ deadline[j] <= clock
    /\ reserved' = [reserved EXCEPT ![p] = @ \ {j}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, deadline, mounted, circulating>>

    /\ clock' = clock + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<reserved, deadline, mounted, circulating>>

    /\ \A p \in Presses : reserved[p] = {}
    /\ clock' = 0
    /\ circulating' = {}

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A power-grid load shedder allocates fixed megawatt blocks to feeders. A block that a
generator has committed is accounted for in exactly one of two ways: it is either held in the
shedder's escrow, waiting to be allocated, or it is allocated to a feeder. Nothing else may
ever be true of a committed block -- a block that fell out of escrow without landing on a
feeder would be power the grid thinks it has and does not.

Allocations are made under optimistic locking. A controller stages the block and feeder it
intends to pair, together with the allocation table's version as it read it, and the staged
pairing is applied only if that version is still the table's version, the block is still in
escrow, and the version numbering has room. Otherwise the staging is thrown away and the
controller starts over.

A controller can fail silently, and it can fail with a staging outstanding. That is safe
precisely because a staging does not move the block: the block sits in escrow until an
application actually lands, so a controller that dies mid-decision costs the grid nothing but
the staging, which is later thrown away like any other unusable one. A failed controller may
come back.

The shedder behaves as follows. A generator may commit a block that is not yet committed,
which puts it into escrow. A live controller with nothing staged may stage a block that is in
escrow against a feeder, recording the table's version. A live controller may apply its
staging when the version still matches, the block is still in escrow, and the numbering has
room, which takes the block out of escrow, allocates it to the feeder and moves the version
on. A staging that fails any of those tests, or whose controller has failed, is thrown away.
A controller may fail silently, so long as not all of them have. A failed controller may come
back. An allocated block may be released back into escrow. A block sitting in escrow may be
decommitted, which withdraws it from the grid's committed set entirely. When the version
numbering is spent it is reindexed, which also throws away every staging.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The committed blocks are exactly those held in escrow together with those
allocated to feeders, so no committed block is ever conjured up or mislaid.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every staging a controller makes is eventually cleared.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An air-traffic runway allocator hands departure slots to flights. It keeps two records that
must always agree: a per-slot record of the flight occupying it, and the set of flights the
allocator has confirmed a slot to. A slot handed out twice would evict the flight that had it,
leaving that flight confirmed with no slot to stand on, which is exactly the disagreement
between the two records that must never arise.

Allocation is done by whichever tower is currently leading, and leadership is carried by a
term number: a tower may allocate only while the term it believes it holds is the allocator's
current term. A tower can fail silently, so the others cannot tell a failed tower from a quiet
one and any tower may take over, which raises the term and leaves the previous leader believing
a term that no longer counts. A failed tower may come back, still believing whatever term it
believed when it went down.

The allocator behaves as follows. A live tower whose believed term is the current term may
allocate a free slot to a flight that has no slot confirmed, which records the flight against
the slot and confirms the slot to the flight. A slot's allocation may be cancelled, which
clears the slot and withdraws the confirmation together. Any tower may fail silently, so long
as not every tower has failed, and a failed tower may come back. A live tower whose believed
term is not the current term may take over, raising the term and taking it for itself, so long
as the term numbering has room. When the numbering is spent, a live tower believing the
current term may restart the numbering with itself leading and every other tower believing
nothing.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The set of flights confirmed a slot is exactly the set of flights appearing
in the per-slot record, so no slot is ever handed out a second time behind the first flight's
back.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

    /\ confirmed \in SUBSET Flights
    /\ believes \in [Towers -> 0..MaxTerm]
    /\ term \in 1..MaxTerm
    /\ dead \in SUBSET Towers

    /\ confirmed = {}
    /\ believes = [t \in Towers |-> 1]
    /\ term = 1
    /\ dead = {}

\* Only the tower whose believed term is the live one may hand out a slot; a
\* tower demoted while it was merely quiet finds its belief worthless.
Leading(t) == t \notin dead /\ believes[t] = term

Allocate(t, f, s) ==

    /\ onSlot[s] = NoFlight
    /\ f \notin confirmed
    /\ onSlot' = [onSlot EXCEPT ![s] = f]
    /\ confirmed' = confirmed \cup {f}

Restore(t) ==

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A car-wash conveyor line assigns arriving vehicles to wash bays. It keeps a per-bay record of
the vehicle in it and a per-vehicle record of the bay it was given, and these must be exact
mirrors of one another: a bay given out twice would leave the first vehicle still pointing at
a bay that now holds someone else.

Assignment is a two-step handshake. The controller in charge posts a claim naming a vehicle
and a bay; the claim is only turned into an assignment when the line acknowledges it, and only
if the bay is still empty and the vehicle still has no bay. Controllers can be slow but never
fail, so a posted claim may sit unacknowledged for arbitrarily long, yet it is always resolved
in the end, one way or the other.

Because a controller can be slow, the line may elect a different controller while a claim of
the old one is still outstanding, which raises the term. The stale controller's claim is not
recalled; it simply has to fail the acknowledgement test if the bay it named has been taken in
the meantime, and is withdrawn instead.

The line behaves as follows. The controller whose term is the line's current term may post a
claim naming an empty bay and a vehicle with no bay, if it has no claim outstanding. An
outstanding claim whose bay is still empty and whose vehicle still has no bay may be
acknowledged, which writes both records and clears the claim. An outstanding claim that fails
either test is withdrawn. An occupied bay may be emptied, which clears both records together.
Any controller other than the one in charge may take over, which raises the term, so long as
the term numbering has room. When the numbering is spent, the controller in charge may restart
it.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every vehicle that has been given a bay is the vehicle that bay records
holding, so no bay is ever handed out a second time.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every claim a controller posts is eventually resolved, leaving that
controller with no claim outstanding.

A university course-registration system keeps its course catalogue as a chain of revisions. A
single compare-and-swap register holds the head of the chain. A department that wants to change
the catalogue starts a draft revision, recording as the draft's parent whatever the head was at
the moment the draft began. Publishing swaps the head to the draft, but only if the head is
still the revision the draft was parented on; otherwise the draft is stale, because publishing
it would hang the chain off an old head and cut loose everything published in between, and the
department has to abandon it and start again.

A department can fail silently, so the others cannot tell a failed department from a slow one.
A department that fails with a draft outstanding costs the catalogue nothing: the draft was
never on the chain, so abandoning it later loses no published work. A failed department may
come back.

The system behaves as follows. A live department with no draft outstanding may start a draft on
a revision number that is unused -- not parented on anything, not published, not the head, and
not being drafted elsewhere -- recording the current head as that revision's parent. A live
department may publish its draft when the head is still the revision the draft is parented on,
which makes the draft the new head and records it as published. A department may abandon a
draft whose parent is no longer the head, clearing the revision number for reuse. A department
may fail silently, so long as not every department has failed, and a failed department may come
back.

running back from the current head, so no published revision is ever cut loose by a later
publish.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A library reservation system runs a hold shelf with a fixed number of shelf permits. A permit
is what entitles a book to occupy space: the shelf's whole capacity is accounted for at every
moment as permits still free, permits travelling with a placement instruction that has not
landed yet, and permits under books already on the shelf.

Pickup requests wait in a bounded work queue. The queue applies backpressure by refusing to
grow beyond its limit. Dispatching a request takes a free permit and sends a placement
instruction; instructions do not land in the order they were sent, so several may be
outstanding at once and any of them may be the next to land. An instruction may also be
recalled in transit, which hands its permit straight back.

The system behaves as follows. A pickup request may join the queue while the queue is below
its limit. A queued request may be dispatched while a permit is free, which takes that permit
and puts a placement instruction in transit. A queued request is deferred off the queue
instead when no permit is free. A placement instruction in transit may land, putting a book on
the shelf under the permit it was carrying. A placement instruction in transit may be recalled,
returning its permit to the free pool. A book on the shelf may be collected by its patron,
which returns its permit to the free pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The permits still free, the permits travelling with instructions in transit,
and the permits under books on the shelf always add up to exactly the shelf's capacity, so the
hold shelf can never be committed beyond what it can hold.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every request that joins the queue eventually leaves it.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Requests, Capacity, QueueLimit

VARIABLES free, inTransit, onShelf, queue

vars == <<free, inTransit, onShelf, queue>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ free \in 0..Capacity
    /\ inTransit \in 0..Capacity
    /\ onShelf \in 0..Capacity
    /\ queue \in SUBSET Requests

Init ==
    /\ free = Capacity
    /\ inTransit = 0
    /\ onShelf = 0
    /\ queue = {}

\* Backpressure: the queue simply will not grow past its limit.
Join(r) ==
    /\ r \notin queue
    /\ Cardinality(queue) < QueueLimit
    /\ queue' = queue \cup {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<free, inTransit, onShelf>>

\* Dispatching moves a permit from the free pool onto an instruction; the permit
\* is spoken for from that moment, not from when the instruction lands.
Dispatch(r) ==
    /\ r \in queue
    /\ free > 0
    /\ free' = free - 1
    /\ inTransit' = inTransit + 1
    /\ queue' = queue \ {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED onShelf

Defer(r) ==
    /\ r \in queue
    /\ free = 0
    /\ queue' = queue \ {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<free, inTransit, onShelf>>

\* Instructions land in whatever order they get to; which one lands is not fixed
\* by which was sent first.
Land ==
    /\ inTransit > 0
    /\ inTransit' = inTransit - 1
    /\ onShelf' = onShelf + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<free, queue>>

Recall ==
    /\ inTransit > 0
    /\ inTransit' = inTransit - 1
    /\ free' = free + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<onShelf, queue>>

Collect ==
    /\ onShelf > 0
    /\ onShelf' = onShelf - 1
    /\ free' = free + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<inTransit, queue>>

Clear(r) == Dispatch(r) \/ Defer(r)

Next ==
    \/ \E r \in Requests : Join(r) \/ Clear(r)
    \/ Land
    \/ Recall
    \/ Collect

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars
        /\ \A r \in Requests : WF_vars(Clear(r))

PermitsAccountForCapacity == free + inTransit + onShelf = Capacity

EveryQueuedRequestLeaves ==

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home door lock network keeps a shared automation record: a setting for each automation
the household runs. A setting starts blank and is filled in exactly once; the record only ever
gains settings and never changes one that is already filled in. Editing is protected by a lease. Only the node holding the lease number
the network most recently issued may write, and a write replaces the whole record with the
editing node's working copy, so a copy that was taken before somebody else's edit landed would
carry that edit away with it.

Issuing a lease hands the new holder a fresh copy of the record in the same breath, and a node
may only refresh its copy while it holds the current lease. That is what keeps a working copy
from ever being older than the lease it is written under. Nodes can be slow but never fail: a
node may go on fiddling with a copy it took under a lease that has since been handed to
somebody else, and it will still be there later, but its writes will no longer be taken.

When a node writes, it is told which automation it has just set and to what, and it holds on to
that acknowledgement.

The network behaves as follows. The next lease number may be issued to any node, so long as the
lease budget is not spent; issuing hands that node a fresh copy of the record. A node holding
the current lease may refresh its copy from the record. Any node may fill in a still-blank automation in
its own working copy, whether or not it holds a lease; it may not change one already filled in. A node holding the current lease may
write its working copy over the record, and is acknowledged for one automation its copy has
actually filled in, together with the value it filled in; a still-blank automation is not
something the record acknowledges. When the lease budget is spent the numbering is reissued from the start and
every node is left holding no lease.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every acknowledgement a node holds still matches the record -- the automation
it names still carries the value it was acknowledged for -- so no acknowledged edit is ever
carried away by a later write reverting it to blank.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

Copies == [Automations -> 0..MaxSetting]
Acks == [auto : Automations, value : 0..MaxSetting]

VARIABLES record, copy, leaseOf, lease, ack

vars == <<record, copy, leaseOf, lease, ack>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ record \in Copies
    /\ copy \in [Nodes -> Copies]
    /\ leaseOf \in [Nodes -> 0..MaxLease]
    /\ lease \in 0..MaxLease
    /\ ack \in [Nodes -> {NoAck} \cup Acks]

Init ==
    /\ record = [a \in Automations |-> 0]
    /\ copy = [n \in Nodes |-> [a \in Automations |-> 0]]
    /\ leaseOf = [n \in Nodes |-> 0]
    /\ lease = 0
    /\ ack = [n \in Nodes |-> NoAck]

Holder(n) == leaseOf[n] = lease /\ lease > 0

\* Issuing the lease and handing over a fresh copy are the same step, so a
\* working copy can never predate the lease it will be written under.
Issue(n) ==
    /\ lease < MaxLease
    /\ lease' = lease + 1
    /\ leaseOf' = [leaseOf EXCEPT ![n] = lease + 1]
    /\ copy' = [copy EXCEPT ![n] = record]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, ack>>

Refresh(n) ==
    /\ Holder(n)
    /\ copy' = [copy EXCEPT ![n] = record]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, leaseOf, lease, ack>>

\* A setting is filled in once and never changed, so the record only ever gains
\* settings; a slow node keeps filling in its own copy regardless of the lease.
Adjust(n, a, v) ==

    /\ copy[n][a] = 0
    /\ copy' = [copy EXCEPT ![n] = [copy[n] EXCEPT ![a] = v]]

\* Only a setting the copy has actually filled in is acknowledged; a blank is
\* not something the record has promised to keep.
WriteBack(n, a) ==

    /\ copy[n][a] > 0
    /\ record' = copy[n]
    /\ ack' = [ack EXCEPT ![n] = [auto |-> a, value |-> copy[n][a]]]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<copy, leaseOf, lease>>

Reissue ==
    /\ lease = MaxLease
    /\ lease' = 0
    /\ leaseOf' = [n \in Nodes |-> 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, copy, ack>>

Next ==
    \/ \E n \in Nodes : Issue(n) \/ Refresh(n)
    \/ \E n \in Nodes, a \in Automations, v \in 1..MaxSetting : Adjust(n, a, v)
    \/ \E n \in Nodes, a \in Automations : WriteBack(n, a)
    \/ Reissue

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

AcknowledgedEditsStand ==
    \A n \in Nodes : ack[n] # NoAck => record[ack[n].auto] = ack[n].value

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A subway signalling block system lets maintenance crews release a track block for work. A
release is irreversible: the block's interlock seal is broken for the rest of the session, and
the system records both which crew broke it and, on the crew's own sheet, which block that crew
is credited with. Those two records are what stop a block being released twice -- a second
release would take the block's record away from the first crew while that crew's sheet still
claimed it.

Which crews are on duty is settled by an epoch-numbered reconfiguration. Only a crew on the
current roster may be assigned a block or perform a release, and the roster may only be
reconfigured when no crew is holding an assignment, so a reconfiguration never strands a crew
part-way through a release. The control-room supervisor holds a privileged override and may
break a block's seal directly, without a roster or an assignment, a bounded number of times per
session; the override is still credited on the supervisor's own sheet like any other release.

The system behaves as follows. A crew on the current roster, holding no assignment and not yet
credited with a block, may be assigned a block whose seal is still intact. A crew is credited with at most one release per session. A crew on the roster
that is not yet credited and holds an assignment on a block whose seal is still intact may
release it, which breaks the
seal, records the crew against the block, credits the block on the crew's sheet, and clears the
assignment. A crew holding an assignment may stand down from it instead. The roster may be
reconfigured to any different roster while no crew holds an assignment, which takes the system
to the next epoch. The supervisor may break the seal of a block directly, spending one of the
session's overrides, provided the supervisor is not already credited with a block. When the
epoch numbering is spent and no crew holds an assignment, the numbering restarts.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every block whose seal is broken is credited on the sheet of the very crew
recorded against it, so the irreversible release happens at most once per block.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every assignment a crew takes on is eventually cleared.

vars == <<epoch, roster, assignment, credited, brokenBy, overrides>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ epoch \in 1..MaxEpoch
    /\ roster \in SUBSET Crews
    /\ assignment \in [Crews -> {NoBlock} \cup Blocks]
    /\ credited \in [Crews -> {NoBlock} \cup Blocks]
    /\ brokenBy \in [Blocks -> {NoOne} \cup Crews]
    /\ overrides \in 0..MaxOverrides

    /\ roster = Crews
    /\ assignment = [c \in Crews |-> NoBlock]
    /\ credited = [c \in Crews |-> NoBlock]
    /\ brokenBy = [b \in Blocks |-> NoOne]

Assign(c, b) ==
    /\ c \in roster
    /\ assignment[c] = NoBlock
    /\ credited[c] = NoBlock
    /\ brokenBy[b] = NoOne
    /\ assignment' = [assignment EXCEPT ![c] = b]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, roster, credited, brokenBy, overrides>>

\* Breaking the seal is the irreversible step; both records are written with it.
Release(c) ==
    /\ c \in roster
    /\ assignment[c] # NoBlock
    /\ credited[c] = NoBlock
    /\ brokenBy[assignment[c]] = NoOne
    /\ brokenBy' = [brokenBy EXCEPT ![assignment[c]] = c]
    /\ credited' = [credited EXCEPT ![c] = assignment[c]]
    /\ assignment' = [assignment EXCEPT ![c] = NoBlock]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, roster, overrides>>

Override(b) ==

    /\ credited[Supervisor] = NoBlock
    /\ brokenBy' = [brokenBy EXCEPT ![b] = Supervisor]
    /\ credited' = [credited EXCEPT ![Supervisor] = b]
    /\ overrides' = overrides + 1

    \/ \E c \in Crews : Settle(c)
    \/ \E b \in Blocks : Override(b)
    \/ \E r \in SUBSET Crews : Reconfigure(r)
    \/ Renumber

ReleasedAtMostOnce ==

A hospital operating-room scheduler hands theatre slots to surgical teams as leases. Every
lease carries a number, and the numbers are handed out in sequence and never reused within a
scheduling round. A slot carries the number of the lease currently on it, or nothing if it is
free, and a team that has taken up a lease holds the slot and the number it was granted.

Grant notices reach the teams out of order and can be arbitrarily late. A team therefore takes
up a notice only if the slot it names still carries exactly the lease number on the notice; a
notice naming a lease number the slot has moved past is a leftover from an earlier grant and is
thrown away. That check is the whole of the defence against a slot being handed to two teams.

Leases expire. When the scheduler pulls a slot's lease it frees the slot and takes the lease
away from whatever team was holding it, so no team is left holding a number the slot no longer
carries.

The scheduler behaves as follows. The scheduler may grant a free slot to a team, taking the
next lease number, marking the slot with it and putting a grant notice into circulation. A
team with no lease in hand may take up a circulating notice addressed to it whose slot still
carries the notice's lease number. A circulating notice addressed to a team that already holds
a lease, or whose slot no longer carries its number, is thrown away. A team holding a lease may
give it up, freeing the slot. The scheduler may pull a slot's lease, freeing the slot and
taking the lease from any team holding it. When the lease numbering is spent and no slot is
leased, no team is holding, and no notice is in circulation, a fresh round of numbering begins.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every team holding a lease finds its slot still carrying exactly the lease
number that team was granted, so a slot is never handed out to a second team while the first
still holds it.

CONSTANTS Teams, Slots, MaxLease, NoGrant

Grants == [slot : Slots, id : 1..MaxLease]
Notices == [to : Teams, slot : Slots, id : 1..MaxLease]

vars == <<onSlot, holding, issued, circulating>>

    /\ onSlot \in [Slots -> 0..MaxLease]
    /\ holding \in [Teams -> {NoGrant} \cup Grants]
    /\ issued \in 0..MaxLease
    /\ circulating \in SUBSET Notices

    /\ holding = [t \in Teams |-> NoGrant]

Grant(t, s) ==

    /\ issued < MaxLease
    /\ issued' = issued + 1
    /\ onSlot' = [onSlot EXCEPT ![s] = issued + 1]
    /\ circulating' = circulating \cup {[to |-> t, slot |-> s, id |-> issued + 1]}

\* past is a leftover, however plausible it looks.

    /\ holding[n.to] = NoGrant
    /\ onSlot[n.slot] = n.id
    /\ holding' = [holding EXCEPT ![n.to] = [slot |-> n.slot, id |-> n.id]]

    \/ \E s \in Slots : Pull(s)
    \/ Renumber

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A print shop job spooler burns jobs onto printing plates. Burning is irreversible: the plate is
etched for that job and can never carry another, and the job can never be burned again. The
spooler keeps both halves of that pairing -- the plate a job was burned onto, and the job a
plate was used for -- and a job burned a second time would leave its first plate recorded
against it while the job itself pointed at the second.

Burning goes through optimistic locking. An operator stages the job and plate it intends to
pair, together with the job board's version as it read it. The staging is carried out only if
that version is still the board's version, the job is still unburned, the plate is still
unused, the number of plates in use is below the shop's current plate limit, and the version
numbering has room. Otherwise the staging is thrown away and the operator starts over.

The plate limit is set at runtime and the shop foreman may retune it up or down at any time,
including below the number of plates already in use, in which case nothing more is burned until
the count is back below the limit.

The spooler behaves as follows. An operator with nothing staged may stage an unburned job
against an unused plate, recording the board's version. An operator may carry out its staging
when all of the tests above pass, which burns the job onto the plate, records the pairing both
ways and moves the version on. A staging that fails any test is thrown away and the operator
starts over. The foreman may retune the plate limit to any value in the shop's permitted range.
When the version numbering is spent it is reindexed to the start, which also throws away every
staging.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every plate that has been used is the very plate its job records being burned
onto, so the irreversible burn happens at most once per job.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every staging an operator makes is eventually cleared.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

vars == <<burnedOn, usedBy, version, staged, limit>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ burnedOn \in [Jobs -> {NoPlate} \cup Plates]
    /\ usedBy \in [Plates -> {NoJob} \cup Jobs]
    /\ version \in 0..MaxVersion
    /\ staged \in [Operators -> {NoStage} \cup Stagings]
    /\ limit \in MinLimit..MaxLimit

Init ==
    /\ burnedOn = [j \in Jobs |-> NoPlate]
    /\ usedBy = [p \in Plates |-> NoJob]
    /\ version = 0
    /\ staged = [o \in Operators |-> NoStage]
    /\ limit = MinLimit

InUse == Cardinality({p \in Plates : usedBy[p] # NoJob})

Stage(o, j, p) ==
    /\ staged[o] = NoStage
    /\ burnedOn[j] = NoPlate
    /\ usedBy[p] = NoJob
    /\ staged' = [staged EXCEPT ![o] = [job |-> j, plate |-> p, base |-> version]]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<burnedOn, usedBy, version, limit>>

\* The version test is what stops two operators staging against the same board
\* and both burning; the limit test is the shop's current plate ceiling.
Ready(o) ==
    /\ staged[o].base = version
    /\ burnedOn[staged[o].job] = NoPlate
    /\ usedBy[staged[o].plate] = NoJob
    /\ InUse < limit
    /\ version < MaxVersion

Burn(o) ==
    /\ staged[o] # NoStage
    /\ Ready(o)

    /\ usedBy' = [usedBy EXCEPT ![staged[o].plate] = staged[o].job]
    /\ version' = version + 1
    /\ staged' = [staged EXCEPT ![o] = NoStage]
    /\ UNCHANGED limit

StartOver(o) ==
    /\ staged[o] # NoStage
    /\ ~Ready(o)
    /\ staged' = [staged EXCEPT ![o] = NoStage]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<burnedOn, usedBy, version, limit>>

\* count has come back under the limit.
Retune(v) ==

    /\ limit' = v
    /\ UNCHANGED <<burnedOn, usedBy, version, staged>>

Reindex ==

    /\ version' = 0
    /\ staged' = [o \in Operators |-> NoStage]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<burnedOn, usedBy, limit>>

    \/ \E o \in Operators : Settle(o)
    \/ \E v \in MinLimit..MaxLimit : Retune(v)
    \/ Reindex

BurnedAtMostOnce ==
    \A p \in Plates : usedBy[p] # NoJob => burnedOn[usedBy[p]] = p

EveryStagingClears ==

<|start|>user<|message|>Write a TLA+ specification that implements EXACTLY the system described below, and a TLC .cfg to model-check it. The system's safety property described in the NL text must be captured as a real, non-trivial INVARIANT (not `Inv == TRUE`) in the .cfg.

Name the module `W4Od18m7p0t3`.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home door lock network has one programming mode on its master keypad that only a single
app session may be inside at a time. The right to be inside is held in a compare-and-swap
register carrying two things read together: who holds the mode, and a tag that moves on every
time the register changes. An app reads the pair, and later swaps itself in only if the tag it
read is still the register's tag and the read showed the mode unheld. Because every change moves
the tag, a read taken before somebody else's change can never pass that test.

Apps can be slow but never fail. An app may sit on a read for arbitrarily long before trying to
swap, which is exactly why the tag rather than the read's own picture of the holder is what the
swap is judged on. An app whose read has gone stale abandons it and reads again.

The network behaves as follows. An app may read the register, recording both the holder it saw
and the tag it saw. An app holding a read that showed the mode unheld, whose tag is still the
register's tag and while the tag numbering has room, may swap itself in: it becomes the holder,
the tag moves on, and the app records the tag it entered under. An app inside the mode may leave
while the tag numbering has room, which clears the holder and moves the tag on. An app holding a
read whose tag is no longer the register's tag abandons that read. When the tag numbering is
spent, the mode is unheld and nobody is inside, the register may be resealed: the tag returns to
zero and every outstanding read is thrown away, so no read survives the reseal to be mistaken
for a current one.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every app inside the programming mode is the register's recorded holder and
entered under the tag the register still carries, so two apps can never be inside it at once.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

\* which is what makes the tag a sound test on the pair.
Reads == [who : {NoOne} \cup Apps, tag : 0..MaxTag]

VARIABLES holder, tag, inside, seen

vars == <<holder, tag, inside, seen>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ holder \in {NoOne} \cup Apps
    /\ tag \in 0..MaxTag
    /\ inside \in [Apps -> {NoTag} \cup (0..MaxTag)]
    /\ seen \in [Apps -> {NoRead} \cup Reads]

Init ==
    /\ holder = NoOne
    /\ tag = 0
    /\ inside = [a \in Apps |-> NoTag]
    /\ seen = [a \in Apps |-> NoRead]

Read(a) ==
    /\ seen' = [seen EXCEPT ![a] = [who |-> holder, tag |-> tag]]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<holder, tag, inside>>

\* The swap is judged on the tag, not on the picture of the holder the read
\* happened to carry; a slow app's read fails here rather than getting in.
SwapIn(a) ==
    /\ seen[a] # NoRead
    /\ seen[a].tag = tag
    /\ seen[a].who = NoOne
    /\ tag < MaxTag
    /\ holder' = a
    /\ tag' = tag + 1
    /\ inside' = [inside EXCEPT ![a] = tag + 1]
    /\ seen' = [seen EXCEPT ![a] = NoRead]

Leave(a) ==
    /\ inside[a] # NoTag
    /\ tag < MaxTag
    /\ holder' = NoOne
    /\ tag' = tag + 1
    /\ inside' = [inside EXCEPT ![a] = NoTag]
    /\ UNCHANGED seen

Abandon(a) ==
    /\ seen[a] # NoRead
    /\ seen[a].tag # tag
    /\ seen' = [seen EXCEPT ![a] = NoRead]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<holder, tag, inside>>

Reseal ==

    /\ holder = NoOne
    /\ \A a \in Apps : inside[a] = NoTag
    /\ tag' = 0
    /\ seen' = [a \in Apps |-> NoRead]

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An airport runs two independent baggage routers, one per terminal, that share a single pool of
loading carts. A cart is taken by holding a lease on it, and a lease carries a deadline on the
shift clock; a terminal may hold at most one cart lease across all of its loaders at a time, so
neither terminal can corner the pool.

Dispatching a bag to a flight is irreversible: the bag goes onto that flight's manifest and its
own record is stamped with the flight, and it can never be dispatched again. The manifest and the
bag's own stamp are the two halves that keep this honest -- a bag dispatched a second time would
be left sitting on the first flight's manifest while its stamp named the second.

The routers behave as follows. A loader may be granted a lease on a free cart, provided no loader
on its terminal already holds one and the lease deadline would fall inside the shift; the deadline
is set a fixed span ahead of the clock. A loader holding a cart lease whose deadline is still
ahead of the clock may dispatch a bag that has never been dispatched to a flight, which stamps the
bag with the flight and puts it on that flight's manifest. A loader holding a cart lease may return
the cart to the pool. The clock may tick. A cart whose lease deadline has been reached may be
reclaimed into the pool. When the shift clock has run out and no cart is leased, a fresh shift
begins with the clock back at the start.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every bag on a flight's manifest is stamped with that very flight, so the
irreversible dispatch happens at most once per bag.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every leased cart is eventually returned to the pool.

CONSTANTS TerminalA, TerminalB, Carts, Bags, Flights, ShiftLength, Span, NoOne, NotSent

Loaders == TerminalA \cup TerminalB

\* Which terminal a loader belongs to decides whether the shared pool already
\* owes that terminal a cart.
SideOf(l) == IF l \in TerminalA THEN TerminalA ELSE TerminalB

VARIABLES stamp, manifest, leaseOf, deadline, clock

vars == <<stamp, manifest, leaseOf, deadline, clock>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ stamp \in [Bags -> {NotSent} \cup Flights]
    /\ manifest \in [Flights -> SUBSET Bags]
    /\ leaseOf \in [Carts -> {NoOne} \cup Loaders]
    /\ deadline \in [Carts -> 0..ShiftLength]
    /\ clock \in 0..ShiftLength

Init ==
    /\ stamp = [b \in Bags |-> NotSent]
    /\ manifest = [f \in Flights |-> {}]
    /\ leaseOf = [c \in Carts |-> NoOne]
    /\ deadline = [c \in Carts |-> 0]
    /\ clock = 0

GrantLease(l, c) ==
    /\ leaseOf[c] = NoOne
    /\ \A x \in SideOf(l) : \A d \in Carts : leaseOf[d] # x
    /\ clock + Span <= ShiftLength
    /\ leaseOf' = [leaseOf EXCEPT ![c] = l]
    /\ deadline' = [deadline EXCEPT ![c] = clock + Span]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<stamp, manifest, clock>>

\* Both halves of the record are written together; the bag can never come back.
Dispatch(l, c, b, f) ==
    /\ leaseOf[c] = l
    /\ deadline[c] > clock
    /\ stamp[b] = NotSent
    /\ stamp' = [stamp EXCEPT ![b] = f]
    /\ manifest' = [manifest EXCEPT ![f] = @ \cup {b}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<leaseOf, deadline, clock>>

ReturnCart(c) ==
    /\ leaseOf[c] # NoOne
    /\ leaseOf' = [leaseOf EXCEPT ![c] = NoOne]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<stamp, manifest, deadline, clock>>

Reclaim(c) ==
    /\ leaseOf[c] # NoOne
    /\ deadline[c] <= clock
    /\ leaseOf' = [leaseOf EXCEPT ![c] = NoOne]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<stamp, manifest, deadline, clock>>

Tick ==
    /\ clock < ShiftLength
    /\ clock' = clock + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<stamp, manifest, leaseOf, deadline>>

NewShift ==

    /\ \A c \in Carts : leaseOf[c] = NoOne

EveryLeasedCartComesBack ==

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A print shop runs two independent job spoolers that draw press slots from one shared pool. The
pool has a capacity that is smaller than the number of slots on the floor: only so many slots may
be claimed at once across both spoolers together, whatever either of them would like.

The pool is guarded by a compare-and-swap register. A spooler reads the register, taking both the
tag it carries and the set of slots that were free at that moment, and later claims a slot only if
the tag it read is still the register's tag. Every claim and every release moves the tag on, so a
read taken before somebody else's change cannot pass. The claim is judged against what the read
saw, not against the live pool -- that is the point of the tag test, since a stale read would show
the pool emptier than it is. The register serves one read at a time.

The shop behaves as follows. A spooler may read the register when no read is outstanding anywhere,
recording the tag and the free set it saw. A spooler holding a read whose tag is still the
register's tag may claim a slot that its read showed free, provided its read also showed the pool
below capacity and the tag numbering has room; claiming records the slot against that spooler and
moves the tag on. A spooler may release a slot it has claimed, which moves the tag on. A spooler
holding a read whose tag is no longer current abandons it, and so does one holding a read taken
once the tag numbering is spent, since no claim can be made against it. When the tag numbering is spent and no
read is outstanding, the register is resealed and the tag returns to zero.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The slots claimed by the two spoolers together never number more than the pool's
capacity.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

    /\ tag \in 0..MaxTag
    /\ seenTag \in [Spoolers -> {NoTag} \cup (0..MaxTag)]
    /\ seenFree \in [Spoolers -> SUBSET Slots]

Init ==
    /\ claimed = [s \in Spoolers |-> {}]
    /\ tag = 0
    /\ seenTag = [s \in Spoolers |-> NoTag]
    /\ seenFree = [s \in Spoolers |-> Slots]

Taken == UNION {claimed[s] : s \in Spoolers}

\* The register serves one read at a time.
Read(s) ==
    /\ \A x \in Spoolers : seenTag[x] = NoTag
    /\ seenTag' = [seenTag EXCEPT ![s] = tag]
    /\ seenFree' = [seenFree EXCEPT ![s] = Slots \ Taken]

\* The claim is judged against what the read saw; the tag test is what makes that
\* picture trustworthy, since a stale one would show the pool emptier than it is.

    /\ Cardinality(Slots \ seenFree[s]) < PoolSize

    /\ tag' = 0

long as the numbering has room. Any surviving member may regenerate the token when no live member
is seated on the current generation. Any member may fail silently, so long as not every member has

\* stall the whole book.

    /\ gen \in 1..MaxGen

    /\ gen = 1
    /\ seat = [m \in Members |-> IF m = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0]
    /\ dead = {}

Resting == UNION {book[l] : l \in Levels}

Seated(m) == m \notin dead /\ seat[m] = gen

\* Nobody alive is seated on the current generation: the ring is stranded.
Stranded == \A m \in Members : seat[m] = gen => m \in dead

Rest(m, l, o) ==

    /\ o \notin Resting
    /\ Cardinality(book[l]) < Depth
    /\ book' = [book EXCEPT ![l] = @ \cup {o}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<gen, seat, dead>>

Pull(m, l, o) ==

    /\ o \in book[l]
    /\ book' = [book EXCEPT ![l] = @ \ {o}]

    /\ gen < MaxGen
    /\ gen' = gen + 1
    /\ seat' = [seat EXCEPT ![m] = 0, ![Onward(m, k)] = gen + 1]

    /\ m \notin dead
    /\ gen < MaxGen
    /\ gen' = gen + 1
    /\ seat' = [seat EXCEPT ![m] = gen + 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<book, dead>>

Fail(m) ==

    /\ Cardinality(dead) < Cardinality(Members) - 1
    /\ dead' = dead \cup {m}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<book, gen, seat>>

Recover(m) ==

    /\ dead' = dead \ {m}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<book, gen, seat>>

A warehouse robot fleet keeps a shared assignment record: for each aisle, which robot is working
it and a stamp that moves on every time that aisle's entry changes. Robots update the record with
a compare-and-swap: a robot reads one aisle's entry, taking the stamp it saw, and later writes only
if that stamp is still the aisle's stamp. An aisle's entry may only be written by the robot that
already owns it or by anyone when it is unowned, so a robot's own write is the only thing that can
supersede its own write.

Robots can be slow but never fail. A robot may sit on a read for arbitrarily long before trying to
write, which is exactly why the stamp rather than the robot's memory of the entry is what the write
is judged on. A read that can no longer be written is abandoned and the robot reads again.

When a robot writes, it remembers the aisle and the stamp its write produced, and that memory is
what it relies on afterwards.

The fleet behaves as follows. A robot may read any aisle's entry, recording the aisle and the stamp
it saw. A robot holding a read may write when the aisle's stamp is still the one it read, the aisle
is either unowned or already its own, and the stamp numbering has room; writing takes ownership,
moves the aisle's stamp on and records the aisle and new stamp as the robot's own. A robot holding a
read it cannot write abandons it. A robot may give up an aisle it owns, which leaves the aisle
unowned, moves its stamp on and clears that robot's memory of it. When the stamp numbering is spent
the record is reindexed: every stamp returns to zero, every aisle is left unowned, and every
memory and outstanding read is cleared.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every robot that remembers writing an aisle finds that aisle still carrying
exactly the stamp its write produced, so no robot's write is ever silently overwritten.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every read a robot takes is eventually resolved, leaving it holding no read.

A power-grid load shedder writes every shed instruction into a shared append-only dispatch log.
Control desks append under optimistic locking: a desk prepares an instruction together with the log
length it read, and the append lands only if the log is still that length. If another desk got
there first the log has grown, the prepared instruction is thrown away, and the desk starts again.
When an append lands, the desk is told the index its entry occupies, and that index is what it
relies on from then on.

Desks can be slow but never fail. A prepared instruction may sit for arbitrarily long before the
desk tries to append it, which is exactly why the length the desk read, rather than the desk's own
sense of where the log stood, is what the append is judged on.

Each desk also carries a running total of megawatts it has shed, capped by its allowance; shed load
may be restored one megawatt at a time. When the log has run to its full length and no desk has an
instruction prepared, the log is rolled: it is emptied and every index a desk was told is cleared,
since those indices mean nothing against a fresh log.

The shedder behaves as follows. A desk with nothing prepared may prepare an instruction for a number
of megawatts, recording the log's current length. A desk may append its prepared instruction when
the log is still that length, the log has room, and its running total would stay within its
allowance; appending adds its entry to the end of the log, tells the desk the index it landed at,
and raises its running total. A prepared instruction failing any of those tests is thrown away and
the desk starts again. A desk may restore a megawatt of shed load. When the log is full and nothing
is prepared anywhere, the log may be rolled.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a desk has been told an index for its entry, the log still runs at least
that far and that index still holds that desk's entry, so no landed append is ever overwritten or
lost.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A hospital operating-room scheduler divides a fixed daily budget of theatre minutes. Minutes are
never created or destroyed: at every moment the budget is accounted for as minutes still in the
unallocated pool, minutes allotted to a theatre, and minutes travelling with a grant that has been
issued but not yet applied.

Grants are issued and applied under optimistic locking on the pool. A grant carries the pool
version it was issued against, and applying it requires that version still to be the pool's version;
grants circulate and are applied out of order, so a grant issued earlier may well be overtaken.
A grant that can no longer be applied is returned, and its minutes go straight back into the pool
rather than evaporating in transit.

The scheduler behaves as follows. A grant naming a theatre and a number of minutes may be issued
against the pool's current version while the pool holds at least that many minutes and the version
numbering has room; issuing takes the minutes out of the pool, puts the grant into circulation and
moves the version on. A circulating grant whose version is still the pool's version may be applied
while the numbering has room, which adds its minutes to that theatre's allotment and moves the
version on. A circulating grant whose version is no longer the pool's, or any circulating grant once
the numbering is spent, is returned, putting its minutes back in the pool. A theatre may release
minutes from its allotment back to the pool. When the numbering is spent and nothing is in
circulation, the version is reindexed to the start.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The minutes in the pool, the minutes allotted across the theatres and the minutes
travelling with circulating grants always add up to exactly the day's budget, so no theatre minute
is ever conjured up or lost in transit.

\* has to be counted alongside what is banked.
Grants == [to : Theatres, mins : 1..MaxGrant, base : 0..MaxVersion]

VARIABLES pool, allotted, circulating, version

vars == <<pool, allotted, circulating, version>>

RECURSIVE Banked(_)
Banked(S) ==
    IF S = {} THEN 0
    ELSE LET t == CHOOSE x \in S : TRUE IN allotted[t] + Banked(S \ {t})

RECURSIVE Carried(_)
Carried(S) ==
    IF S = {} THEN 0
    ELSE LET g == CHOOSE x \in S : TRUE IN g.mins + Carried(S \ {g})

    /\ circulating = {}

Issue(g) ==

    /\ g.base = version
    /\ pool >= g.mins
    /\ version < MaxVersion

    /\ circulating' = circulating \cup {g}
    /\ version' = version + 1

    /\ version < MaxVersion

Return(g) ==

    /\ circulating' = circulating \ {g}

A library's rare-books reading room is entered with a single key that one patron at a time may
hold. The key is held on a lease with a countdown rather than a wall clock: a grant sets the

be inside the room while it holds the key and the countdown has not run out; when the countdown
reaches zero anyone inside is shown out there and then, and the lapsed lease is later cleared so

A lease may be renewed back to its full span, but only a fixed number of times per grant, so a
patron cannot sit on the key indefinitely.

The head librarian holds a privileged override and may, a bounded number of times per day, take
the key off whoever has it and hand it straight to another patron. The override shows the room out
in the same movement, sets the new lease to its full span and returns the renewal allowance,
because a patron left inside under a lease that has just changed hands would be exactly the
overlap the key exists to prevent.

desk, setting the countdown to its full span and returning the renewal allowance. The patron
holding the key with countdown left may go into the room. A patron inside may come out. The
holder's lease may be renewed to its full span while the countdown has not run out and the renewal
allowance is not spent. The timer may tick, taking one off the countdown and showing the room out
if that brings it to zero. A lapsed lease whose countdown has run out may be cleared, returning the
key to the desk. The head librarian may override, taking the key from its holder and handing it to
another patron.

countdown has not run out, so two patrons are never inside at once.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Whenever the key is out with a patron, it eventually comes back to the desk.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A bank's interbank settlement batch keeps a shared record of settled amounts per account. Amounts
only ever rise: a bank raises a figure in its own working copy of the whole record and later posts
that copy over the shared record. Because a post replaces the record wholesale, a copy taken before
somebody else's post would carry away every figure raised in between.

The batch is organised by epochs. Taking a copy stamps it with the epoch in force at that moment,
and a post is accepted only from a copy stamped with the epoch still in force. Every post itself
moves the batch to the next epoch, so at most one post can ever be made from any one epoch's copies;
a reconfiguration of the batch likewise moves the epoch on. Banks can be slow but never fail, so a
bank may go on raising figures in a copy stamped with an epoch that has long since passed, and its
post will simply not be accepted.

When a post is accepted the posting bank is acknowledged for one account and the figure its copy
carried for it.

The batch behaves as follows. A bank may take a fresh copy of the record, stamped with the epoch in
force. A bank may raise any account's figure in its own copy above what that copy holds, whether or
not its stamp is current. A bank whose copy is stamped with the epoch in force may post it over the
record while the epoch numbering has room, which moves the epoch on, re-stamps and refreshes that
bank's copy, and acknowledges the bank for one account and the figure it posted. The batch may be
reconfigured, moving the epoch on. When the epoch numbering is spent it is renumbered from the
start and every copy's stamp is voided.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every acknowledgement a bank holds is still honoured by the record -- the account
it names stands at least at the figure acknowledged -- so no settled figure is ever carried away by
a later post.

Acks == [acct : Accounts, figure : 0..MaxFigure]

VARIABLES settled, working, stamp, acked, epoch

vars == <<settled, working, stamp, acked, epoch>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ settled \in Copies
    /\ working \in [Banks -> Copies]
    /\ stamp \in [Banks -> 0..MaxEpoch]
    /\ acked \in [Banks -> {NoAck} \cup Acks]
    /\ epoch \in 1..MaxEpoch

Init ==

    /\ working = [b \in Banks |-> [a \in Accounts |-> 0]]
    /\ stamp = [b \in Banks |-> 0]
    /\ acked = [b \in Banks |-> NoAck]

\* A slow bank goes on raising figures in a copy whose stamp has long passed.
Raise(b, a, v) ==

\* Every post moves the epoch on, so no two posts can be made from copies taken

Post(b, a) ==

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A library reservation system has one returns chute that a single branch may feed at a time. Which
branches are eligible is settled by an epoch-numbered reconfiguration, and the chute is handed out
by admitting one branch at a time as its recorded holder. A reconfiguration is only allowed while
the chute has no holder, so an eligibility change can never strip the branch that is currently
holding it.

The chute empties into a bin whose capacity is set at runtime, and the depot may retune that
capacity up or down at any moment. Feeding is only possible while the bin still has room: a branch
that fills the bin with its last item is taken off the chute there and then, and a retune that
leaves the bin with no room takes off whoever is feeding in the same movement. The bin may be
emptied one item at a time.

The system behaves as follows. An eligible branch may be admitted as the chute's holder while the
chute is unheld and the bin has room. The holder may start feeding while the bin has room. A branch
that is feeding may push an item into the bin while the bin has room, and if that item fills the bin
the chute is cleared. A branch that is feeding may stop. A holder that is not feeding may give the
chute up. The bin may be emptied by one item. The depot may retune the bin capacity to any value in
its permitted range, clearing the chute if the new capacity leaves no room. The eligible set may be
reconfigured to any different set while the chute is unheld, which takes the system to the next
epoch. When the epoch numbering is spent and the chute is unheld, the numbering restarts.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every branch feeding the chute is the chute's recorded holder and the bin still has
room, so two branches can never be feeding it at once.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Whenever the chute has a holder, it is eventually unheld again.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

    /\ feeding \in SUBSET Branches

    /\ binCap \in MinBin..MaxBin

    /\ eligible = Branches
    /\ holder = NoOne
    /\ feeding = {}
    /\ bin = 0
    /\ binCap = MinBin

Admit(b) ==
    /\ b \in eligible
    /\ holder = NoOne
    /\ bin < binCap
    /\ holder' = b

Start(b) ==

    /\ b \notin feeding
    /\ bin < binCap

Push(b) ==

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An elevator bank in a skyscraper limits how many people each car may be committed to. A car's
commitment is everything it owes space to: passengers holding a reservation for it and passengers
already aboard it. That total may never exceed the car's capacity.

Reservations are made by a two-phase commit across the bank's participants -- the car controllers
and the lobby panels. A ballot is opened naming one car, participants vote on it, and the
reservation is only taken once a quorum has voted and the car still has room. A participant can
fail silently, so the bank cannot wait for everybody and works to a quorum instead; a ballot that
stalls is simply abandoned and can be opened again.

The bank behaves as follows. A ballot may be opened for a car that still has room, when no ballot
is open, which clears the vote tally. A live participant that has not yet voted on the open ballot
may vote. The open ballot may be taken once a quorum has voted and the named car still has room,
which adds a reservation to that car. The open ballot may be abandoned at any time. A passenger
holding a reservation for a car may board it, which turns the reservation into an occupancy without
changing what the car is committed to. A reservation may lapse, freeing the commitment. A passenger
aboard a car may get out. A participant may fail silently, so long as not all of them have, and a
failed participant may come back.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every car, the reservations held for it plus the passengers already aboard it
never exceed that car's capacity.

    /\ ballot \in {NoBallot} \cup Ballots
    /\ votes \in SUBSET Participants
    /\ dead \in SUBSET Participants

Init ==

    /\ aboard = [c \in Cars |-> 0]
    /\ ballot = NoBallot
    /\ votes = {}
    /\ dead = {}

Open(c) ==

    /\ Committed(c) < Capacity
    /\ ballot' = [car |-> c]
    /\ votes' = {}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<reserved, aboard, dead>>

Vote(p) ==

    /\ p \notin dead
    /\ p \notin votes
    /\ votes' = votes \cup {p}

\* The room test is made again at commit time, not just when the ballot opened.
Take ==
    /\ ballot # NoBallot
    /\ Cardinality(votes) >= Quorum
    /\ Committed(ballot.car) < Capacity
    /\ reserved' = [reserved EXCEPT ![ballot.car] = @ + 1]
    /\ ballot' = NoBallot
    /\ votes' = {}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<aboard, dead>>

Abandon ==

    /\ ballot' = NoBallot
    /\ votes' = {}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<reserved, aboard, dead>>

    /\ aboard' = [aboard EXCEPT ![c] = @ + 1]

    /\ reserved[c] > 0
    /\ reserved' = [reserved EXCEPT ![c] = @ - 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<aboard, ballot, votes, dead>>

GetOut(c) ==
    /\ aboard[c] > 0
    /\ aboard' = [aboard EXCEPT ![c] = @ - 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<reserved, ballot, votes, dead>>

    /\ p \notin dead
    /\ Cardinality(dead) < Cardinality(Participants) - 1
    /\ dead' = dead \cup {p}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<reserved, aboard, ballot, votes>>

    /\ p \in dead

    /\ UNCHANGED <<reserved, aboard, ballot, votes>>

    \/ \E p \in Participants : Vote(p) \/ Fail(p) \/ Recover(p)
    \/ Take
    \/ Abandon

tests is discarded. The set of cabins in service may be reconfigured to any different set, which

A blood-bank inventory tracker hands transfusion slots to wards as leases. The pairing is recorded
twice -- each slot records the ward holding it, and each ward records the slot it holds -- and those
two records must mirror one another, since a slot handed to a second ward would leave the first
ward still pointing at a slot that now records somebody else.

Every lease carries a deadline on the bank's clock. A lease whose deadline has been reached is
expired and may be cleared, which frees the slot and clears the ward's record together. The
haematology consultant holds a privileged override and may, a bounded number of times per cycle,
take a slot whose lease has expired and hand it straight to another ward; the override clears the
previous holder's record in the same movement, because leaving it pointing at the slot is precisely
the double allocation the two records exist to rule out. The override may not touch a lease that is
still live.

The tracker behaves as follows. A ward holding no slot may be assigned a free slot, provided the new
deadline would fall inside the cycle; the deadline is set a fixed span ahead of the clock. A ward
holding a slot may give it back, freeing the slot. An expired lease may be cleared, freeing the slot
and the ward's record. The consultant may override an expired lease in favour of a ward holding no
slot, clearing the previous holder's record and setting a fresh deadline. The clock may tick. When
the cycle clock has run out and no slot is held, a fresh cycle begins with the clock back at the
start.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every ward that records holding a slot is the ward that slot records as its holder,
so a slot is never allocated to two wards at once.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every expired lease is eventually cleared, freeing its slot.

CONSTANTS Wards, Slots, Cycle, Span, MaxOverrides, NoWard, NoSlot

VARIABLES holder, slotOf, deadline, clock, overrides

vars == <<holder, slotOf, deadline, clock, overrides>>

TypeOK ==
    /\ holder \in [Slots -> {NoWard} \cup Wards]
    /\ slotOf \in [Wards -> {NoSlot} \cup Slots]
    /\ deadline \in [Slots -> 0..Cycle]
    /\ clock \in 0..Cycle
    /\ overrides \in 0..MaxOverrides

Init ==
    /\ holder = [s \in Slots |-> NoWard]
    /\ slotOf = [w \in Wards |-> NoSlot]
    /\ deadline = [s \in Slots |-> 0]
    /\ clock = 0
    /\ overrides = 0

Assign(w, s) ==
    /\ holder[s] = NoWard
    /\ slotOf[w] = NoSlot
    /\ clock + Span <= Cycle
    /\ holder' = [holder EXCEPT ![s] = w]
    /\ slotOf' = [slotOf EXCEPT ![w] = s]
    /\ deadline' = [deadline EXCEPT ![s] = clock + Span]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, overrides>>

GiveBack(w) ==
    /\ slotOf[w] # NoSlot
    /\ holder' = [holder EXCEPT ![slotOf[w]] = NoWard]
    /\ deadline' = [deadline EXCEPT ![slotOf[w]] = 0]
    /\ slotOf' = [slotOf EXCEPT ![w] = NoSlot]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, overrides>>

Clear(s) ==
    /\ holder[s] # NoWard
    /\ deadline[s] <= clock
    /\ slotOf' = [w \in Wards |-> IF slotOf[w] = s THEN NoSlot ELSE slotOf[w]]
    /\ holder' = [holder EXCEPT ![s] = NoWard]
    /\ deadline' = [deadline EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, overrides>>

\* The override takes the previous holder's record with it; leaving it behind is
\* exactly the double allocation the two records rule out.
Override(w, s) ==
    /\ overrides < MaxOverrides
    /\ holder[s] # NoWard
    /\ deadline[s] <= clock
    /\ slotOf[w] = NoSlot
    /\ clock + Span <= Cycle
    /\ holder' = [holder EXCEPT ![s] = w]
    /\ slotOf' = [x \in Wards |->
                    IF x = w THEN s
                    ELSE IF slotOf[x] = s THEN NoSlot ELSE slotOf[x]]
    /\ deadline' = [deadline EXCEPT ![s] = clock + Span]
    /\ overrides' = overrides + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED clock

Tick ==
    /\ clock < Cycle
    /\ clock' = clock + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<holder, slotOf, deadline, overrides>>

NewCycle ==
    /\ clock = Cycle
    /\ \A s \in Slots : holder[s] = NoWard
    /\ clock' = 0
    /\ deadline' = [s \in Slots |-> 0]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<holder, slotOf, overrides>>

Clearing == \E s \in Slots : Clear(s)

Next ==
    \/ \E w \in Wards, s \in Slots : Assign(w, s) \/ Override(w, s)
    \/ \E w \in Wards : GiveBack(w)
    \/ Clearing
    \/ Tick
    \/ NewCycle

RecordsMirror ==
    \A w \in Wards : slotOf[w] # NoSlot => holder[slotOf[w]] = w

ExpiredLeasesAreCleared ==

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home door lock network keeps one shared configuration record that maps each lock to its current keypad-code generation number. A hub owns the record and stamps it with a version that advances by one every time a change is written. Because the radio link to the locks is slow, changes are not written directly: a phone app first reads the record, computes the new generation number for the lock it wants to change, and hands that change to the hub as a job. Each job therefore carries the lock it targets, the new generation number the app computed, and the record version the app read when it computed it.

The hub holds those jobs in a bounded work queue. The queue's admission limit is a live tuning parameter: a homeowner or an installer can raise it when the house is busy and lower it when the hub is thermally throttled, and the new limit takes effect immediately even if more jobs are already parked in the queue than the new limit allows. When a job arrives and the queue is already at its limit, the hub does not silently forget it and does not grow the queue; it applies backpressure, refusing the job outright and incrementing a shed counter that the app can read to learn it must retry.

The hub drains the queue from the front, one job at a time. Before writing a job it compares the version the job was computed against with the record's current version. If they match, the job is fresh: the hub writes the computed generation number into the record for that lock, advances the record version, and notes the value it just committed for that lock in a per-lock high-water mark. If they do not match, the record has moved on since the app read it, so the job is stale and the hub discards it from the front of the queue without writing anything; the app will observe the version change and recompute.

The full set of actions the hub network can take is: Submit, which places a fresh job on the queue while there is room under the current limit; Shed, which refuses an arriving job and bumps the shed counter when the queue is at its limit; Commit, which writes the front job when its base version matches the record version and advances both the record and the lock's high-water mark; Discard, which drops the front job when its base version is stale; and Retune, which changes the queue's admission limit at runtime to any value in the supported range.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every lock, the generation number currently stored in the shared record is exactly the highest generation number ever committed for that lock, so no committed change to a lock is ever clobbered by a job computed from an older view of the record.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

EXTENDS Naturals, Sequences

CONSTANTS Locks, MaxGen, MaxShed, MinLimit, MaxLimit

VARIABLES record, mark, version, queue, limit, shed

vars == <<record, mark, version, queue, limit, shed>>

\* A job is the app's read-modify-write intent: which lock, the generation it
\* computed, and the record version it read while computing.
Job == [lock: Locks, gen: 1..MaxGen, base: 0..MaxGen]

TypeOK ==
    /\ record \in [Locks -> 0..MaxGen]
    /\ mark \in [Locks -> 0..MaxGen]
    /\ version \in 0..MaxGen
    /\ queue \in Seq(Job)
    /\ limit \in MinLimit..MaxLimit
    /\ shed \in 0..MaxShed

Init ==
    /\ record = [l \in Locks |-> 0]
    /\ mark = [l \in Locks |-> 0]
    /\ version = 0
    /\ queue = <<>>
    /\ limit = MinLimit
    /\ shed = 0

Fresh(l) == [lock |-> l, gen |-> record[l] + 1, base |-> version]

Submit(l) ==
    /\ Len(queue) < limit
    /\ record[l] < MaxGen
    /\ queue' = Append(queue, Fresh(l))
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, mark, version, limit, shed>>

\* Backpressure: a job arriving at a full queue is refused, never buffered.
Shed ==
    /\ Len(queue) >= limit
    /\ shed < MaxShed
    /\ shed' = shed + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, mark, version, queue, limit>>

Commit ==
    /\ queue # <<>>
    /\ Head(queue).base = version
    /\ LET j == Head(queue) IN
        /\ record' = [record EXCEPT ![j.lock] = j.gen]
        /\ mark' = [mark EXCEPT ![j.lock] = IF j.gen > mark[j.lock]
                                            THEN j.gen ELSE mark[j.lock]]
    /\ version' = version + 1
    /\ queue' = Tail(queue)
    /\ UNCHANGED <<limit, shed>>

\* The front job was computed against a record version that has since moved on.
Discard ==
    /\ queue # <<>>
    /\ Head(queue).base # version
    /\ queue' = Tail(queue)
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, mark, version, limit, shed>>

\* The admission limit is retuned live and may drop below the current backlog.
Retune ==
    /\ \E n \in MinLimit..MaxLimit : limit' = n
    /\ UNCHANGED <<record, mark, version, queue, shed>>

Next == \/ \E l \in Locks : Submit(l)
        \/ Shed \/ Commit \/ Discard \/ Retune

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* No lost update: the live value never regresses below one already committed.
NoLostUpdate == \A l \in Locks : record[l] = mark[l]

StateBound == version <= MaxGen

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An air-traffic runway allocator hands departure slots to flights. Slots are grouped by sector, and the allocator protects them with a two-level scheme: a flight must first take the sector's coarse latch, and only then may it take a specific slot inside that sector. Taking the coarse latch is what lets a flight trust what it sees, because at the moment it takes the latch the allocator hands it a snapshot listing exactly which slots in that sector were unassigned. The flight then picks a slot out of that snapshot without re-checking the board; the whole point of the coarse latch is that nobody else can be picking in that sector at the same time, so the snapshot cannot go stale underneath it.

Slot requests reach the allocator over a datalink that does not preserve order. Requests sit in the allocator's pending pool and are picked up in whatever order the allocator gets to them, so a request filed later may well be latched earlier.

Taking a slot ends the coarse phase: as the flight records the slot as its own, it drops the sector latch so other flights can proceed. If the snapshot the flight received was empty, the sector was full when it latched, and the flight drops the latch and refiles its request into the pending pool to try again later. A flight that already holds a slot never files a new request and never takes a latch; it releases its slot when it departs, which returns the slot to the unassigned pool.

The full set of actions is: File, in which a flight with no slot and no request outstanding puts a request for a sector into the pending pool; Latch, in which the allocator picks any pending request whose sector is unlatched, gives that flight the coarse latch, and hands it a snapshot of the sector's currently unassigned slots; Take, in which a latched flight records one slot from its snapshot as its own and simultaneously drops the sector latch; Release, in which a flight holding a slot departs and returns the slot to the unassigned pool; and Refile, in which a latched flight whose snapshot is empty drops the latch and puts its request back into the pending pool.

A stock exchange runs an opening auction. Each price level in the opening book has exactly one crossing slot, and a member firm that wants to cross at a level must first be granted that level's slot. Because the book is rebuilt continuously right up to the cross, the exchange guards it with two nested locks: a member must first take the whole-book lock, and only while holding it may it take the slot at a single price level. Taking the level slot immediately releases the book lock, so the coarse lock is held only for the instant it takes to pick a level.

Once a firm holds a level's slot it may begin executing at that level, which is the irreversible part: matching engines start printing the cross. Executing finishes by printing the last lot, which both ends the execution and returns the level's slot to the exchange for the next auction phase.

Member firms can crash silently. A crashed firm stops taking locks, stops executing, and sends no notice; the exchange learns nothing directly. What the exchange has instead is a supervisor that may declare any member suspect at any time, on nothing more than a hunch about latency. Once a member is suspect the supervisor may pull back the book lock it holds, and may pull back a level slot it holds — but only a level slot at which the member has not started executing. A level with an execution in progress is never pulled back on suspicion alone, because the supervisor cannot tell a slow firm from a dead one and printing the same level twice would be a market-integrity failure. A firm that was wrongly declared suspect can come back: it reconnects, the supervisor clears the suspicion, and it resumes.

A clearing bank posts interbank settlement batches through a single posting engine. The engine is the critical resource: it holds the ledger open, applies a batch's debits and credits, and closes the ledger again, and it can only ever be working one batch at a time. A batch that is being posted is said to be in the window, and the engine records which batch is in its window.

Batches do not go straight to the engine. They are admitted into a bounded intake queue and posted strictly in the order they were admitted, oldest first, so an older batch is never overtaken by a newer one. The queue's admission depth is a live operational parameter: the operations desk raises it when the correspondent banks are sending heavily and lowers it when the ledger is running close to its cut-off, and the change takes effect on the next admission decision.

Backpressure is explicit rather than silent. When a batch is presented and the queue already holds as many batches as the current admission depth allows, the batch is refused outright rather than buffered, and the submitting desk is told so. A refused batch is not lost: the desk can present it again later, when the depth may have been raised or the queue may have drained.

The full set of actions is: Admit, in which a freshly presented batch is placed at the back of the intake queue because the queue is below the current admission depth; Refuse, in which a freshly presented batch is rejected because the queue is already at the current admission depth; Represent, in which a refused batch is presented again as fresh; Begin, in which the idle engine takes the oldest queued batch into its window and starts posting it; Complete, in which the engine finishes the batch in its window, marks it posted, and goes idle again; and Retune, in which the operations desk changes the queue's admission depth to any value in the supported range.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A skyscraper is served by two independent elevator banks, a low-rise bank and a high-rise bank, each with its own dispatcher and its own schedule. What they are not independent about is standby hoist drives: the building keeps one shared pool of spare drive units in the machine room, and either bank can draw units out of that pool to bring extra cars into service. Drive units are physical objects. The building's engineer accounts for every one of them, and the total number in the building never changes on its own — a unit is either sitting in the pool, installed in one of the two banks, or in the middle of being moved.

Because the two banks would otherwise race each other for the same units, no bank may take units on its own authority. Each transfer is put to a panel of building controllers and needs a quorum of them to approve. A proposal names one bank and a number of units, and the units it asks for are pulled out of the pool the instant the proposal is filed and set aside in a staging cage, so that a second proposal cannot be written against units the first has already spoken for. Controllers then vote one at a time. When enough controllers have voted to reach quorum, the proposal commits: the staged units are installed in the named bank and the staging cage is emptied. Units also come back. When a bank takes a car out of service it returns drive units to the pool directly, which needs no vote, but it may only do so while no proposal is open.
