===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A subway signalling system must decide which train is given the movement authority for a particular track block. Handing out that authority is irreversible: the signal clears, the train commits to the block at line speed, and nothing the interlocking does afterwards can take it back. The decision is therefore not made by any single signalling node. It is made by a panel of interlocking nodes voting in numbered rounds, and a round only takes effect once a quorum of nodes has voted in it.

A round is opened by naming one train as that round's candidate. Rounds are opened one at a time and numbered in order. The rule that keeps the system honest is the carry-over rule: if any earlier round has already carried, a newly opened round is not free to name a different train — it must name the train that carried. Only when no round has carried yet is the choice open.

Nodes vote for the candidate of the round that is currently open, one vote per node per round, and only while that round has not yet carried. When the votes in the open round reach quorum, the round carries and the signal clears for that round's candidate.

One node can crash silently. It stops voting and gives no notice; the rest of the panel cannot distinguish it from a slow node, which is why the quorum is set below the panel size. A crashed node can later be restored by a technician on site, at which point it resumes voting. At most one node is ever down at a time, so a quorum of the remaining nodes is always reachable.

The full set of actions is: Open, in which the next round is opened naming a candidate train, subject to the carry-over rule; Vote, in which a live node casts its vote in the open round; Carry, in which the open round reaches quorum and carries, clearing the signal for its candidate; Crash, in which a node silently stops while every other node is still up; and Restore, in which the crashed node is brought back and resumes voting.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Any two rounds that have carried name the same train, so the block's movement authority is never irreversibly granted to two different trains.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Some round eventually carries, so the block's authority is eventually granted rather than left undecided.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A hospital keeps one shared operating-room day plan. The plan is not stored as a table that people overwrite; it is stored as an append-only revision journal, one entry per booking change, and every entry records which surgical team made the change, which room it concerns, and how many earlier entries that team believed already existed for that room. That last number is the whole point: a team must state what it thought it was building on.

Each room exposes a small compare-and-swap register holding the count of journal entries written for that room so far. Booking is a read-modify-write: a team first reads a room's register and prepares a draft change carrying the count it read; later it tries to swap the draft into the journal. The swap goes through only if the room's register still holds the count the draft was prepared against. If it does, the entry is appended and the room's register advances by one. If another team has booked that room in the meantime, the register has moved, the swap is refused, and the team throws the draft away and starts over from a fresh read.

The number of rooms actually open changes during the day. Theatre management opens or closes rooms as anaesthetic staff arrive or are pulled to emergencies, and the change takes effect immediately. A team may only read a register for a room that is currently open, and a team holding a draft for a room that has since been closed abandons that draft. A team holds at most one draft at a time. The journal for the day has a fixed maximum length; once it is full no further entries are appended.

The full set of actions is: Read, in which a team with no draft in hand reads an open room's register and prepares a draft carrying the count it read; Swap, in which a team's draft is appended to the journal because the room's register still matches the draft's count, advancing that register; Refuse, in which a team's draft is discarded because the room's register no longer matches; Abandon, in which a team discards a draft for a room that management has since closed; and Staff, in which management changes how many rooms are open.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every entry in the journal, the count the entry was built on is exactly the number of earlier journal entries for that same room, so no booking change is ever written on top of a room state it did not actually see.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A stock exchange runs its opening auction on a cross engine that must be driven by exactly one matching node. Driving the engine is the critical section: while a node is on the engine it is computing and printing the opening price, and a second node computing at the same time would produce two different opening prints for the same symbol.

Ownership of the engine is handed out as a lease rather than as a permanent assignment, because a matching node can go quiet without warning and the auction cannot wait for it. Nodes that want the engine put a bid for it into the registrar's request set. That set has no order to it — bids arrive over an unordered fabric, and the registrar picks whichever bid it happens to look at first, so a bid filed earlier may well be served later. The registrar grants a lease only when no lease is outstanding.

A lease is kept alive by heartbeats. The holder must renew within each renewal window; the window then lapses and must be renewed again. If the window lapses and the holder has not renewed, the registrar expires the lease, and expiring a lease also takes its holder off the cross engine in the same instant — that is what makes it safe to hand the engine to somebody else. A node steps onto the engine only while it actually holds a live lease, and it prints the opening cross from the engine, which ends its turn and gives the lease back.

The full set of actions is: Bid, in which a node without a lease adds itself to the registrar's unordered request set; Grant, in which the registrar picks any bid from that set and gives that node a lease, provided no lease is currently outstanding; Renew, in which the holder of a lease sends its heartbeat for the current renewal window; Lapse, in which the current renewal window closes and the heartbeat must be sent again; Mount, in which a node holding a live lease steps onto the cross engine; Print, in which a node on the engine computes and prints the opening cross, then steps off and gives up its lease; and Expire, in which the registrar reclaims a lease whose renewal window lapsed without a heartbeat, removing its holder from the engine at the same moment.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every node standing on the cross engine holds a live lease at that moment, and since the registrar never grants a second lease while one is outstanding, two nodes are never on the engine together.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: The opening cross is eventually printed, because leases keep being granted and a node that holds one repeatedly gets the chance to mount the engine and print.

A university runs two independent registration front ends against one shared seat pool for a capstone course: the student self-service portal and the advising office's override portal. The lease is time-bounded and lapses on its own. That is the awkward part, because a front end whose lease has lapsed does not find out at the moment it lapses — it goes on believing it is authorised until something tells it otherwise. The seat pool itself does the checking. It records the fencing number of every draw it accepts, and it refuses any draw whose number is not higher than the last number it accepted. A front end acting on a lapsed lease is therefore carrying an old number, and the pool turns it away rather than trusting it.

A front end uses its fencing number for a single draw: taking a seat consumes both the seat and the number. A front end that notices the lease is no longer held by it gives up its number without drawing.     /\ UNCHANGED <<holder, counter, carried, admitted>>

    /\ holder = NOBODY

Re-forming a lobby tears down its roster completely and advances its formation number, and it does this whether or not a client is sitting on that lobby's lock — the matchmaker will not let one client stall a whole region's matchmaking.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A print shop runs two spoolers — the sheet-fed spooler and the web spooler — that schedule jobs completely independently of one another. What ties them together is paper: both draw reams of the same house stock from a single store room, and the shop's stock control is only meaningful if reams are never conjured up and never quietly vanish. A ream is always in exactly one of three places: on the shelf in the store room, cut and set aside against one of the spoolers, or loaded into that spooler's press.

Neither spooler may take stock on its own say-so, because a spooler that grabs reams for a long run can starve the other one mid-shift. Instead each spooler's draw is put to the shift supervisors and needs a quorum of them to endorse it. The two spoolers can have draws in flight at the same time and are voted on separately — one spooler's pending draw does not block the other's.

A draw begins by setting reams aside: the reams come off the shelf immediately and sit in that spooler's cut pile, because paper that has been physically cut for a run cannot also be counted as available on the shelf. The supervisors then endorse one at a time. When a spooler's endorsements reach quorum, the draw is loaded: the cut pile goes into that spooler's press and the tally of endorsements is wiped ready for the next draw. A draw that has not reached quorum can instead be rescinded, in which case the cut pile goes back on the shelf whole and the endorsements are wiped. A spooler has at most one draw in flight at a time. Reams that a press did not end up needing are returned to the shelf directly, which needs no vote.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A multiplayer game lobby matchmaker keeps one shared lobby record listing which loadout slots have been claimed. Party leaders edit that record, and because the record is a single blob that clients read and write back whole, an edit is a read-modify-write: a leader reads the current claim list, adds the slot it wants, and writes the whole list back. That is exactly the shape in which one leader's edit can silently erase another's.

The matchmaker's defence is a write lease. Only the leader currently holding the lease may prepare an edit or write one back, and preparing an edit is what captures the snapshot the leader will write from. Leases expire on their own — a leader that goes quiet does not hold the record hostage — and a leader whose lease has gone must throw away the snapshot it captured rather than write from it, because that snapshot may already be behind. A leader with a snapshot in hand cannot take a fresh lease until it has thrown the stale one away, so a snapshot captured under one lease is never written back under another.

When a leader writes, the record becomes exactly the snapshot it captured plus the slot it claimed, and the leader keeps a note of the claim it just committed as its own receipt from the matchmaker. Writing also gives up the lease.

The lobby's size is tuned at runtime — the matchmaker grows or shrinks the lobby as queue depth and server capacity change — and a write is only accepted if the resulting claim list fits within the size then in force. The matchmaker never shrinks the lobby below the number of claims already in the record, because a claim already accepted cannot be revoked by a resize.

The full set of actions is: Take, in which a leader that holds no snapshot takes the free write lease; Prepare, in which the lease holder captures the current claim list as its snapshot and picks an unclaimed slot; Write, in which the lease holder replaces the record with its snapshot plus its chosen slot, provided the result fits the current lobby size, records its receipt, and gives up the lease; Expire, in which an outstanding lease lapses on its own; Discard, in which a leader that no longer holds the lease throws away the snapshot it captured; and Resize, in which the matchmaker sets the lobby size to any supported value that still covers every claim already in the record.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every claim a leader holds a receipt for is still present in the shared record, so no committed claim is ever erased by another leader writing back an older view of the record.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: No leader is left holding a captured snapshot forever — every snapshot is eventually either written back or thrown away.

A vending operator runs two separate machine networks in one building — the snack network and the cold-drink network — under two independent route controllers that do not coordinate with each other. Both networks report telemetry through a single shared uplink modem installed in the riser. The modem is the critical resource: it has one carrier, and if two machines key it at the same time the traffic is garbage and both batches are lost.

Exclusive use of the modem is arranged with a token ring. Every machine in the building, regardless of which network it belongs to, sits in one ring, and a single transmit token circulates around it. A machine may take the modem only while it is the machine holding the token. Its own controller records that one of its machines is on the modem, so each network knows whether it is currently keying the carrier.

The token only moves while the modem is idle. A machine that has taken the modem holds the token until it lets the modem go, and only then does the token move on to the next machine in the ring — passing the token out from under a machine that is mid-transmission is precisely what would let a machine on the other network key the carrier at the same time.

A machine that has readings to send raises a request; while its network is not on the modem, the machine's own request can be picked up when the token reaches it. Once on the modem the machine uploads telemetry batches, up to the number its buffer holds, and then releases the modem, clearing its request.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a network records one of its machines as being on the modem, that machine is the one holding the ring's transmit token, so the two networks can never be keying the shared carrier at the same time.

A university keeps each student's degree-audit record — the approved credit total for the term — replicated across several registrar nodes. Advisors edit that total, and because two advisors can be looking at the same student at the same time, an edit that is written blindly can wipe out an edit made a moment earlier. The registrar's rule is that no single node may accept an edit on its own: every edit is put to the nodes and needs a quorum of them before it counts as made.

An edit is proposed as a numbered revision. The proposing advisor reads the highest revision number any node is currently carrying and proposes the next one up; that is what stops a second edit from being written at a revision number that some node has already used for a different value. Only one proposal is open at a time. Nodes then accept it one at a time, and accepting means the node writes the proposed value and revision into its own copy — a node only accepts a revision newer than the one it is already carrying.

A proposal that has reached a quorum of acceptances is committed and closed. A proposal that has not reached quorum can instead be abandoned and closed, which is the awkward case: some nodes may already have written it into their copies, and those partial writes stay. That is exactly why the next proposal takes its number from the highest revision any node carries rather than from the last committed one.

The approved credit cap is retuned during the term as the senate adjusts overload policy, and an advisor may only propose a total that fits the cap in force when the proposal is made.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Any two registrar nodes carrying the same revision number carry the same credit total, so no advisor's edit is ever overwritten by another edit issued at the same revision.

Each car in a skyscraper's elevator bank carries a single-use pyrotechnic safety brake. Firing it is as irreversible as anything in the building: the charge is spent, the car is clamped to the rails, and it comes off the rails only with a crew and a crane. Firing a car's brake twice is not merely wasteful, it is a certification failure, so every firing is written into the bank's permanent journal along with how many earlier firings that car had already had when the entry was written.

Taking the car's lock releases the bank lock immediately, so the coarse lock is held only long enough to pick a car, and other technicians can go on working on other cars. A hospital runs two operating-room suites that schedule independently of one another: the main theatre block and the day-surgery block. They share one central store of anaesthetic machines. The building's lift-service contract buys a fixed number of duty hours per day, and those hours are the quantity the bank has to account for: an hour is either assigned to a specific car or sitting unassigned in the bank's reserve. A subway signalling system drives its point machines from a control centre, but which controller is allowed to drive a given point is not fixed. Areas of the railway are vested in controllers and re-vested as shifts change, as a possession is taken for engineering work, or as a fault forces a hand-back. Every change of vesting — taking an area, and giving it up — advances that point's control epoch, and the epoch is what tells a stale command from a current one.

Commands do not reach the point machines in the order they were sent. They go onto an unordered command bus and are picked up in whatever order the bus manages, so a command sent under an old vesting can easily arrive after the area has been re-vested to somebody else. Each command carries the controller that sent it, the point it addresses, and the control epoch that was in force when it was sent. A controller has at most one command outstanding per point.

A point machine acts on a command only when the command's epoch still matches the point's current epoch and the point is still vested in the controller that sent it. When it acts, it records the command as the standing command for that point, keeping both the sending controller and the epoch. A command that fails either check is not acted on and is dropped off the bus.

The full set of actions is: Vest, in which an unvested point is vested in a controller, advancing its epoch; Send, in which the controller a point is vested in puts a command for that point onto the bus, stamped with the point's current epoch, provided it has none outstanding for that point; Act, in which a point machine takes a command off the bus whose epoch still matches and whose sender is still the vested controller, and records it as the point's standing command; Drop, in which a command whose epoch is stale or whose sender no longer holds the vesting is taken off the bus unacted; and Release, in which a point's vesting is given up, advancing its epoch.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: No command sits on the bus forever — every command put onto the bus is eventually taken off it, either acted on or dropped.

Handlers are slow but they do not fail. A handler always finishes what it started, but it may take a long time about it: it prepares a divert command against a chute, recording the chute's version at the moment it prepared, and only later gets around to committing that command to the belt controller. The belt controller therefore re-checks at commit time. A prepared command is committed only if the chute's version register still holds the value the command recorded and the chute is still owned by the handler that prepared it. A container terminal keeps one shared stow plan listing which bay slots on the berthed ship have been committed to cargo. Gantry cranes edit that plan, and because the plan is transmitted and stored as one document, an edit is a read-modify-write: a crane takes the plan as it stands, adds the slot it is about to fill, and sends the whole revised plan back to the planning office. That is the shape in which one crane's commitment can be wiped out by another crane's write.

Editing rights are handed out as a lease. Only the crane holding the lease may compose a write, and composing captures the copy of the plan the crane will send. Leases expire on their own, because a crane that stops working — driver change, a spreader fault, a wind stop — must not hold the plan shut.

Writes reach the planning office over the yard's radio link, which does not preserve order. Composed writes sit on the link and are taken up in whatever order they arrive, so a write composed under an earlier lease can arrive after a write composed under a later one. A crane has at most one write outstanding at a time.

The office therefore checks the lease when a write lands, not when it was composed. A write is applied only if its author is still the crane holding the lease; applying replaces the plan with exactly the copy that crane captured plus the slot it committed, notes the newly committed slot in the terminal's permanent commitment record, and gives the lease back. A write whose author no longer holds the lease is binned unapplied, because the copy it captured is no longer a safe basis for a whole-document overwrite.

The full set of actions is: Grab, in which a crane with no write outstanding takes the free editing lease; Compose, in which the lease-holding crane captures the current plan and picks a slot not yet in it, putting the resulting write onto the radio link; Land, in which a write whose author still holds the lease is applied, replacing the plan, recording the committed slot permanently, and releasing the lease; Bin, in which a write whose author no longer holds the lease is discarded unapplied; and Expire, in which an outstanding lease lapses on its own.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every slot in the terminal's permanent commitment record is still present in the shared stow plan, so no committed slot is ever erased by a crane writing back a copy of the plan taken before that commitment.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A clearing bank settles interbank payment instructions against a central ledger. Settling an instruction is irreversible: the funds move across the central bank's books and there is no unwind, so an instruction that settles twice is a duplicated payment that has to be chased manually between two institutions.

The ledger is not locked while an instruction is being prepared. The bank works optimistically instead: a member reads the ledger's current version, prepares a commit request naming the instruction and the version it read, and sends it in. Requests reach the ledger over the settlement network, which does not preserve order — a request prepared earlier can arrive after one prepared later. A member has at most one request outstanding for a given instruction.

The ledger accepts a request only if the version it names is still the ledger's version and the instruction has not already settled. Accepting appends the instruction to the settlement log, advances the version by one, and records against that instruction the position in the log where it landed. A request naming a superseded version is not settled; it is simply dropped, and the member is free to read the ledger again and prepare a fresh one — that is what optimistic working means here. A request for an instruction that has already settled is dropped as well, because the payment has already moved. The settlement log runs to a fixed length for the cycle, and once it is full no further requests can be accepted, so those are dropped for retry in the next cycle too.

The full set of actions is: Prepare, in which a member reads the ledger's version and puts a commit request for an unsettled instruction onto the settlement network; Settle, in which the ledger accepts a request whose version still matches, appending its instruction to the log, advancing the version, and recording the log position against that instruction; Retry, in which a request naming a superseded version, or arriving when the log is already full, is dropped so it can be prepared again; Drop, in which a request for an instruction that has already settled is discarded; and Closed, in which the ledger simply waits once every instruction has settled and nothing is left in flight.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every position in the settlement log, the instruction sitting there has that exact position recorded against it as the place it settled, so no instruction appears in the log more than once and no payment settles twice.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: No commit request sits on the settlement network forever — every request that is sent in is eventually taken off it, whether by settling, by being dropped for retry, or by being discarded as already settled.

    /\ version \in 0..LogLimit

A game publisher runs two matchmaking regions that make their own decisions independently — the European region and the North American one — but both draw dedicated game servers from a single shared server pool. A dedicated server is the critical resource here: it hosts one match at a time, and two regions starting matches on the same box is a live incident, not a scheduling inefficiency.

The pool hands out grants. A region asks the pool for a server, the pool records that server as granted to that region, and only then may the region put a match on it. A region runs at most one match at a time, and asks for a server only while it is not running one. Finishing a match takes the region off the server and gives the grant back.

The server fleet is reconfigured under an epoch number: boxes are drained for patching, a new rack comes online, the capacity plan changes. Every reconfiguration advances the fleet epoch, and each grant carries the epoch it was issued under, so a grant written against the old fleet layout is recognisably stale. A stale grant is revoked rather than honoured, and a region can only put a match on a server whose grant is both its own and current.

The one thing the publisher will not do is reconfigure the fleet underneath a running match. A reconfiguration is only permitted while no region is running a match at all — draining is a precondition of the epoch bump, not a consequence of it — because advancing the epoch invalidates grants, and invalidating the grant under a live match is exactly how the same box ends up handed to the other region.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a region is running a match on a server, the pool's books show that server granted to exactly that region, so the two regions can never both be running matches on the same box.

A vending machine network runs a promotion with a single grand prize. Paying the grand prize out is irreversible — the machine opens the prize bay, the customer walks off with it, and there is no recalling it — and the promotion is funded for exactly one payout across the whole estate. Two machines paying it out is a loss the operator eats.

The machines take turns at the prize register using a token ring: they are wired in a ring, one payout token circulates, and a machine may only touch the register while it holds the token. The token keeps moving around the ring whether or not anybody is doing anything with it.

Machines are slow but they do not fail. A machine decides to pay out the prize while it holds the token and while the register still shows the prize unclaimed, but the actual payout comes later, after the coin mechanism has cycled and the bay has unlatched. In the meantime the token may have gone right around the ring and another machine may have paid the prize out already.

That is why the register carries a claim generation, which advances every time the prize is paid. A machine's decision records the generation it saw. When the machine is finally ready, it pays out only if the generation on its decision still matches the register and it still holds the token; the register then records that machine as the winner and advances the generation, and the machine notes internally that it was the one that paid. A decision whose generation has moved on, or whose machine no longer holds the token, is dropped rather than acted on.

A smart-home door lock network shares battery charge between its locks peer to peer, with no hub holding a reserve. Charge is measured in whole units and the installed total is fixed for the day: every unit is either sitting in one of the locks or riding in a donation that one lock has sent to another and that has not yet been taken up.

Donations travel over the home's mesh radio, which does not preserve order. Several donations can be in the air at once and they are taken up in whatever order the mesh manages, so a donation sent first may well arrive last. A lock will not have more than one donation outstanding to the same neighbour at a time. The donor debits itself the moment it sends — the units are physically committed to the transfer — and each donation records the version number the receiving lock was showing when the donation was composed.

There is no lock held over the receiver while a donation is in flight. The network works optimistically instead: when a donation is taken up, the receiver compares the version it recorded against its own version now. If they match, the units are credited to the receiver. If they do not — the receiver has re-paired, had its keypad re-keyed, or taken a firmware bump in the meantime — the donation is not credited; the units go back whole to the donor, who is free to compose a fresh donation against the receiver's new version. That is what retrying means here: nothing is held, nothing is lost, the transfer is simply attempted again.

Retrying is not free. Each returned donation counts against the donor's retry budget, and a lock that has used its budget up stops composing new donations for the rest of the day rather than churning the mesh.

The full set of actions is: Donate, in which a lock with retry budget left debits itself and puts a donation to a neighbour onto the mesh, recording that neighbour's current version, provided it has none outstanding to that neighbour; Credit, in which a receiving lock takes up a donation whose recorded version still matches and adds the units to its own charge; Return, in which a donation whose recorded version no longer matches its receiver is taken off the mesh, its units given back whole to the donor, and the donor's retry budget charged; Bump, in which a lock's version advances because it was re-paired or re-keyed; and Quiet, in which the network simply rests once nothing is in flight and no lock has any version change left to make.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The charge units held across all the locks, plus the units riding in donations still on the mesh, always add up to exactly the total the installer configured.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A stock exchange runs its opening auction with a hard limit on how many member firms may have an order-entry session open against any one symbol's book at the same time. The limit is a matching-engine capacity figure, not a policy preference: exceeding it means the book cannot be crossed within the auction window.

Sessions are handed out as leases. A member does not get a session by asking for one directly; the exchange puts a grant onto the member link, and the member's session begins when the grant is taken up. The member link does not preserve order, so grants are taken up in whatever order they arrive, and a grant issued earlier may be acted on later. A member has at most one grant outstanding per symbol.

Because a grant that has been issued but not yet taken up is a session that is going to exist, the exchange counts it against the symbol's capacity from the moment it issues it, not from the moment the member takes it up. Issuing a grant is only permitted while the sessions already open, counted together with the grants still outstanding for that symbol, leave room under the limit.

Each symbol carries an admission epoch, and a grant records the epoch in force when it was issued. Leases expire: a session that is not kept up lapses, and lapsing advances the symbol's epoch. That advance is what makes the accounting safe — every grant still outstanding for that symbol was written against the old epoch, so it can no longer be taken up and stops counting against the limit. A grant whose epoch no longer matches is simply taken off the link. A member may also give a session up voluntarily, which does not disturb the epoch.

Books can be halted for a volatility interruption. While a symbol is halted the exchange issues no new grants for it and takes up none of the outstanding ones; sessions already open are unaffected, and the halt is lifted when the interruption ends.

The full set of actions is: Issue, in which the exchange puts a grant for a member onto the link for an unhalted symbol, stamped with that symbol's epoch, provided the open sessions plus outstanding grants leave room under the limit; TakeUp, in which a grant whose epoch still matches its unhalted symbol is taken off the link and becomes an open session; Discard, in which a grant whose epoch no longer matches is taken off the link; Lapse, in which an open session expires, closing it and advancing that symbol's epoch; Surrender, in which a member closes an open session voluntarily; Halt, in which a symbol's book is suspended for a volatility interruption; and Resume, in which a halted symbol's book reopens.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A stock exchange's opening auction ends with an uncrossing run on the matching engine. The engine is the critical resource: it walks the whole book computing the opening price, and two firms running uncrossings at the same time would produce two different opening prints.

Access is arranged in two levels. A firm that wants the engine first joins the queue of firms asking for it. From the queue it takes the auction session lock, which is the coarse one covering the whole opening process, and only while holding that may it take the engine lock itself. Taking the engine lock releases the session lock in the same step, so the coarse lock is held only long enough to reach the engine, and other firms can carry on queueing behind it.

Holding the engine lock is what lets a firm start uncrossing. A firm that has started keeps its own internal flag saying it is uncrossing, and clears that flag when it finishes; finishing also releases the engine lock and records that the firm has completed an uncrossing at least once in the day's log.

Firms are slow but they do not fail. A firm that has the engine lock may take a long time to get started and a long time to finish — its risk checks are slow, its book is large, its network is congested — but it always gets there in the end, and nothing takes the engine lock away from it in the meantime. A firm holding only the coarse session lock may also simply drop it without reaching the engine.

The full set of actions is: Queue, in which a firm that is not uncrossing joins the queue of firms asking for the engine; TakeSession, in which a queued firm takes the free session lock and leaves the queue; TakeEngine, in which a firm holding the session lock takes the free engine lock and releases the session lock in the same step; DropSession, in which a firm gives up the session lock without reaching the engine; Start, in which a firm holding the engine lock begins its uncrossing and raises its own flag; and Finish, in which a firm that is uncrossing lowers its flag, releases the engine lock, and is recorded in the day's log.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A clearing bank runs two settlement engines that operate independently of each other: the real-time gross engine and the end-of-cycle netting engine. They draw intraday liquidity from one shared pool that the central bank has collateralised to a fixed ceiling. The ceiling is a hard limit on aggregate exposure — the bank's own drawings plus anything it has committed to draw must never exceed it.

Because the two engines do not coordinate, the shared pool exposes a single compare-and-swap register. An engine that wants liquidity first reads the register, which gives it two things: the register's current version, and the headroom left under the ceiling at that instant. The engine then works from what it read, not from a fresh look at the pool; that is the point of the read.

Committing is where the compare-and-swap happens. An engine may commit a reservation for an amount only if the register's version still equals the version it read, and only if the amount fits inside the headroom it read. A successful commit sets that engine's reservation aside and advances the register's version, which immediately makes the other engine's outstanding read worthless. An engine whose read has been overtaken throws it away and reads again. An engine holds at most one read and at most one reservation at a time.

A reservation is turned into an actual drawing when the engine settles the payments it reserved for. Repaying reduces an engine's drawing and advances the register's version, because headroom has changed.

The full set of actions is: Read, in which an engine with no read outstanding takes the register's version and the headroom currently left under the ceiling; Reserve, in which an engine commits a reservation for an amount that fits the headroom it read, provided the register's version still matches what it read, advancing the version; Discard, in which an engine whose read has been overtaken by a version change throws it away; Draw, in which an engine turns its reservation into an actual drawing; and Repay, in which an engine repays part of its drawing, advancing the register's version.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The liquidity drawn by the two engines, counted together with the amounts they have reserved and not yet drawn, never exceeds the collateralised ceiling on the shared pool.

    /\ Booked(a) < Occupancy

Enter(r) ==

    /\ UNCHANGED <<era, shut>>

Void(r) ==

    /\ \/ era[permit[r].aisle] # permit[r].era

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An air-traffic runway allocator limits how many departures may be rolling on any one runway at the same time. The figure comes from wake-turbulence separation and is not negotiable: once that many aircraft are rolling, no further departure may be cleared onto that runway until one of them is airborne.

Clearances are written by controllers, and controllers reach a runway through two levels of lock. A controller must first take the field lock, which covers the whole airport, and only while holding it may it take the lock on one runway. Taking a runway's lock releases the field lock in the same step, so the coarse lock is held only long enough to choose a runway and other controllers can keep working.

Holding a runway's lock is what lets a controller prepare a departure clearance for it. A clearance that has been prepared but not yet acted on is a departure that is going to be rolling, so the allocator counts prepared clearances against the runway's limit alongside the aircraft already rolling. A controller holds at most one prepared clearance and only prepares while the aircraft rolling plus the clearances prepared leave room under the limit.

Controllers are slow but they do not fail. A controller that has taken a runway lock and prepared a clearance will get round to issuing it, but it may sit on that lock for a long time — coordinating with the tower, waiting on a wake check — and nothing takes the lock away from it. Issuing the clearance puts the aircraft onto the runway rolling, consumes the prepared clearance, and releases the runway lock. An aircraft that gets airborne frees its place on the runway. A controller that has taken the field lock, or a runway lock, and decided against a departure simply gives it back.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every runway, the aircraft rolling on it counted together with the departure clearances prepared for it never exceeds that runway's wake-separation limit.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending machine network keeps one shared price schedule for a product line. Machines revise it as costs move, and a revision is a read-modify-write: a machine reads the price now published, works out the next price up from what it read, and writes that back as the new published price. Two machines revising at once is how a revision gets lost — the second one writes a price computed from a schedule that has already moved.

The schedule sits behind a compare-and-swap register. Reading gives a machine two things: the price as published, and the register's current value. Writing back succeeds only if the register still holds the value the machine read; a successful write publishes the new price and turns the register over, which makes any other machine's outstanding read worthless. A machine whose read has been overtaken throws it away and reads again. A machine holds at most one read at a time.

The network also keeps a high-water mark: the highest price ever published on this schedule. It is what the operations team audits against, because a schedule that has gone backwards means a revision was computed from stale data and somebody's price increase was silently undone.

Machines can crash silently. A crashed machine stops reading and stops writing and gives no notice; a read it was holding is simply reaped by the network so the register does not stay pinned behind a machine that is not coming back on its own. A crashed machine can be power-cycled by the route driver and rejoins. At most one machine is down at a time. The register is turned over only a fixed number of times per pricing day; once it has been, outstanding reads are reaped rather than written back.

The full set of actions is: Read, in which a machine that is up and holding no read takes the published price and the register's current value; Write, in which a machine that is up writes back one above the price it read, provided the register still holds what it read and the day's turnover budget is not spent, publishing the new price, raising the high-water mark if it is higher, and turning the register over; Reap, in which an outstanding read is thrown away because the register has moved on, because the day's turnover budget is spent, or because the machine holding it has crashed; Crash, in which a machine that is up silently stops while every other machine is still up; and Rejoin, in which the crashed machine is power-cycled and comes back.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The published price is never below the highest price ever published on the schedule, so no revision is ever lost by being overwritten with a price computed from an older read.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: No machine is left holding a read forever — every read taken is eventually either written back or reaped.

\* reg: the compare-and-swap register. held: the read a machine is carrying.
\* up: a crashed machine acts no further and says nothing.

vars == <<price, peak, reg, held, up>>

Reads == [saw: 0..MaxPrice, reg: 0..Turnovers]

TypeOK ==

    /\ peak \in 0..MaxPrice
    /\ reg \in 0..Turnovers
    /\ held \in [Machines -> Reads \cup {NOREAD}]
    /\ up \in [Machines -> BOOLEAN]

    /\ peak = 0
    /\ reg = 0
    /\ held = [m \in Machines |-> NOREAD]

    /\ held[m] = NOREAD
    /\ price < MaxPrice
    /\ held' = [held EXCEPT ![m] = [saw |-> price, reg |-> reg]]

\* the only thing standing between a stale read and a lost revision.
Write(m) ==

    /\ UNCHANGED <<price, peak, reg, held>>

A robot may only put pallets into a bay, or take pallets out of one, while it holds that bay's lease. Leases are used rather than permanent assignments because robots are slow: a robot that has claimed a bay may take a long time over the transfer — it is re-planning its route, its lift is cycling, the aisle ahead is congested — and if bays were assigned permanently one slow robot would sterilise a bay for the rest of the shift. Robots are slow but they do not fail, and a lapse takes nothing away from them. A warehouse robot fleet closes out outbound trailers. Sealing a trailer is irreversible: the robot fits the numbered customs seal, the paperwork is cut against that seal number, and the trailer cannot be reopened on the yard. Fitting a second seal to a trailer that already has one is a customs discrepancy that has to be resolved with the carrier, so a trailer is sealed once or not at all.

The yard register is the authority on what has been sealed: for each trailer it records the robot that sealed it, or that it is still open. Every robot also keeps its own on-board log of the trailers it has sealed, which is what the fleet's end-of-day reconciliation reads.

The dock plan is reconfigured under an epoch number as doors are reassigned and trailers are re-spotted. Advancing the epoch changes which trailer is at which door, so a decision made under the old plan no longer points at the trailer the robot thought it did.

Robots are slow but they do not fail. A robot decides to seal a particular open trailer, recording the epoch it decided under, and then takes its time getting there — it is finishing another move, its seal magazine is being reloaded, it is waiting for a door to clear. By the time it arrives the dock plan may have been reconfigured, or another robot may have sealed that trailer already. So the robot checks twice before it fits the seal: the epoch it decided under must still be the current one, and the yard register must still show the trailer open. A smart-home door lock network hands out guest access through a small fixed set of keypad code slots. ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home door lock network is rolling out a security fix that permanently blows a one-time fuse inside each lock, closing off the factory recovery path for good. Blowing the fuse is irreversible in the strongest sense available to a consumer device: the silicon is altered, there is no undo, and blowing it a second time is not merely wasteful but would draw a second fuse charge out of a hub that has only so many.

The hub holds a stock of fuse charges, and each lock model draws a different, known amount of that stock when its fuse is blown. The stock is what the installer audits: charges that are still in the hub, plus the charges consumed by the locks that have been blown, must always account for exactly what the hub started with.

The rollout runs as a two-phase commit. The hub opens a round and puts the question to a batch of locks: each lock asked in the round answers yes if it is ready to blow its fuse or no if it is not. Only when every lock in the round has answered yes does the hub move the round into its commit phase; a single no aborts the round outright and nobody blows anything. In the commit phase the locks that answered yes blow their fuses one at a time, each drawing its own charge from the hub's stock, and a lock that has blown is marked done and is never asked again in a later round. A lock already blown is never put into a batch.

How many locks the hub will put into one round is retuned at runtime — a bigger batch when the house is quiet and the mesh is idle, a smaller one when the radio is busy or the hub is on battery — and the limit in force is what caps the batch as it is being assembled. A round whose locks have all blown is closed and the hub goes idle.

The full set of actions is: Open, in which the idle hub opens a new round with nobody yet asked; Ask, in which the hub puts the question to an unasked, unblown lock and receives a yes or a no, permitted only while the batch is below the current limit; Abort, in which a round in which some lock answered no is closed without anything being blown; Commit, in which a round whose asked locks all answered yes moves into its commit phase; Blow, in which a lock that answered yes in a committed round blows its fuse, draws its charge from the hub's stock, and is marked done; Close, in which a committed round with nothing left to blow returns the hub to idle; and Retune, in which the hub sets the batch limit to any supported value.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The fuse charges remaining in the hub's stock, plus the charges drawn by the locks that have been blown, always add up to exactly the stock the hub started with, so no lock's fuse is ever blown twice.

    /\ answer \in [Locks -> Answers]
    /\ blown \subseteq Locks
    /\ stock \in 0..Stocked
    /\ limit \in MinBatch..LockCount

    /\ phase = "idle"
    /\ answer = [l \in Locks |-> "unasked"]
    /\ blown = {}
    /\ stock = Stocked
    /\ limit = MinBatch

Drawn(S) ==
    LET add[T \in SUBSET Locks] ==
        IF T = {} THEN 0
        ELSE LET l == CHOOSE x \in T : TRUE IN Charge(l) + add[T \ {l}]
    IN add[S]

    /\ phase' = "voting"
    /\ answer' = [l \in Locks |-> "unasked"]

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home door lock network keeps one shared setting that every lock in the house obeys: the auto-relock delay. Household members change it from their phones, and a change is a read-modify-write — the phone reads the delay as it stands, works out the next step up, and sends that value back to the hub. Two phones doing that at once is how somebody's change quietly disappears.

The hub arbitrates with a write lease. Only the phone currently holding the lease may compose a change, and only a change from the phone that holds the lease is applied. Leases expire on their own, so a phone that goes out of range or gets locked in a pocket does not freeze the setting for everybody else.

Changes reach the hub over the house mesh, which does not preserve order. A composed change sits on the mesh and is picked up in whatever order the radio manages, so a change composed under an earlier lease can easily be picked up after a change composed under a later one. A phone has at most one change outstanding.

The hub does not re-derive the value when a change lands — it writes what the phone sent. What it checks is the lease: a change is applied only if the phone that composed it is still the lease holder. That check is the whole safety mechanism, because a phone whose lease has gone composed its value against a delay the hub has since moved past, and writing it would step the setting backwards. A change from a phone that no longer holds the lease is binned unapplied. Applying a change also acknowledges it back to the composing phone, which remembers the value the hub confirmed, and releases the lease.

The full set of actions is: Take, in which a phone with nothing outstanding takes the free write lease; Compose, in which the lease-holding phone reads the delay, works out the next step up, and puts the resulting change onto the mesh; Apply, in which a change whose composer still holds the lease is written to the setting, acknowledged back to that phone, and the lease released; Bin, in which a change whose composer no longer holds the lease is discarded unapplied; and Expire, in which an outstanding lease lapses on its own.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: No change stays on the mesh forever — every change a phone composes is eventually taken off it, either applied or binned.

A public library runs its hold-and-pickup service through a single intake queue. When a patron asks to reserve a title, the request is appended to the intake queue together with a snapshot of the serial number currently printed on that patron's library card. Pickup is performed against the physical card, so a request written under an old serial number can no longer be honoured by anyone. The clerk therefore examines only the head of the queue: if the head belongs to a patron whose privileges are intact and whose card serial still matches the snapshot taken at submission time, the clerk hands over the book and records the hold under that serial number. Otherwise the clerk shreds the slip and moves on. Either way the head leaves the queue, so the desk never wedges on a dead request.

Holds already granted are also affected. Suspending a patron confiscates any book currently on hold for them, and reissuing a card voids the hold that was tied to the old serial. A patron may return a held book at any time, and a suspended patron may be reinstated once the fines are settled.

A metro line is divided into fixed signalling blocks. After a block has been taken out of service for track work, it cannot simply be handed back to traffic: the control centre must commission it, which means breaking the tamper seal on the block's safety certificate and writing the block into the line's permanent commissioning register. Breaking a seal is irreversible. A certificate can never be re-sealed, and the regulator treats a second register entry for the same block as evidence that the first commissioning was never real, so a duplicate entry is a reportable incident rather than a harmless retry.

Commissioning orders travel through a bounded dispatch queue. When the maintenance gang finishes work on a block, the block becomes ready, and a dispatcher may push a commissioning order for it onto the queue. The queue applies backpressure: no new order is accepted once the queue has reached the depth limit currently in force. That depth limit is adjusted while the system runs, because the control centre allows a deeper backlog during the overnight engineering window than it does during service hours. Shrinking the limit never throws away orders that are already queued; it only stalls new pushes until the backlog works down.

The controller works strictly from the head of the queue. If the block at the head still has an unbroken seal, the controller commissions it: the seal is broken and the block's identifier is appended to the commissioning register. If the block instead fails its final check at the head of the queue, the order is torn up and the block is marked faulted, which sends it back to the gang; a faulted block can be repaired and become ready again, but only if it has not already been commissioned. The register has a fixed physical size and the control centre stops commissioning when it is full.

The action set is exactly: mark a block ready when it is not already ready, faulted, queued, or commissioned; push a commissioning order for a ready block onto the queue while the queue is below the current depth limit, removing it from the ready set; commission the block at the head of the queue when its seal is unbroken and the register has room; fail the final check on the head of the queue, marking that block faulted; repair a faulted block back to ready provided it has not been commissioned; and change the queue depth limit to another configured value.

A regional blood bank keeps its rare-phenotype units in a shared cold store, and every release of a unit to an operating theatre is authorised collectively by the region's transfusion sites rather than by whoever happens to be at the fridge. Releasing a unit is irreversible: once a unit leaves the cold chain it can never be returned to inventory, and the regional registry treats a unit as permanently gone the moment the release is recorded.

Authorisation works by ballot. A site opens a release ballot for a specific unit; opening a ballot assigns it a fresh round number and clears any votes carried over from an earlier round. Each site independently checks the crossmatch paperwork and casts its yes-vote into the ballot. When strictly more than half of the sites have voted, the ballot has a quorum and the unit may be released: the unit is recorded as issued and the ballot is closed. A ballot may only be opened for a unit that has not already been issued, and a unit's ballot may only be opened a limited number of times before the regional registry refuses further rounds.

Sites in this region are slow, not unreliable. A site can fall behind — its paperwork terminal queues up, its technician is in theatre, its link to the registry is congested — and while it is behind it cannot cast a vote. But no site ever fails outright. Individual sites do sometimes catch up on their own, and in addition the registry runs a reconciliation pass that brings every lagging site current in one sweep, so a period in which sites are behind is always followed by a period in which they can vote again. This is what lets the region promise that authorisation is a matter of delay rather than of deadlock.

A commercial print shop runs one large press fed by a spooler. Every job that arrives has a fixed sheet count, decided when the customer's file is prepared and unchanged thereafter. What the spooler must protect is not the number of jobs but the amount of paper committed at once: the shop's finishing line can only absorb a fixed number of sheets of work-in-progress, so the total sheet count of everything the spooler has taken responsibility for must stay within that ceiling.

Requests reach the spooler over a shared print bus, and the bus makes no ordering promises. Submissions land in an unordered inbox and the spooler may look at them in any order; likewise, once a job has been admitted, its actual page data streams in over the same bus and jobs finish streaming in an order unrelated to the order in which they were admitted. A spec that decided admission based on the order requests were sent would be wrong here, so the spooler re-evaluates the sheet ceiling at the moment it admits a job, counting everything it is already committed to: jobs admitted but still streaming, jobs fully spooled to disk, and the job currently mounted on the press.

When the spooler picks a request out of the inbox it either admits it, if the ceiling still has room for that job's sheets, or bounces it back to the customer, if it does not. A bounced request simply disappears from the inbox; the customer is free to submit it again later, and by then the press may well have freed up room. ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A branch library runs a reserve shelf behind the circulation desk. A patron who wants a title that is currently out places a reservation; when a copy becomes free it is moved onto the reserve shelf and offered to one waiting patron. An offer is a lease with a clock on it: the copy is held under that patron's name for a fixed number of ticks of the desk's shift timer and no longer. While the lease is running the patron may come in and collect.

Collection is the irreversible step. When the patron collects, the copy leaves the reserve shelf for good — it is charged to the patron's account and the reservation coupon that entitled them to it is discharged. A discharged coupon is not reissued: the patron is no longer on the waiting list, holds no offer, and cannot place the same reservation again in this cycle. This is deliberate, because the branch's audit reconciles collected copies against discharged coupons one-for-one, and a coupon that got discharged twice would mean a copy left the building without a matching record.

The failure mode the lease exists for is a patron who goes quiet. Someone places a reservation, gets an offer, and then simply stops responding — the phone number is dead, they moved away, they forgot. They never announce this; from the desk's point of view the offer is simply not being collected. A quiet patron cannot collect, and the desk has no way of knowing whether a silent patron is gone for good or will resurface later. The lease clock is what stops such a patron from pinning a copy forever: the shift timer ticks down every running lease, and when a lease reaches zero the desk sweeps it, pulling the copy back onto the shelf as unoffered so it can go to somebody else. The patron whose offer lapsed drops off the list and would have to place the reservation again.

The action set is exactly: place a reservation for a patron who is not already waiting, not holding an offer, and whose coupon has not been discharged; offer an unoffered shelf copy to a waiting patron, starting that copy's lease clock at full and taking the patron off the waiting list; tick the shift timer, decrementing every running lease clock that has not yet reached zero; sweep every lease whose clock has reached zero, returning those copies to the shelf as unoffered; collect a copy whose lease is still running, by a patron who has not gone quiet, discharging that patron's coupon and taking the copy off the shelf permanently; have a patron go quiet; and have a quiet patron resurface, once a new contact number finally reaches the desk.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every lease that starts eventually ends — the copy is either collected or swept back onto the shelf — so no offer to a patron who has gone quiet can hold a copy forever.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A metro line's signalling is done by a panel of interlocking computers. Before a train may be given a movement authority over a route, a strict majority of the panel must vote for it: each interlocking independently checks track circuits, point positions and conflicting routes, and casts its vote. Only when the votes on a route exceed half the panel is the route cleared and the authority handed to the train.

What makes this interesting is that the panel is not a fixed set. Interlockings are commissioned and decommissioned while the line is in service — a spare is brought online for the peak, a unit is taken out for a firmware change, a depot extension adds a new one. Each such change is a reconfiguration: it publishes a new configuration under a strictly higher configuration number and names the new panel. Because the size of the panel is exactly what determines how many votes a majority takes, changing the panel changes the threshold under everyone's feet. Reconfiguration therefore also cancels every movement authority currently outstanding and throws away every vote cast under the old configuration; routes must be re-voted from scratch under the new panel.

An interlocking learns about a reconfiguration by resynchronising, which brings its own configuration number up to the published one. Until it resynchronises it is running superseded logic — its view of which points are motorised and which routes conflict may simply be wrong — so its vote must not be counted. An interlocking that has been decommissioned is no longer in the panel at all and its vote must not be counted either, whatever configuration number it thinks it is running. A cleared route can be cancelled by the controller, which also discards the votes that cleared it.

The action set is exactly: reconfigure to a different non-empty panel under the next configuration number, cancelling all cleared routes and discarding all votes; resynchronise an interlocking whose configuration number is behind the published one; cast a vote on a route that is not already cleared, from an interlocking that is in the current panel, is running the current configuration, and has not already voted on that route; clear a route whose votes exceed half the current panel; and cancel a cleared route, discarding its votes.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every route currently holding a movement authority is backed by a set of votes drawn entirely from the currently commissioned panel, cast only by interlockings running the current configuration number, and larger than half of that panel.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

\* itself moves; reconfiguration bumps the configuration number, cancels every
\* cleared route and discards every vote taken under the old panel.
\* The invariant rejects authority backed by decommissioned or unsynchronised units.

VARIABLES config, panel, unitConfig, votes, cleared
vars == <<config, panel, unitConfig, votes, cleared>>

Majority(r) == 2 * Cardinality(votes[r]) > Cardinality(panel)

TypeOK ==
  /\ config \in 0..MaxConfig
  /\ panel \subseteq Interlockings
  /\ unitConfig \in [Interlockings -> 0..MaxConfig]
  /\ votes \in [Routes -> SUBSET Interlockings]

  /\ unitConfig = [i \in Interlockings |-> 0]
  /\ votes = [r \in Routes |-> {}]
  /\ cleared = {}

Reconfigure(g) ==
  /\ g # {}
  /\ g # panel
  /\ config < MaxConfig
  /\ config' = config + 1
  /\ panel' = g
  /\ votes' = [r \in Routes |-> {}]
  /\ cleared' = {}
  /\ UNCHANGED unitConfig

Resync(i) ==
  /\ unitConfig[i] < config
  /\ unitConfig' = [unitConfig EXCEPT ![i] = config]

  /\ unitConfig[i] = config
  /\ r \notin cleared
  /\ i \notin votes[r]

  /\ UNCHANGED <<config, panel, unitConfig, cleared>>

  /\ UNCHANGED <<config, panel, unitConfig>>

  \/ \E i \in Interlockings : Resync(i)

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A skyscraper is served by two dispatch controllers — the low-rise controller and the high-rise controller — which were installed by different vendors at different times and know nothing about each other's internals. After a refit they were wired to a single shared pool of cars, so both now write into the same per-car assignment record. Each record holds the car's current call list together with a revision number that the record's own hardware stamps on every accepted write.

Amending a car's assignment is a read-modify-write. The controller reads the record, notes the revision it read, works out the new call list, and writes it back stamped with the next revision. The danger the refit introduced is the classic one: if both controllers read revision n and both write revision n+1, one controller's amendment is silently thrown away — a floor call vanishes and a passenger waits for a car that is never coming. Nothing about the record hardware prevents that; the discipline has to come from outside.

The discipline is a two-level claim. To touch anything, a controller must first take the pool-wide claim, of which there is one. Holding the pool claim, it may then take the per-car claim on one specific car and read that car's record, which stages an amendment: the controller remembers the revision it read as the basis for its write. Having staged, it releases the pool claim so the other controller can get on with a different car, but it keeps the per-car claim until it writes. Writing back bumps the record's revision to one past the basis and releases the per-car claim. A controller may also give up on a staged amendment without writing, releasing the per-car claim and leaving the revision alone. A controller stages at most one amendment at a time, and the record hardware refuses to go past its maximum revision, so a controller only stages against a record that still has room to advance.

The action set is exactly: take the pool-wide claim when it is free; release the pool-wide claim; stage an amendment by taking a free per-car claim while holding the pool claim, on a car whose revision has not reached the maximum, when the controller has nothing staged; write back a staged amendment, bumping the record's revision past the basis and releasing the per-car claim; and abandon a staged amendment, releasing the per-car claim without changing the revision.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a controller has an amendment staged, the basis revision it read is still the record's current revision, so no write can ever be built on a revision that another controller has already superseded.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every staged amendment is eventually resolved — the controller either writes it back or abandons it — so a staged amendment never pins a car's record indefinitely.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS Controllers, Cars, MaxRevision

\* Two independently built dispatch controllers share one pool of car records.
\* Amendments are read-modify-write, so the spec tracks the revision each controller
\* read as the basis of its pending write; the coarse pool claim then the fine per-car
\* claim are what keep that basis from going stale under it.
\* The invariant is the no-lost-update condition, not an exclusion claim.

Free == "free"
Nothing == "nothing"

VARIABLES poolClaim, carClaim, staged, basis, revision
vars == <<poolClaim, carClaim, staged, basis, revision>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ poolClaim \in Controllers \cup {Free}
  /\ carClaim \in [Cars -> Controllers \cup {Free}]
  /\ staged \in [Controllers -> Cars \cup {Nothing}]
  /\ basis \in [Controllers -> 0..MaxRevision]
  /\ revision \in [Cars -> 0..MaxRevision]

Init ==
  /\ poolClaim = Free
  /\ carClaim = [c \in Cars |-> Free]
  /\ staged = [k \in Controllers |-> Nothing]
  /\ basis = [k \in Controllers |-> 0]
  /\ revision = [c \in Cars |-> 0]

TakePool(k) ==
  /\ poolClaim = Free
  /\ poolClaim' = k
  /\ UNCHANGED <<carClaim, staged, basis, revision>>

DropPool(k) ==
  /\ poolClaim = k
  /\ poolClaim' = Free
  /\ UNCHANGED <<carClaim, staged, basis, revision>>

StageAmend(k, c) ==
  /\ poolClaim = k
  /\ staged[k] = Nothing
  /\ carClaim[c] = Free
  /\ revision[c] < MaxRevision
  /\ carClaim' = [carClaim EXCEPT ![c] = k]
  /\ staged' = [staged EXCEPT ![k] = c]
  /\ basis' = [basis EXCEPT ![k] = revision[c]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<poolClaim, revision>>

WriteBack(k) ==
  /\ staged[k] # Nothing
  /\ LET c == staged[k] IN
       /\ revision' = [revision EXCEPT ![c] = basis[k] + 1]
       /\ carClaim' = [carClaim EXCEPT ![c] = Free]
  /\ staged' = [staged EXCEPT ![k] = Nothing]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<poolClaim, basis>>

Abandon(k) ==
  /\ staged[k] # Nothing
  /\ carClaim' = [carClaim EXCEPT ![staged[k]] = Free]
  /\ staged' = [staged EXCEPT ![k] = Nothing]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<poolClaim, basis, revision>>

SomeWriteBack == \E k \in Controllers : WriteBack(k)

Next ==
  \/ \E k \in Controllers : TakePool(k) \/ DropPool(k) \/ WriteBack(k) \/ Abandon(k)
  \/ \E k \in Controllers, c \in Cars : StageAmend(k, c)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ WF_vars(SomeWriteBack)

BasisNeverGoesStale ==
  \A k \in Controllers :
    staged[k] # Nothing => basis[k] = revision[staged[k]]

StagedWorkResolves ==
  \A k \in Controllers : (staged[k] # Nothing) ~> (staged[k] = Nothing)

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
Before the market opens, an exchange runs an opening auction whose order book is a single shared record. Two matching engines write into it: the lit engine that handles ordinary member flow and the auction engine that handles the crossing session. They were built years apart by different teams and neither knows how the other works internally; the refit that merged the two sessions simply pointed both at the same book.

An amendment to the book is prepared as a complete replacement image. An engine that wants to add an order reads the current book, builds the image it intends to install — the book as it read it, plus the new order — and then runs a two-phase commit across the exchange's order-book shards. In the voting phase the engine asks each shard in turn. A shard that is not already committed to another engine's transaction inspects the proposed image and votes yes only if that image still contains everything the shared book currently contains; if the image has fallen behind, the shard refuses and the transaction is torn down. A shard that votes yes is committed to that engine and will not vote for anybody else until the transaction finishes. When every shard has voted yes, the engine commits: the proposed image becomes the book, and every shard the engine was holding is released. An engine may also abandon its transaction at any point, releasing whatever shards it holds.

The hazard this exists to prevent is the ordinary lost update. Both engines read the same book, both build an image from it, and if both were allowed to install their image, whichever installs second silently erases the other's order. An order that a member believes is in the auction but which is not in the book is an unwinnable dispute for the exchange, so the shard vote is the only thing standing between the two engines and that outcome. Orders may also be cancelled outright, but only while the book is quiescent — when neither engine has a transaction in flight.

The action set is exactly: begin an amendment for an engine with nothing in flight, adding an order that is not already in the book and fixing the proposed image; grant a shard's yes-vote to an in-flight engine when the shard is uncommitted and the proposed image still covers the current book; refuse a shard's vote and tear down the transaction when the proposed image no longer covers the book; commit an engine's amendment once every shard has voted yes, installing the image and releasing the shards; abandon an in-flight transaction, releasing its shards; and cancel an order out of the book while no transaction is in flight.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever an engine has collected a yes-vote from every shard, the image it is about to install still contains every order currently in the shared book, so committing it cannot erase another engine's order.

The pickup shelf at a busy library branch is divided into numbered cubbies. When a reserved title comes in, it has to be put somewhere a patron can find it, and the branch's whole retrieval workflow depends on two things staying in agreement: the slip stapled to the book, which says which cubby the book went into, and the shelf index at the desk, which says which book is in each cubby. If those two ever disagree — if a book's slip points at a cubby that the index says holds a different book — then two books have been filed into one cubby and one of them is, for practical purposes, lost.

Incoming titles are handled through a short intake queue. A title that is not already queued, not already shelved, and not sitting in the bounced pile can be added to the queue while the queue is below its depth limit; once the queue is full the desk simply refuses new intake until the clerk works some off. The clerk always deals with the front of the queue. If a cubby is free, the title goes into it and both the slip and the index are written. If every cubby is occupied, the title is bounced instead, and it goes onto the bounced pile from which it can be re-queued later. Either way the front of the queue is consumed, so a full queue always drains.

The branch manager has an override. She can flag a title as urgent — an interlibrary loan going back tomorrow, a reserve for a course that starts in the morning — and a flagged title can be filed straight into a free cubby without waiting its turn, which also pulls it out of the intake queue if it happens to be sitting there. The override skips the queue but not the cubby discipline: she still has to pick a cubby that the index says is empty, and she still writes both the slip and the index. Patrons collect books, which empties the cubby and clears the slip.

The action set is exactly: queue a title that is unqueued, unshelved and not bounced, while the queue is below its depth limit; file the front of the queue into a free cubby, writing slip and index; bounce the front of the queue onto the bounced pile when no cubby is free; re-queue a bounced title by taking it off the pile; collect a shelved title, emptying its cubby and clearing its slip; flag a title as urgent; and use the manager's override to file a flagged, unshelved title directly into an empty cubby, removing it from the intake queue if present.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every title whose slip names a cubby, the shelf index for that cubby names that same title, so no two titles are ever filed into the same cubby.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Whenever the intake queue is at its depth limit and intake is being refused, the queue eventually drops below the limit again, so backpressure at this desk is always temporary.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An online shooter runs a lobby matchmaker. Every player connected to the region is in exactly one of three situations: sitting in the lobby waiting for a game, holding a seat in a match that is being formed, or actually playing. The matchmaker's whole job is to move players between those three situations without ever losing one or cloning one. A player who ends up in neither the lobby nor a match has fallen off the service and will sit staring at a loading screen; a player who somehow appears both in the lobby and in a live match gets matched into a second game while already shooting in the first, which the anti-cheat treats as an exploit.

Forming a match is a two-phase commit with the players' clients as the participants. The matchmaker picks a full team's worth of players out of the lobby and invites them; each invited client is asked to hold a seat. A client that accepts moves its player out of the lobby and into the held state, and its acceptance is recorded. The matchmaker only commits the match once every invited client has accepted, at which point all the held players become playing. If any invited client declines, or if the matchmaker gives up waiting, the attempt is torn down and every player who was holding a seat for that attempt goes straight back to the lobby.

The lobby's network is a best-effort mesh and it does not preserve ordering. Acceptances come back in whatever order the routing happens to deliver them, which need not be the order the invitations went out, and the matchmaker must not assume otherwise: it works from the set of acceptances it has, not from a sequence. That is why acceptance is modelled as an unordered collection and any outstanding invitee may be the next to reply.

The action set is exactly: propose a match by inviting a full team's worth of lobby players when no attempt is in flight; record an acceptance from any outstanding invitee, moving that player out of the lobby into the held state; decline from any outstanding invitee, which tears the attempt down and returns every held player of that attempt to the lobby; commit the attempt once every invitee has accepted, moving all its held players into play; time the attempt out, returning its held players to the lobby; and have a playing player leave their match back to the lobby.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The lobby, the set of players holding seats, and the set of players in a live match always partition the region's player roster — every player is in exactly one of the three, so no player is ever lost or duplicated by a match attempt.

\* a sequence; any outstanding invitee may be the next to reply.
\* The invariant is conservation of the roster: lobby, held and playing partition it.
