===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A consortium of library branches shares one reservation ledger. Reservations are not written by whoever takes the phone call: at any moment exactly one branch holds the reservation authority, and only that branch appends to the ledger. The authority is assigned by epoch-numbered reconfiguration. When the consortium reconfigures, it moves to the next epoch number and names the branch that will hold the authority for that epoch; the epoch-to-branch assignment for an epoch is fixed once and never rewritten, which is what makes the ledger auditable years later.

Branches do not all learn about a reconfiguration at the same time. Each branch carries the epoch number it currently believes is in force, and it stamps that number onto anything it writes. A branch that is behind can be brought up to date, and the consortium periodically runs a gossip round that brings every branch that is currently up to the published epoch in one pass.

Branches also fail, and they fail silently: a branch's server simply stops answering, with no notice to anyone, and it may come back hours later still believing the epoch it believed when it died. That is the dangerous case. A recovered branch that was the authority two epochs ago may well try to append a reservation stamped with its stale epoch number, and if the ledger accepted it the audit trail would show a reservation authorised by a branch that had already been superseded, out of order with everything appended since. Appends are therefore refused unless the appending branch is the authority for the currently published epoch, is up, and believes the currently published epoch. Reconfiguration itself may only be initiated by a branch that is up, and the branch that takes the authority learns the new epoch as part of taking it. The ledger has a fixed number of pages.

The action set is exactly: reconfigure to the next epoch, naming an up branch as the new authority and bringing that branch's believed epoch up to date; run a gossip round that sets every up branch's believed epoch to the published one; crash a branch silently; recover a crashed branch with its believed epoch untouched; and append a reservation for an unreserved title, stamped with the appending branch's believed epoch and name, when that branch is up and is the authority for the published epoch.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every entry in the reservation ledger names, as its author, the branch that was assigned the authority for the epoch stamped on that entry, and the stamped epochs never decrease as the ledger is read from first page to last.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Whenever some branch that is up believes an epoch other than the published one, the consortium eventually reaches a state in which every up branch believes the published epoch.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

\* that never run backwards down the pages.

  /\ down \subseteq Branches
  /\ ledger \in Seq(Entries)

  /\ authorityOf = [e \in 0..MaxEpoch |-> IF e = 0 THEN FirstAuthority ELSE Unassigned]
  /\ believed = [b \in Branches |-> 0]

Reconfigure(b) ==

An automatic car wash moves vehicles through the tunnel on a chain conveyor divided into numbered positions. A car waits in the forecourt, is loaded onto the first position when that position is clear, rides the conveyor one position at a time, and is pushed off the far end into the exit apron, where its driver eventually collects it and drives away. The site's whole accounting rests on knowing where every vehicle on the premises is: a car that the system thinks is nowhere has effectively been lost inside the tunnel, and a car the system thinks is at two positions at once means the conveyor has been double-counted and the next vehicle will be loaded on top of somebody's bonnet.

Advancing the conveyor is not a decision any single component is allowed to make. Position sensors, the brush-pressure monitor and the dryer interlock each vote on whether the chain may move; the chain advances only once a strict majority of them has voted for the current advance. Once the chain moves, all outstanding votes are discarded and the sensors must vote again for the next advance.

The shift manager carries a key card that overrides the vote. When a sensor has failed dirty and the tunnel is backing up, she can force a single advance without a majority. The override is not free: the key card allows only a limited number of forced advances per shift and every use is logged for the site's insurer. What the override does not change is the physical bookkeeping — a forced advance moves the chain exactly the way a voted advance does, pushing the car at the far end onto the exit apron and clearing the first position.

The action set is exactly: a car arrives in the forecourt if it is not already on the premises; a sensor casts its vote for the current advance; the conveyor advances when a strict majority of sensors has voted, discarding the votes; the manager forces an advance without a majority while her override budget lasts, also discarding the votes; a waiting car is loaded onto the first conveyor position when that position is clear; and a car on the exit apron is driven away, leaving the premises.

A regional library consortium runs interlibrary loans. When a patron at one branch asks for a title held elsewhere, the request has to be committed jointly: the lending branch must agree to release the volume, the receiving branch must agree to take custody of it, and both must agree before anything physically moves. The consortium therefore runs each request as a two-phase commit across the branches. The request starts idle, goes out for voting, and each branch that is up records its vote. Once every branch that is currently up has voted, the request is written into the consortium's recovery log and becomes prepared.

Becoming prepared is the moment that costs something. Each branch keeps a holding shelf behind its desk for interlibrary volumes that are inbound or waiting to be collected, and that shelf has a fixed number of spaces. A request that is prepared has already reserved a space on its destination branch's holding shelf, and a request that has been committed occupies one for real. The consortium therefore refuses to let a request become prepared unless the destination branch's shelf can still take it, counting both the reserved spaces and the occupied ones. A patron collecting their volume frees the space again.

Branches crash silently. A branch's desk system goes offline without warning and without telling anybody, and while it is offline it casts no votes; requests in voting simply wait for the branches that are still up. The awkward consequence is that a request can sit prepared indefinitely — in doubt, holding a shelf space, with nobody to hand the volume to. The consortium's recovery manager exists for exactly this: it holds the log and periodically runs an in-doubt sweep that commits every prepared request in the log at once, whether or not the branches involved are currently reachable. Requests may also be committed one at a time on the normal path, and a request that has not yet been committed may be abandoned, returning it to idle and giving back whatever it had reserved.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home installation has several hub controllers wired into a ring, and a set of electronic door locks. Each lock ships with a one-time-programmable key slot: the household master key can be burned into the slot exactly once, and after that the slot is spent. There is no erase. A lock whose slot has been spent still works, but it can never be re-keyed, so a second burn attempt is not merely wasteful — it is the event the installer's audit is designed to catch, because it means the hub believed a lock was unkeyed when it was not.

Only the hub currently holding the ring token may drive a burn, and the token moves round the ring one hop at a time. The hubs share a work order: a short list of locks scheduled to be keyed. The token holder may add a lock to the work order if the lock's slot is still fresh and the lock is not already on the list, and the token holder may burn the lock at the front of the work order, which spends that lock's slot, writes the holder's identity into the lock's burn record, and takes the lock off the front of the list.

The hubs in this installation are slow, not broken. A hub that is busy — running a firmware check, waiting on a congested radio channel, mid-way through a scene update — will hang on to the token rather than passing it on, and the ring simply waits. It always finishes eventually and passes the token along; no hub ever drops off the ring or loses the token. Slowness therefore costs latency, not correctness.

There is one other way a slot gets spent. An installer standing at the door panel can burn a lock by hand. Because the installer cannot see the hubs' work order and the hubs cannot see the installer, hand burning is only permitted on a lock the hubs have not scheduled; that restriction is what keeps the two routes from racing for the same slot. A hand burn also writes a burn record, naming the installer rather than a hub.

The action set is exactly: pass the token one hop round the ring, provided the current holder is not busy; make a hub busy; let a busy hub finish and stop being busy; schedule a lock onto the work order, by the token holder, when the lock's slot is fresh and the lock is not already scheduled; burn the lock at the front of the work order, by the token holder, spending its slot and writing the burn record; and hand burn an unscheduled lock with a fresh slot at the door panel, writing an installer burn record.

A regional blood service tracks its plasma stock in whole donation units. Every unit the service owns is in exactly one of three places: on the shelf at one of the depots, in quarantine at a depot pending a repeat screening result, or on a van somewhere between depots. The service's regulator does not care where a unit is on any given day, but it cares enormously that the arithmetic closes: the total across shelves, quarantine and vans must always equal the stock the service is accountable for. A unit that goes missing from the count is a unit that cannot be traced to a recipient, and a unit that appears from nowhere means a transfer was double-counted.

Moving stock between depots is not a unilateral decision. A depot proposes a transfer — so many units, from this depot to that one — and the depots then vote on it. The proposal is only executed once strictly more than half the depots have voted for it, at which point the units leave the sending depot's shelf and go onto the van as stock in transit to the destination. A proposal can also be dropped without executing, which discards the votes.

The depots communicate over a store-and-forward network that makes no ordering promise at all. Votes on a proposal are collected as a set, not as a sequence: they arrive in whatever order the network happens to deliver them and the proposer must not assume the order it sent the requests in. The same is true of arrivals — vans are unloaded at whichever depot happens to have a free bay first, so the receipt of stock in transit is not tied to the order in which shipments were dispatched. To stop stock sitting on vans indefinitely, the service also runs a nightly round that unloads every van at once.

Quarantine works locally: a depot can move units off its shelf into quarantine while a repeat screen is pending, and can release quarantined units back to the shelf when the screen comes back clean. Neither movement changes the total.

The action set is exactly: propose a transfer of a positive number of units from one depot to a different depot, when no proposal is outstanding and the sender's shelf covers it; cast a depot's vote on the outstanding proposal; execute the outstanding proposal once a strict majority has voted, moving the units onto a van bound for the destination; drop the outstanding proposal, discarding its votes; unload the van stock waiting for one depot onto that depot's shelf; run the nightly round that unloads every depot's van stock at once; move units from a depot's shelf into quarantine; and release quarantined units back onto the shelf.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total number of units on depot shelves, in quarantine, and in transit on vans is always exactly the stock the service is accountable for.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Stock never stays on a van forever — whenever any depot has stock in transit, every depot's in-transit stock is eventually unloaded onto its shelf.

A busy airport is worked by two approach control positions — the north arrivals desk and the south arrivals desk — that were commissioned years apart and run on separate consoles. They are independent in every respect except one: they draw landing slots from a single shared pool for the same runway complex, and the pool has a hard size. Only so many aircraft can be committed to final approach at once, and the number depends on which runway configuration is in force.

The runway configuration changes during the day. A wind shift, a closure for a rubber removal crew, a switch to reduced separation in good visibility — each of these is published as a reconfiguration under the next configuration number, and each publication comes with the pool size that applies from then on. Because a reconfiguration can shrink the pool, slots that were granted under the previous configuration cannot simply be carried across; a desk that is still working to a superseded configuration is holding slots that the new configuration may not have room for. So a desk that finds itself behind the published configuration adopts the new one, which means surrendering everything it was holding and starting again under the new number. The two desks adopt independently, and the tower also runs a sweep that pulls every desk that is behind onto the published configuration in one go.

A desk that is working to the published configuration may take a free slot from the pool for an inbound aircraft, provided the pool still has room counting the slots both desks are holding under the published configuration. A university enrols students into capped courses through a registration engine that will not act on any single office's word. The line is only restarted once every bay is empty, so no vehicle can be sitting in a bay under a stale ticket when the conveyor starts moving again. A hospital blood bank keeps its inventory in a set of monitored fridges, and the arrangement of that inventory is governed by a storage plan. The plan says how many units a single fridge shelf assembly may hold — a figure that moves with the fridge model in use, the shelf inserts fitted, and the standing order in force for reserved capacity. Whenever any of that changes, the bank publishes a new storage plan under the next plan number.

Republishing a plan is disruptive on purpose. Every unit in the bank has to be re-shelved under the new plan, because the plan is what the audit reconciles against, and a unit sitting on a shelf under a superseded plan number cannot be shown to be stored correctly. Individual units can also be shelved one at a time into a fridge with room, and a unit can be pulled off a shelf back onto the trolley — for a crossmatch, for a temperature excursion check, for a label reprint. holding a lock while it decides, a controller working on behalf of some
aircraft first takes a snapshot of a slot's current version number, works out
whether the slot looks free, and only later attempts to commit that decision.
The commit is only honored if the slot's version has not moved since the
snapshot was taken and no other aircraft currently holds the slot; otherwise
the attempt is simply rejected and the controller must go back and take a
fresh snapshot to retry. Because these snapshot and commit messages travel
independently and are not guaranteed to arrive in the order they were sent,
several aircraft's attempts -- for the same slot or different ones -- can be
resolved in essentially any order. The full action set is: (1) StartRead, in
which a controller for an aircraft that currently holds no slot takes a fresh
snapshot of some slot's live version number; (2) CommitSuccess, in which a
previously taken snapshot is acted on, and because its version still matches
the slot's live version and no aircraft currently holds that slot, the
aircraft is assigned the slot and the slot's version is bumped; (3)
CommitFail, in which a previously taken snapshot is acted on but is found to
be stale (the version moved) or the slot is already taken, so the attempt is
simply discarded and the controller's retry count for that aircraft goes up;
and (4) Release, in which an aircraft that holds a slot gives it up, which
also bumps that slot's version so that any other aircraft's outstanding
stale snapshot for it is invalidated. No matter how many attempts race each
other or how their snapshot-and-commit messages get reordered, two different
aircraft must never end up holding the exact same runway slot.

the same time, no matter how snapshot-and-commit messages for optimistic
locking attempts are reordered or retried.

During the opening auction of a stock exchange, matched orders move shares between settlement accounts. Instead of locking both the seller's and buyer's account for the whole transfer, the settlement engine uses optimistic concurrency: each order first records a snapshot of the current version numbers on the seller and buyer accounts it will touch, without changing any balance yet. The four actions in this system are: an order taking a fresh version snapshot of its seller and buyer accounts, an order applying its transfer once both snapshotted versions still match, an order aborting because the seller account's version moved, and an order aborting because the buyer account's version moved. (* roster (capacity) can grow or shrink at runtime. Only the elected      *)

(* failover re-elects a leader whenever the fleet goes leaderless.        *)

ASSUME NoLeader \notin Robot

    /\ leader \in Robot \cup {NoLeader}
    /\ active \subseteq Robot

    /\ leader = NoLeader
    /\ active = Robot

    /\ active' = active \cup {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<term, leader, using>>

    /\ leader # r
    /\ Cardinality(active) > 1
    /\ active' = active \ {r}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<term, leader, using>>

    /\ leader = NoLeader
    /\ leader' = r
    /\ term' = (term + 1) % MaxTerm

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home door lock network issues temporary guest access credentials across all of a home's doors at once, using a hierarchical locking scheme. A single coarse, home-wide lock admits only one guest-issuance transaction at a time and immediately reserves that transaction's slot against the home's configured limit on simultaneously active guest credentials. Once admitted, the transaction takes a fine-grained lock on each individual door in turn to write the new credential into that door's local memory, then releases the door's lock and sends an acknowledgement back to the hub confirming the write.

The twist is that these per-door write acknowledgements travel through an unordered network buffer, so they can arrive late or out of order -- and in particular, an acknowledgement can still be in flight when its own issuance transaction gets cancelled (for example, if the guest declines partway through setup). The hub handles this by only crediting an acknowledgement toward an issuance's progress if the sender is still the currently active coarse-lock holder; a stale acknowledgement that arrives after its issuance has already been cancelled is simply dropped rather than mistakenly counted.

The full action set is: StartIssue(g), where guest g's issuance transaction takes the coarse lock, provided no other issuance is in progress and the home is under its configured limit on active credentials -- this is the point where g's capacity slot is reserved; AcquireFineWrite(g, d), where the current coarse-lock holder g takes the fine lock on door d to write g's credential there; ReleaseFineAndAck(g, d), where g releases door d's fine lock and sends the write's acknowledgement into the network; ProcessAck(g, d), where a previously sent acknowledgement from g for door d is delivered -- it counts toward g's progress only if g is still the current coarse-lock holder, and is otherwise dropped as stale; FinishIssue(g), where g's transaction completes once every door has been written, releasing the coarse lock; CancelIssue(g), where g's transaction is abandoned before every door was written, releasing the coarse lock and g's reserved capacity slot immediately; and Revoke(g), where a guest g with an already-active credential has it revoked, freeing its capacity slot for reuse.

SAFETY PROPERTY: the number of simultaneously active guest credentials never exceeds the home's configured limit, no matter how the per-door write acknowledgements are delayed, reordered, or rendered stale by a cancelled issuance.

\* this is the single point that enforces the bound, regardless of how

A neighborhood print shop runs several printer workers off one job spooler.
Every job starts out sitting in an intake pile before it is released into the
shop's active spool. Once released, ownership of a job is protected by a
compare-and-swap register: a printer worker may only become a job's owner by
successfully CAS-ing the job's owner register from "unowned" to itself, which
only succeeds if no other worker currently owns that job. Actually printing a
job -- ink physically hitting paper -- is a separate, irreversible action
that a worker may only perform while it owns the job, and it too is guarded
by a compare-and-swap: the worker CAS-es the job's print counter from 0 to 1,
which can only ever succeed once per job, so a given job can never be
physically printed a second time.

The twist is that a printer worker can crash silently at any moment,
including while it currently owns a job it has not yet printed. A crashed
worker does nothing further -- it never prints and never claims another job.

by the crashed worker that has not yet been printed and CAS-es its owner
register back to "unowned" (expected value: the crashed worker) so a
different, still-working worker can claim it and finish the job. Reclaim only
ever touches a job that has not yet been printed, so it can never itself
cause a job to be printed twice.

The full action set is:
  - Spool(j): a job j sitting in the intake pile is released into the active
    spool, making it eligible for a worker to claim.
  - Claim(w, j): a non-crashed worker w that does not currently own any other

  - Print(w, j): a non-crashed worker w that owns job j CAS-es the job's

    its ownership of the job.
  - Crash(w): at most one worker, chosen nondeterministically, crashes

  - Reclaim(j): a job j still owned by the crashed worker, and not yet

  - Archive(j): a job j that has already been physically printed is filed
    into the shop's completed-jobs archive, a separate clerical bookkeeping
    step that happens strictly after printing and can never affect whether
    or how many times a job gets printed.

is ever physically printed more than once.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every job that starts out in the intake pile is eventually
printed exactly once, even though the worker that first claims it may crash
silently before finishing it.

One of the participant hospitals can crash silently at any point in the protocol -- once crashed it stops casting further votes for the round it was in, but the coordinator can still (eventually) resolve the round: it may only commit a round if every participant, including one that later turns out to be unresponsive, actually voted YES before the crash, and it must abort any round in which a participant crashed before voting. A regional stock exchange runs a single-threaded opening-auction price-discovery
engine. Before the opening bell, member firms submit indicative order requests
that must each be fed, one at a time, into the auction engine so it can fold
that firm's interest into the running opening-price calculation. Because the
exchange's inbound gateway can reorder packets under load, requests do not
arrive at the engine's intake queue in the order the firms sent them -- the
intake queue is modeled as an unordered pool of pending requests rather than a
FIFO, so any pending request can be the next one pulled into the engine
regardless of when it was submitted.

The intake queue is a bounded work queue with backpressure: it can hold at
most the queue's current live capacity worth of pending requests at once,
starting at QueueCap. A firm whose request arrives while the queue is full is
not queued at all -- it is immediately rejected (backpressure signal) and
must resubmit later once the queue has drained enough to accept it again (a
retry). The auction engine itself is a single critical resource: at most one
firm's request may be "in the engine" being folded into the price
calculation at any moment, and while an engine slot is occupied no other
firm's request may be pulled in. Separately, exchange operations can raise
the intake queue's live capacity mid-session (for example by provisioning
more gateway throughput before a busy open), one unit at a time up to a
fixed ceiling MaxQueueCap; this capacity only ever grows, so it can loosen
backpressure but never suddenly reject a request that was already accepted.

The full action set is:
  - Submit(w): a waiting firm w hands its request to the intake queue, which
    succeeds only if the queue currently has room under its current live
    capacity.
  - Reject(w): a waiting firm w's request arrives while the queue is full
    (at its current live capacity), so it is dropped by backpressure and
    marked rejected instead of queued.
  - Retry(w): a previously rejected firm w resubmits its request, which
    succeeds only if the queue currently has room under its current live
    capacity.
  - Admit: whenever the engine is free and the intake queue is non-empty, one
    pending request is pulled from the pool nondeterministically (reflecting
    that reordering means arrival order is not preserved) and occupies the
    sole engine slot.
  - Release: the firm currently occupying the engine slot finishes being
    folded into the opening price and is marked served, freeing the slot.
  - Expand: exchange operations raise the intake queue's live capacity by
    one, provided it has not yet reached the fixed ceiling MaxQueueCap.
  - Shrink: exchange operations lower the intake queue's live capacity by
    one under load-shedding, provided it has not yet fallen back to the
    original QueueCap floor; firms already pending, in the engine, or
    served are unaffected -- only future Submit/Retry admissions face the
    tighter limit.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At every reachable state, at most one firm's request occupies
the auction engine's single processing slot at a time.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every member firm that starts out waiting to submit its
opening-auction request is eventually served by the engine, even though its
first attempt may be bounced by backpressure and its request may be pulled
into the engine out of submission order due to reordering.

\* Workers are member firms; the intake queue is an unordered pool (not a
\* sequence) because the gateway can reorder arrivals, so Admit may pull any
\* pending request next regardless of submission order. MutualExclusion
\* protects the single-slot auction engine: holders never grows past size 1.
\* cap is the queue's live capacity: it only ever grows (bounded by
\* MaxQueueCap), so raising it can loosen Submit/Reject but never blocks or
\* reverses progress already made toward admitting and serving a firm.

\* A waiting firm enters the bounded queue if there is room under the
\* current live capacity.

             /\ UNCHANGED <<rejected, holders, served, cap>>

\* Backpressure: a waiting firm arriving while the queue is full is dropped.
Reject(w) == w \in waiting /\ PendingCount = cap

             /\ UNCHANGED <<pending, holders, served, cap>>

\* A rejected firm resubmits once the queue has room again.
Retry(w) == w \in rejected /\ PendingCount < cap

\* mid-session. Monotonic and bounded, so it can only ever relax the

MutualExclusion == Cardinality(holders) <= 1

An airport baggage router moves bags toward the loading bay for their assigned flight. Each bag has a manifest slot with a version counter, and loading a bag onto its flight is irreversible: once done it cannot be undone or repeated. Handlers process bags using optimistic locking with retry instead of exclusive locks: a handler snapshots a bag's current slot version, does other work, and then attempts a compare-and-swap against that snapshot; if the slot's version has not moved, the compare-and-swap succeeds and the load happens; if it has moved, the handler must refresh its snapshot and try again.

Concretely, the full action set is: (1) StartAttempt — an idle handler picks a bag that has not yet been loaded and snapshots that bag's current slot version, becoming busy on it; (2) LoadSuccess — a busy handler whose snapshot still matches the bag's current slot version performs the irreversible load: the bag's load count moves from 0 to 1, the slot version is bumped, and the handler becomes idle again; (3) RetryAfterConflict — a busy handler whose snapshot no longer matches the bag's current slot version, and whose bag is still not loaded, refreshes its snapshot to the current version so it can attempt again later; (4) AbandonCompleted — a busy handler discovers that the bag it was working on has already been loaded by someone else in the meantime, and gives up on it, becoming idle; (5) RescanSlot — the router's manifest system may, a strictly limited number of times overall, revise a not-yet-loaded bag's slot (for example, a late gate reassignment), bumping its version and invalidating any handler's outstanding snapshot for that bag, which forces a later retry; (6) CrashHandler — the twist: at most one handler, at any point, may silently crash and permanently stop taking any further action, abandoning whatever it was doing without releasing any exclusive resource (there is none, since locking here is optimistic), so other handlers are never blocked by it.

A group of banks settle a shared end-of-day net position through a single
settlement coordinator cluster. Exactly one coordinator is the elected leader
at any moment, and leadership can fail over to a different coordinator at any
time (leader election with failover). Each pending settlement instruction
must be folded into one shared settlement record whose optimistic version
number advances by exactly one with every successful update. Because more
than one instruction can be in flight in the coordinator's working set at
once, each instruction first reads (prepares against) the record's current
version before it is allowed to write; it may only actually commit its
result if the version it read is still exactly the record's current version
at the moment it tries to commit. If some other instruction committed in the
meantime, the read is stale and the write must be discarded (aborted) rather
than blindly applied, because applying a write based on a stale version would
silently overwrite -- and thereby lose -- whatever the intervening commit had
already recorded.

The twist is that the coordinator's working capacity -- the maximum number of
instructions that may be simultaneously prepared (holding a read of the
record's version) but not yet committed -- can change at runtime as the
cluster is resized up or down; the safety of the settlement record must not
depend on holding that capacity fixed. Leadership failover is likewise
independent of the per-instruction optimistic check: a change of leader never
resets or forges an instruction's recorded read-version, so the version-based
guard keeps working exactly the same way no matter who is currently leader.

The full action set is:
  - Prepare(u): an instruction u that has not yet committed and is not
    currently holding a read snapshots the settlement record's current
    version, provided the number of instructions currently holding a
    snapshot is below the coordinator's current capacity.
  - Commit(u): an instruction u whose held snapshot exactly equals the
    record's current version plus one writes that snapshot in as the
    record's new version and records that same value as u's commit version,
    releasing its snapshot; this is the only way the shared record's version
    advances.
  - Abort(u): an instruction u whose held snapshot has gone stale (no longer
    equal to the record's current version plus one) because some other
    instruction committed in the meantime releases its snapshot without
    writing anything, so it can retry later with a fresh read.
  - Withdraw(u): an instruction u whose held snapshot is still exactly
    current (equal to the record's current version plus one, i.e. not
    stale) voluntarily gives up that snapshot without committing -- for
    example a business decision to cancel the settlement instruction --
    releasing its snapshot without writing anything. This is distinct from
    Abort: Withdraw only applies to a still-fresh snapshot, Abort only to
    an already-stale one, so the two guards never overlap for the same
    instruction.
  - Failover(l): leadership moves to a different coordinator l; this changes
    only who is recognized as leader and never touches the settlement
    record, capacity, or any instruction's held snapshot.
  - CapacityUp: the coordinator cluster is resized up, raising the maximum
    number of concurrently prepared instructions by one (up to a fixed
    ceiling).
  - CapacityDown: the coordinator cluster is resized down, lowering the
    maximum number of concurrently prepared instructions by one (down to a
    fixed floor).

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every settlement instruction that has ever committed,
the version number it recorded for itself at commit time never exceeds the
settlement record's current version -- no instruction's already-recorded
commit is ever left stranded ahead of the record itself, which is exactly
what would happen if a stale, superseded write were ever allowed through and
silently lost a later instruction's already-applied update.

A consortium of banks runs a nightly interbank settlement batch. Each participating bank must, in turn, acquire exclusive use of the single shared clearing account (the critical resource that actually posts debits and credits between banks) before it can settle its net position; only one bank may hold the clearing account at a time. Because only a limited number of banks can be mid-flight at once, admission to the clearing account is mediated by a bounded work queue: a bank that wants to settle first enqueues a settlement request, and if the queue is already at its capacity the bank is subject to backpressure and simply cannot enqueue yet -- it must wait for room to open up. When the clearing account is free and the queue is non-empty, the bank at the head of the queue is dequeued and granted exclusive use of the clearing account. Once a bank finishes posting its settlement it releases the clearing account and is marked settled. A container-ship crane yard moves a fixed number of shipping containers among a small set of storage locations (for example the ship's hold, the yard stack, and a truck chassis). ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A container-ship crane yard runs a small pool of gantry cranes that load
containers onto a departing ship. Every container destined for the ship must
first pass through a bounded dispatch queue before a crane can pick it up:
the dispatcher can hold at most QueueCap containers waiting for a crane at
once. A container whose turn to enter the dispatch queue comes up while the
queue is already full is bounced by backpressure and marked as bounced; a
bounced container must be resubmitted later once the queue has room again.
Once a container reaches the front of the dispatch queue, an idle crane (one
not already carrying another container) picks it up. Loading a container
onto the ship is irreversible -- once a crane has actually swung a given
container aboard, that specific container can never be loaded a second time.

The twist is that a crane can crash silently while it is carrying a
container it has picked up but not yet loaded. A crashed crane freezes
exactly where it was -- it never loads its container and never picks up
another one. To keep the yard moving, a reassignment step notices when a
container is still attached to a crashed crane and returns that container to
the dispatch queue so a different, working crane can pick it up and load it;
reassignment only ever happens to a container that has not yet been loaded,
so it can never cause a container to be loaded twice.

The full action set is:
  - Submit(k): a waiting container k enters the dispatch queue, provided the
    queue currently has room under QueueCap.
  - Bounce(k): a waiting container k arrives while the queue is full, so it
    is bounced by backpressure instead of queued.
  - Retry(k): a previously bounced container k re-enters the dispatch queue
    once the queue has room again.
  - Assign(cr, k): an idle, non-crashed crane cr picks up container k from
    the front of the dispatch queue.
  - Load(cr, k): crane cr, currently carrying container k, irreversibly
    loads k onto the ship; this can only ever happen once per container.
  - Crash(cr): at most one crane, chosen nondeterministically, crashes
    silently while carrying whatever container it currently holds (if any).
  - Reassign(k): a container k still attached to a crashed crane, and not
    yet loaded, is returned to the dispatch queue so another crane can take
    it over.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No container is ever loaded onto the ship more than once --
for every container, the number of times it has been loaded never exceeds
one.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every container that starts out waiting for the dispatch
queue is eventually loaded onto the ship exactly once, even though it may
first be bounced by backpressure and even though the crane that first picks
it up may crash silently before loading it.

A university's course-registration system lets a fixed set of registration terminals write to a single shared enrollment ledger (the resource that actually commits seat assignments). Exclusive write access to the ledger is granted by a single circulating token that moves around the terminals in a fixed ring order (each terminal has one designated next-terminal in the ring). Only the terminal currently holding the token may open the ledger for writing; when it is done it closes the ledger and passes the token on to the next terminal in the ring. Once the token is lost because its holder crashed, any other still-live terminal may mint a freshly numbered replacement token for itself so registration can eventually resume, but a crashed terminal itself may never again request access, hold the token, or write to the ledger.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A hospital's operating-room scheduler controls how many procedures may run at once, bounded by the number of anesthesia teams the hospital can staff at the same time (its concurrency capacity), not by the number of physical rooms. Surgical teams request a time-bounded lease on that shared capacity before starting a procedure, and must eventually release it (or let it expire) when done. Communication between a surgical team's terminal and the central scheduler runs over an unreliable hospital network where acquire and release messages can be reordered in transit -- a release sent after an acquire can arrive at the scheduler before it, or a stale duplicate can arrive late -- so the scheduler tags every message with a per-team sequence number and only honors a message if its sequence number is strictly newer than the last one it already applied for that team; older or duplicate messages are silently dropped.

The full set of actions is:
1. SendAcquire(t): a team t that does not currently hold a capacity lease sends a freshly sequenced "acquire" message into the network.
2. SendRelease(t): a team t that currently holds a capacity lease sends a freshly sequenced "release" message into the network.
3. DeliverMessage(m): the scheduler picks any message currently in the network (delivery order is unconstrained, modeling reordering) and processes it: if the message's sequence number is not newer than the last one already applied for that team, it is dropped with no effect; otherwise the scheduler records it as the newest applied sequence number for that team, and if it is an "acquire" it grants the lease (recording an expiry time) only if the number of currently held leases is still below capacity, and if it is a "release" it frees the team's lease immediately.
4. ExpireLease(t): a team t holding a lease whose recorded expiry time has passed has its lease reclaimed automatically by the scheduler, even if no release message was ever delivered.
5. Tick: the global clock advances by one unit, up to a bounded horizon.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At every reachable state, the number of teams simultaneously holding a granted capacity lease never exceeds the hospital's fixed concurrency capacity, no matter what order the acquire, release, and expiry events are delivered or interleaved in.

\* auto-reclaims once its recorded expiry passes, even without a release
\* message. Because the network can reorder acquire/release messages, the
\* scheduler only applies a message whose sequence number is strictly newer
\* than the last one it already applied for that team -- this is what keeps
\* stale or duplicate deliveries from corrupting the capacity count below.

    /\ leaseExpiry \in [Teams -> 0..(MaxTime + MaxLeaseTerm)]

    /\ now = 0
    /\ teamSeq = [t \in Teams |-> 0]
    /\ lastSeq = [t \in Teams |-> 0]
    /\ network = {}
    /\ leaseHeld = [t \in Teams |-> FALSE]
    /\ leaseExpiry = [t \in Teams |-> 0]

ActiveCount == Cardinality({t \in Teams : leaseHeld[t]})

SendAcquire(t) ==
    /\ ~leaseHeld[t]
    /\ teamSeq[t] < MaxSeq
    /\ teamSeq' = [teamSeq EXCEPT ![t] = @ + 1]
    /\ network' = network \cup {<<t, "acquire", teamSeq[t] + 1>>}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<now, lastSeq, leaseHeld, leaseExpiry>>

    /\ teamSeq[t] < MaxSeq
    /\ teamSeq' = [teamSeq EXCEPT ![t] = @ + 1]

\* which is exactly what lets the network reorder messages.

\* catches up to the current epoch -- it may be slow to do so (patchy field

    /\ roster \subseteq Drones

\* reports are scoped to the epoch during which they were filed.

\* and processes the latest reconfiguration, catching its own epoch up to

An airport baggage router moves bags through a physical sortation corridor that is shared by several zone controllers. Each bag has a shared routing record consisting of a version counter that must be bumped every time some zone controller updates it. ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A small group of banks runs a periodic interbank settlement batch. Only one bank may hold exclusive access to the shared settlement ledger (the critical resource) at a time, so that it can compute and post net positions without another bank's concurrent writes corrupting the batch. Access is not granted by a simple lock but by quorum voting: each bank has a single pledge (vote) it can hold at any moment, and a bank that wants the ledger must collect pledges from at least a quorum of banks (counting its own) before it may enter. A participant bank can be arbitrarily slow to respond to a vote request -- it never crashes or refuses outright, it just may take a long time -- and the protocol must still make progress despite that.

The full set of actions is:
1. Request: an idle bank whose own single vote-token is currently free asks for the ledger. It stamps its request with the next tick of a shared logical clock (an older tick means higher priority) and immediately pledges its own vote to itself. (A bank whose vote-token is presently lent out to another requester must wait for that pledge to come back before it can start its own request, so a lent-out vote is never silently orphaned.)
2. CastVote: a bank whose pledge is currently free backs some other requesting bank's bid, handing that requester its pledge.
3. Preempt: if a bank's pledge is currently sitting with some requester that has a strictly later (lower-priority) timestamp than another, still-waiting requester, the bank reclaims its pledge from the lower-priority requester and gives it to the higher-priority one instead. This is what keeps a slow voter from permanently stalling an older, higher-priority request -- eventually every outstanding pledge gets sorted toward whichever pending request has been waiting longest.
4. Enter: once a requesting bank has collected pledges from at least a quorum of banks, it is granted exclusive access to the ledger.
5. Release: the bank holding the ledger finishes settlement and releases it, freeing every pledge that was sitting with it so those banks are available to help the next requester.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At every reachable state, at most one bank holds exclusive access to the settlement ledger at the same time.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every bank that is waiting for the ledger is eventually granted exclusive access to it, even though some voters may be arbitrarily slow to cast or reassign their pledge, as long as they are never permanently failed.

\* access to the shared settlement ledger (the critical resource) so that
\* net positions are computed without interference. Access is granted not by
\* a lock but by quorum voting: a requester needs pledges from enough banks
\* (Quorum of them, counting itself) before it may enter. Because a bank can
\* be slow to respond but never fails outright, a pledge it is still sitting
\* on can be reclaimed by an older, higher-priority request (Preempt) so that
\* a slow voter can never permanently stall someone else's progress.

TypeOK ==
    /\ pc \in [Banks -> {"idle", "reqing", "holding"}]
    /\ ts \in [Banks -> Nat]
    /\ clock \in Nat
    /\ votedFor \in [Banks -> Banks \cup {NoBank}]
    /\ votes \in [Banks -> SUBSET Banks]

Init ==
    /\ pc = [b \in Banks |-> "idle"]
    /\ ts = [b \in Banks |-> 0]
    /\ clock = 0
    /\ votedFor = [b \in Banks |-> NoBank]
    /\ votes = [b \in Banks |-> {}]

\* An idle bank asks for the ledger, stamping its request with the next tick
\* of the shared clock (older tick = higher priority) and immediately
\* pledging its own vote to itself. A bank may only start a request while its
\* own single vote-token is free, so a vote it lent out elsewhere is never
\* silently orphaned in another requester's tally.
Request(b) ==
    /\ pc[b] = "idle"
    /\ votedFor[b] = NoBank
    /\ clock < MaxClock
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![b] = "reqing"]
    /\ ts' = [ts EXCEPT ![b] = clock]
    /\ clock' = clock + 1
    /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![b] = b]
    /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![b] = {b}]

\* A currently unpledged bank v backs some requester b's bid.
CastVote(v, b) ==
    /\ votedFor[v] = NoBank
    /\ v # b
    /\ pc[b] = "reqing"
    /\ v \notin votes[b]
    /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![v] = b]
    /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![b] = @ \cup {v}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pc, ts, clock>>

\* The slow-but-not-failed twist: if v's pledge is currently sitting with a
\* requester cur that is strictly younger (later timestamp) than b, v may
\* reclaim its pledge from cur and give it to the older, higher-priority
\* request b instead -- this is what keeps a slow voter from stalling
\* everyone else forever.
Preempt(v, b) ==
    LET cur == votedFor[v] IN
    /\ cur # NoBank
    /\ cur # b
    /\ pc[b] = "reqing"
    /\ pc[cur] = "reqing"
    /\ ts[b] < ts[cur]
    /\ v \notin votes[b]
    /\ votedFor' = [votedFor EXCEPT ![v] = b]
    /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![cur] = @ \ {v}, ![b] = @ \cup {v}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<pc, ts, clock>>

\* granted exclusive access to the ledger.

    /\ Cardinality(votes[b]) >= Quorum
    /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![b] = "holding"]

\* pledge that was sitting with it so those banks can help someone else next.
Release(b) ==

    /\ votedFor' = [v \in Banks |-> IF votedFor[v] = b THEN NoBank ELSE votedFor[v]]
    /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![b] = {}]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<ts, clock>>

    \/ \E v, b \in Banks : CastVote(v, b)
    \/ \E v, b \in Banks : Preempt(v, b)
    \/ \E b \in Banks : Enter(b)
    \/ \E b \in Banks : Release(b)

\* Mutual exclusion of the critical resource: at most one bank ever holds
\* exclusive access to the settlement ledger at once.
AtMostOneHolder == Cardinality({b \in Banks : pc[b] = "holding"}) <= 1

\* Every bank that is waiting for the ledger eventually gets it, despite

RequestEventuallyGranted == \A b \in Banks : (pc[b] = "reqing") ~> (pc[b] = "holding")

====

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A container-ship crane yard tracks how many containers currently sit in its staging area against a capacity bound that yard operations can raise or lower at runtime (for example, closing off part of the yard for maintenance, or reopening it later). Gantry cranes place containers into the staging area using an optimistic, versioned update: a crane first snapshots the current occupancy count and a version number, then later tries to commit one more container by comparing the live version against the one it snapshotted. If the version has moved (someone else committed in the meantime) the crane refreshes its snapshot and retries. If the version still matches but the yard's live, current capacity bound has no room left for one more container, the crane abandons this attempt and may start a fresh one later. Critically, the commit step always re-checks the *current* capacity, never a cached value from when the crane started -- so a capacity reduction that happens mid-attempt is still respected. Separately, containers also depart the yard from time to time, freeing up room and advancing the version counter just like a commit does.

The full set of actions is:
1. ChangeCapacity: yard operations set a new capacity bound, chosen freely within the allowed range but never below the number of containers currently occupying the staging area (operations cannot strand already-placed containers), independent of any crane's in-progress attempt.
2. StartAttempt(c): an idle crane snapshots the current version and occupancy count and moves into an in-progress attempt.
3. CommitAttempt(c): a crane with an in-progress attempt whose snapshotted version still matches the live version, and for whom the live occupancy is still below the live capacity, commits one more container -- occupancy and version both advance -- and returns to idle.
4. RetryStale(c): a crane with an in-progress attempt whose snapshotted version no longer matches the live version (someone else committed or a container departed) refreshes its snapshot and keeps trying.
5. RetryFull(c): a crane with an in-progress attempt whose snapshotted version still matches the live version, but whose live occupancy has reached the live capacity, abandons the attempt and returns to idle.
6. Depart: one container leaves the staging area, decrementing occupancy and advancing the version counter.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At every reachable state, the number of containers occupying the staging area never exceeds the yard's current capacity bound, even though that bound can change at runtime and cranes commit optimistically with retries rather than holding an exclusive lock.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A container-ship crane yard is divided into zones, and each zone contains several bays. Each bay holds a shared manifest record (the recorded container count for that bay) that traveling gantry cranes must update whenever they move containers through it. To touch a bay's record, a crane must first acquire the zone's coarse-grained lock, then acquire the bay's fine-grained lock nested inside it; only after holding both does it read the record and later commit a new value. A crane can be slow -- it may take an arbitrarily long time between reading the record and committing its new value, or between committing and releasing the coarse zone lock -- but it never crashes or abandons its locks, so it always eventually finishes its cycle.

The full set of actions is:
1. AcquireZone(c): an idle crane picks some bay, and if that bay's zone lock is free, takes the zone lock and marks itself as holding the zone.
2. AcquireBay(c): a crane holding its chosen bay's zone lock takes the bay's fine lock (if free) and immediately snapshots the bay's current manifest value into its own local reading.
3. StartWrite(c): a crane that has snapshotted the record (and may have been slow up to this point) moves to the writing phase, still holding both locks.
4. CommitWrite(c): a crane in the writing phase picks a new record value and writes it into the bay's manifest, then releases the bay's fine lock, without yet releasing the zone lock.
5. ReleaseZone(c): a crane that has committed its write releases the zone lock and returns to idle, free to start a new cycle on any bay.

Because a crane holds the bay's fine lock exclusively from the moment it snapshots the record until it commits, no other crane can modify that bay's manifest value in between -- so the update a crane commits is never silently clobbered by, or built on top of, someone else's concurrent write. The hierarchical (coarse-then-fine) locking is what makes this true even though individual cranes may dawdle for a long time between phases.

A container-ship terminal operates two independent crane-yard control instances (a north-side crane team and a south-side crane team) that share one physical container-storage pool of bounded capacity. Each instance manages its own local numbering of storage slots, but every container either instance places ultimately occupies space in the same shared pool, so the two instances must coordinate before adding anything. Admission into the pool follows a two-level, hierarchical scheme that mirrors coarse-then-fine locking: an instance must first hold the single, pool-wide admission permit (the coarse level, held by at most one instance at a time) before it is allowed to make a fine-grained reservation of one of its own local slots and then actually commit a container into the shared pool. Only after committing (or abandoning) its reservation does an instance give the pool-wide permit back up, letting the other instance proceed.

The full set of actions is:
1. Request: an instance with an idle local slot registers that it wants to place a new container in the shared pool.
2. AcquireAdmission: an instance with an outstanding request takes the pool-wide admission permit, provided no other instance currently holds it.
3. ReserveSlot: while holding the pool-wide permit, an instance picks one of its own not-yet-placed local slots and marks it as its fine-grained in-progress reservation.
4. CommitPlacement: while holding the permit with an in-progress reservation, if the shared pool's combined occupancy (counted across both instances) is below the bound, the instance commits its reserved slot's container into the shared pool, clears its request and reservation, and gives the pool-wide permit back.
5. AbandonReservation: while holding the permit with an in-progress reservation, if the shared pool is already at its bound (so the commit cannot proceed), the instance drops the reservation and gives the pool-wide permit back so the other instance is not starved; its request stays outstanding to retry later.
6. DepartContainer: any instance may remove one of its own already-committed containers from the shared pool at any time, freeing a unit of shared capacity.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At every reachable state, the total number of containers committed into the shared pool across both crane-yard instances together never exceeds the pool's fixed bound.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every outstanding placement request, from either instance, is eventually satisfied (its container is committed into the shared pool), even though the two instances contend for the single pool-wide admission permit and the shared pool can transiently be full.

  /\ wantCS \in [Nodes -> BOOLEAN]

  /\ override = FALSE

Request(n) ==

A university's course-registration system replicates the roster for one popular, capacity-limited course across a small cluster of registrar replicas for fault tolerance. Every change to the roster -- enrolling a student or dropping a student -- is first proposed, then voted on by the replicas, and only takes effect once a quorum of replicas has endorsed it. Each replica endorses a proposal by consulting only its own local copy of the roster, which is kept up to date by sync messages that can be reordered or delivered out of turn, so a replica's local copy may lag behind or apply changes in a different order than they actually happened. To guard against this staleness, the coordinator that ultimately commits an action always re-checks it against the true, authoritative roster (not any one replica's local copy) before applying it.

The full set of actions is:
1. Propose: a student's enrollment or drop is proposed, as long as it is currently sensible against the true roster (you can't propose to enroll someone already enrolled, and you can't propose to drop someone not currently enrolled).
2. CastVote: a replica endorses a pending proposal using only its own local roster copy -- it always endorses a drop, but only endorses an enrollment if its own (possibly stale) local copy believes there is still room.
3. Commit: once a quorum of replicas has endorsed a pending proposal, the coordinator commits it, but only after re-validating the proposal against the true authoritative roster (rejecting it if, in truth, the course is already full or the student's true membership no longer matches what was proposed). A successful commit updates the true roster and broadcasts a sync message to every replica.
4. ApplySync: a replica applies one pending sync message to its own local roster copy. Because the network can reorder these messages, a replica may apply a later change before an earlier one, so its local copy can transiently disagree with the true commit order.

SAFETY PROPERTY: At every reachable state, the true, authoritative course roster never holds more students than the course has seats for, no matter how stale or out-of-order any individual replica's local view of the roster becomes.

CONSTANTS Students, Replicas, Capacity, Quorum

\* A university course-registration system replicates one course's roster
\* across several registrar replicas for fault tolerance. Every enroll/drop
\* action is first proposed, then voted on by replicas (each replica checks

\* only takes effect once a quorum of replicas has endorsed it -- at which
\* point the coordinator re-validates against the true authoritative roster
\* before committing. Sync messages that propagate a commit out to each
\* replica's local copy can be reordered/delivered out of turn, so a
\* replica's local view may transiently look inconsistent, but the
\* authoritative roster (the thing that actually holds a seat) is the only
\* thing the safety property protects.

VARIABLES enrolled, pending, voteMsgs, localView, syncMsgs

TypeOK ==
    /\ enrolled \subseteq Students
    /\ pending \subseteq [student: Students, kind: {"enroll", "drop"}]
    /\ voteMsgs \subseteq [replica: Replicas, student: Students, kind: {"enroll", "drop"}]
    /\ localView \in [Replicas -> SUBSET Students]
    /\ syncMsgs \subseteq [replica: Replicas, student: Students, kind: {"add", "remove"}]

Init ==
    /\ enrolled = {}
    /\ pending = {}
    /\ voteMsgs = {}
    /\ localView = [r \in Replicas |-> {}]
    /\ syncMsgs = {}

\* A student's enroll or drop is proposed, if it is currently sensible
\* against the true roster (can't propose to enroll someone already in,
\* can't propose to drop someone not in).
Propose(s, k) ==
    /\ [student |-> s, kind |-> k] \notin pending
    /\ (k = "enroll" => s \notin enrolled)
    /\ (k = "drop" => s \in enrolled)
    /\ pending' = pending \cup {[student |-> s, kind |-> k]}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<enrolled, voteMsgs, localView, syncMsgs>>

\* A replica endorses a pending action using only its own local roster copy:
\* it always endorses a drop, but only endorses an enroll it believes there
\* is room for -- its local copy may be stale, so this is a heuristic, not
\* the authoritative check.
CastVote(r, s, k) ==
    /\ [student |-> s, kind |-> k] \in pending
    /\ [replica |-> r, student |-> s, kind |-> k] \notin voteMsgs
    /\ (k = "enroll" => Cardinality(localView[r]) < Capacity)
    /\ voteMsgs' = voteMsgs \cup {[replica |-> r, student |-> s, kind |-> k]}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<enrolled, pending, localView, syncMsgs>>

\* Once a quorum of replicas has endorsed an action, the coordinator commits
\* it -- but only after re-checking the action against the true authoritative
\* roster, which is what actually keeps capacity from ever being exceeded no
\* matter how stale the individual votes were. A commit also broadcasts a
\* sync diff to every replica.
Commit(s, k) ==
    LET diffKind == IF k = "enroll" THEN "add" ELSE "remove" IN
    /\ [student |-> s, kind |-> k] \in pending
    /\ Cardinality({r \in Replicas : [replica |-> r, student |-> s, kind |-> k] \in voteMsgs}) >= Quorum
    /\ (k = "enroll" => (s \notin enrolled /\ Cardinality(enrolled) < Capacity))
    /\ (k = "drop" => s \in enrolled)
    /\ enrolled' = IF k = "enroll" THEN enrolled \cup {s} ELSE enrolled \ {s}
    /\ pending' = pending \ {[student |-> s, kind |-> k]}
    /\ voteMsgs' = {m \in voteMsgs : m.student # s}
    /\ syncMsgs' = syncMsgs \cup {[replica |-> r, student |-> s, kind |-> diffKind] : r \in Replicas}
    /\ UNCHANGED localView

\* A replica applies one pending sync diff to its local copy. The network
\* can deliver these out of order, so a replica may apply a later commit's
\* diff before an earlier one's, leaving its local view transiently
\* inconsistent with the true commit order (though never with the true
\* roster's authoritative membership once fully caught up).
ApplySync(r, s, k) ==
    /\ [replica |-> r, student |-> s, kind |-> k] \in syncMsgs
    /\ localView' = [localView EXCEPT ![r] = IF k = "add" THEN @ \cup {s} ELSE @ \ {s}]
    /\ syncMsgs' = syncMsgs \ {[replica |-> r, student |-> s, kind |-> k]}

    \/ \E r \in Replicas, s \in Students, k \in {"enroll", "drop"} : CastVote(r, s, k)
    \/ \E s \in Students, k \in {"enroll", "drop"} : Commit(s, k)
    \/ \E r \in Replicas, s \in Students, k \in {"add", "remove"} : ApplySync(r, s, k)

vars == <<enrolled, pending, voteMsgs, localView, syncMsgs>>

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* Bounds the amount of simultaneously in-flight coordination bookkeeping so
\* the reachable state space stays finite and small for model checking; it
\* does not restrict which actions are semantically allowed.
StateSpaceBound == Cardinality(pending) + Cardinality(voteMsgs) + Cardinality(syncMsgs) <= 5

\* The one thing that actually matters operationally: the authoritative,
\* quorum-committed roster never holds more students than the course has
\* seats for, regardless of how stale or reordered any replica's own view
\* of the roster becomes in the meantime.
CapacityRespected == Cardinality(enrolled) <= Capacity

====

A wildfire surveillance swarm is flown by two independent ground controllers, north and south. Each controller keeps its own bounded dispatch queue of drones waiting to stream imagery, but both controllers draw from a single shared pool of transmit credits, and there is exactly one physical relay channel that carries a drone feed to the incident command post.

Either controller may admit a pending drone into its own queue, but only while a transmit credit is free and that controller's queue is below its capacity; admitting consumes one credit from the shared pool. A controller may key the relay for the drone at the head of its queue only when the relay is idle for both controllers. Once a keyed drone's imagery has been taken, the controller logs the drone, drops it from the head of its queue, unkeys the relay, and returns the credit to the shared pool. A controller may also requeue: if its queue is non-empty and it is not currently keyed, it can push the head drone back to pending and return that drone's credit, which is how a controller sheds load when the shared pool runs dry for the other side.

Finally, a logged drone may be rearmed: it is dropped from the logged set and becomes eligible to report a fresh sighting on its next pass.

An elevator bank in a skyscraper keeps one shared hall-call ledger recording which cars have filed their accumulated batch of floor requests. Each car updates the ledger through a compare-and-swap register: the ledger carries a stamp that is bumped on every successful write.

A car that has not yet filed reads the ledger, taking a private copy of the ledger contents and of the current stamp, but only while the number of cars currently holding a copy is below the bank's live concurrency limit. A car holding a copy swaps its merged copy -- its own view plus its own batch -- back into the ledger, but only if the stamp it read is still the live stamp; a successful swap bumps the stamp, marks that car as filed, and discards the car's copy. If the stamp has moved on since the read, the car retries: it throws its copy away and goes back for a fresh read. The bank's concurrency limit itself changes while the bank is running: a resize picks a different limit, and a car holding a copy when the number of holders exceeds the new limit sheds that copy without writing anything to the ledger.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every car that has been marked as filed still appears in the ledger, so no successful write is ever erased by a later one.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every car in the bank eventually files its batch, so the ledger eventually records all of them.

Holders == {i \in Cars : snap[i] # NoSnap}

\* Each car reads the hall-call ledger into a private view, then swaps its
\* merged view back only if the stamp it read is still the live one.

  /\ filed \subseteq Cars
  /\ stamp \in 0..NumCars
  /\ snap \in [Cars -> (0..NumCars) \cup {NoSnap}]
  /\ view \in [Cars -> SUBSET Cars]
  /\ cap \in 1..MaxCap

Init ==

  /\ stamp = 0
  /\ snap = [i \in Cars |-> NoSnap]
  /\ view = [i \in Cars |-> {}]
  /\ filed = {}
  /\ cap = 1

Read(i) ==
  /\ i \notin filed
  /\ snap[i] = NoSnap
  /\ Cardinality(Holders) < cap
  /\ snap' = [snap EXCEPT ![i] = stamp]
  /\ view' = [view EXCEPT ![i] = book]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<book, stamp, filed, cap>>

\* The swap writes back the whole merged view, so a stale swap would erase
\* every batch filed since the read -- the stamp guard is what forbids it.
Swap(i) ==

  /\ snap[i] = stamp
  /\ book'  = view[i] \cup {i}
  /\ stamp' = stamp + 1
  /\ snap'  = [snap EXCEPT ![i] = NoSnap]
  /\ view'  = [view EXCEPT ![i] = {}]
  /\ filed' = filed \cup {i}
  /\ UNCHANGED cap

Retry(i) ==

  /\ snap[i] # stamp

A hospital operating-room scheduler books surgeons into theatres from an intake pool of booking slips. The pool is deliberately unordered: slips arrive over a messaging fabric that can deliver them out of order, so the scheduler may pick up any slip in the pool, not the oldest one. Each surgeon has a credential term, and a slip records the term that was in force for its author at the moment it was cut. A slip is current only if its author is credentialed right now and the slip's term still matches that author's term.

A credentialed surgeon may submit a slip, but only while the intake pool is below its bound and that exact slip is not already sitting in the pool; when intake is full the desk refuses new slips outright, which is how backpressure is applied upstream. The scheduler may wheel a case into any free theatre by taking a current slip out of the pool and attaching it to that theatre. Credentials office may revoke a surgeon, provided at least one other surgeon stays credentialed and that surgeon's term has room to advance: revoking drops the surgeon from the credentialed set, advances that surgeon's term, and immediately clears any theatre that surgeon was standing in. The office may also reinstate a surgeon who is not credentialed, which advances that surgeon's term as well, so any slip that surgeon left in the pool is now out of date. Closing a theatre records the surgeon as having completed a case and frees the theatre. Finally, the scheduler may purge any slip in the pool that is no longer current, which is the only way stale slips stop consuming intake capacity.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every theatre that has a case attached is staffed by a surgeon who is credentialed at that moment and whose slip carries that surgeon's current term.

EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Surgeons, Rooms, MaxTerm, Intake, NoCase

VARIABLES pool, live, term, assign, done

vars == <<pool, live, term, assign, done>>

\* The intake pool is an unordered bag of booking slips, so the scheduler may
\* pick them up in any order -- a slip carries the credential term it was cut
\* under, which is how a slip that outlived its author's privileges is spotted.

Slip == [sg : Surgeons, tm : 0..MaxTerm]

Current(r) == live[r.sg] /\ r.tm = term[r.sg]

TypeOK ==
  /\ pool \subseteq Slip
  /\ live \in [Surgeons -> BOOLEAN]
  /\ term \in [Surgeons -> 0..MaxTerm]
  /\ assign \in [Rooms -> Slip \cup {NoCase}]
  /\ done \subseteq Surgeons

Init ==
  /\ pool = {}
  /\ live = [s \in Surgeons |-> TRUE]
  /\ term = [s \in Surgeons |-> 0]
  /\ assign = [rm \in Rooms |-> NoCase]
  /\ done = {}

\* Intake is bounded; when it is full the desk stops taking slips at all.
Submit(s) ==
  /\ live[s]
  /\ Cardinality(pool) < Intake
  /\ [sg |-> s, tm |-> term[s]] \notin pool
  /\ pool' = pool \cup {[sg |-> s, tm |-> term[s]]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<live, term, assign, done>>

Wheel(rm, r) ==
  /\ assign[rm] = NoCase
  /\ r \in pool
  /\ Current(r)
  /\ assign' = [assign EXCEPT ![rm] = r]
  /\ pool'   = pool \ {r}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<live, term, done>>

\* Pulling privileges also clears the theatre: a surgeon whose credential is
\* withdrawn cannot be left standing over an open case.
Revoke(s) ==
  /\ live[s]
  /\ \E o \in Surgeons : o # s /\ live[o]
  /\ term[s] < MaxTerm
  /\ live'   = [live EXCEPT ![s] = FALSE]
  /\ term'   = [term EXCEPT ![s] = @ + 1]
  /\ assign' = [rm \in Rooms |->
                  IF assign[rm] # NoCase /\ assign[rm].sg = s
                    THEN NoCase ELSE assign[rm]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, done>>

Reinstate(s) ==
  /\ ~live[s]
  /\ term[s] < MaxTerm
  /\ live' = [live EXCEPT ![s] = TRUE]
  /\ term' = [term EXCEPT ![s] = @ + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, assign, done>>

Close(rm) ==
  /\ assign[rm] # NoCase
  /\ done'   = done \cup {assign[rm].sg}

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An interbank settlement batch is assembled by several member banks against a fixed settlement window: the total value already written to the batch's ledger lines plus the total value currently pledged but not yet written must fit inside that window. Access is two-level. There is one coarse batch gate, and each ledger line has its own fine claim. A bank is assumed to be slow at times but never to fail outright, so a bank that is holding something will always get around to letting it go.

A bank with nothing pledged may take the batch gate when it is free, and may hand it straight back if it decides not to pledge. While holding the gate, a bank sizes a pledge: it picks an amount and takes it only if the amount still fits in the window alongside everything committed and everything already pledged. A bank holding the gate with a live pledge may claim any unclaimed ledger line, provided it is not already holding a line; claiming the line releases the coarse gate immediately, so the gate is never held across the write. A bank holding a line posts its pledge onto that line: the line's balance grows by the pledged amount, the pledge is cleared, and the line is released. A bank holding the gate with a live pledge may instead cancel: the pledge is cleared and the gate released, with nothing written. When the gate is free, nothing is pledged, no line is claimed, and the batch has value on it, a cutover zeroes every ledger line and reopens the window for the next batch.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The value committed to ledger lines plus the value currently pledged by banks never exceeds the settlement window.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every pledge a bank takes is eventually resolved, so no bank is left holding an unsettled pledge forever.

RECURSIVE Total(_, _)
Total(f, S) ==
  IF S = {} THEN 0
  ELSE LET x == CHOOSE y \in S : TRUE IN f[x] + Total(f, S \ {x})

Committed == Total(book, Lines)
Pledged   == Total(pledge, Banks)

\* Coarse first, fine second: a bank must hold the batch gate to size its
\* pledge against the remaining window, and only then may it claim a ledger
\* line and hand the gate straight back to the next bank in the queue.

TypeOK ==
  /\ gate \in Banks \cup {NoBank}
  /\ pledge \in [Banks -> 0..MaxPledge]
  /\ holder \in [Lines -> Banks \cup {NoBank}]

Init ==

  /\ pledge = [b \in Banks |-> 0]
  /\ holder = [l \in Lines |-> NoBank]
  /\ book = [l \in Lines |-> 0]

TakeGate(b) ==
  /\ gate = NoBank
  /\ pledge[b] = 0
  /\ gate' = b
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pledge, holder, book>>

DropGate(b) ==

  /\ pledge[b] = 0
  /\ gate' = NoBank

\* same remaining headroom and both pledge against it.
Reserve(b, v) ==

  /\ pledge[b] = 0
  /\ Committed + Pledged + v =< Window
  /\ pledge' = [pledge EXCEPT ![b] = v]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<gate, holder, book>>

ClaimLine(b, l) ==
  /\ gate = b
  /\ pledge[b] > 0
  /\ holder[l] = NoBank
  /\ \A k \in Lines : holder[k] # b
  /\ holder' = [holder EXCEPT ![l] = b]
  /\ gate' = NoBank
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pledge, book>>

Post(b, l) ==
  /\ holder[l] = b
  /\ pledge[b] > 0
  /\ book' = [book EXCEPT ![l] = @ + pledge[b]]
  /\ pledge' = [pledge EXCEPT ![b] = 0]
  /\ holder' = [holder EXCEPT ![l] = NoBank]

  /\ pledge[b] > 0
  /\ pledge' = [pledge EXCEPT ![b] = 0]
  /\ gate' = NoBank

  /\ Committed > 0
  /\ Pledged = 0
  /\ \A l \in Lines : holder[l] = NoBank

  \/ \E b \in Banks : Cancel(b)

  /\ [][Next]_vars
  /\ \A b \in Banks : WF_vars(Cancel(b))
  /\ \A b \in Banks : \A l \in Lines : WF_vars(Post(b, l))

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A wildfire drone surveillance swarm is planned by two independent mission planners that share one pool of orbit slots over the fire ground. Neither planner is authoritative, so no slot is handed out on a planner's say-so alone: a ring of ground stations votes, and a slot is only awarded once a quorum of stations has endorsed the same offer.

A planner may put an offer on a free slot -- a slot with no live ballot and no standing grant -- naming a drone that is not currently seated and not already named in another live ballot; a planner may only have one ballot open at a time, so the two planners interleave rather than flooding the pool. Any ground station may endorse a live ballot for a slot once. When a ballot for a slot reaches the quorum and the slot has no standing grant, the slot is awarded to the drone named in the ballot, and the ballot and its endorsements are cleared. A ballot that has not yet reached the quorum may instead be abandoned, clearing the ballot and its endorsements with no grant cut. A drone that is not seated may take the orbit of any slot granted to it. A seated drone may be recalled: it leaves its slot and the slot's grant is torn down, returning the slot to the shared pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Any drone occupying an orbit slot is the drone that slot's standing grant names, so a slot is never flown by two drones at once.
===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

CONSTANTS Planners, Stations, Drones, Slots, Quorum, NoBid, NoDrone, NoSlot

VARIABLES bid, tally, grant, seat

vars == <<bid, tally, grant, seat>>

Offer == [pl : Planners, dr : Drones]

\* Two mission planners run side by side over one pool of orbit slots. Neither
\* trusts the other's view, so a slot is only handed out once a quorum of
\* ground stations has voted for the same offer.

TypeOK ==
  /\ bid \in [Slots -> Offer \cup {NoBid}]
  /\ tally \in [Slots -> SUBSET Stations]
  /\ grant \in [Slots -> Drones \cup {NoDrone}]
  /\ seat \in [Drones -> Slots \cup {NoSlot}]

Init ==
  /\ bid = [s \in Slots |-> NoBid]
  /\ tally = [s \in Slots |-> {}]
  /\ grant = [s \in Slots |-> NoDrone]
  /\ seat = [d \in Drones |-> NoSlot]

Busy(p) == \E t \in Slots : bid[t] # NoBid /\ bid[t].pl = p

Offered(d) == \E t \in Slots : bid[t] # NoBid /\ bid[t].dr = d

Propose(p, s, d) ==
  /\ bid[s] = NoBid
  /\ grant[s] = NoDrone
  /\ seat[d] = NoSlot
  /\ ~Busy(p)
  /\ ~Offered(d)
  /\ bid' = [bid EXCEPT ![s] = [pl |-> p, dr |-> d]]
  /\ tally' = [tally EXCEPT ![s] = {}]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<grant, seat>>

Endorse(g, s) ==
  /\ bid[s] # NoBid
  /\ g \notin tally[s]
  /\ tally' = [tally EXCEPT ![s] = @ \cup {g}]

\* A grant is only cut when the ballot is over the line; both planners see the
\* same grant table afterwards, which is what stops a slot going out twice.
Award(s) ==

  /\ grant[s] = NoDrone
  /\ Cardinality(tally[s]) >= Quorum
  /\ grant' = [grant EXCEPT ![s] = bid[s].dr]
  /\ bid' = [bid EXCEPT ![s] = NoBid]
  /\ tally' = [tally EXCEPT ![s] = {}]
  /\ UNCHANGED seat

Abandon(s) ==
  /\ bid[s] # NoBid
  /\ Cardinality(tally[s]) < Quorum
  /\ bid' = [bid EXCEPT ![s] = NoBid]
  /\ tally' = [tally EXCEPT ![s] = {}]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<grant, seat>>

  /\ seat[d] = NoSlot
  /\ seat' = [seat EXCEPT ![d] = s]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<bid, tally, grant>>

Recall(d) ==

  /\ grant' = [grant EXCEPT ![seat[d]] = NoDrone]
  /\ seat' = [seat EXCEPT ![d] = NoSlot]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<bid, tally>>

  \/ \E g \in Stations, s \in Slots : Endorse(g, s)
  \/ \E s \in Slots : Award(s)
  \/ \E s \in Slots : Abandon(s)
  \/ \E d \in Drones, s \in Slots : TakeOrbit(d, s)
  \/ \E d \in Drones : Recall(d)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* Intent: a drone sitting in an orbit slot must be the one that slot was
\* awarded to. Since grant holds a single drone per slot, that rules out the
\* same slot being flown by two drones at once.
NoSlotHandedOutTwice ==
  \A d \in Drones : seat[d] # NoSlot => grant[seat[d]] = d

====
