===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A pharmacy keeps a patient's medication chart in three places that must not drift apart: the dispensing robot, the counter terminal, and the insurer link. Adding a line to the chart is settled as a two-phase commit over those three desks.

A new line starts fresh and is put out to poll. A desk that votes yes writes the line into its own copy of the chart there and then, on the understanding that it comes back out again if the line is dropped. A desk that votes no writes nothing. The line stands once all three desks have voted yes, and is dropped if any desk voted no.

The pharmacist in charge has an override. She can make a line stand over a desk's refusal -- which is what happens when the insurer link refuses a drug the patient plainly needs -- and she can pull a line that is still being polled. Neither override touches a line that already stands: once a line stands it stays standing.

A desk that has not got a standing line in its copy back-fills it, which is how a desk that voted no or never voted at all catches up after an override. A desk that has a dropped line in its copy takes it back out again. The patient is told a line is on file only once the line stands and every one of the three desks has it in its copy.

The full action set is: put a fresh line out to poll, vote yes and write the line into that desk's copy, vote no, let a line stand on a full set of yes votes, drop a line that got a no, override a polling line into standing, override a polling line into dropped, back-fill a standing line into a desk that lacks it, take a dropped line back out of a desk's copy, and tell the patient about a standing line that every desk has.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every line the patient has been told is on file is present in all three desks' copies of the chart, so no acknowledged update is ever lost from any copy.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every line put out to poll eventually ends up either standing or dropped.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

VARIABLES chart, stage, ballot, told
vars == <<chart, stage, ballot, told>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ chart \in [Desks -> SUBSET Entries]
  /\ stage \in [Entries -> {"fresh", "polling", "standing", "dropped"}]
  /\ ballot \in [Entries -> [Desks -> {"quiet", "yes", "no"}]]
  /\ told \subseteq Entries

Init ==
  /\ chart = [d \in Desks |-> {}]
  /\ stage = [e \in Entries |-> "fresh"]
  /\ ballot = [e \in Entries |-> [d \in Desks |-> "quiet"]]
  /\ told = {}

OpenPoll(e) ==
  /\ stage[e] = "fresh"
  /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![e] = "polling"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<chart, ballot, told>>

\* A yes vote writes the line into that desk's chart straight away, on the
\* understanding that it comes back out again if the entry is dropped.
VoteYes(e, d) ==
  /\ stage[e] = "polling"
  /\ ballot[e][d] = "quiet"
  /\ ballot' = [ballot EXCEPT ![e][d] = "yes"]
  /\ chart' = [chart EXCEPT ![d] = chart[d] \cup {e}]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<stage, told>>

VoteNo(e, d) ==
  /\ stage[e] = "polling"
  /\ ballot[e][d] = "quiet"
  /\ ballot' = [ballot EXCEPT ![e][d] = "no"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<chart, stage, told>>

Stand(e) ==
  /\ stage[e] = "polling"
  /\ \A d \in Desks : ballot[e][d] = "yes"
  /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![e] = "standing"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<chart, ballot, told>>

Drop(e) ==
  /\ stage[e] = "polling"
  /\ \E d \in Desks : ballot[e][d] = "no"
  /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![e] = "dropped"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<chart, ballot, told>>

\* The pharmacist in charge can push an entry through over a refusal, or pull
\* one that is still being polled. Neither override touches a standing entry.
OverrideStand(e) ==
  /\ stage[e] = "polling"
  /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![e] = "standing"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<chart, ballot, told>>

OverrideDrop(e) ==
  /\ stage[e] = "polling"
  /\ stage' = [stage EXCEPT ![e] = "dropped"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<chart, ballot, told>>

BackFill(e, d) ==
  /\ stage[e] = "standing"
  /\ e \notin chart[d]
  /\ chart' = [chart EXCEPT ![d] = chart[d] \cup {e}]

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An airfield's ground movement is rated for only so many aircraft out on the manoeuvring area at once. Access is governed by two levels of lock, always taken coarse first and fine second: there is one apron lock covering the whole movement area, and one strip lock for each departure strip.

An aircraft at its stand takes the apron lock. Holding the apron lock, it pushes off: the movement tally goes up by one and the aircraft is now taxiing out on the area. With a strip in hand the aircraft lines up, and from lined up it rolls: it leaves the area, the strip lock is dropped, and the tally comes down by one.

An aircraft can go dead on the ground without warning -- no radio, no movement, nothing. A dead aircraft keeps whatever locks it was holding and, far more to the point, keeps its metal sitting out on the manoeuvring area. It stays there until a tug physically drags it off, and that tow is what drops its locks and brings the tally down; dropping the tally for an aircraft that is still sitting out there would be exactly the wrong thing to do.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A central bank runs interbank settlement in batches. Member banks lodge batches into a settlement queue that has a hard length limit; when the queue is at that limit a member simply cannot lodge, however urgent its batch, and has to wait for the queue to drain. That is the whole of the backpressure arrangement.

A member may only lodge while its mandate to settle is live, and every lodged batch is stamped with the serial of the mandate it was lodged under. Batches leave the queue from the front: while the settlement window is open the batch at the head is put through and marked settled.

The duty officer at the central bank has overrides that ordinary members do not. She can pull a member's mandate, which marks it pulled and moves it to a new serial; pulling a mandate scrubs that member's batches out of the settlement queue in the same stroke, because a batch lodged under a mandate that no longer stands must not be sitting there waiting to be put through. She can reinstate a pulled mandate, again on a new serial, after which the member may lodge afresh. She can also shut the settlement window and open it again, which stops and restarts the draining of the queue without touching anything in it.

The full action set is: lodge a batch under a live mandate while the queue is below its limit, settle the batch at the head of the queue while the window is open, pull a member's mandate and scrub its batches from the queue, reinstate a pulled mandate on a new serial, shut the settlement window, and open the settlement window.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every batch sitting in the settlement queue was lodged under a mandate that still stands today at exactly the serial it was stamped with, so nothing lodged by a member whose mandate has been pulled or superseded is ever waiting to settle.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every batch that reaches the settlement queue eventually leaves it.

Standing(m, s) == mandate[m].state = "live" /\ mandate[m].serial = s
Waiting(k) == \E i \in 1 .. Len(queue) : queue[i].tkt = k

TypeOK ==
  /\ mandate \in [Members -> [state : {"live", "pulled"}, serial : 0 .. MaxSerial]]
  /\ lodged \subseteq Batches
  /\ settled \subseteq Batches
  /\ window \in {"open", "shut"}

Init ==
  /\ queue = <<>>
  /\ mandate = [m \in Members |-> [state |-> "live", serial |-> 0]]
  /\ lodged = {}
  /\ settled = {}
  /\ window = "open"

\* Backpressure: a member with a live mandate simply cannot lodge while the
\* settlement queue is at its length limit.
Lodge(k, m) ==
  /\ k \notin lodged
  /\ mandate[m].state = "live"
  /\ Len(queue) < QueueCap
  /\ queue' = Append(queue, [bank |-> m, serial |-> mandate[m].serial, tkt |-> k])
  /\ lodged' = lodged \cup {k}

SettleHead ==

PullMandate(m) ==

  /\ UNCHANGED <<queue, mandate, lodged, settled>>

OpenWindow ==

  /\ window' = "open"

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An airport tower allocates its runways by cutting timed slips. A slip names one runway, one flight, a slip number, the tower wall-clock reading it was cut at, and the reading it runs out at. The tower will not cut a new slip for a runway while an older slip for that runway is still inside its window, so the slips on any one runway never overlap in time.

Cockpit panels do not read the same time as the tower. A panel always trails the tower wall clock, and the certification rule is that it never trails by more than a fixed skew; the tower will not advance its own clock past the point where some panel would fall further behind than that. Panels creep forward towards the tower reading on their own. A flight is never treated as lost, only as slow: its panel is behind, and it will catch up.

A slip reaches a flight by radio, and that can happen at any point after it was cut, including well after the window it describes has already run out. A flight carries whatever slip reached it most recently.

To roll onto a runway a crew works entirely from its own panel, because that is all it has. It requires that its panel has reached the start of the slip's window, and, crucially, that its panel plus a full skew of margin is still short of the end of that window. That margin is the whole point: it is what makes the roll legal in tower time and not merely in cockpit time. Every roll is recorded by the tower with the runway, the flight, the slip number quoted, and the tower wall-clock reading at the moment it happened.

The full action set is: advance the tower wall clock while no panel would fall outside the certified skew, creep a lagging cockpit panel forward, cut a slip for a runway with no slip currently inside its window, radio an already-cut slip to the flight it names, and roll out on the carried slip when the panel plus a skew of margin is still inside the window.

A university course-registration system hands out seats in a single popular lecture course. Every seat in the course is a physical unit of capacity: it either sits unclaimed in the registrar's open pool, or it is held by a student under a short-lived reservation lease, or it has been turned into a confirmed enrollment. The registrar's accounting rule is that seats are never manufactured and never quietly vanish; a seat always sits in exactly one of those three places.

If a student lets the lease deadline pass without acting, the lease expires and the seat goes straight back into the open pool so somebody else can take it. If the student acts in time, the lease is converted into a confirmed enrollment and the lease record is torn up. A confirmed student may later drop the course, which releases the seat back into the open pool.

Because registration disputes happen, the system also carries a privileged registrar override: the registrar may administratively revoke a confirmed enrollment outright, without the student's cooperation, and the revoked seat is returned to the open pool exactly like a voluntary drop. ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A national clearing house runs an interbank settlement batch. A fixed amount of settlement money exists on the books at the start of the batch, spread across the participating banks, and the whole point of the batch is that the money only moves -- the clearing house never mints a unit and never lets one evaporate.

Any participant may originate a payment instruction at any time. Originating debits the payer's own balance immediately and parks the amount in that bank's escrow slot, together with a note of which bank is to receive it and a snapshot of the shared settlement ledger's version stamp at the moment the instruction was drawn up. Nothing is locked: this is optimistic. The ledger's version stamp advances every time some payment is actually posted, so a parked instruction that was drawn up before somebody else's posting is now working from a stale snapshot and must not be posted as it stands.

The clearing house drives the batch with a single settlement agent that walks the participants in a fixed cyclic order. The agent works on exactly one participant at a time, and it does not move on to the next participant until the one in front of it has nothing parked in escrow. Participants are known to be slow -- a bank's back office may take a long while to answer -- but no participant is treated as failed, so the agent waits rather than skipping. When the agent is at a participant whose parked instruction carries the current version stamp, it posts the payment: the escrowed amount is credited to the receiving bank, the escrow slot empties, and the ledger's version stamp advances. When the parked instruction carries a stale stamp, the agent refreshes the snapshot to the current stamp and the instruction stays parked for another try. The agent may also give up on a parked instruction and return the escrowed amount to the originator's own balance.

The full action set is: a participant originates a payment instruction, debiting itself into escrow with a version snapshot; the agent posts the current participant's parked instruction when its snapshot is current, crediting the receiver and advancing the version stamp; the agent refreshes a stale snapshot and leaves the instruction parked; the agent returns a parked escrow amount to its originator; and the agent advances to the next participant in the cycle once the current one has an empty escrow slot.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The total settlement money held across all participants' balances plus everything sitting in escrow always equals the amount the batch started with, so no unit of money is created or destroyed by any posting, refresh, return, or origination.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Any amount a participant parks in escrow is eventually cleared out of that escrow slot, either by being posted to its receiver or by being returned to the originator.

Banks == 0 .. (NumBanks - 1)
NoPayee == NumBanks

Money == 0 .. TotalFunds

SumOf(f, S) ==
  IF S = {} THEN 0
  ELSE LET x == CHOOSE y \in S : TRUE IN f[x] + SumOf(f, S \ {x})

  /\ stampSeen \in [Banks -> Stamps]
  /\ stamp \in Stamps
  /\ agentAt \in Banks

Init ==
  /\ balance = [b \in Banks |-> IF b = 0 THEN TotalFunds ELSE 0]
  /\ escrow = [b \in Banks |-> 0]
  /\ payee = [b \in Banks |-> NoPayee]
  /\ stampSeen = [b \in Banks |-> 0]
  /\ stamp = 0
  /\ agentAt = 0

\* Optimistic origination: debit now, remember the stamp we drew against.
Originate(b, d, amt) ==

  /\ amt \in 1 .. MaxAmount

  /\ balance' = [balance EXCEPT ![b] = balance[b] - amt]
  /\ escrow' = [escrow EXCEPT ![b] = amt]
  /\ payee' = [payee EXCEPT ![b] = d]

\* every other participant's snapshot.

  /\ stampSeen[agentAt] = stamp
  /\ balance' = [balance EXCEPT ![payee[agentAt]] = @ + escrow[agentAt]]
  /\ escrow' = [escrow EXCEPT ![agentAt] = 0]
  /\ payee' = [payee EXCEPT ![agentAt] = NoPayee]
  /\ stamp' = (stamp + 1) % StampCycle

  /\ stampSeen[agentAt] # stamp

  /\ UNCHANGED <<balance, escrow, payee, stamp, agentAt>>

Return ==

  /\ escrow' = [escrow EXCEPT ![agentAt] = 0]
  /\ payee' = [payee EXCEPT ![agentAt] = NoPayee]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<stampSeen, stamp, agentAt>>

StepOn ==

  /\ agentAt' = (agentAt + 1) % NumBanks

AgentWork == Post \/ Refresh \/ Return

Next ==
  \/ \E b \in Banks, d \in Banks, amt \in Amounts : Originate(b, d, amt)

  \/ StepOn

  /\ WF_vars(AgentWork)
  /\ SF_vars(StepOn)

FundsConserved ==
  SumOf(balance, Banks) + SumOf(escrow, Banks) = TotalFunds

A warehouse runs a fleet of mobile robots under a single fleet coordinator. The coordinator publishes a configuration that says which robot is responsible for which pallet, and every configuration carries an epoch number. Reconfiguration happens while the floor is live: the coordinator bumps the epoch and republishes a fresh pallet-to-robot assignment, for instance when a robot is pulled off for charging.

The irreversible action in this warehouse is scrapping a pallet down the compaction chute. Once a pallet goes down the chute it is crushed; there is no way to retrieve it, and there is no way to un-scrap it. The chute sits on a load cell that accumulates the total mass it has swallowed, and pallets have different masses, so the load cell reading is an independent physical witness of what has actually gone down. The chute also keeps a manifest listing which pallets it has taken.

Orders travel over the warehouse's radio mesh, which does not preserve order: an order issued under an older epoch can arrive after an order issued under a newer one, and orders can sit in the air for a long time before they land. A robot therefore learns about epochs only from the orders it receives, and its own notion of the current epoch lags the coordinator's. A robot will act on an order whose epoch is at least as new as the epoch the robot itself currently believes in, and acting on an order also advances the robot's belief to that order's epoch. A robot may also simply adopt a newer epoch it hears about in an order addressed to it without acting on that order, and it may discard any order addressed to it. Because two robots can hold orders for the same pallet from two different epochs, the chute manifest is the one shared thing that keeps a pallet from being scrapped twice: the chute refuses a pallet already on its manifest.

The full action set is: the coordinator bumps the epoch and republishes a pallet-to-robot assignment; the coordinator issues a scrap order for a pallet to that pallet's currently assigned robot, stamped with the current epoch; a robot adopts a newer epoch it learns from an order addressed to it; a robot discards an order addressed to it; and a robot presents a pallet to the chute under an order at least as new as the robot's own epoch, whereupon the chute adds the pallet to its manifest and its mass to the load cell.

A subway line is divided into signalling blocks, and each block is a physical stretch of track with a hard occupancy limit set by its length and its emergency-braking distance. A short block near a station throat admits only one train; a long open-air block admits two. Exceeding a block's limit is the thing the signalling system exists to prevent.

A train does not enter the line one block at a time. It is granted a whole route at once, and a route may span several blocks, so the grant is arranged as a two-phase commit across the interlockings that own those blocks. In the first phase the train's route controller asks each interlocking on the route to reserve a place. An interlocking that still has room below its block's limit takes a tentative hold on behalf of that train; an interlocking that is already at its limit refuses. Tentative holds count against the block's limit exactly like real occupancy does, because a held place is a place that must be there when the train arrives.

Interlockings are relay-based and can be slow: an interlocking that is mid-cycle simply does not answer for a while. Slow is not the same as failed here -- the route controller does not conclude anything from silence, and it never re-asks a block behind the interlocking's back. It waits. When every interlocking on the route has taken a hold, the route controller commits: each hold on that route turns into real occupancy and the train runs. If any interlocking on the route refuses, the route controller aborts, and every hold that route had taken anywhere is dropped. A train that has finished running clears out of its blocks, and an aborted route may be attempted again from scratch.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A subway line's signalling centre keeps one shared movement-authority record for the line. The record carries a revision number, and every accepted change bumps that revision by exactly one. The centre also keeps a revision journal: an append-only strip that records the revision number produced by each change as it is written. A healthy line produces revisions 1, 2, 3, and so on with no repeats and no gaps in that strip, because each change is supposed to be built on top of the revision immediately before it.

Changes arrive from trackside as authority-update jobs and are held in a bounded staging queue in front of the single applier. The queue has a fixed depth, and that depth is the line's backpressure: when the staging queue is full, trackside submissions are simply not admitted, and the centre also refuses to admit more work than the record's remaining revision budget for the shift. When a job is admitted it records the revision the record showed at the moment of admission -- that is the revision the job was built against.

The applier takes jobs off the front of the queue one at a time. The applier is a relay-driven unit and it can be slow: it goes into a busy sub-cycle during which it does nothing at all, and it comes out again. Slow is not failed here -- it always comes back out, and nothing is ever taken away from it while it is quiet. When the applier is responsive and the job in its hand was built against the record's current revision, it writes the change: the record moves to the job's base revision plus one and that number is stamped on the journal strip. When the job in its hand was built against an older revision, writing it would silently discard whatever landed in between, so instead the applier rebases the job onto the record's current revision and keeps it in hand for another go.

The full action set is: trackside submits a job, which is admitted only when the staging queue is below its depth limit and the shift's revision budget still allows it; the applier takes the front job off the queue into its hand; the applier enters its busy sub-cycle; the applier leaves its busy sub-cycle; the responsive applier writes a job whose base matches the record's current revision, bumping the record and stamping the journal; and the responsive applier rebases a job whose base is older than the record's current revision.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The revision journal strip always reads exactly 1, 2, 3, ... with the entry in position i being the number i, so no write ever reuses or skips a revision number and no accepted change is ever silently overwritten by one built on stale data.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every job admitted into the staging queue is eventually written to the shared record, so the record's revision eventually reaches the count of everything ever admitted.

A regional power grid is protected by a set of load-shedding controllers, one per substation district, that all edit a single shared shed plan. The shed plan is a list of which feeders are currently marked for shedding, and it is the only authoritative copy: there is no per-district version of it. Each controller cares about exactly one feeder, its own, and its job is to get that feeder onto the plan when its district is in trouble and off the plan when the district recovers.

Editing the plan is a read-then-write affair, not a single atomic operation. A controller first copies the plan into a local working sheet, then later writes the working sheet back with its own feeder added. If the plan had moved on between the copy and the write-back -- because some other controller had meanwhile added its own feeder -- writing the old sheet back would quietly erase that other feeder from the plan. That is the lost update this system has to avoid, and it matters physically: a feeder that a controller has been told is on the plan but which has silently fallen off will not actually be shed when the grid needs it.

Editing rights circulate on a ring. A single editing baton travels around the controllers in fixed cyclic order, and only the controller currently holding the baton may copy the plan, write a sheet back, or take its own feeder off the plan. A controller passes the baton onward only when it is not in the middle of an edit, so a working sheet never survives across a baton handover. Controllers are known to be slow: a controller can go quiet for a long stretch while it polls its district's telemetry, and while it is quiet it neither edits nor passes the baton. Nothing ever pulls the baton away from a quiet controller -- the ring treats slowness as slowness, not as failure -- and a quiet controller always comes back. A controller may also give up on a working sheet and throw it away.

Whenever a controller successfully writes its feeder onto the plan, it records an acknowledgement that its feeder is on the plan; when it takes its feeder off the plan it withdraws that acknowledgement.

The full action set is: the baton holder, if not quiet and not mid-edit, passes the baton to the next controller on the ring; the baton holder copies the plan into its working sheet; the baton holder writes its working sheet back with its own feeder added and records the acknowledgement; the baton holder throws away its working sheet; the baton holder takes its own feeder off the plan and withdraws its acknowledgement; a controller goes quiet; and a quiet controller comes back.

A public library system runs a reservation service backed by a single hold shelf at the central depot. The shelf has a fixed number of numbered slots, and a patron reservation that has been filled occupies exactly one slot until the patron collects it. Two branch servers, east and west, each handle their own patrons' reservations and place filled reservations onto the shelf.

The shelf layout is not static. Periodically the depot reconfigures it -- reindexing slots after shelving work, or repartitioning capacity between branches -- and each reconfiguration carries a new epoch number. A reservation records the epoch in force when it was placed. After a reconfiguration, a reservation still sitting on a slot from a previous epoch no longer corresponds to the shelf's current arrangement, and the branch that placed it must lift it off and place it again under the current epoch.

Placement is recorded in two independent places: the branch's own reservation record says which slot a reservation went into, and the shelf's slot register says which reservation is sitting in each slot. These two must tell the same story, because the whole point of the slot register is that a slot can hold one reservation and the depot staff go to the slot the reservation record names.

A branch server can crash silently. There is no failure announcement and no last message: the branch simply stops answering, and a crashed branch never comes back and never places or lifts anything again. A shed window can be allocated to exactly one district, because two districts blacking out in the same window would drop more load than the interties can absorb. Allocating a window is agreed by two-phase commit across the region's substations, because every substation has to know the schedule before it takes effect. A district that wants a currently unheld window opens a round and asks the substations; each substation votes yes as long as the window is still unheld when it is asked. A district may also give a window back, clearing it from the register and from its own list.

In an emergency the operator can seize a window for a district outright, with no round and no substation votes, and the seizure takes precedence over whatever was there before: the register is rewritten to name the seizing district, and the window is struck off the promised list of whichever district previously held it. An airport baggage router feeds bags from the check-in kerb onto a single make-up chute that loads them into an aircraft container. Dropping a bag down the make-up chute is the irreversible step: the bag lands inside the container, the container is on a live loading cycle, and there is no mechanism to lift a bag back out. A bag that went down the chute twice would mean the airline's records show one bag but two things happened to it, which is exactly the fault this router is designed to make impossible.

Between the kerb and the chute sits the induction queue, a physical line of totes on the sorter loop. The queue is served strictly from its front. The queue's depth limit is not fixed: lanes of the sorter loop open and close during the shift as maintenance crews work on them, so the limit rises and falls while bags are moving. When the queue is at its current depth limit, kerb inductions are refused outright -- that is the router's backpressure -- and a lane may only be taken out of service when the queue is short enough to fit under the reduced limit.

Two things can happen to the bag at the front of the queue. It can be dropped down the make-up chute, or the scanner can fail to read its tag, in which case the bag is kicked back out to the kerb to be re-inducted later. Only a bag standing at the kerb may be inducted, and a bag that has already gone down the chute is never at the kerb again, which is what keeps a bag from making a second trip.

Every drop is written to the container's loading manifest, in order, and at the same moment the bag's own baggage tag is overprinted with the manifest position it just took. The manifest and the tag overprints are meant to be a consistent pair of records: the bag written at manifest position i must be carrying an overprint reading i.

The full action set is: a maintenance crew brings a sorter lane back into service, raising the queue's depth limit; a crew takes a lane out of service, lowering the limit, which is only allowed when the queue already fits under the lower limit; a bag standing at the kerb is inducted into the back of the queue when the queue is below its current limit; the bag at the front of the queue is dropped down the make-up chute, appended to the loading manifest, and overprinted with its manifest position; and the bag at the front of the queue is kicked back out to the kerb after a failed tag read.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every position i of the container's loading manifest, the bag recorded at that position carries an overprint reading exactly i, which can only hold if no bag was ever dropped down the make-up chute more than once.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: No bag ever sits in the induction queue forever; every bag that is inducted eventually leaves the queue, either down the chute or back out to the kerb.

A power-grid load shedder divides its rolling-blackout schedule into rotation slots. A rotation slot is a chunk of shedding duty, and it may be allocated to only one dispatch node at a time: if two nodes both believed they owned the same rotation slot, both would open their breakers in that window and the grid would lose double the intended load.

Ownership lives in a compare-and-swap register, one per rotation slot. Each register holds two fields: who owns the slot, and a stamp that is bumped every time the register changes hands in either direction. A dispatch node that wants a slot first takes a snapshot of a register it finds unowned, noting the stamp it saw. Later it attempts the swap: the swap goes through only if the register is still unowned and still carries the exact stamp from the snapshot. If either has moved, the attempt is dead and the node throws its snapshot away. A successful swap bumps the stamp and, in the same indivisible step, writes the node's own grant slip recording which slot it took and at which stamp. Giving a slot back is also a compare-and-swap: the node swaps the register back to unowned, again only if the register still carries the stamp on its grant slip, and the stamp bumps once more.

Dispatch nodes are slow. A node may go quiet for a long stretch -- it is polling feeder telemetry, or its link is congested -- and while quiet it takes no snapshots, attempts no swaps, and gives nothing back. Quiet is not failure here: nothing reclaims a slot from a quiet node, and a quiet node always becomes responsive again, so a held slot always comes back on the node's own initiative. This is exactly why a node's snapshot can be arbitrarily old by the time it tries to use it.

While a node holds a slot it may actually perform the shed for that slot, which it does at most once per grant.

The full action set is: a responsive node with no slot in hand snapshots an unowned register and notes its stamp; a responsive node completes a compare-and-swap on a register that still matches its snapshot, taking ownership, bumping the stamp and writing its grant slip; a responsive node throws away a snapshot whose register no longer matches; a node holding a slot performs the shed for it; a responsive node compare-and-swaps its slot back to unowned using the stamp on its grant slip; a node goes quiet; and a quiet node becomes responsive.

During the auction the book is organised by price level, and each price level admits only a bounded number of resting orders: the deep levels around the indicative opening price take two resting orders, the thin outer levels take one. The matching engine's opening cross allocates against a fixed-size array per level, and a level that ever carried more resting orders than its bound would corrupt the cross.

A firm may also simply give up on an intention. Every accepted submission and every pulled order bumps the level's change stamp. The room check happens at the moment of acceptance against the level as it stands then, not against what the firm read earlier.

One member firm can crash silently during the auction. There is no disconnect message and no cancel-on-disconnect notice; the firm just stops, and it never submits, retries, or gives up again. A firm that crashes while holding a live reading leaves that reading dangling, and the exchange's auction supervisor sweeps dangling readings belonging to firms that have gone quiet. ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An operator runs a network of vending machines backed by a single central cash vault. Every coin in the business is at any moment in exactly one of three places: sitting in a machine's hopper, riding in a sealed courier bag on its way to the vault, or lying in the vault itself. Coins are not minted and not lost, and the operator's daily reconciliation depends on that being literally true.

A machine sends cash in by sealing a bag: coins leave its hopper and go into the bag, and the bag is stamped with the vault ledger's change stamp as the machine last saw it. This is deliberately optimistic -- the machine takes no lock on the ledger and does not wait for the vault's permission to seal a bag.

Courier bags do not arrive in the order they were sealed. Routes differ, vans break down, and the vault takes whichever bag is in front of it. When the vault picks up a bag whose stamp matches the ledger's current stamp, it books the bag in: the coins land in the vault and the ledger's stamp moves on. When the vault picks up a bag whose stamp is out of date -- because some other machine's bag was booked in first -- it cannot book it in as it stands, so it restamps the bag with the ledger's current stamp and the bag waits for another attempt. The operator may also recall a bag, sending its coins straight back to the machine's hopper. Separately, the operator refills a machine's hopper with change drawn from the vault.

The full action set is: a machine seals coins from its hopper into a courier bag stamped with the ledger's current stamp; the vault books in a bag whose stamp matches the ledger, moving the coins into the vault and advancing the stamp; the vault restamps a bag whose stamp is out of date, leaving the coins in the bag; a bag is recalled and its coins returned to the machine's hopper; and the operator moves change from the vault into a machine's hopper.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The coins in the vault, the coins in every machine hopper and the coins in every courier bag always add up to exactly the amount of cash the network started with, so no sealing, booking, restamping, recall or refill ever creates or destroys a coin.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: A courier bag never stays out of date forever; every bag carrying a stale stamp is eventually either restamped to the ledger's current stamp or emptied back to its machine.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

--------------------------- MODULE W4Od13m0p2t1 ---------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS NumMachines, TotalCoins, BagLimit, MaxStamp

Machines == 1 .. NumMachines
Stamps == 0 .. MaxStamp

VARIABLES vault, hopper, bag, mark, ledger
vars == <<vault, hopper, bag, mark, ledger>>

RECURSIVE Held(_)
Held(k) == IF k = 0 THEN 0 ELSE hopper[k] + bag[k] + Held(k - 1)

TypeOK ==
  /\ vault \in 0 .. TotalCoins
  /\ hopper \in [Machines -> 0 .. TotalCoins]
  /\ bag \in [Machines -> 0 .. BagLimit]
  /\ mark \in [Machines -> Stamps]
  /\ ledger \in Stamps

Init ==
  /\ vault = TotalCoins
  /\ hopper = [m \in Machines |-> 0]
  /\ bag = [m \in Machines |-> 0]
  /\ mark = [m \in Machines |-> 0]
  /\ ledger = 0

\* Sealing is optimistic: the machine copies the stamp it last saw, no locking.
Seal(m, k) ==
  /\ bag[m] = 0
  /\ k \in 1 .. BagLimit
  /\ hopper[m] >= k
  /\ hopper' = [hopper EXCEPT ![m] = hopper[m] - k]
  /\ bag' = [bag EXCEPT ![m] = k]
  /\ mark' = [mark EXCEPT ![m] = ledger]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<vault, ledger>>

\* Bags arrive in any order; only a bag whose stamp still matches books in.
BookIn(m) ==
  /\ bag[m] > 0
  /\ mark[m] = ledger
  /\ ledger < MaxStamp
  /\ vault' = vault + bag[m]
  /\ bag' = [bag EXCEPT ![m] = 0]
  /\ ledger' = ledger + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<hopper, mark>>

Restamp(m) ==
  /\ bag[m] > 0
  /\ mark[m] # ledger
  /\ mark' = [mark EXCEPT ![m] = ledger]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<vault, hopper, bag, ledger>>

Recall(m) ==
  /\ bag[m] > 0
  /\ hopper' = [hopper EXCEPT ![m] = hopper[m] + bag[m]]
  /\ bag' = [bag EXCEPT ![m] = 0]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<vault, mark, ledger>>

Refill(m, k) ==
  /\ k \in 1 .. BagLimit
  /\ vault >= k
  /\ vault' = vault - k
  /\ hopper' = [hopper EXCEPT ![m] = hopper[m] + k]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<bag, mark, ledger>>

RestampAny == \E m \in Machines : Restamp(m)

Next ==
  \/ \E m \in Machines, k \in 1 .. BagLimit : Seal(m, k)
  \/ \E m \in Machines : BookIn(m)
  \/ RestampAny
  \/ \E m \in Machines : Recall(m)
  \/ \E m \in Machines, k \in 1 .. BagLimit : Refill(m, k)

Spec ==
  /\ Init
  /\ [][Next]_vars
  /\ WF_vars(RestampAny)

\* Vault plus hoppers plus bags is the network's unchanging cash total.
CoinsConserved ==
  vault + Held(NumMachines) = TotalCoins

StaleBagsGetRestamped ==
  \A m \in Machines :
    (bag[m] > 0 /\ mark[m] # ledger) ~> (bag[m] = 0 \/ mark[m] = ledger)
===========================================================================

    BagLimit = 2
    MaxStamp = 3

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
At the terminus of a metro line there are a small number of turnback sidings, and a siding is a slot that exactly one incoming service may be allocated at a time. Several area controllers share responsibility for the terminus, and any of them may allocate a siding, so the terminus needs a rule about who is entitled to allocate at any given moment.

The rule is a circulating baton. The baton moves around the controllers in a fixed cyclic order, and each handover starts a new lap. The terminus keeps a lap book: an ordered record that writes down, for every lap number, which controller was holding the baton during that lap. Only the controller currently holding the baton may allocate a free siding, and when it does, the siding's register entry records both the allocating controller and the lap number in force at that moment. The controller holding the baton may also key the physical lock on a siding it has allocated, unkey it again, and give a siding back, which clears the register entry. A siding that is keyed cannot be given back until it is unkeyed.

Above all this sits the duty controller's privileged override. In a disruption the duty controller can seize a siding for any controller at all: the seizure starts a fresh lap, writes that controller into the lap book for the new lap, hands the baton to that controller, unkeys the siding and rewrites the register entry to that controller at the new lap, regardless of who held the siding before. The duty controller can also force a siding free outright, unkeying it and clearing its register entry no matter whose it was.

The point of writing the lap number into the register is that every live allocation can be audited back to the lap book: an allocation claiming lap n must have been made by the controller the lap book shows holding the baton during lap n.

The full action set is: the baton is passed to the next controller on the ring, starting a new lap and writing that controller into the lap book; the baton holder allocates a free siding, recording itself and the current lap in the register; the baton holder keys the lock on a siding it holds; the baton holder unkeys a siding it holds; the baton holder gives back an unkeyed siding it holds, clearing the register; the duty controller seizes a siding for a controller, starting a new lap, writing the lap book, handing over the baton, unkeying the siding and rewriting the register; and the duty controller forces a siding free, unkeying it and clearing the register.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every siding whose register entry names an owner names a controller that the lap book shows was holding the baton during the lap recorded in that same entry, so no siding is ever allocated by a controller that was not entitled to allocate, and no siding carries two live allocations.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

--------------------------- MODULE W4Od10m1p3t5 ---------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS NumControllers, NumSidings, MaxLap

Controllers == 1 .. NumControllers
Sidings == 1 .. NumSidings
Unheld == 0
Laps == 0 .. MaxLap
NextOnRing(c) == (c % NumControllers) + 1

VARIABLES baton, lap, lapBook, register, keyed
vars == <<baton, lap, lapBook, register, keyed>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ baton \in Controllers
  /\ lap \in Laps
  /\ lapBook \in [Laps -> Controllers \cup {Unheld}]
  /\ register \in [Sidings -> [owner : Controllers \cup {Unheld}, lap : Laps]]
  /\ keyed \in [Sidings -> BOOLEAN]

Init ==
  /\ baton = 1
  /\ lap = 0
  /\ lapBook = [l \in Laps |-> IF l = 0 THEN 1 ELSE Unheld]
  /\ register = [s \in Sidings |-> [owner |-> Unheld, lap |-> 0]]
  /\ keyed = [s \in Sidings |-> FALSE]

\* Each handover opens a lap and is written into the lap book straight away.
PassBaton ==
  /\ lap < MaxLap
  /\ baton' = NextOnRing(baton)
  /\ lap' = lap + 1
  /\ lapBook' = [lapBook EXCEPT ![lap + 1] = NextOnRing(baton)]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<register, keyed>>

Allocate(s) ==
  /\ register[s].owner = Unheld
  /\ register' = [register EXCEPT ![s] = [owner |-> baton, lap |-> lap]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<baton, lap, lapBook, keyed>>

KeyLock(s) ==
  /\ register[s].owner = baton
  /\ ~keyed[s]
  /\ keyed' = [keyed EXCEPT ![s] = TRUE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<baton, lap, lapBook, register>>

UnkeyLock(s) ==
  /\ register[s].owner = baton
  /\ keyed[s]
  /\ keyed' = [keyed EXCEPT ![s] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<baton, lap, lapBook, register>>

GiveBack(s) ==
  /\ register[s].owner = baton
  /\ ~keyed[s]
  /\ register' = [register EXCEPT ![s] = [owner |-> Unheld, lap |-> 0]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<baton, lap, lapBook, keyed>>

\* The override opens its own lap so the seizure is still auditable.
Seize(s, c) ==
  /\ lap < MaxLap
  /\ lap' = lap + 1
  /\ lapBook' = [lapBook EXCEPT ![lap + 1] = c]
  /\ baton' = c
  /\ keyed' = [keyed EXCEPT ![s] = FALSE]
  /\ register' = [register EXCEPT ![s] = [owner |-> c, lap |-> lap + 1]]

ForceFree(s) ==
  /\ register[s].owner # Unheld
  /\ register' = [register EXCEPT ![s] = [owner |-> Unheld, lap |-> 0]]
  /\ keyed' = [keyed EXCEPT ![s] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<baton, lap, lapBook>>

Next ==
  \/ PassBaton
  \/ \E s \in Sidings : Allocate(s)
  \/ \E s \in Sidings : KeyLock(s)
  \/ \E s \in Sidings : UnkeyLock(s)
  \/ \E s \in Sidings : GiveBack(s)
  \/ \E s \in Sidings, c \in Controllers : Seize(s, c)
  \/ \E s \in Sidings : ForceFree(s)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* Provenance: every live allocation traces back to the lap book.
AllocationsTraceToLapBook ==
  \A s \in Sidings :
    register[s].owner # Unheld => lapBook[register[s].lap] = register[s].owner
===========================================================================

<|start|>user<|message|>Write a TLA+ specification that implements EXACTLY the system described below, and a TLC .cfg to model-check it. The system's safety property described in the NL text must be captured as a real, non-trivial INVARIANT (not `Inv == TRUE`) in the .cfg.

Name the module `W4Od4m2p3t3`.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A car-wash site runs a conveyor line that ends in a row of numbered drying bays. A drying bay is a slot: one vehicle at a time occupies it for the whole of its drying cycle, and two vehicles sent to the same bay would collide on the conveyor exit.

A vehicle is not simply pushed into a bay. Before a vehicle may run, every station along the line -- the prewash arch, the foam arch, the rinse arch -- has to have booked that bay for that vehicle in its own local plan, because each station has to set its nozzles and timing for the bay the car is heading to. So the grant is a two-phase commit. A waiting vehicle names the bay it wants and starts asking. Each station, when it is not mid-cycle, books that bay for that vehicle in its own plan, provided the station has not already booked that bay for somebody else. When every station on the line has the bay booked for the same vehicle, the site controller commits and the vehicle runs. If the vehicle finds that some station has that bay booked for a different vehicle, it balks: it gives up on the attempt and all the bookings it did manage to get are dropped. A balked vehicle goes back to waiting and may name a bay again.

Stations are slow. An arch that is mid-cycle simply does not book anything for a while. Slowness is not failure here: no station is ever declared dead, nothing is booked on a station's behalf, and a mid-cycle arch always comes back and books eventually. The site controller never proceeds on partial agreement, no matter how long a station takes.

A vehicle that has run is pushed off the end of the conveyor: its drying cycle finishes, all of its bookings across every station are dropped, and it leaves the site for good rather than queueing again.

The full action set is: a waiting vehicle that has not yet been through names a bay and starts asking; a station that is not mid-cycle books the asked-for bay for an asking vehicle, provided that station has that bay free in its plan; the controller commits a vehicle whose asked-for bay is booked for it at every station, and the vehicle runs; an asking vehicle balks because some station has its bay booked for another vehicle, dropping all of its own bookings; a balked vehicle returns to waiting; a running vehicle finishes its cycle, drops all its bookings and leaves the site; and a station enters or leaves its mid-cycle state.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every vehicle that is running has a bay named, and at every single station on the line that bay is booked for that very vehicle, so no drying bay is ever allocated to two vehicles at the same time.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every vehicle that starts running eventually stops running, finishing its drying cycle and freeing its bay.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

---------------------------- MODULE W4Od4m2p3t3 ---------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS NumStations, NumBays, NumCars

Stations == 1 .. NumStations
Bays == 1 .. NumBays
Cars == 1 .. NumCars
NoCar == 0
NoBay == 0

VARIABLES booked, phase, wants, midCycle, gone
vars == <<booked, phase, wants, midCycle, gone>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ booked \in [Stations -> [Bays -> Cars \cup {NoCar}]]
  /\ phase \in [Cars -> {"waiting", "asking", "running", "balked"}]
  /\ wants \in [Cars -> Bays \cup {NoBay}]
  /\ midCycle \in [Stations -> BOOLEAN]
  /\ gone \subseteq Cars

Init ==
  /\ booked = [st \in Stations |-> [b \in Bays |-> NoCar]]
  /\ phase = [c \in Cars |-> "waiting"]
  /\ wants = [c \in Cars |-> NoBay]
  /\ midCycle = [st \in Stations |-> FALSE]
  /\ gone = {}

DropBookings(c) ==
  [st \in Stations |->
     [b \in Bays |-> IF booked[st][b] = c THEN NoCar ELSE booked[st][b]]]

NameBay(c, b) ==
  /\ phase[c] = "waiting"
  /\ c \notin gone
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![c] = "asking"]
  /\ wants' = [wants EXCEPT ![c] = b]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<booked, midCycle, gone>>

\* Each station books into its own plan; nothing is ever booked on its behalf.
Book(st, c) ==
  /\ phase[c] = "asking"
  /\ ~midCycle[st]
  /\ booked[st][wants[c]] = NoCar
  /\ booked' = [booked EXCEPT ![st][wants[c]] = c]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<phase, wants, midCycle, gone>>

\* The controller only ever proceeds on unanimity across the whole line.
StartRun(c) ==
  /\ phase[c] = "asking"
  /\ \A st \in Stations : booked[st][wants[c]] = c
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![c] = "running"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<booked, wants, midCycle, gone>>

Balk(c) ==
  /\ phase[c] = "asking"
  /\ \E st \in Stations : booked[st][wants[c]] \notin {NoCar, c}
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![c] = "balked"]
  /\ booked' = DropBookings(c)
  /\ UNCHANGED <<wants, midCycle, gone>>

BackToWaiting(c) ==
  /\ phase[c] = "balked"
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![c] = "waiting"]
  /\ wants' = [wants EXCEPT ![c] = NoBay]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<booked, midCycle, gone>>

LeaveSite(c) ==
  /\ phase[c] = "running"
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![c] = "waiting"]
  /\ wants' = [wants EXCEPT ![c] = NoBay]
  /\ booked' = DropBookings(c)
  /\ gone' = gone \cup {c}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<midCycle>>

FlipCycle(st) ==
  /\ midCycle' = [midCycle EXCEPT ![st] = ~midCycle[st]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<booked, phase, wants, gone>>

LeaveAny == \E c \in Cars : LeaveSite(c)

Next ==
  \/ \E c \in Cars, b \in Bays : NameBay(c, b)
  \/ \E st \in Stations, c \in Cars : Book(st, c)
  \/ \E c \in Cars : StartRun(c)
  \/ \E c \in Cars : Balk(c)
  \/ \E c \in Cars : BackToWaiting(c)
  \/ LeaveAny
  \/ \E st \in Stations : FlipCycle(st)

Spec ==
  /\ Init
  /\ [][Next]_vars
  /\ WF_vars(LeaveAny)

\* Unanimity holds for the whole run, not merely at the moment of commit.
RunningCarOwnsItsBayEverywhere ==
  \A c \in Cars :
    phase[c] = "running" =>
      /\ wants[c] # NoBay
      /\ \A st \in Stations : booked[st][wants[c]] = c

EveryRunEnds ==
  \A c \in Cars : (phase[c] = "running") ~> (phase[c] # "running")
===========================================================================

PROPERTY EveryRunEnds

<|start|>user<|message|>Write a TLA+ specification that implements EXACTLY the system described below, and a TLC .cfg to model-check it. The system's safety property described in the NL text must be captured as a real, non-trivial INVARIANT (not `Inv == TRUE`) in the .cfg.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A hospital keeps one master theatre list: a single shared record holding the day's operating-room schedule. Several schedulers -- the surgical coordinator, the anaesthetics desk -- revise it during the day. The record carries a revision number, and alongside it the hospital keeps a provenance strip: for every revision the record has ever reached, the strip records which revision that one was built on top of.

Revising is a read-modify-write, and there are no locks anywhere. A scheduler first reads the record, noting the revision number it saw, and then works out its change offline -- ringing a surgeon, checking a bed. When it is ready it attempts a compare-and-swap: the change is written only if the record's revision number is still exactly the one the scheduler noted. If somebody else revised the list in the meantime the swap does not go through, because writing the change as it stands would silently discard whatever that other person did. A scheduler in that position may refresh its noted revision to the record's current one and carry on preparing, or it may abandon the change entirely.

Every swap that does go through bumps the revision number by one and writes into the provenance strip the revision the scheduler had noted. A healthy list therefore has a provenance strip in which revision 1 was built on revision 0, revision 2 on revision 1, and so on with no revision ever grafted onto an older ancestor.

One scheduler can crash silently. There is no error, no message, no handover: the terminal simply stops, and that scheduler never reads, refreshes, swaps or abandons again. A scheduler that crashes while holding a noted revision leaves it dangling, and the hospital's records office sweeps dangling notes belonging to schedulers that have gone silent. At most one scheduler crashes during the day.

The full action set is: a live scheduler with nothing in hand reads the record and notes its revision; a live scheduler whose noted revision still matches the record swaps its change in, bumping the revision and writing the provenance strip; a live scheduler whose noted revision is out of date refreshes it to the record's current revision; a live scheduler abandons what it had in hand; a scheduler crashes silently; and the records office sweeps the dangling note of a scheduler that has gone silent.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every entry on the provenance strip shows that revision as having been built on the revision immediately before it, so no accepted change was ever grafted onto a stale ancestor and no revision of the theatre list was ever silently overwritten.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS NumSchedulers, MaxRevision

Schedulers == 1 .. NumSchedulers
Revisions == 0 .. MaxRevision
Written == 1 .. MaxRevision
Unwritten == 0

VARIABLES revision, builtOn, noted, inHand, live
vars == <<revision, builtOn, noted, inHand, live>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ revision \in Revisions
  /\ builtOn \in [Written -> Revisions]
  /\ noted \in [Schedulers -> Revisions]
  /\ inHand \in [Schedulers -> BOOLEAN]
  /\ live \in [Schedulers -> BOOLEAN]

Init ==
  /\ revision = 0
  /\ builtOn = [v \in Written |-> Unwritten]
  /\ noted = [p \in Schedulers |-> 0]
  /\ inHand = [p \in Schedulers |-> FALSE]
  /\ live = [p \in Schedulers |-> TRUE]

ReadList(p) ==
  /\ live[p]
  /\ ~inHand[p]
  /\ noted' = [noted EXCEPT ![p] = revision]
  /\ inHand' = [inHand EXCEPT ![p] = TRUE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<revision, builtOn, live>>

\* The swap goes through only against the exact revision the scheduler noted,
\* and it records that revision as the new one's ancestor.
Swap(p) ==
  /\ live[p]
  /\ inHand[p]
  /\ noted[p] = revision
  /\ revision < MaxRevision
  /\ revision' = revision + 1
  /\ builtOn' = [builtOn EXCEPT ![revision + 1] = noted[p]]
  /\ inHand' = [inHand EXCEPT ![p] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<noted, live>>

Refresh(p) ==
  /\ live[p]
  /\ inHand[p]
  /\ noted[p] # revision
  /\ noted' = [noted EXCEPT ![p] = revision]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<revision, builtOn, inHand, live>>

Abandon(p) ==
  /\ live[p]
  /\ inHand[p]
  /\ inHand' = [inHand EXCEPT ![p] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<revision, builtOn, noted, live>>

\* A silent crash: no message, and at most one terminal ever goes quiet.
CrashOut(p) ==
  /\ \A q \in Schedulers : live[q]
  /\ live' = [live EXCEPT ![p] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<revision, builtOn, noted, inHand>>

SweepNote(p) ==
  /\ ~live[p]
  /\ inHand[p]
  /\ inHand' = [inHand EXCEPT ![p] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<revision, builtOn, noted, live>>

Next ==
  \/ \E p \in Schedulers : ReadList(p)
  \/ \E p \in Schedulers : Swap(p)
  \/ \E p \in Schedulers : Refresh(p)
  \/ \E p \in Schedulers : Abandon(p)
  \/ \E p \in Schedulers : CrashOut(p)
  \/ \E p \in Schedulers : SweepNote(p)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* Every revision reached must name its immediate predecessor as ancestor.
RevisionChainUnbroken ==
  \A v \in Written : v <= revision => builtOn[v] = v - 1
===========================================================================

A regional blood bank tracks individual units of packed red cells by barcode across several hospital sites. Every unit that exists is, at any moment, in exactly one of three custodies: sitting in some site's fridge, riding in a sealed courier box between sites, or lying out on the crossmatch bench. A barcode that appeared in two custodies at once, or that appeared in none, would mean the bank has either invented a unit of blood or lost one, and both are reportable incidents.

Custody changes are written into one shared inventory ledger, and the right to write into that ledger circulates. A single write baton passes around the sites in a fixed cyclic order, and only the site currently holding the baton may move a unit out of its own fridge, take delivery of a unit, or work at the crossmatch bench. Courier boxes do not arrive in the order they were sealed. A unit shipped out carries a transfer note naming its destination site, and the destination takes delivery whenever it next holds the baton, in whatever order boxes happen to turn up at its door. A box in transit may also be rerouted, its transfer note rewritten to name a different destination while the unit is still on the road. What never changes is the custody arithmetic: a unit leaving a fridge into a box has left the fridge and is in the box, a unit taken out of a box is in the receiving fridge, and a unit on the bench came out of the baton holder's own fridge.

Nothing in the signalling estate can undo an earthing, and a section that somehow got earthed twice would mean a second strap had been clamped on top of a first one that nobody could then account for.

Earthing straps are the estate's physical currency for this. Each strap carries its own serial number and lives in the traction store when it is not in use. Clamping a strap takes it out of the store and puts it on exactly one section. The estate's audit rule is simple: at any moment every strap in the estate is either lying in the traction store or hanging on one section, and never both and never neither.

Authorising an earthing is the job of the controlling centre. Which centre is controlling is decided by an election carrying a term number, and each election installs a centre and moves the estate on to the next term. A controlling centre can fail, leaving the estate with nobody in charge and no earthings possible until an election installs a replacement. Elections can be run at any time, so a failure is always recoverable.

How many sections may stand earthed at once is not a fixed number. It is the traction allowance, and it is adjusted during the day as the depot changes how much of the line it needs alive for stock movements. The allowance may be raised freely, but it may never be set below the number of sections already standing earthed, since straps already clamped cannot be recalled.

Several member banks each hold a batch of payment instructions that must be pushed through a single shared posting engine, and the engine can only work one bank's batch at a time. The token moves one position around the ring at a time, and the clearing house only lets the token move while the posting engine is standing idle and while the bank the token is parked on has nothing queued, so the token never slides away underneath a batch that is mid-post and never abandons a member that is still waiting for its turn.

A waiting bank may seize the posting engine only when the settlement token is currently parked on it and the engine is free; at that moment the engine records that bank as its owner and the bank moves into the posting phase. When the bank has pushed its batch through, it releases the engine, returns to idle, and its batch is marked settled.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An online game runs a lobby matchmaker. A lobby has a fixed number of numbered player slots, and seating a player into a slot has to be agreed by every region server that mirrors the lobby, because each region server serves the lobby view to its own players. The matchmaker acts as the transaction coordinator and runs one seating transaction at a time.

A seating transaction begins when the matchmaker proposes to seat a currently unseated player into a particular slot; the proposal is recorded and every region server's ballot is cleared. Each region server then casts its ballot on the open proposal. A region server casts a yes ballot when, according to the lobby view it holds, the proposed slot has nobody in it and the proposed player is not already seated somewhere; otherwise it casts a no ballot. The region servers are known to be slow but not failed: a server may take arbitrarily long to answer, but it always answers eventually, which is why the matchmaker simply waits rather than timing anybody out.

Once every region server has balloted, the matchmaker takes the decision. It moves the transaction into the committing phase only if every ballot was yes and the proposed slot is still empty at decision time; otherwise it moves the transaction into the aborting phase. Committing writes the seating through: the slot records the player as its occupant and the player records the slot as its seat, and the transaction closes. Aborting simply closes the transaction and leaves the lobby untouched. Separately, a seated player may stand up at any time, which clears both the slot's occupant record and the player's seat record.

The full action set is: propose a seating of an unseated player into a slot, cast a region server's ballot on the open proposal, take the commit-or-abort decision once all ballots are in, apply a committed seating, close an aborted transaction, and stand a seated player up.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The slot occupancy records and the player seating records always agree with each other in both directions, so a player's recorded seat always names a slot that records that same player as its occupant and vice versa, which means no slot is ever allocated to two different players at once.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every seating transaction that reaches the balloting phase eventually reaches a decision and closes.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending machine network shares one physical coin-refill dock at the depot. Only one machine may be standing in the dock being refilled at any moment, so the dock is the network's critical resource. Access to it is arbitrated entirely through a single compare-and-swap register at the depot controller. The register carries two fields: the identity of the machine that currently holds the dock claim, and a version counter that is bumped on every successful swap. The version counter only runs up to a fixed ceiling before the controller stops accepting swaps.

A machine that wants coins first announces that it is trying. A trying machine, or a machine that still believes it holds a claim that has since been swapped away, may attempt the compare-and-swap: if the register's holder field currently reads nobody, the machine swaps its own identity in, the version counter goes up by one, and the machine privately writes down the version it just wrote as its claim ticket. A machine that has swapped itself in is a claimant.

A claimant may actually roll into the dock and start refilling only if the register still names it as holder and its private claim ticket still matches the register's live version, and only if the depot's refill allowance for the shift is greater than zero; rolling in consumes one unit of that allowance. When the refill is finished the machine rolls out and the register's holder field is set back to nobody.

The depot controller may also revoke a claim that is only a claim: if a machine holds the register but has not yet rolled into the dock, the controller may swap the holder field back to nobody and bump the version, which silently invalidates that machine's claim ticket. The refill allowance is not a fixed number for the shift: the depot may raise it by one at any time and may also cut it by one at any time, so the capacity available to the network genuinely changes while the network is running. The depot always does eventually top the allowance back up when it is below its ceiling.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A clearing bank runs its interbank settlement batch against a shared intraday credit line. The credit line has a hard drawn-down ceiling: the amount drawn at any instant must never exceed it, because an overdrawn line stops the whole batch. Several member desks push settlement legs against the same line, and there is no lock on the line at all; the desks work optimistically.

A desk that is standing by may prepare a leg. Preparing reads the currently drawn amount off the line and copies it into the desk's own worksheet, and a desk is only allowed to prepare a leg if the amount it just read leaves room for a leg under the ceiling. The desk now holds a snapshot that may go stale at any moment, because other desks and the drain both move the real drawn amount.

A prepared desk may push its leg through only if its worksheet snapshot still matches the line's live drawn amount; that comparison is the whole of the optimistic scheme. On success the drawn amount goes up by one leg and the desk records its leg as posted. If the desk finds that its snapshot no longer matches the live figure, it tears the worksheet up and goes back to standing by, which is the retry. Separately, settlement traffic drains the line: whenever the drawn amount is above zero it can fall by one.

The batch supervisor holds a privileged override. The supervisor may flag one prepared desk at a time, and a flagged desk is taken out of the ordinary optimistic scheme entirely: it may no longer push through on a snapshot match and may no longer tear up its worksheet and retry. Instead the supervisor pushes the flagged desk's leg through directly, reading the live drawn amount rather than the stale worksheet, and it still refuses to push if the leg would break the ceiling. A supervisor push posts the leg and clears the flag.

The full action set is: prepare a leg at a standing-by desk when the freshly read drawn amount leaves room under the ceiling, push a prepared leg through when the worksheet snapshot still matches the live drawn amount, tear up a stale worksheet and go back to standing by, drain one leg's worth off the line, flag a prepared desk for the supervisor override, and have the supervisor push a flagged desk's leg through against the live drawn amount.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The drawn amount on the credit line never exceeds the ceiling, and every prepared desk's worksheet snapshot was itself checked to leave room for a leg under the ceiling, which is what makes an optimistic push safe.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every desk that the supervisor flags for the override eventually has its leg posted.

vars == <<drawn, worksheet, desk, flagged, posted>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ drawn \in Amounts
  /\ worksheet \in [Desks -> Amounts]
  /\ desk \in [Desks -> {"standby", "prepared"}]
  /\ flagged \in Desks \cup {NoDesk}
  /\ posted \in [Desks -> BOOLEAN]

  /\ worksheet = [d \in Desks |-> 0]
  /\ desk = [d \in Desks |-> "standby"]

  /\ posted = [d \in Desks |-> FALSE]

\* Preparing takes a snapshot, and it is refused unless the figure just read
\* already leaves room for a leg; that check is what the push relies on.
PrepareLeg(d) ==
  /\ desk[d] = "standby"
  /\ drawn + LegSize <= Ceiling
  /\ worksheet' = [worksheet EXCEPT ![d] = drawn]
  /\ desk' = [desk EXCEPT ![d] = "prepared"]
  /\ posted' = [posted EXCEPT ![d] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<drawn, flagged>>

\* The optimistic push: the snapshot must still equal the live figure.
PushThrough(d) ==
  /\ desk[d] = "prepared"
  /\ flagged # d
  /\ worksheet[d] = drawn

  /\ desk' = [desk EXCEPT ![d] = "standby"]

  /\ flagged' = d

\* but it is still refused if the leg would break the ceiling.

CeilingHolds ==

  /\ \A d \in Desks : desk[d] = "prepared" => worksheet[d] + LegSize <= Ceiling

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A blood-bank inventory tracker guards each cold-storage fridge with a lease. A technician who wants to work a fridge is granted a lease on it, and the lease carries a deadline taken from the bank's shift clock at the moment of grant. Only the technician named on a fridge's live lease is authorised to have that fridge open, and only under the deadline that the lease currently carries.

Commands from technicians do not reach the fridge controllers instantly, and the bank's messaging fabric gives no ordering guarantee at all: commands sit in flight and may be delivered in any order, so a command issued early can overtake one issued later, and a command can easily arrive after the situation that justified it has gone away. Every command therefore carries a stamp: the lease deadline that was live on that fridge when the technician issued it.

A technician holding a live lease on a fridge, one whose deadline has not yet passed on the shift clock, may issue an open command, which goes into the in-flight set stamped with that deadline. When an in-flight command is delivered, the controller accepts it only if the fridge is currently shut, the command's sender is the fridge's current lease holder, the command's stamp equals the fridge's live lease deadline, and the shift clock has not yet reached that deadline. An accepted command opens the fridge and records both who opened it and the deadline stamp it came in under. A delivered command that fails any of those tests is simply discarded.

An open fridge may be shut again at any time. The shift clock ticks forward while it is below the end of the shift. A fridge's lease may be granted to a technician only when the fridge has no lease holder and is shut, and only if the new deadline still falls within the shift. A lease whose deadline the clock has reached may be torn down, but only while the fridge is shut, so a lease is never pulled out from under an open door. When the clock has reached the end of the shift, every fridge is shut and unleased and nothing is left in flight, the bank resets the clock and a fresh shift begins.

The full action set is: grant a lease on an unleased, shut fridge to a technician, issue an open command stamped with the live lease deadline, deliver an in-flight command and accept it when sender, stamp, shut state and clock all check out, deliver an in-flight command and discard it when any of those checks fails, shut an open fridge, tick the shift clock, tear down an expired lease on a shut fridge, and start a fresh shift once the floor is completely quiet at the end of the old one.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a fridge is open, the technician who opened it is that fridge's current lease holder and the deadline stamp recorded at opening is still exactly the fridge's live lease deadline, so no reordered, stale, or unauthorised command ever leaves a fridge standing open.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A power-grid operator runs an automatic load shedder over a set of feeders. Taking a feeder off supply is a serious act, so it is never done on one controller's say-so: each shedding decision must be carried by a quorum of the region's control nodes, and the operator cares very much that the approvals counted are both from nodes that are actually on the live control roster and from the round of deliberation that is currently open.

Deliberation is organised in numbered rounds. Opening a proposal to shed a particular feeder bumps the round number and names that feeder as the live proposal; only one proposal is open at a time. A control node that is on the live roster may approve the open proposal, and its approval is recorded against the round number that was live when it approved. Approvals are never wiped: a node's recorded approval simply becomes stale the moment the round moves on, and a stale approval carries no weight at all in a later round.

The grid also carries a shedding budget, which is the number of feeders the operator is willing to have off supply at once, and that budget is adjusted at runtime as demand and reserve margin change. The shedder begins taking the proposed feeder off supply only when a strict majority of the on-roster control nodes have approvals recorded against the currently live round and the number of feeders already off supply is below the live budget. A feeder that is being taken off supply is then confirmed off, which also closes the proposal. A feeder that is off supply may later be restored to service.

The control roster itself changes: a node can be taken off the roster or put back on it. That amendment is only permitted while no feeder is actually mid-shed, so the quorum that a shed is standing on can never be dissolved underneath it.

The full action set is: open a proposal to shed a live feeder, which bumps the deliberation round; record an on-roster node's approval against the live round; begin taking the proposed feeder off supply when a majority of live-round approvals is in hand and the budget has room; confirm a mid-shed feeder as off supply and close the proposal; restore an off-supply feeder to service; amend the control roster while nothing is mid-shed; and adjust the shedding budget at runtime.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every feeder that the shedder has begun taking off supply is eventually confirmed as off supply.

vars == <<round, proposal, approval, onRoster, supply, budget>>

\* An approval is only worth anything if the node is on the live roster and
\* the approval was recorded against the round that is open now.
FreshBackers == {n \in Nodes : onRoster[n] /\ approval[n] = round}
OffSupplyCount == Cardinality({f \in Feeders : supply[f] # "live"})

TypeOK ==
  /\ round \in Rounds
  /\ proposal \in Feeders \cup {NoFeeder}
  /\ approval \in [Nodes -> Rounds]
  /\ onRoster \in [Nodes -> BOOLEAN]
  /\ supply \in [Feeders -> {"live", "shedding", "off"}]
  /\ budget \in 0 .. MaxBudget

  /\ round = 0
  /\ proposal = NoFeeder
  /\ approval = [n \in Nodes |-> 0]
  /\ onRoster = [n \in Nodes |-> TRUE]
  /\ supply = [f \in Feeders |-> "live"]
  /\ budget = MaxBudget

OpenProposal(f) ==
  /\ proposal = NoFeeder
  /\ supply[f] = "live"
  /\ round < MaxRound
  /\ round' = round + 1
  /\ proposal' = f
  /\ UNCHANGED <<approval, onRoster, supply, budget>>

RecordApproval(n) ==
  /\ onRoster[n]
  /\ proposal # NoFeeder
  /\ approval[n] # round
  /\ approval' = [approval EXCEPT ![n] = round]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, proposal, onRoster, supply, budget>>

BeginShed(f) ==

  /\ supply[f] = "live"
  /\ 2 * Cardinality(FreshBackers) > Cardinality(Nodes)
  /\ OffSupplyCount < budget
  /\ supply' = [supply EXCEPT ![f] = "shedding"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, proposal, approval, onRoster, budget>>

ConfirmOff(f) ==

  /\ proposal' = NoFeeder
  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, approval, onRoster, budget>>

RestoreFeeder(f) ==

  /\ supply' = [supply EXCEPT ![f] = "live"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, proposal, approval, onRoster, budget>>

AmendRoster(n) ==

  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, proposal, approval, supply, budget>>

AdjustBudget(k) ==

  /\ budget' = k
  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, proposal, approval, onRoster, supply>>

ConfirmAny == \E f \in Feeders : ConfirmOff(f)

  \/ \E f \in Feeders : BeginShed(f)

  \/ \E f \in Feeders : RestoreFeeder(f)
  \/ \E n \in Nodes : AmendRoster(n)

A car-wash conveyor line pulls a batch of cars through a tunnel in a fixed order, position one first, then position two, and so on to the end of the batch. Near the end of the tunnel sits the hot-wax bay. Baking hot wax onto a car is irreversible: the finish cannot be stripped and re-baked, and a car that goes through the bake twice comes out scorched. The line therefore keeps a wax book, an append-only list of the conveyor positions that have actually been baked, and that book must read exactly position one, then position two, and so on with no gaps and no repeats.

The tunnel is driven by a small cluster of line controllers, one of which is the leader. Leadership is carried by a term number: an election bumps the term and installs the electing controller as leader for it, which is how the line fails over when a controller drops out. A controller may act only while the term it believes it leads is the live term. Crucially, a controller does not refresh its own idea of which position comes next when it takes over; it keeps whatever counter it was carrying, so a fresh leader can easily believe the line is further back than it really is.

The wax bay itself is slow but never fails. When the leader sends a car into the bake, the bay starts running with that conveyor position on its slip; it may take arbitrarily long, but it always eventually reports the bake as complete. Once the bay reports complete, the leader looks at the wax book. If the slip's position is exactly the next position the book is waiting for, the leader writes it into the book, advances its own counter past it and releases the bay. If the slip's position is one the book already covers, the bake was a duplicate rerun by a leader that was behind, so the result is thrown away without any write, the leader resets its counter to the position the book is actually waiting for, and the bay is released. When the whole batch has been baked and the bay is idle, the tunnel takes a fresh batch, which empties the wax book and resets every controller's counter to position one.

The full action set is: elect a controller as leader by bumping the term, send the position on the leader's counter into the wax bay when the bay is free, have the slow bay report a running bake as complete, write a completed bake into the wax book when its position is the one the book is waiting for, throw away a completed bake whose position the book already covers, and start a fresh batch once the book is full and the bay is free.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The wax book always reads as the plain ascending run of conveyor positions, entry one being position one, entry two being position two and so on, so no conveyor position is ever written into it twice and the irreversible hot-wax bake is booked at most once per car.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Any bake that the wax bay has started eventually leaves the bay free again.
