===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A regional power-grid load shedder moves whole blocks of demand between substations. The megawatt blocks on the network are a fixed inventory for the shift: a block moved off one substation must land on another, and the control room keeps a double-entry book so that no block can be conjured into existence or quietly lost when a transfer goes wrong.

The book works like any double-entry ledger. Each substation has an opening figure for the shift, a running credit total for blocks that have landed on it, and a running debit total for blocks that have left it. The control room's rule is that each substation's live load must always equal its opening figure plus its credits minus its debits, and that the credits across the whole region must always equal the debits across the whole region.

A transfer is agreed by two-phase commit across the grid's protection relays. The control room proposes moving one block from a source substation that has a block to give to a destination substation that has headroom, which clears every relay's ballot. Each relay then votes: yes if the destination still has headroom, no otherwise. Once every relay has voted, the transfer commits if the ballots are unanimous, the source still has a block, the destination still has headroom and neither substation's ledger column has run out of room; committing takes one block off the source, puts one on the destination, and writes one debit and one credit in the same stroke. If a fully balloted transfer cannot be applied for any of those reasons it is abandoned outright, and no ledger line is written.

The control room supervisor also holds a privileged override. The supervisor may force a proposed transfer through without waiting for the relays to agree at all, which is used when a cascade is developing and there is no time to poll. The override skips the ballots entirely but it does not skip the books: it still checks that the source has a block, that the destination has headroom and that the ledger columns have room, and it still writes the matching debit and credit.

The full action set is: propose a one-block transfer between substations and clear the relay ballots, cast a relay's ballot on the open transfer according to the destination's headroom, commit a unanimously balloted transfer that can still be applied by writing the matching debit and credit, abandon a fully balloted transfer that cannot be applied, and have the supervisor force a proposed transfer through on the override while still writing both ledger lines.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every substation's live load always equals its opening figure plus its credits minus its debits, and the region's total credits always equal its total debits, so no megawatt block is ever created or destroyed by a transfer, an abandonment or a supervisor override.

---------------------------- MODULE W4Od9m2p2t5 ----------------------------
EXTENDS Integers

CONSTANTS NumStations, Relays, OpeningLoad, MaxLoad, LedgerRoom

Stations == 1 .. NumStations
NoStation == 0
NoTransfer == [src |-> NoStation, dst |-> NoStation]

VARIABLES load, credits, debits, transfer, ballot
vars == <<load, credits, debits, transfer, ballot>>

RECURSIVE SumOf(_, _)
SumOf(f, k) == IF k = 0 THEN 0 ELSE f[k] + SumOf(f, k - 1)

AllBalloted == \A r \in Relays : ballot[r] # "open"
Unanimous == \A r \in Relays : ballot[r] = "yes"

TypeOK ==
  /\ load \in [Stations -> 0 .. MaxLoad]
  /\ credits \in [Stations -> 0 .. LedgerRoom]
  /\ debits \in [Stations -> 0 .. LedgerRoom]
  /\ transfer \in [src : Stations \cup {NoStation}, dst : Stations \cup {NoStation}]
  /\ ballot \in [Relays -> {"open", "yes", "no"}]

Init ==
  /\ load = [b \in Stations |-> OpeningLoad]
  /\ credits = [b \in Stations |-> 0]
  /\ debits = [b \in Stations |-> 0]
  /\ transfer = NoTransfer
  /\ ballot = [r \in Relays |-> "open"]

\* A transfer can only be applied if both sides and both ledger columns can
\* take it; this is the guard the abandon path mirrors.
Applicable ==
  /\ load[transfer.src] > 0
  /\ load[transfer.dst] < MaxLoad
  /\ debits[transfer.src] < LedgerRoom
  /\ credits[transfer.dst] < LedgerRoom

ProposeTransfer(s, d) ==
  /\ transfer = NoTransfer
  /\ s # d
  /\ load[s] > 0
  /\ transfer' = [src |-> s, dst |-> d]
  /\ ballot' = [r \in Relays |-> "open"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<load, credits, debits>>

CastBallot(r) ==
  /\ transfer # NoTransfer
  /\ ballot[r] = "open"
  /\ ballot' = [ballot EXCEPT ![r] =
        IF load[transfer.dst] < MaxLoad THEN "yes" ELSE "no"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<load, credits, debits, transfer>>

\* One block moves and the matching debit and credit are written together.
ApplyBlock ==
  /\ load' = [load EXCEPT ![transfer.src] = load[transfer.src] - 1,
                         ![transfer.dst] = load[transfer.dst] + 1]
  /\ debits' = [debits EXCEPT ![transfer.src] = debits[transfer.src] + 1]
  /\ credits' = [credits EXCEPT ![transfer.dst] = credits[transfer.dst] + 1]
  /\ transfer' = NoTransfer

CommitTransfer ==
  /\ transfer # NoTransfer
  /\ AllBalloted
  /\ Unanimous
  /\ Applicable
  /\ ApplyBlock
  /\ UNCHANGED ballot

AbandonTransfer ==
  /\ transfer # NoTransfer
  /\ AllBalloted
  /\ ~(Unanimous /\ Applicable)
  /\ transfer' = NoTransfer
  /\ UNCHANGED <<load, credits, debits, ballot>>

\* The supervisor override skips the ballots but never skips the books.
SupervisorForce ==
  /\ transfer # NoTransfer
  /\ Applicable
  /\ ApplyBlock
  /\ UNCHANGED ballot

Next ==
  \/ \E s \in Stations, d \in Stations : ProposeTransfer(s, d)
  \/ \E r \in Relays : CastBallot(r)
  \/ CommitTransfer
  \/ AbandonTransfer
  \/ SupervisorForce

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* Double entry: every station's live load reconciles against its own ledger
\* columns, and the region's credits and debits match exactly.
GridBooksBalance ==
  /\ \A b \in Stations : load[b] = OpeningLoad + credits[b] - debits[b]
  /\ SumOf(credits, NumStations) = SumOf(debits, NumStations)
=============================================================================

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A hospital pharmacy runs two independent compounding robots, robot A and robot B, and both of them draw work from the same shared pool of prescriptions. Neither robot owns a set of prescriptions; whichever robot picks one up out of the pool carries it.

The finished dose is put away in a numbered drawer of the compounding cabinet, and the drawers are grouped into two temperature zones. Applying the tamper seal to a dose is irreversible: the seal is a single-use foil that carries the batch record, it cannot be lifted and re-applied, and a dose that gets sealed twice has to be destroyed. Every seal that is applied leaves its tamper tag in the drawer it was applied in, so the cabinet's drawers are the physical record of which prescriptions have been sealed.

Access to the cabinet is layered. A robot carrying a prescription must first take the coarse lock on a temperature zone, and only while it holds a zone's coarse lock may it take the fine lock on an individual drawer inside that zone. A robot may seal its dose into a drawer only while it holds both the coarse lock on that drawer's zone and the fine lock on that drawer, and only if the drawer has no tamper tag in it yet; sealing marks the prescription sealed, leaves the tamper tag in the drawer and leaves the robot's hands empty. A robot may give back every lock it holds, but only once its hands are empty, so it never abandons a job halfway through the cabinet.

When every drawer in the cabinet holds a tamper tag, the locks are all free and neither robot is carrying anything, the cabinet is emptied for the next batch: the tamper tags come out, the prescriptions go back into the shared pool and the seal records are cleared together.

The full action set is: pick a prescription out of the shared pool with empty hands, take the coarse lock on a temperature zone while carrying a prescription, take the fine lock on a drawer inside a zone whose coarse lock is already held, seal the carried dose into a fully locked untagged drawer, give back all of a robot's locks once its hands are empty, and empty the cabinet for a new batch once every drawer is tagged and everything is quiet.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every prescription, the number of drawers holding that prescription's tamper tag is exactly one if the prescription is marked sealed and zero otherwise, so the irreversible seal is applied to a given prescription at most once even though two robots draw from the same pool.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: A robot that is carrying a prescription and already holds both the coarse lock on a zone and the fine lock on an untagged drawer in that zone eventually ends up with empty hands.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Scripts, NumDrawers, ColdUpTo

Robots == {"A", "B"}
Drawers == 1 .. NumDrawers
Zones == {"cold", "ambient"}
FreeLock == "unlocked"
NoScript == "emptyhands"

ZoneOf(d) == IF d <= ColdUpTo THEN "cold" ELSE "ambient"

VARIABLES zoneLock, drawerLock, carrying, sealed, tamperTag, inPool
vars == <<zoneLock, drawerLock, carrying, sealed, tamperTag, inPool>>

TagsFor(p) == Cardinality({d \in Drawers : tamperTag[d] = p})

TypeOK ==
  /\ zoneLock \in [Zones -> Robots \cup {FreeLock}]
  /\ drawerLock \in [Drawers -> Robots \cup {FreeLock}]
  /\ carrying \in [Robots -> Scripts \cup {NoScript}]
  /\ sealed \in [Scripts -> BOOLEAN]
  /\ tamperTag \in [Drawers -> Scripts \cup {NoScript}]
  /\ inPool \in [Scripts -> BOOLEAN]

Init ==
  /\ zoneLock = [z \in Zones |-> FreeLock]
  /\ drawerLock = [d \in Drawers |-> FreeLock]
  /\ carrying = [rb \in Robots |-> NoScript]
  /\ sealed = [p \in Scripts |-> FALSE]
  /\ tamperTag = [d \in Drawers |-> NoScript]
  /\ inPool = [p \in Scripts |-> TRUE]

PickUp(rb, p) ==
  /\ carrying[rb] = NoScript
  /\ inPool[p]
  /\ carrying' = [carrying EXCEPT ![rb] = p]
  /\ inPool' = [inPool EXCEPT ![p] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<zoneLock, drawerLock, sealed, tamperTag>>

TakeZoneLock(rb, z) ==
  /\ carrying[rb] # NoScript
  /\ zoneLock[z] = FreeLock
  /\ zoneLock' = [zoneLock EXCEPT ![z] = rb]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<drawerLock, carrying, sealed, tamperTag, inPool>>

\* The fine lock is only reachable through the coarse lock on its zone.
TakeDrawerLock(rb, d) ==
  /\ zoneLock[ZoneOf(d)] = rb
  /\ drawerLock[d] = FreeLock
  /\ drawerLock' = [drawerLock EXCEPT ![d] = rb]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<zoneLock, carrying, sealed, tamperTag, inPool>>

\* The irreversible step: one foil seal, one tamper tag left behind.
SealInto(rb, d) ==
  /\ carrying[rb] # NoScript
  /\ zoneLock[ZoneOf(d)] = rb
  /\ drawerLock[d] = rb
  /\ tamperTag[d] = NoScript
  /\ sealed' = [sealed EXCEPT ![carrying[rb]] = TRUE]
  /\ tamperTag' = [tamperTag EXCEPT ![d] = carrying[rb]]
  /\ carrying' = [carrying EXCEPT ![rb] = NoScript]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<zoneLock, drawerLock, inPool>>

\* Locks only go back when the robot's hands are empty.
GiveBackLocks(rb) ==
  /\ carrying[rb] = NoScript
  /\ (\E z \in Zones : zoneLock[z] = rb) \/ (\E d \in Drawers : drawerLock[d] = rb)
  /\ zoneLock' = [z \in Zones |-> IF zoneLock[z] = rb THEN FreeLock ELSE zoneLock[z]]
  /\ drawerLock' = [d \in Drawers |-> IF drawerLock[d] = rb THEN FreeLock ELSE drawerLock[d]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<carrying, sealed, tamperTag, inPool>>

EmptyCabinet ==
  /\ \A d \in Drawers : tamperTag[d] # NoScript
  /\ (\A z \in Zones : zoneLock[z] = FreeLock)
  /\ (\A d \in Drawers : drawerLock[d] = FreeLock) /\ (\A rb \in Robots : carrying[rb] = NoScript)
  /\ tamperTag' = [d \in Drawers |-> NoScript]
  /\ sealed' = [p \in Scripts |-> FALSE]
  /\ inPool' = [p \in Scripts |-> TRUE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<zoneLock, drawerLock, carrying>>

SealByA == \E d \in Drawers : SealInto("A", d)
SealByB == \E d \in Drawers : SealInto("B", d)

Next ==
  \/ \E rb \in Robots, p \in Scripts : PickUp(rb, p)
  \/ \E rb \in Robots, z \in Zones : TakeZoneLock(rb, z)
  \/ \E rb \in Robots, d \in Drawers : TakeDrawerLock(rb, d)
  \/ SealByA
  \/ SealByB
  \/ \E rb \in Robots : GiveBackLocks(rb)
  \/ EmptyCabinet

Spec ==
  /\ Init
  /\ [][Next]_vars
  /\ WF_vars(SealByA)
  /\ WF_vars(SealByB)

\* Exactly one tamper tag exists for a sealed prescription and none for an
\* unsealed one, so the single-use foil is spent at most once per script.
SealAppliedAtMostOnce ==
  \A p \in Scripts : TagsFor(p) = (IF sealed[p] THEN 1 ELSE 0)

\* A robot holding both locks over a clean drawer always gets to put its
\* dose away, so it never stands there loaded for ever.
LoadedRobotSealsThrough ==
  \A rb \in Robots :
    ( carrying[rb] # NoScript /\ \E d \in Drawers :
        zoneLock[ZoneOf(d)] = rb /\ drawerLock[d] = rb /\ tamperTag[d] = NoScript )
      ~> (carrying[rb] = NoScript)
===========================================================================

A skyscraper's elevator bank is run by a cluster of dispatch computers, one of which is the elected leader. Leadership is carried by a term number: an election bumps the bank's term and installs the electing computer as leader of that term, and a computer may only dispatch while the term it believes it leads is the bank's live term. That is how the bank fails over when a dispatch computer drops out.

Two capacity limits govern the bank. Each car has a rated load: the people already riding in it plus the people the dispatcher has committed to it but who have not yet stepped in must never exceed that rating. On top of that the building fire code sets a bank-wide limit on how many people may be in transit at once, counting everyone riding and everyone committed to a car across the whole bank, and that limit is deliberately lower than the sum of the car ratings.

People wait in the lobby. The live leader may commit one waiting person to a car, but only if that car's riding-plus-committed count is still below its rating and the bank-wide in-transit count is still below the fire-code limit; committing takes the person out of the lobby. A person committed to a car with a working controller steps into the car, turning a commitment into a rider. A rider in a car with a working controller alights and returns to the lobby.

One car controller in the bank can crash silently: at most one controller ever fails, and it fails without telling anybody, so nothing in the dispatcher's records changes when it does. A crashed car simply stops loading and unloading, and its riders and commitments stay charged against both limits. A building engineer may hand-walk one person out of a crashed car, whether that person was riding or merely committed, and back to the lobby.

The full action set is: elect a dispatch computer as leader by bumping the bank's term, commit a waiting person to a car that has room under both its own rating and the bank-wide limit, step a committed person into a car with a working controller, alight a rider from a car with a working controller back to the lobby, crash the one car controller that is allowed to fail, and hand-walk one person out of a crashed car back to the lobby.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No car's riders plus commitments ever exceed that car's rated load, and the bank-wide count of riders plus commitments across all cars never exceeds the fire-code in-transit limit, even after a car controller has crashed silently and stopped clearing its load.

EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS NumCars, Dispatchers, CarRating, BankLimit, LobbyPeople, MaxTerm

Cars == 1 .. NumCars
Terms == 0 .. MaxTerm

VARIABLES term, believes, riding, committed, carUp, lobby
vars == <<term, believes, riding, committed, carUp, lobby>>

RECURSIVE SumOf(_, _)
SumOf(f, k) == IF k = 0 THEN 0 ELSE f[k] + SumOf(f, k - 1)

LeadsNow(n) == believes[n] = term
InTransit == SumOf(riding, NumCars) + SumOf(committed, NumCars)

TypeOK ==
  /\ term \in Terms
  /\ believes \in [Dispatchers -> Terms]
  /\ riding \in [Cars -> 0 .. LobbyPeople]
  /\ committed \in [Cars -> 0 .. LobbyPeople]
  /\ carUp \in [Cars -> BOOLEAN]
  /\ lobby \in 0 .. LobbyPeople

Init ==
  /\ term = 0
  /\ believes = [n \in Dispatchers |-> 0]
  /\ riding = [c \in Cars |-> 0]
  /\ committed = [c \in Cars |-> 0]
  /\ carUp = [c \in Cars |-> TRUE]
  /\ lobby = LobbyPeople

\* Failover: an election bumps the live term and leaves earlier leaders inert.
ElectLeader(n) ==
  /\ term < MaxTerm
  /\ term' = term + 1
  /\ believes' = [believes EXCEPT ![n] = term + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<riding, committed, carUp, lobby>>

\* A commitment is charged against both the car rating and the bank limit
\* the moment it is made, not when the passenger steps in.
CommitToCar(n, c) ==
  /\ LeadsNow(n)
  /\ lobby > 0
  /\ riding[c] + committed[c] < CarRating
  /\ InTransit < BankLimit
  /\ committed' = [committed EXCEPT ![c] = committed[c] + 1]
  /\ lobby' = lobby - 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<term, believes, riding, carUp>>

StepIn(c) ==
  /\ carUp[c]
  /\ committed[c] > 0
  /\ committed' = [committed EXCEPT ![c] = committed[c] - 1]
  /\ riding' = [riding EXCEPT ![c] = riding[c] + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<term, believes, carUp, lobby>>

Alight(c) ==
  /\ carUp[c]
  /\ riding[c] > 0
  /\ riding' = [riding EXCEPT ![c] = riding[c] - 1]
  /\ lobby' = lobby + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<term, believes, committed, carUp>>

\* At most one controller fails, and it leaves no trace when it does.
CrashController(c) ==
  /\ \A d \in Cars : carUp[d]
  /\ carUp' = [carUp EXCEPT ![c] = FALSE]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<term, believes, riding, committed, lobby>>

HandWalkOut(c) ==
  /\ ~carUp[c]
  /\ riding[c] + committed[c] > 0
  /\ riding' = [riding EXCEPT ![c] = IF riding[c] > 0 THEN riding[c] - 1 ELSE 0]
  /\ committed' = [committed EXCEPT ![c] =
        IF riding[c] > 0 THEN committed[c] ELSE committed[c] - 1]
  /\ lobby' = lobby + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<term, believes, carUp>>

Next ==
  \/ \E n \in Dispatchers : ElectLeader(n)
  \/ \E n \in Dispatchers, c \in Cars : CommitToCar(n, c)
  \/ \E c \in Cars : StepIn(c)
  \/ \E c \in Cars : Alight(c)
  \/ \E c \in Cars : CrashController(c)
  \/ \E c \in Cars : HandWalkOut(c)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* Two independent ceilings: each car's own rating, and the fire-code cap on
\* everybody in transit across the whole bank.
LoadWithinBothLimits ==
  /\ \A c \in Cars : riding[c] + committed[c] <= CarRating
  /\ SumOf(riding, NumCars) + SumOf(committed, NumCars) <= BankLimit

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A warehouse floor is worked by a fleet of picking robots. Each aisle is handed out to one robot at a time under a lease, and a robot may only move stock in an aisle whose lease it genuinely holds right now. Leases are the whole authorisation story here: the warehouse controller does not track robot positions, so if a robot were to act on an aisle whose lease had moved on without it, nothing else would catch the mistake.

Every aisle carries a lease holder, a lease generation number and a run-down timer. Granting a free aisle's lease to a robot bumps that aisle's generation, refills the timer and hands the robot a ticket naming the aisle and the generation it was granted at. Renewing a live lease for the robot that already holds it bumps the generation again, refills the timer and reissues that robot's ticket. A ticket is therefore only good for the generation printed on it: the moment the aisle's generation moves on, every ticket printed under an earlier generation is stale and worthless. The generation counter runs only up to a fixed ceiling.

A robot may start moving stock in an aisle only if its ticket names that aisle, the aisle's lease holder is that same robot, the aisle's generation still matches the generation printed on the ticket, and the aisle's timer has not run out. The robots are slow but they never fail: a robot may take arbitrarily long over a job, but it always eventually finishes and goes idle. Aisle timers run down on their own. An aisle whose timer has run out has its lease torn down, but only once no robot is actually working in it, so a lease is never yanked out from under a robot mid-job; because robots always finish, the controller never has to wait for ever.

When every aisle is unleased, every robot is idle and some aisle's generation has reached the ceiling, the warehouse starts a new shift: generation counters go back to zero, timers are emptied and every robot's ticket is torn up together, so no ticket from the old shift can survive into the new one.

The full action set is: grant a free aisle's lease to a robot with a fresh generation and ticket, renew a live lease for its current holder with a new generation and ticket, start moving stock in an aisle against a matching, unexpired, live-generation ticket, finish a job and go idle, run an aisle's timer down by one, tear down an expired lease on an aisle nobody is working in, and start a new shift once everything is quiet and the generation ceiling has been reached.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Any robot that is moving stock is working an aisle that its own ticket names, whose lease holder is that same robot, and whose lease generation still equals the generation printed on that ticket, so no unauthorised robot and no robot carrying a stale ticket ever moves stock.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Any aisle whose lease timer has run out while a lease is still held on it eventually has that lease torn down.

EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS NumAisles, GenCeiling, TimerFull

Aisles == 1 .. NumAisles
Robots == {"r1", "r2"}
Gens == 0 .. GenCeiling
NoRobot == "unleased"
NoAisle == 0
BlankTicket == [aisle |-> NoAisle, gen |-> 0]

VARIABLES holder, generation, timer, ticket, phase
vars == <<holder, generation, timer, ticket, phase>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ holder \in [Aisles -> Robots \cup {NoRobot}]
  /\ generation \in [Aisles -> Gens] /\ timer \in [Aisles -> 0 .. TimerFull]
  /\ ticket \in [Robots -> [aisle : Aisles \cup {NoAisle}, gen : Gens]]
  /\ phase \in [Robots -> {"idle", "moving"}]

Init ==
  /\ holder = [a \in Aisles |-> NoRobot]
  /\ generation = [a \in Aisles |-> 0] /\ timer = [a \in Aisles |-> 0]
  /\ ticket = [rb \in Robots |-> BlankTicket]
  /\ phase = [rb \in Robots |-> "idle"]

\* Every grant and every renewal bumps the generation, which is what makes
\* all older tickets for that aisle worthless.
GrantLease(a, rb) ==
  /\ holder[a] = NoRobot
  /\ generation[a] < GenCeiling
  /\ holder' = [holder EXCEPT ![a] = rb]
  /\ generation' = [generation EXCEPT ![a] = generation[a] + 1]
  /\ timer' = [timer EXCEPT ![a] = TimerFull]
  /\ ticket' = [ticket EXCEPT ![rb] = [aisle |-> a, gen |-> generation[a] + 1]]
  /\ UNCHANGED phase

RenewLease(a, rb) ==
  /\ holder[a] = rb
  /\ timer[a] > 0

  \/ \E a \in Aisles : RunDown(a)

  /\ WF_vars(FinishR1)
  /\ WF_vars(FinishR2)
  /\ WF_vars(TearDownAny)

\* its ticket generation still matches the aisle's live generation.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A regional power-grid operator runs a two-phase-commit protocol across a small set of substation controllers to decide whether to shed load on a feeder during a demand spike. Each round, the operator (acting as coordinator) opens a new epoch, asking every substation controller to vote "yes" (able to shed safely) or "no" (must stay online) for that specific epoch. A controller may only cast a vote once it has synchronized its local epoch counter with the operator's current epoch -- a controller that has not yet synchronized is considered stale for that round and is barred from voting or acting.

Only if every controller votes "yes" does the operator move the round to "committed"; if any controller votes "no", the round is "aborted" instead. Feeder shedding -- the actual physical action of cutting load -- is only performed by a controller that is both caught up to the live epoch and holds a "yes" vote recorded for that same epoch. Once a round resolves (committed or aborted), the operator resets to idle and may open the next epoch. Controllers synchronize asynchronously and independently: a controller can be slow to catch up to the current epoch (it may sit stale for a while before syncing), but it never crashes or drops out permanently -- it always eventually catches up if given the chance, it just cannot be assumed to act promptly.

This models the real hazard in feeder-shedding coordination: a controller that missed the current round's vote (because it was still processing the prior epoch) must never shed load on the strength of an old, no-longer-valid authorization, and a controller that never actually voted "yes" this round must never act as though it had.

The full action set is: StartRound (operator opens a new epoch and clears votes), Sync (a controller catches up its local epoch to the operator's current epoch), CastVote (a synchronized controller records a yes/no vote for the live epoch), Commit (operator moves to committed once all votes are yes), Abort (operator moves to aborted once any vote is no), Shed (a synchronized, yes-voting controller actually cuts load for the live epoch), and ResetRound (operator returns to idle after a round resolves).
SAFETY PROPERTY: whenever a controller's recorded shed-epoch equals the operator's current live epoch, that controller must actually be synchronized to the live epoch and hold a yes-vote for it -- no stale or unauthorized controller ever performs the shed action.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home vendor runs several hub controllers (a front-door hub, a garage hub, a side-gate hub) that all share one access schedule: the set of guest door codes currently authorized in the house. Rather than a central coordinator, the hubs cooperate through a compare-and-swap register: the shared schedule carries a version token, and a hub wishing to add its own guest code must first take a snapshot of that token, then attempt to swap in the new schedule only if the token still matches its snapshot. If another hub updated the schedule first, the token has moved on and the swap is rejected, so the hub must re-snapshot the current token and try again -- this is exactly what prevents one hub's addition from silently clobbering another hub's already-committed addition.

Concretely, each hub starts idle and, at some point, decides it wants to add its own code to the shared schedule. From then on it repeatedly re-synchronizes its local snapshot of the version token until the token it has last seen matches the register's live token, at which point its compare-and-swap succeeds: the code joins the shared schedule, the token advances by one, and the hub records the exact token value at which its own addition landed. Because every successful swap bumps the token, no two hubs can ever believe they landed at the same token value -- each committed addition gets its own distinct, traceable slot, so updates are never lost or overwritten without a trace.

One hub in the whole network can, at any point, crash silently -- its firmware simply stops responding, with no notification to the others. A crashed hub takes no further actions ever again (in particular it never lands its own pending addition), but crucially the other hubs' snapshot-and-swap retries are completely unaffected by another hub's crash: they keep re-synchronizing and re-attempting until their own addition succeeds. The mechanism guarantees that any hub which wants to add its code, and which never crashes, eventually gets that addition durably recorded in the shared schedule.

The full action set is: Request (a hub decides it wants to add its own guest code to the shared schedule), SyncHub (a hub re-synchronizes its local snapshot of the register's version token to the current live value), AddCode (a hub whose snapshot matches the live token swaps its code into the shared schedule and the token advances), and CrashHub (the one hub in the network permitted to crash does so silently and takes no further action).
SAFETY PROPERTY: no two hubs ever have their additions recorded at the same version token -- every committed addition to the shared schedule lands at its own distinct token, so no hub's update is ever silently lost or overwritten by another's.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: every hub that has requested to add its code eventually either gets that addition durably recorded in the shared schedule or crashes -- a slow hub competing with others is never left waiting forever.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A university course-registration system lets several advisors edit one shared registration record for a course (its roster overrides: manual add/drop exceptions to the automated enrollment engine). Because two advisors editing the record at once could silently clobber each other's changes, the system uses lease-based ownership: an advisor must first acquire a lease on the record, which is only granted while no one else currently holds it, and the lease carries a fixed expiry measured against a shared clock. Only the current lease holder may commit an edit, and only while the shared clock has not yet passed the lease's expiry -- once the clock passes expiry, the lease lapses on its own and the record becomes free for the next advisor to claim.

Each time a lease is granted -- whether through the normal acquire path or through the registrar's admin override -- the system stamps a fresh lease generation number, and any edit an advisor commits is tagged with the generation under which it was made. This generation tag is what protects against lost updates: because a new generation is stamped every time ownership changes hands, no two different advisors can ever have their edits tagged with the same generation, so no advisor's committed edit can ever be silently attributed to, or overwritten by, another advisor's turn with the record.

The registrar holds a privileged admin override: unlike an ordinary advisor, the registrar may force the lease directly onto a chosen advisor at any moment, regardless of who currently holds it or whether that lease has expired yet -- for example to break a session where an advisor's client has hung. The override still goes through the same generation-stamping path as a normal acquire, so the protection against lost updates holds even when the registrar exercises this privileged power.

The full action set is: Tick (the shared clock advances by one), AcquireLease (an advisor claims the record's lease once it is free, stamping a new generation and expiry), Edit (the current lease holder commits an edit tagged with the live generation, only while the clock has not passed expiry), NaturalExpiry (the lease lapses on its own once the clock passes its expiry, freeing the record), and AdminOverride (the registrar forcibly hands the lease to a chosen advisor at any time, stamping a new generation regardless of the current holder or expiry).
SAFETY PROPERTY: no two different advisors ever have committed edits tagged with the same lease generation -- every committed edit is attributable to exactly the one advisor who held that generation's lease, so updates are never lost or silently overwritten.

    /\ expiry = 0
    /\ gen = 0

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A container-ship crane yard operates several gantry cranes that compete for the job of hoisting containers off an incoming vessel. Each container on the ship has its own claim register: a compare-and-swap token that starts at zero. A crane that wants to service a container first moves into position and takes a snapshot of that container's current token. It then attempts a compare-and-swap claim: the claim succeeds, and the crane becomes the container's recorded claimant, only if no one else has claimed the container yet and the crane's snapshot still matches the register's live token (the token is bumped the instant a claim succeeds). If another crane's claim beat it to the register, the snapshot is now stale and the crane must abandon that container and move on to another one.

Only the crane recorded as a container's claimant may actually perform the hoist -- the physical, irreversible act of lifting the container off the ship. Once a container has been hoisted it can never be hoisted again, so the claim register's compare-and-swap step is what prevents two cranes from both believing they are clear to lift the same container at once. After a crane either completes its hoist or abandons a losing claim, it becomes free to move on and take aim at another still-unclaimed, unhoisted container.

Any crane in the yard can be arbitrarily slow -- it might sit in position for a long time before taking its snapshot, before attempting its claim, or before actually swinging into the hoist -- but no crane ever breaks down or drops out permanently; every crane that still has work available to it keeps making progress eventually, just not necessarily promptly. Because of this, the yard is guaranteed to eventually hoist every container exactly once, no matter how the cranes' relative speeds play out.

The full action set is: PickTarget (an idle crane moves onto an unclaimed, unhoisted container and snapshots its token), ClaimCAS (a crane whose snapshot still matches the live token wins the compare-and-swap claim on its target container), Hoist (the recorded claimant of a container performs the irreversible lift), ReleaseDone (a crane that finished hoisting its container becomes idle again), and Abandon (a crane whose target was claimed by someone else gives up on it and becomes idle again).

LIVENESS PROPERTY: every container in the yard is eventually hoisted, regardless of how slowly any individual crane moves.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An airport baggage router moves bags between conveyor-belt segments feeding the sorting hall, and it uses a two-phase-commit protocol to decide each single bag transfer between two segments. To move a bag from a source segment to a destination segment, the router first opens a transfer round: both the source and the destination segment are asked to vote. The source votes "yes" only if it actually still holds a bag to hand off; the destination votes "yes" only if accepting one more bag would not push its occupancy past its fixed belt capacity. Only when both segments vote "yes" does the router commit the round -- the bag count moves from source to destination -- otherwise the round is aborted and no bag moves.

This capacity check by the destination segment is the crux of the safety mechanism: a destination segment that is already at capacity must always vote "no," and it is exactly that vote that stops the transfer from ever pushing its occupancy over the limit. Once a round resolves (committed or aborted), the router returns to idle and may open a new transfer round between any pair of segments.

A segment can be slow to cast its vote in a round -- the router may wait an arbitrary amount of time for a segment's belt-load sensor to respond -- but a segment never goes offline or drops out of a round entirely; every vote it owes eventually gets cast, it simply cannot be assumed to respond promptly. The router never commits a transfer on partial information: both votes must actually be in before it decides, so a slow segment can delay a round but can never cause its capacity limit to be silently violated.

The full action set is: StartTransfer (the router opens a new round between a chosen source and destination segment), VoteSource (the source segment votes yes only if it currently holds a bag to give up), VoteDest (the destination segment votes yes only if accepting a bag would not exceed its belt capacity), Commit (the router moves the bag once both votes are yes), Abort (the router cancels the round once either vote is no), and ResetRound (the router returns to idle once a round has resolved).
SAFETY PROPERTY: no conveyor-belt segment's occupancy ever exceeds its fixed capacity.

A consortium of correspondent banks runs an interbank settlement batch: on each settlement cycle, one bank acts as the settlement coordinator ("leader") that gathers payment instructions from the other banks into a single batch destined for the next settlement window. The clearing infrastructure enforces a hard capacity on how many instructions a single batch may hold before it must be closed and presented, because the downstream settlement engine can only reconcile a bounded number of legs per window without risking exposure limits being breached.

Leadership of the batch is decided by an election with failover: at the start, there is no coordinator, so any bank may be elected. If the acting coordinator is later observed by its peers to be running slow -- not crashed, just lagging behind the expected cadence of admitting instructions -- the peers can trigger a failover election that hands coordination to a (possibly different) bank and advances an election term counter, without discarding the instructions already accumulated in the batch. A slow coordinator is never treated as failed: it keeps the batch state intact and remains capable of resuming, so failover here is a hand-off of responsibility rather than a recovery from crash.

While a batch is open, the coordinator admits instructions into it one at a time, refusing to admit past the configured capacity limit. The coordinator (whichever bank currently holds the role) may close the open batch at its discretion, moving it to a closing state; a closed batch is then flushed at the settlement window, after which a fresh batch is opened for the next cycle.

SAFETY PROPERTY: While a settlement batch is open or awaiting settlement, the number of instructions it holds never exceeds the configured capacity limit.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every settlement batch that is opened is eventually flushed at a settlement window, even when its coordinating bank becomes slow.

An airport's runway allocator decides which aircraft may use the single active runway next, and it must never let a second flight's clearance be finalized while an earlier flight's clearance for the same runway is still being resolved. Granting the runway goes through a two-phase commit across the controllers who must agree before a clearance is final: several aircraft may have open requests for the runway at once, and the radio and data links carrying each controller's vote back to the allocator do not guarantee delivery in the order the votes were cast, so votes and requests can arrive out of sequence.

To stay safe under this reordering, every request that opens is stamped with a fresh fencing term, a counter that only ever increases. Participants (the tower and approach control) cast their votes for a specific flight's request independently of one another and of any other flight's request, so the order in which votes and competing requests land is never fixed. A flight's clearance is only finalized once every participant has voted for it and its fencing term still matches the allocator's current term; if some other, later request has since advanced the term, the earlier request's votes -- however complete -- are recognized as stale and cannot be used to grant the runway, and that earlier request instead gives up so its flight can try again.

A flight holding the runway eventually vacates it, freeing the runway for the next clearance to be finalized. An open request that has been superseded does not linger forever: it is always eventually resolved, either by being granted the runway or by giving up once a newer request has taken over the fencing term.

The full action set is: Request (a flight opens a request for the runway, advancing the fencing term), Vote (a participant casts its vote for a specific flight's open request, independently of any other flight's request), Commit (a flight is granted the runway once every participant has voted for it and its fencing term is still current), Reset (an open request whose fencing term has been superseded by a later request gives up), and Release (a flight holding the runway gives it up).

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every flight's open request eventually stops being open -- it is always eventually either granted the runway or superseded and given up, never stuck pending forever.

A small swarm of surveillance drones patrols a wildfire perimeter, reporting hotspots that must be inspected up close. Ground control keeps the inspection requests in a bounded work queue: a request first sits in an unbounded backlog, and control admits it into the small active queue only while the number of requests currently queued-or-in-progress is below the queue's fixed capacity. This backpressure keeps at most a handful of inspection jobs in flight at once, so a burst of new hotspots cannot overwhelm the swarm's limited bandwidth. Once a job is in the active queue, any drone that is not currently known to be down may pick it up and start flying the inspection.

Because the radio link is unreliable, ground control never learns instantly that a drone has crashed -- one drone, and only one, can go silently unresponsive mid-flight without announcing anything. Each drone carries its own fencing generation number, which starts at zero and is bumped the moment control detects that particular drone has crashed. Every job a drone picks up keeps a stamp equal to that drone's generation at pickup time, so a job's stamp only ever goes stale relative to its own holder's generation, never because some unrelated healthy drone happened to crash. Only a job whose stamp still equals its holder's live generation may be reported complete by that holder. A job orphaned because its holder's generation moved past its stamp is reclaimed back into the active queue -- with its holder cleared -- so a still-healthy drone can pick it up fresh and carry the inspection through to completion.

A regional power-grid load shedder protects a single critical shedding actuator: the
physical relay bank that actually disconnects a distribution feeder when demand gets too

that one actuator pool, but only one of them may be driving it at any moment. Rather than
taking a hard lock up front, each instance uses optimistic locking with retry: it first
takes a lightweight snapshot of the actuator's version counter, and only afterward tries
to commit its claim to the actuator by checking that the version has not moved since the
snapshot was taken.

The version counter toggles between an even value (actuator free) and an odd value
(actuator held) every time it changes. An instance stages a snapshot of the current
version only once grid load has actually crossed the shedding threshold. If, when it
attempts to commit, the live version still matches its stale snapshot and the actuator is
free, the commit succeeds: the instance becomes the holder and the version flips to odd.
If the version has since moved -- because the other instance grabbed the actuator first,
or because the actuator is currently held -- the attempt fails and the instance must
discard its snapshot and retry later. Whoever is holding the actuator eventually releases
it, flipping the version back to even so a waiting instance's next attempt can succeed.
Independently of all this, the grid's load level itself keeps drifting up and down as
demand changes throughout the day.

at or above the shedding threshold), CommitLock (an instance whose snapshot still matches
the live, even version becomes the actuator holder), RetryFail (an instance whose snapshot
is stale or finds the actuator held discards it), Release (the current holder gives up the
actuator and flips the version), RaiseLoad (grid load increases by one step), and
LowerLoad (grid load decreases by one step).

LIVENESS PROPERTY: every instance that stages a version snapshot eventually resolves it, either by committing the lock or by retrying it away.

override still goes through the very same irreversible bookkeeping as an ordinary

privileged admin dispenses a specific not-yet-dispensed request immediately, pulling it
out of the queue if it was waiting there).

A power-grid load shedder coordinates a synchronized shed action across three feeder

right now; only once every live participant has voted yes does the coordinator declare
the round committed, and only then may a participant actually execute the shed action
for that round.

Exactly one participant can crash silently, and it always does so before ever casting a
vote in the round it crashes during -- it simply goes quiet instead of responding, rather
than voting no. The coordinator must not wait forever on a silently crashed participant:
the commit decision only ever depends on the votes of the participants that are still
alive. A round that gets a live no vote is aborted instead of committed. Once a round is
decided, either way, a fresh round begins: votes are cleared and a new round number
starts, bounded so it wraps back around rather than growing forever.

The full action set is: Vote (a live participant that has not yet voted in the current
round casts yes or no), CrashSilently (a participant that has not yet voted goes silently
quiet for the rest of time, before ever casting a vote), DecideCommit (every live
participant has voted yes, so the round is declared committed), DecideAbort (some live
participant voted no, so the round is declared aborted), Execute (a participant that
voted yes in a now-committed round actually carries out the shed action for that round),
and StartNextEpoch (a decided round closes and a fresh round begins).

A regional vending machine network lets field vendors remotely restock and adjust prices on machines using an optimistic-locking protocol over an unreliable wireless link. Before writing to a machine's inventory record, a vendor first fetches the record's current version counter; the vendor's handheld terminal caches this version alongside the change it intends to make. When the vendor is ready to commit, the machine only accepts the write if the vendor's cached version still equals the machine's live version counter, meaning the record was not modified by anyone else since the last fetch. If the versions disagree the commit is simply not enabled, and the vendor is expected to re-fetch and retry with a fresh version.

Each vendor additionally requires a valid dispatch credential (authorization) issued by network operations, and this credential can be revoked mid-session, for example after a vendor's route is reassigned to someone else. Because vendors carry cheap handheld terminals that periodically go offline for good with no distress signal, a vendor's terminal may crash silently at any time; nobody else in the network is notified, and the vendor simply stops taking any further actions from that point on. To keep the network's audit trail trustworthy, whenever a vendor is revoked or discovered crashed, operations proactively invalidates that vendor's most recently recorded write on every machine it touched, so the chain of custody for that machine is marked as needing re-validation until a currently-valid vendor writes to it again.

Vendors otherwise operate independently of one another: any non-crashed vendor may fetch a machine's live version at any time, may commit its pending update only if its cached version is still fresh and its credential is currently valid, may have its credential revoked by operations, may have its terminal crash silently, or may be re-authorized by operations after a review -- but only while its terminal is still alive, since a silently crashed terminal never comes back online.

The full action set is: FetchVersion (a vendor reads a machine's current version into its local cache), CommitUpdate (a vendor applies its pending change, but only if its cached version still matches the machine's live version and its credential is valid), RevokeAuthorization (operations revokes a vendor's credential and invalidates that vendor's last recorded write on every machine), CrashSilently (a vendor's terminal fails permanently with no notification, and its last recorded write is likewise invalidated), and Reauthorize (operations restores a still-alive vendor's credential after review).
SAFETY PROPERTY: At every reachable state, whichever vendor is recorded as a machine's most recent writer currently holds a valid, non-revoked, non-crashed credential.

A public library runs its book-reservation system across a small cluster of replica servers so that patrons can still file holds even if one machine goes down. At any time exactly one replica acts as the leader, and only the leader is allowed to accept a patron's reservation request and durably commit it into the shared reservation record; the other replicas hold their own local copies of the record that are kept in sync by asynchronous replication in the background.

If the current leader's process crashes, it crashes silently: there is no graceful shutdown message, the rest of the cluster simply notices (eventually) that the leader is unresponsive and must fail over. The failover protocol is deliberately conservative about data loss: a replica is only allowed to take over as the new leader once its own local copy of the record already contains every reservation that has ever been committed cluster-wide. This prevents the classic failover hazard where a freshly-promoted leader "forgets" a reservation that patrons were already told succeeded, silently reverting or overwriting a shared record that other patrons may already be relying on.

Because only one machine is ever leader at a time and a crash is permanent for the machine it happens to, the model keeps at least one replica alive at every moment so that a new leader can always eventually be found; reservation requests keep arriving from patrons independently of whatever is happening to the cluster's leadership.

The full action set is: Submit (a patron files a new reservation request), ApplyByLeader (the current, live leader applies a filed request to its own copy of the record and commits it cluster-wide), ReplicateToFollower (a non-leader replica copies a committed reservation into its own local record in the background), CrashSilently (a replica's process fails permanently with no notice, provided at least one other replica stays alive), DetectFailure (the cluster notices the crashed machine was the leader and declares the leadership vacant), and Elect (a live replica whose local record already contains everything committed so far takes over as the new leader).

A hospital's operating-room scheduler keeps a bounded backlog of surgery requests waiting to be assigned a room. Surgeons submit requests over an asynchronous messaging fabric that does not preserve order: a request message sent earlier can be delivered to the scheduler later than one sent afterward, and two operating-room-freed notifications can likewise arrive out of sequence. Because the fabric offers no ordering guarantee, the scheduler must never rely on messages showing up in send order, only on what has actually been delivered so far.

A warehouse robot fleet uses a two-phase commit protocol to decide whether to carry out a shared task, such as jointly relocating a heavy pallet that requires several robots to agree before anyone moves. A coordinator opens a round by advancing to a fresh round number and entering a "prepare" phase, in which every robot that is currently on the authorized roster for this task is expected to broadcast a vote. Because the warehouse network can drop and re-deliver packets out of order, votes are modeled as messages sitting in a shared inbox rather than a strict queue: a vote is simply present or absent, and nothing guarantees it arrives in the order it was sent, so a vote tagged with an old round number can still be sitting around when a new round starts.

Each robot keeps a local belief about which round is current. Robots do not always sync this belief immediately, so a robot can cast a vote that is tagged with a round number older than the coordinator's actual round -- a "stale" vote. The coordinator only declares the round committed once every robot on the authorized roster has a "yes" vote in the inbox tagged with the exact current round number; a stale vote or a vote from a robot that is not on the authorized roster never counts toward that decision. Only after the round is committed may a robot carry out the physical action (moving the pallet), and it may only do so if its own "yes" vote for the current round is present in the inbox and it is on the authorized roster -- this is the one truly irreversible step in the scenario.

Some robots are simply never on the authorized roster for this particular task (for example, a robot from a different zone that overhears the broadcast and could still emit a vote message), and any robot's cached round belief can lag behind the coordinator's, producing exactly the stale-vote scenario the protocol must reject. The coordinator can also abort a round if any authorized robot reports "no", after which a fresh round can be opened.

The full action set is: Advance (coordinator opens a new commit round and moves to "prepare"), Sync (a robot updates its locally cached round number to match the coordinator's current round), SendVote (a robot casts a "yes" or "no" vote tagged with its own locally cached round number, right or wrong), Commit (the coordinator declares the round committed once every authorized robot has a matching "yes" vote at the current round), Abort (the coordinator abandons the round if an authorized robot voted "no"), Act (an authorized robot performs the physical pallet-move action once the round is committed and its own current-round "yes" vote is present), and Quiesce (once a round has settled into committed or aborted, the system simply holds still).

Several matchmaker workers independently try to build a match by optimistically grabbing a pair of players out of the shared lobby pool, without taking any lock first. Each worker's grab is exclusive while it holds the pair: it either commits the pair into a finished match, or it gives up and releases the pair back to the lobby pool so another worker (or itself, later) can retry with a fresh optimistic attempt. A bank's interbank settlement batch system accepts settlement instructions from a small set of member banks and processes them through a single shared work queue with backpressure. Each member bank accumulates its own backlog of settlement instructions that still need to be submitted into the shared batch queue. A bank may submit one backlogged instruction into the queue only if there is spare shared capacity: the queue's current length plus the number of instructions currently being processed by settlement workers must stay strictly below the fixed system capacity, otherwise the submission is simply not possible yet and the bank must wait -- this is the backpressure.

A settlement worker pulls the oldest instruction off the front of the queue into active processing, and later finishes processing it, at which point it is durably settled and no longer occupies any shared capacity at all. The system's whole point is to guarantee that the combined footprint of work sitting in the shared queue and work currently being processed never exceeds the fixed capacity of the settlement system, no matter how bursty the banks' submissions are.

One participant bank in this batch can be arbitrarily slow -- it may sit on a large backlog for a long time before submitting anything, or interleave its submissions sparsely compared to the others -- but it is never treated as failed or removed from the system, and its backlog can still grow at any time as new settlement instructions arrive for it. There is no notion of timing out or excluding a slow bank; the shared queue simply keeps enforcing backpressure against everyone equally regardless of how fast or slow any single bank happens to submit.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending machine network uses quorum voting before any machine is allowed to carry out an irreversible action, such as dispensing the very last unit of a scarce promotional item. Instead of a single coordinator deciding, each machine in the network independently casts a vote endorsing a specific proposed action, and that proposal may only be carried out once a quorum -- a fixed minimum number of endorsing votes -- has been gathered for it. Votes are sent as independent messages into the network and the network itself may reorder them arbitrarily: a vote that was cast first can be delivered after one cast later, and delivery order has nothing to do with sending order.

Because delivery can be reordered, the tally that decides whether a quorum has been reached is always computed over votes that have actually been delivered, never over votes that have merely been sent but are still stranded somewhere in transit. A machine may also withdraw its endorsement for a proposal before the action has been carried out, removing its vote from both the sent and delivered records, which models a machine changing its mind before the irreversible step happens; once the action for a proposal has actually been carried out, no further withdrawal for that proposal is meaningful.

Once a proposal's delivered votes reach the required quorum size, the network carries out that proposal's action exactly once, and it permanently records the exact set of delivered votes that justified the decision. No proposal can ever be carried out a second time, and whenever a proposal has been carried out, the votes credited as its justification must all actually have been delivered and must number at least the quorum size -- a reordered-but-undelivered vote can never by itself be the basis for the action.

The full action set is: SendVote (a machine casts a vote endorsing a proposal, entering the network), Deliver (the network delivers a previously sent vote to the tally process, in no particular order relative to other sends), Execute (the network carries out a proposal's irreversible action once its delivered votes reach the quorum size, recording exactly which delivered votes justified it), Withdraw (a machine retracts its vote for a proposal that has not yet been carried out, removing it from both the sent and delivered records), and Idle (once every send, deliver, execute, and withdraw option is exhausted, the network simply holds still).
SAFETY PROPERTY: whenever a proposal has been carried out, the exact set of votes recorded as its justification were all actually delivered and numbered at least the quorum size, so the irreversible action for that proposal happens at most once and only on genuinely delivered endorsements.

A busy print shop runs a single high-capacity printer whose paper tray is the scarce critical resource. Before any worker's job can touch the tray, the worker must first acquire a coarse-grained lock on the whole printer cabinet, and only after holding that outer lock may it acquire a fine-grained lock on the paper tray itself. This hierarchical locking discipline exists so that a worker never fiddles with the tray while some other worker is mid-operation on the cabinet: the outer lock is grabbed first, then the inner one, and both must be released together when the job finishes.

The twist is that a worker's control software can crash silently while it is holding either the cabinet lock or the tray lock (or both) - it simply stops responding, with no warning message and no orderly release. Nothing else about the shop notices immediately. A shop floor monitor periodically scans for such stalled workers and marks them as detected; only once a crashed worker has been detected can its held locks be forcibly reclaimed and handed back to the pool, letting some other worker's job proceed. Because the monitor keeps scanning and reclaiming rather than giving up, every crash is eventually cleaned up.

Ordinary jobs cycle through requesting the cabinet lock, then the tray lock, then finishing and releasing both locks together, over and over, competing with other workers for the same two nested locks. The crash-and-reclaim path runs concurrently with this ordinary cycle, so at any moment some workers may be idle, mid-job, or stuck crashed while the monitor works through its backlog.

The full action set is: AcquireCoarse (a worker takes the free cabinet lock), AcquireFine (a worker already holding the cabinet lock takes the free tray lock), Release (a worker holding both locks finishes its job and releases both), Crash (a worker holding one or both locks silently dies), DetectCrash (the monitor notices a crashed worker), and Reclaim (the monitor forcibly frees the locks of a detected crashed worker and returns it to idle).
SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a worker holds the fine-grained tray lock, that same worker must also hold the coarse-grained cabinet lock, so the critical tray resource is never accessed outside the protecting outer lock.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every worker that silently crashes while holding a lock is eventually detected and has its locks reclaimed, returning it to idle.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A university course-registration system keeps one shared record for a popular course: the number of students currently enrolled. Registering a student is carried out as a two-phase-commit transaction across two backend participants, the Registrar office and the Billing office, both of which must agree before the enrollment count is updated. When a registration transaction starts it first takes a snapshot of the record's current version number, then asks both participants to vote yes; only once both have voted, and the record's version has not moved since the snapshot was taken, may the transaction commit its increment to the enrollment count and bump the version. This version check exists precisely to stop lost updates: if some other transaction had already committed against the same version, a transaction that blindly wrote its own increment on top of a stale read would silently erase that other transaction's update.

The complication is that the Billing office's terminal can crash silently in the middle of a transaction - it just stops sending votes, with no explicit failure signal. When that happens the in-flight transaction can no longer reach unanimity and must be aborted rather than left hanging forever, releasing the transaction slot for a future attempt with a fresh snapshot.

Multiple registration transactions can be started, one at a time contending for the shared enrollment record's transaction slot, vote, commit, or abort, and the Billing participant can crash independently of any particular transaction. The full action set is: StartTxn (a transaction takes a fresh snapshot of the record version and begins collecting votes), Vote (a participant that has not crashed casts its yes vote for the in-flight transaction), Commit (a transaction whose votes are unanimous and whose snapshot is still current writes its increment to the shared record and advances the version), Abort (an in-flight transaction whose snapshot has gone stale or whose vote cannot complete because of a crashed participant is abandoned), and CrashParticipant (the Billing office silently stops voting).
SAFETY PROPERTY: No two distinct committed transactions ever commit against the same snapshot version of the shared enrollment record, so a committed update can never be silently overwritten by another transaction that read the same stale version.

A print shop keeps a fixed total number of blank sheets circulating through three pools: a central supply stack, the printer's loaded tray, and the finished-printed output stack. A sheet only ever moves between these three pools - loading takes a sheet from supply into the tray, and printing takes a sheet from the tray into the finished stack - so the sum of sheets across all three pools never changes, no sheet is ever created or destroyed.

Every shop attendant must weigh in before either kind of move takes effect: moving a sheet is proposed, then each attendant casts a yes vote, and only once a strict majority of attendants have voted yes does the shop actually commit the move and clear the ballot for the next proposal. Attendants are never assumed to fail outright in this shop - the twist is that an attendant can simply be slow to get to the voting station, taking an arbitrary amount of time, but it always eventually shows up and casts its vote rather than vanishing for good.

At any moment the shop may have a load-proposal, a print-proposal, or a restock-proposal pending, or no proposal at all, with some subset of attendants having already voted yes on whatever is pending. A restock move sends a sheet from the finished stack back to the supply stack, which is what keeps the shop's cycle running indefinitely instead of grinding to a halt once every sheet has been printed. Because slow attendants keep arriving rather than staying away forever, any proposal that is put up eventually gathers its majority and gets committed, clearing the way for the next one.

The full action set is: ProposeLoad (a load move is put up for a vote, provided supply has a sheet to give), ProposePrint (a print move is put up for a vote, provided the tray has a loaded sheet), ProposeRestock (a restock move is put up for a vote, provided the finished stack has a sheet to give back), VoteYes (an attendant who has not yet voted on the pending proposal casts its yes vote), CommitLoad (a pending load proposal with majority yes votes moves one sheet from supply to the tray), CommitPrint (a pending print proposal with majority yes votes moves one sheet from the tray to the finished stack), and CommitRestock (a pending restock proposal with majority yes votes moves one sheet from the finished stack back to supply).

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A stock exchange runs a single opening auction each morning to set the day's opening price. Because a stalled attempt must be retryable, the exchange tracks the auction as a small set of independent rounds: each round separately collects yes votes from the member trading firms in a two-phase-commit style handshake, and only a round whose votes are unanimous may proceed to actually cross the book and publish the opening price. Publishing the opening price is irreversible - once it happens the market has opened and trading history cannot be rewritten - so the exchange must guarantee that at most one round is ever allowed to perform that irreversible clearing action, no matter how many rounds were started or retried.

The complication is that a member firm's order-entry gateway can crash silently partway through a round's voting - it simply stops sending votes, with no disconnect notice. When that happens, the round it was participating in can never gather unanimous votes, so the exchange abandons that round and may start a fresh round to try again from a clean slate. Because two or more rounds might be live at once (an old stalled round alongside a fresh retry), the exchange keeps a single ledger slot recording which round, if any, has actually executed the irreversible clear, and every round's clearing action must check that ledger slot is still empty before it is allowed to write to it.

At any time some rounds may be quietly collecting votes, some may have reached full unanimity and be ready to clear, one (at most) may have actually cleared and published a price, and any round can be abandoned if a firm it depended on has crashed. The full action set is: Vote (a firm that has not crashed casts its yes vote in a round that is still collecting votes), Prepare (a round whose votes are unanimous moves to ready-to-clear), Clear (a ready round checks the single-clear ledger is still empty, then writes itself into it and publishes its opening price, an irreversible action), AbortRound (a round still collecting votes is abandoned because some firm it needed has crashed), and CrashFirm (a member firm's gateway silently stops voting).
SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a round has reached the cleared phase, the single-clear ledger must record that exact round, so no two distinct rounds can ever both perform the irreversible opening-price clear.

A metropolitan subway signalling installation divides its running track into
regions, and each region into numbered signalling blocks. Before a train may
roll into a block it must climb a two-level authority ladder held by the
interlocking: first it takes the coarse region authority for the region that
contains the block, and only then may it take the fine authority for the
individual block. Every coarse grant is stamped with the interlocking's current
issue epoch. The interlocking periodically re-issues the region timetable,
which advances the epoch; any train that is already under way inside a block
has its stamp re-confirmed as part of the re-issue, while a train that is merely
holding paper authority on a platform is left carrying an epoch that no longer
matches. Trains on this network are slow but never failed: a train sitting on a
stale stamp will always eventually notice and hand its coarse and fine authority
back, after which it may queue for a fresh grant. The full action set is: a train
takes coarse region authority and receives a stamp at the current epoch; a train
holding fresh coarse authority for a region takes fine authority for one free
block inside that region; a train holding fresh coarse and fine authority rolls
into its block; a train inside a block clears the block and surrenders both
levels of authority; the interlocking re-issues the region and advances the epoch,
re-confirming stamps only for trains already under way; and a train that
discovers its stamp is stale drops its coarse and fine authority without moving.

still holds fine authority for exactly that block and whose coarse stamp equals
the interlocking's current epoch, so no stale or unauthorized train is ever on
the track.

Blocks == Regions \X (1 .. BlocksPerRegion)

NoRegion == "noregion"
NoBlock  == <<"noblock", 0>>
NoTrain  == "notrain"
NoStamp  == EpochBound + 1

RegionOf(b) == b[1]

VARIABLES epoch, coarse, stamp, fine, occ

vars == <<epoch, coarse, stamp, fine, occ>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ epoch \in 0 .. EpochBound
  /\ coarse \in [Trains -> Regions \cup {NoRegion}]
  /\ stamp \in [Trains -> (0 .. EpochBound) \cup {NoStamp}]
  /\ fine \in [Trains -> Blocks \cup {NoBlock}]
  /\ occ \in [Blocks -> Trains \cup {NoTrain}]

UnderWay(t) == \E b \in Blocks : occ[b] = t

Init ==
  /\ epoch = 0
  /\ coarse = [t \in Trains |-> NoRegion]
  /\ stamp = [t \in Trains |-> NoStamp]
  /\ fine = [t \in Trains |-> NoBlock]
  /\ occ = [b \in Blocks |-> NoTrain]

\* Coarse rung: the region authority is exclusive and is stamped with the epoch
\* that was current when the interlocking handed it over.
TakeRegion(t, r) ==
  /\ coarse[t] = NoRegion
  /\ \A u \in Trains \ {t} : coarse[u] # r
  /\ coarse' = [coarse EXCEPT ![t] = r]
  /\ stamp' = [stamp EXCEPT ![t] = epoch]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, fine, occ>>

\* Fine rung: only a train whose coarse stamp is still current may reach for a
\* block, and only for a block inside the region it already holds.
TakeBlock(t, b) ==
  /\ coarse[t] = RegionOf(b)
  /\ stamp[t] = epoch
  /\ fine[t] = NoBlock
  /\ occ[b] = NoTrain
  /\ \A u \in Trains \ {t} : fine[u] # b
  /\ fine' = [fine EXCEPT ![t] = b]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, coarse, stamp, occ>>

Roll(t) ==
  /\ fine[t] # NoBlock
  /\ stamp[t] = epoch
  /\ occ[fine[t]] = NoTrain
  /\ occ' = [occ EXCEPT ![fine[t]] = t]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, coarse, stamp, fine>>

Clear(t) ==
  /\ UnderWay(t)
  /\ occ' = [b \in Blocks |-> IF occ[b] = t THEN NoTrain ELSE occ[b]]
  /\ fine' = [fine EXCEPT ![t] = NoBlock]
  /\ coarse' = [coarse EXCEPT ![t] = NoRegion]
  /\ stamp' = [stamp EXCEPT ![t] = NoStamp]
  /\ UNCHANGED epoch

  /\ stamp' = [t \in Trains |-> IF UnderWay(t) THEN epoch + 1 ELSE stamp[t]]

\* authority back and re-queue.
DropStale(t) ==
  /\ ~UnderWay(t)
  /\ stamp[t] # NoStamp
  /\ stamp[t] # epoch
  /\ stamp' = [stamp EXCEPT ![t] = NoStamp]
  /\ coarse' = [coarse EXCEPT ![t] = NoRegion]
  /\ fine' = [fine EXCEPT ![t] = NoBlock]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, occ>>

  \/ \E t \in Trains : \E r \in Regions : TakeRegion(t, r)
  \/ \E t \in Trains : \E b \in Blocks : TakeBlock(t, b)
  \/ \E t \in Trains : Roll(t) \/ Clear(t) \/ DropStale(t)
  \/ Reissue

\* Nothing rolling is stale or unauthorized: the occupant of a block still owns
\* the fine authority for that exact block and its coarse stamp is current.
NoStaleOccupancy ==

easily arrive after a newer claim has already landed. The registrar accepts a
claim only if the version it carries still matches the register, the sending
client still holds a live registration hold, and seats remain; accepting the
claim decrements the seat count, bumps the version, and writes the claim into the
accepted-writes log. Any claim failing those conditions is turned away as stale
or unauthorized. The registrar may also revoke a client's hold at any moment,
which makes that client's outstanding claim unauthorized. A client whose claim
has been answered may retire the result and go back to idle, and a client with no
hold may be granted one again. The full action set is: grant a hold, post a
claim, accept a claim, turn a claim away, revoke a hold, and retire a finished
result.

Claims == [c : Clients, v : 0 .. VerBound]

vars == <<ver, seats, pool, holds, outcome, log>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ ver \in 0 .. VerBound
  /\ seats \in 0 .. Seats
  /\ pool \in SUBSET Claims
  /\ holds \in SUBSET Clients
  /\ outcome \in [Clients -> {"idle", "pending", "accepted", "refused"}]
  /\ log \in SUBSET Claims

Init ==
  /\ ver = 0
  /\ seats = Seats
  /\ pool = {}
  /\ holds = {}
  /\ outcome = [c \in Clients |-> "idle"]
  /\ log = {}

Grant(c) ==
  /\ c \notin holds
  /\ outcome[c] = "idle"
  /\ holds' = holds \cup {c}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<ver, seats, pool, outcome, log>>

\* A client posts the version it read; the pool is a set, so the registrar is
\* free to serve claims in any order at all.
Post(c) ==
  /\ c \in holds
  /\ outcome[c] = "idle"
  /\ pool' = pool \cup {[c |-> c, v |-> ver]}
  /\ outcome' = [outcome EXCEPT ![c] = "pending"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<ver, seats, holds, log>>

Fresh(m) ==
  /\ m.v = ver
  /\ m.c \in holds
  /\ seats > 0
  /\ ver < VerBound

\* Compare-and-swap: the observed version must still be the live one, otherwise
\* the write is someone else's stale news and is refused.
Accept(m) ==
  /\ m \in pool
  /\ Fresh(m)
  /\ ver' = ver + 1
  /\ seats' = seats - 1
  /\ log' = log \cup {m}
  /\ pool' = pool \ {m}
  /\ outcome' = [outcome EXCEPT ![m.c] = "accepted"]
  /\ UNCHANGED holds

Refuse(m) ==
  /\ m \in pool
  /\ ~Fresh(m)
  /\ pool' = pool \ {m}
  /\ outcome' = [outcome EXCEPT ![m.c] = "refused"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<ver, seats, holds, log>>

Revoke(c) ==
  /\ c \in holds
  /\ holds' = holds \ {c}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<ver, seats, pool, outcome, log>>

Retire(c) ==
  /\ outcome[c] \in {"accepted", "refused"}
  /\ outcome' = [outcome EXCEPT ![c] = "idle"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<ver, seats, pool, holds, log>>

\* Every claim a client has outstanding can always be answered one way or another.
Resolve(c) == \E m \in pool : m.c = c /\ (Accept(m) \/ Refuse(m))

Next ==
  \/ \E c \in Clients : Grant(c) \/ Post(c) \/ Revoke(c) \/ Retire(c)
  \/ \E m \in Claims : Accept(m) \/ Refuse(m)

Spec ==
  /\ Init
  /\ [][Next]_vars
  /\ \A c \in Clients : WF_vars(Resolve(c))

\* The accepted-writes log holds exactly one entry per version below the live
\* version: no gap (a version advanced without a write) and no duplicate (two
\* writes landing on the same version, which is what a stale accept would do).
LogIsGaplessPrefix ==
  /\ {m.v : m \in log} = 0 .. (ver - 1)
  /\ \A m1, m2 \in log : m1.v = m2.v => m1 = m2

EveryClaimAnswered ==
  \A c \in Clients : (outcome[c] = "pending") ~> (outcome[c] # "pending")

NoReq == "noreq"

VARIABLES master, decision, votes, cur, view

TypeOK ==

  /\ decision \in [Reqs -> {"none", "commit", "abort"}]
  /\ votes \in [Branches -> {"none", "yes", "no"}]
  /\ cur \in Reqs \cup {NoReq}
  /\ view \in [Branches -> SUBSET Reqs]

  /\ decision = [x \in Reqs |-> "none"]
  /\ votes = [b \in Branches |-> "none"]
  /\ cur = NoReq
  /\ view = [b \in Branches |-> {}]

  /\ decision[x] = "none"
  /\ cur' = x
  /\ votes' = [b \in Branches |-> "none"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<master, decision, view>>

\* Prepare phase. A slow branch simply has not answered yet; there is no timeout
\* that would let the coordinator move on without it.
Vote(b, v) ==

  /\ votes[b] = "none"
  /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![b] = v]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<master, decision, cur, view>>

\* step, which is what keeps a committed reservation from being lost.

  /\ \A b \in Branches : votes[b] = "yes"
  /\ master' = master \cup {cur}
  /\ decision' = [decision EXCEPT ![cur] = "commit"]
  /\ cur' = NoReq
  /\ votes' = [b \in Branches |-> "none"]
  /\ UNCHANGED view

  /\ cur # NoReq
  /\ \E b \in Branches : votes[b] = "no"
  /\ decision' = [decision EXCEPT ![cur] = "abort"]
  /\ cur' = NoReq
  /\ votes' = [b \in Branches |-> "none"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<master, view>>

\* A lagging branch folds one already-committed entry into its own copy.
Install(b, x) ==
  /\ x \in master
  /\ x \notin view[b]
  /\ view' = [view EXCEPT ![b] = view[b] \cup {x}]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<master, decision, votes, cur>>

\* from the active record; record and copies are trimmed together.
Retire(x) ==
  /\ x \in master
  /\ \A b \in Branches : x \in view[b]
  /\ cur = NoReq
  /\ master' = master \ {x}
  /\ decision' = [decision EXCEPT ![x] = "none"]
  /\ view' = [b \in Branches |-> view[b] \ {x}]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<votes, cur>>

  /\ cur = NoReq
  /\ decision' = [decision EXCEPT ![x] = "none"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<master, votes, cur, view>>

  \/ \E x \in Reqs : Open(x) \/ Retire(x) \/ Retry(x)
  \/ \E b \in Branches : \E v \in {"yes", "no"} : Vote(b, v)
  \/ Commit
  \/ Abort

\* of it: an update is neither lost on commit nor invented anywhere.

  /\ leader = NoLeader

  /\ b \notin down

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
During a stock exchange's opening auction the indicative opening price is held in
a single compare-and-swap register carried by a version counter, and every
accepted change is stamped into the auction's provenance ledger: slot v of the
ledger names whoever wrote the version-v change. A broker gateway works in the
usual optimistic style - it reads the register's current version as a snapshot,
posts its price update against that snapshot, and the register accepts the update
only if the snapshot still equals the live version. Acceptance stamps the
gateway's name into the ledger slot for that version, advances the version, and
hands the gateway an acknowledgement naming the version its update landed at. If
the snapshot has gone out of date the post is turned away and the gateway must
start over. The exchange supervisor holds a privileged override: it can force a
price into the register without holding any snapshot at all, but the override is
not exempt from the ledger - it stamps itself into the current slot and advances
the version exactly like an ordinary write, so a forced change can never
silently overwrite somebody else's recorded change. A gateway that has been
answered clears its snapshot and returns to idle. The full action set is: a
gateway reads a snapshot and posts, the register accepts a fresh post, the
register turns away a stale post, the supervisor forces an override write, and an
answered gateway resets.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every acknowledgement a gateway holds, the auction ledger
slot named by that acknowledgement still records that same gateway as the author
and lies strictly below the live version, so no accepted update is ever lost or
re-attributed - not even by the supervisor's override.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every posted price update is eventually answered, either
accepted or turned away, so no gateway is left posted forever.
