CONSTANTS Elevators, NoOwner, MaxVer

ASSUME /\ Elevators # {}
       /\ NoOwner \notin Elevators
       /\ MaxVer \in Nat /\ MaxVer > 0

VARIABLES regVer, regOwner, snapshot, committed

vars == <<regVer, regOwner, snapshot, committed>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ regVer \in 0..MaxVer
  /\ regOwner \in Elevators \cup {NoOwner}
  /\ snapshot \in [Elevators -> 0..MaxVer]
  /\ committed \in [Elevators -> 0..MaxVer]

Init ==
  /\ regVer = 0
  /\ regOwner = NoOwner
  /\ snapshot = [e \in Elevators |-> 0]
  /\ committed = [e \in Elevators |-> 0]

\* A controller refreshes its cached view of the dispatch record. This is
\* always available, so a controller can never be permanently stuck -- it
\* is allowed to be slow, but it is always able to keep retrying.
ReadSnapshot(e) ==
  /\ snapshot' = [snapshot EXCEPT ![e] = regVer]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<regVer, regOwner, committed>>

\* version is still exactly what the controller last read. If some other
\* write happened in between, this action is simply not enabled, and the
\* controller must ReadSnapshot again before it can retry.
CAS(e) ==
  /\ regVer < MaxVer
  /\ snapshot[e] = regVer
  /\ regVer' = regVer + 1
  /\ regOwner' = e
  /\ committed' = [committed EXCEPT ![e] = regVer + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED snapshot

\* say), advancing its version without going through any elevator's CAS.
DispatcherOverride ==

  /\ regVer' = regVer + 1
  /\ regOwner' = NoOwner
  /\ UNCHANGED <<snapshot, committed>>

ClearOwner ==
  /\ regOwner # NoOwner
  /\ regOwner' = NoOwner
  /\ UNCHANGED <<regVer, snapshot, committed>>

Next ==

  \/ DispatcherOverride
  \/ ClearOwner

\* an owner is never left crediting an update it did not actually land.

A car-wash conveyor line has a fixed number of cars waiting to be washed
and a fixed number of station controllers who must approve each car before
it is let onto the line. A waiting car is admitted onto the conveyor only
once a quorum of controllers has voted to approve it, and the conveyor can
never physically hold more cars at once than its fixed capacity. Votes are
not applied the instant they are cast: a controller's vote for a car is
first dropped into an unordered inbox of pending votes, and because the

earlier one -- tallying does not have to follow the order votes were sent
in. Each car moves through the line exactly once, from waiting to riding
the conveyor to being washed to finally being picked up. The full action
set is: SendVote, where a controller casts its vote for a still-waiting car
into the pending inbox; TallyOne, where any one pending vote is counted
toward its car's quorum, in no particular order; Admit, where a car that
has reached quorum and finds a free conveyor slot is let onto the conveyor
and takes that slot; Wash, where a car on the conveyor finishes washing and
frees its slot; and Exit, where a washed car is picked up and leaves the
line for good; and AllDone, where, once every car has finished and left,
the line simply idles since there is nothing left to do.

SAFETY PROPERTY: the number of cars riding the conveyor at once never
exceeds the conveyor's fixed capacity.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: every car that starts out waiting for a wash eventually

\* A car-wash conveyor line admits a waiting car onto the bounded-capacity
\* conveyor only once a quorum of station controllers has voted to approve
\* it. Vote messages sit in an unordered inbox and are tallied one at a
\* time in any order, modeling a network that can reorder them. Each car
\* passes through the line exactly once: waiting, on the conveyor, washed,
\* then done.
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Cars, Controllers, QuorumSize, Capacity

ASSUME /\ Cars # {} /\ Controllers # {}
       /\ QuorumSize \in Nat /\ QuorumSize <= Cardinality(Controllers)
       /\ Capacity \in Nat /\ Capacity > 0

Stages == {"waiting", "onconveyor", "washed", "done"}

VARIABLES state, pendingVotes, tally, slot

vars == <<state, pendingVotes, tally, slot>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ state \in [Cars -> Stages]
  /\ pendingVotes \subseteq (Controllers \X Cars)
  /\ tally \in [Cars -> SUBSET Controllers]
  /\ slot \in [Cars -> 0..Capacity]

Init ==
  /\ state = [c \in Cars |-> "waiting"]
  /\ pendingVotes = {}
  /\ tally = [c \in Cars |-> {}]
  /\ slot = [c \in Cars |-> 0]

\* A controller sends its vote for a still-waiting car into the inbox.
SendVote(v, c) ==
  /\ state[c] = "waiting"
  /\ <<v, c>> \notin pendingVotes
  /\ v \notin tally[c]
  /\ pendingVotes' = pendingVotes \cup {<<v, c>>}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<state, tally, slot>>

\* Any pending vote message is tallied, regardless of send order -- this
\* is where message reordering shows up: tallying need not follow sending.
TallyOne ==
  \E vc \in pendingVotes :
    /\ tally' = [tally EXCEPT ![vc[2]] = @ \cup {vc[1]}]
    /\ pendingVotes' = pendingVotes \ {vc}
    /\ UNCHANGED <<state, slot>>

\* Once a car has a quorum of votes and a conveyor slot is free, it is
\* admitted onto the conveyor and takes that slot.
Admit(c) ==
  /\ state[c] = "waiting"
  /\ Cardinality(tally[c]) >= QuorumSize
  /\ \E s \in 1..Capacity :
       /\ \A c2 \in Cars : state[c2] = "onconveyor" => slot[c2] # s
       /\ slot' = [slot EXCEPT ![c] = s]
  /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![c] = "onconveyor"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pendingVotes, tally>>

\* The car finishes washing and vacates its conveyor slot.
Wash(c) ==
  /\ state[c] = "onconveyor"
  /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![c] = "washed"]
  /\ slot' = [slot EXCEPT ![c] = 0]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pendingVotes, tally>>

\* The washed car is picked up and leaves the line for good.
Exit(c) ==
  /\ state[c] = "washed"
  /\ state' = [state EXCEPT ![c] = "done"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pendingVotes, tally, slot>>

\* Once every car has finished, the line has nothing left to do; this
\* keeps an action always enabled so the model never deadlocks at the end.
AllDone ==
  /\ \A c \in Cars : state[c] = "done"
  /\ UNCHANGED vars

Next ==
  \/ \E v \in Controllers, c \in Cars : SendVote(v, c)
  \/ TallyOne
  \/ \E c \in Cars : Admit(c) \/ Wash(c) \/ Exit(c)
  \/ AllDone

Spec ==
  /\ Init /\ [][Next]_vars
  /\ \A v \in Controllers, c \in Cars : WF_vars(SendVote(v, c))
  /\ WF_vars(TallyOne)
  /\ \A c \in Cars : WF_vars(Admit(c)) /\ WF_vars(Wash(c)) /\ WF_vars(Exit(c))

\* SAFETY: the conveyor never holds more cars at once than its capacity.
BoundedCapacity == Cardinality({c \in Cars : state[c] = "onconveyor"}) <= Capacity

\* LIVENESS: every car put through the line eventually finishes.
AllCarsFinish == \A c \in Cars : <>(state[c] = "done")

An elevator bank runs two independent dispatch transactions, each trying to
assign a hall call to a car, but both transactions draw candidate cars from
the very same shared pool. Each transaction follows a two-phase-commit
protocol: it first picks a target car from the pool, then tries to
tentatively reserve it, and only turns that tentative reservation into a
permanent dispatch assignment once the reservation succeeds. Because the
pool is shared between the two transactions, a transaction's prepare step
must check both the tentative reservation table and the pool's permanent
assignment record before it locks a car -- a car that already has a
permanent assignment from the other transaction cannot be reserved again,
even if its tentative lock happens to be free at that moment. The full
action set is: Begin, where an idle transaction wakes up and picks a
candidate car from the shared pool; Prepare, where the transaction attempts
to tentatively lock its target car, succeeding only if that car is neither
already tentatively locked nor already permanently assigned, and aborting
otherwise; Commit, where a transaction that holds a successful tentative
lock turns it into a permanent pool assignment; Abort, where a transaction
that is merely prepared gives up and releases its tentative lock without
ever touching the permanent record; and Reset, where a transaction that has
committed or aborted returns to idle so it can attempt a new dispatch
later, leaving any already-committed permanent assignment untouched.

SAFETY PROPERTY: a car in the shared pool is never simultaneously
tentatively reserved by one transaction while already permanently assigned
to a different transaction, so a committed dispatch assignment can never be
silently shadowed or lost to a concurrent reservation from the other
transaction sharing the same pool.

       /\ NoTx \notin Tx

  /\ txTarget \in [Tx -> Participants]
  /\ poolOwner \in [Participants -> Tx \cup {NoTx}]
  /\ reserved \in [Participants -> Tx \cup {NoTx}]

  /\ txPhase' = [txPhase EXCEPT ![t] = "trying"]

  /\ expiry = 0
  /\ editing = {}
  /\ pending = {}

Request(t) ==
  /\ t \notin pending
  /\ t \notin editing
  /\ holder # t
  /\ pending' = pending \cup {t}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, holder, expiry, editing>>

Grant(t) ==
  /\ holder = NoTech
  /\ t \in pending
  /\ holder' = t
  /\ pending' = pending \ {t}
  /\ expiry' = IF clock + LeaseLen > MaxClock THEN MaxClock ELSE clock + LeaseLen
  /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, editing>>

Enter(t) ==
  /\ holder = t
  /\ clock <= expiry
  /\ t \notin editing
  /\ editing' = editing \cup {t}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, holder, expiry, pending>>

Exit(t) ==

  /\ editing' = editing \ {t}
  /\ holder' = NoTech

\* editing -- reclaiming an in-use lease would allow a second technician in.

  /\ holder' = NoTech

  /\ \A t \in Tech : SF_vars(Grant(t))
  /\ \A t \in Tech : SF_vars(Enter(t))
  /\ \A t \in Tech : WF_vars(Exit(t))

\* LIVENESS: every technician that requests the ledger eventually gets in.

\* Pharmacy dispenser: each dispensing slot's occupant is stamped with the

\* property below relies on. A privileged admin may bypass the normal
\* request queue and force-assign a slot directly, but only after evicting
\* whatever is already there, so a slot is never claimed twice at once.
CONSTANTS Drug, Slot, MaxEpoch

NoDrug == "NoDrug"

VARIABLES epoch, assigned, pending, lastEvicted

vars == <<epoch, assigned, pending, lastEvicted>>

Rec(d, s, e) == [drug |-> d, slot |-> s, ep |-> e]

  /\ epoch \in 0..MaxEpoch
  /\ assigned \subseteq [drug: Drug, slot: Slot, ep: 0..MaxEpoch]
  /\ pending \subseteq Drug

  /\ assigned = {}
  /\ pending = {}
  /\ lastEvicted = NoDrug

SlotFree(s) == ~ \E a \in assigned : a.slot = s

  /\ ~HoldsSlot(d)
  /\ pending' = pending \cup {d}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, assigned, lastEvicted>>

\* Ordinary allocation: only a pharmacist who requested may take a free slot.
Allocate(d, s) ==
  /\ d \in pending
  /\ SlotFree(s)
  /\ assigned' = assigned \cup {Rec(d, s, epoch)}
  /\ pending' = pending \ {d}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, lastEvicted>>

  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, pending, lastEvicted>>

Reconfigure ==
  /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
  /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<assigned, pending, lastEvicted>>

\* current occupant of the slot atomically before installing the new one,
\* so the slot is never held by two drugs even for an instant.

This models an airport baggage router where each conveyor zone keeps one
shared manifest tally (a running bag count for that zone). Updating the
tally correctly requires a hierarchical locking dance: a worker first calls
AcquireCoarse to take the whole zone's lock, then AcquireFine to take the
finer-grained lock on the tally record itself (only obtainable by whoever
already holds the zone lock). Once holding the record lock, the worker calls
ReadSnapshot to copy the current tally into its own local scratchpad, and
later calls WriteBack to write the incremented value back and release both
locks in one step. Holding the fine lock continuously across this whole
read-then-write window is what stops a second worker's write from silently
overwriting (losing) the first worker's update. Exactly one worker, at any
point, may Crash silently while mid-transaction, stranding whatever locks and
cached snapshot it was holding; an operator's ForceRelease action can then
reclaim a crashed worker's stranded zone and record locks and discard its
abandoned snapshot so the zone is not stuck forever. The full action set is:
AcquireCoarse, AcquireFine, ReadSnapshot, WriteBack, Crash, and ForceRelease.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The fine record lock is never held without the matching
coarse zone lock, and any worker with an in-flight cached read still holds
that zone's record lock -- so no worker's read-modify-write on a zone's
tally can ever be split open and have its update silently lost.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

---- MODULE W4Od17m8p1t0 ----
EXTENDS Integers, FiniteSets

\* Airport baggage router: each conveyor zone holds one shared manifest tally.
\* Updating it is a coarse-then-fine locking dance: a worker takes the zone
\* lock, then the record lock, snapshots the tally into a local cache, and
\* only later writes the incremented value back. Holding both locks for the
\* whole read-modify-write window is what stops a second worker's write from
\* silently clobbering (losing) the first worker's update. Exactly one
\* worker may crash mid-transaction, silently, leaving its locks stranded
\* until an operator force-releases them.
CONSTANTS Worker, Zone, MaxVal

NoW == "NoW"
NoCache == -1

VARIABLES coarseLock, fineLock, val, cache, crashed

vars == <<coarseLock, fineLock, val, cache, crashed>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ coarseLock \in [Zone -> Worker \cup {NoW}]
  /\ fineLock \in [Zone -> Worker \cup {NoW}]
  /\ val \in [Zone -> 0..MaxVal]
  /\ cache \in [Worker -> (0..MaxVal) \cup {NoCache}]
  /\ crashed \subseteq Worker

Init ==
  /\ coarseLock = [z \in Zone |-> NoW]
  /\ fineLock = [z \in Zone |-> NoW]
  /\ val = [z \in Zone |-> 0]
  /\ cache = [w \in Worker |-> NoCache]
  /\ crashed = {}

AcquireCoarse(w, z) ==
  /\ w \notin crashed
  /\ coarseLock[z] = NoW
  /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![z] = w]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<fineLock, val, cache, crashed>>

AcquireFine(w, z) ==
  /\ w \notin crashed
  /\ coarseLock[z] = w
  /\ fineLock[z] = NoW
  /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![z] = w]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, val, cache, crashed>>

ReadSnapshot(w, z) ==
  /\ w \notin crashed
  /\ fineLock[z] = w
  /\ cache[w] = NoCache
  /\ cache' = [cache EXCEPT ![w] = val[z]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, fineLock, val, crashed>>

\* Writes back the incremented tally and releases both locks in one step,
\* completing the read-modify-write started by ReadSnapshot.
WriteBack(w, z) ==
  /\ w \notin crashed
  /\ fineLock[z] = w
  /\ cache[w] # NoCache
  /\ val' = [val EXCEPT ![z] = (cache[w] + 1) % (MaxVal + 1)]
  /\ cache' = [cache EXCEPT ![w] = NoCache]
  /\ fineLock' = [fineLock EXCEPT ![z] = NoW]
  /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![z] = NoW]
  /\ UNCHANGED crashed

\* Exactly one worker, ever, may crash silently while mid-transaction.
Crash(w) ==
  /\ w \notin crashed
  /\ Cardinality(crashed) = 0
  /\ crashed' = crashed \cup {w}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<coarseLock, fineLock, val, cache>>

\* Operator recovery: reclaim a crashed worker's stranded locks and discard
\* its abandoned in-flight snapshot for that zone.
ForceRelease(z) ==
  /\ coarseLock[z] # NoW
  /\ coarseLock[z] \in crashed
  /\ LET w == coarseLock[z] IN
       /\ coarseLock' = [coarseLock EXCEPT ![z] = NoW]
       /\ fineLock' = IF fineLock[z] = w THEN [fineLock EXCEPT ![z] = NoW] ELSE fineLock
       /\ cache' = [cache EXCEPT ![w] = NoCache]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<val, crashed>>

Next ==
  \/ \E w \in Worker, z \in Zone :
       AcquireCoarse(w, z) \/ AcquireFine(w, z) \/ ReadSnapshot(w, z) \/ WriteBack(w, z)
  \/ \E w \in Worker : Crash(w)
  \/ \E z \in Zone : ForceRelease(z)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* SAFETY: the fine (record) lock never outruns the coarse (zone) lock, and
\* any worker with an in-flight cached read still holds the matching fine
\* lock -- together these guarantee the read-modify-write window on a
\* zone's tally is never split open for a second writer to lose an update.
NoLostUpdate ==
  /\ \A z \in Zone : fineLock[z] # NoW => coarseLock[z] = fineLock[z]
  /\ \A w \in Worker : cache[w] # NoCache => \E z \in Zone : fineLock[z] = w

====

\* Interbank settlement batch: a term-numbered leader bank collects member
\* banks' settlement entries into one clearing batch bounded by a fixed

\* failover elects a survivor. Once the leader settles the batch it starts a

  /\ leader = NoBank

  /\ batch = {}

  /\ crashed' = crashed \cup {b}
  /\ leader' = IF b = leader THEN NoBank ELSE leader

  /\ b \notin crashed
  /\ term < MaxTerm
  /\ leader' = b
  /\ term' = term + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<crashed, batch, settled>>

  /\ b \notin crashed
  /\ b \notin batch
  /\ Cardinality(batch) < Capacity

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A print shop has one shared job spooler and a set of print-shop workers who
take turns operating it. Locking is hierarchical: a worker must first grab
the single coarse shop lock for the whole spooler before it may touch any
individual job, and only after holding the coarse lock may it grab a fine,
per-job lock on a specific print job. AcquireShopLock lets an idle worker
take the coarse lock when nobody else holds it. AcquireJobLock lets whichever
worker currently holds the coarse lock grab the fine lock on a specific job
that nobody else has locked. PrintJob lets the worker holding a job's fine
lock actually run the job to completion, which also releases that job's fine
lock. ReleaseShopLock lets a worker give up the coarse lock once it is not
holding any job's fine lock. Finally, AdminOverride is a privileged action a
shop supervisor can invoke at any time to forcibly strip the coarse lock away
from whoever currently holds it and free every job that worker had fine-
locked, bumping a shop-wide epoch counter so that the ousted worker's
credentials are immediately recognized as stale and cannot be used to touch
any job afterward, even if that worker's own view of the world hasn't caught
up yet.

SAFETY PROPERTY: whenever a print job is fine-locked, the worker holding that lock has credentials matching the shop's current epoch, so no stale or overridden worker's fine lock can linger after it has been stripped of authority.

  /\ workerEpoch = [w \in Workers |-> 0]
  /\ jobLock = [j \in Jobs |-> None]

\* Coarse lock: the whole spooler, taken only when free.
AcquireShopLock(w) ==

  /\ shopLock' = w

AcquireJobLock(w, j) ==

  /\ jobLock[j] = None

A hospital has a fixed, small number of operating rooms shared among several
surgeons who together form the scheduling committee, and admitting a patient
into surgery normally requires a quorum of the committee to sign off first.
Propose lets any committee member put a waiting patient forward as a
candidate for the next open operating room, starting an empty ballot for that
patient. CastVote lets a committee member who has not already voted for a
proposed patient add their vote to that patient's ballot. Admit moves a
proposed patient into an operating room, but only once that patient's ballot
has reached quorum and there is a free operating room to put them in; admitting
clears the patient's ballot. Discharge frees up an operating room by moving a
patient who has finished surgery back out, and is always available so the
schedule can never wedge with every room full and nobody leaving. Finally,
AdminOverride is a privileged action the chief of surgery can invoke to rush a
patient straight into an open operating room in an emergency, completely
skipping the quorum ballot -- but even the chief of surgery cannot invoke it
when every operating room is already full, and the hospital only authorizes
the chief a limited number of such emergency overrides in total.

A blood bank keeps a single shared shelf count of blood units, and each
partner hospital keeps its own locally reserved stock plus a remembered
snapshot of what it last saw on the shelf. Reservations are done through a
compare-and-swap register: a hospital may only pull units off the shelf
through CasReserve, and that action only goes through if the hospital's
remembered snapshot still equals the shelf's actual current count -- if some
other hospital (or the director) has changed the shelf in the meantime, the
attempt is out of date and does nothing until the hospital catches up. Resync
lets a hospital refresh its remembered snapshot to match whatever the shelf
currently holds, which is how a hospital that has fallen behind catches back
up so its next compare-and-swap attempt can go through. Issue lets a hospital
consume some of its own already-reserved units for a transfusion, moving them
out of the reserved pool into permanently-used units, never destroying them
from the tracker's books. Finally, AdminOverride is a privileged action the
bank director can invoke to move units directly from the shelf into a
hospital's reserved stock without going through the compare-and-swap check at
all, which is exactly what can leave other hospitals' remembered snapshots
out of date.

SAFETY PROPERTY: at every moment, the shelf count plus every hospital's reserved units plus all units already used together equal the blood bank's fixed total supply, so no unit is ever created or destroyed, only moved.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: whenever a hospital's remembered snapshot falls out of date with the shelf's actual count, that hospital eventually resyncs and catches back up to the current shelf count.

  /\ snapshot \in [Hospitals -> 0..TotalUnits]

  /\ snapshot = [h \in Hospitals |-> TotalUnits]

Resync(h) ==

specific prescription that nobody else currently has locked. Dispense is the
irreversible step: the pharmacist holding a prescription's fine lock actually
counts out and hands over that medication, and it releases the fine lock when
done. UnlockPrescription lets a pharmacist give up a prescription's fine lock
without dispensing anything, whether because it already dispensed it earlier
or simply changed its mind about which prescription to handle next.

not holding any prescription's fine lock.

\* Lease "time left" is a bounded countdown (not an absolute clock), so a
\* crashed station's stale lease always has a finite path to lapsing.

CONSTANTS Stations, Prescriptions, NoStation, LeaseLen

VARIABLES leaseHolder, leaseTicksLeft, dispensed, timesDispensed, crashed

TypeOK ==
  /\ leaseHolder \in [Prescriptions -> Stations \union {NoStation}]
  /\ leaseTicksLeft \in [Prescriptions -> 0..LeaseLen]
  /\ dispensed \subseteq Prescriptions
  /\ timesDispensed \in [Prescriptions -> 0..2]
  /\ crashed \subseteq Stations

Init ==
  /\ leaseHolder = [p \in Prescriptions |-> NoStation]
  /\ leaseTicksLeft = [p \in Prescriptions |-> 0]
  /\ dispensed = {}
  /\ timesDispensed = [p \in Prescriptions |-> 0]
  /\ crashed = {}

AcquireLease(s, p) ==
  /\ s \notin crashed
  /\ p \notin dispensed
  /\ (leaseHolder[p] = NoStation \/ leaseTicksLeft[p] = 0)
  /\ leaseHolder' = [leaseHolder EXCEPT ![p] = s]
  /\ leaseTicksLeft' = [leaseTicksLeft EXCEPT ![p] = LeaseLen]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<dispensed, timesDispensed, crashed>>

\* The one irreversible step: only the current, not-yet-lapsed lease holder may do it.
Dispense(s, p) ==
  /\ leaseHolder[p] = s
  /\ s \notin crashed
  /\ p \notin dispensed
  /\ leaseTicksLeft[p] > 0
  /\ dispensed' = dispensed \union {p}
  /\ timesDispensed' = [timesDispensed EXCEPT ![p] = @ + 1]
  /\ leaseHolder' = [leaseHolder EXCEPT ![p] = NoStation]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<leaseTicksLeft, crashed>>

\* Advances the shared countdown clock, lapsing any lease whose time has run
\* out. Always enabled (a no-op once nothing is outstanding) so the clock
\* never gets stuck even after every prescription has been dispensed.

  /\ UNCHANGED <<leaseHolder, dispensed, timesDispensed, crashed>>

\* Exactly one station may ever go silent; its lease is left to lapse normally.
Crash(s) ==
  /\ crashed = {}
  /\ crashed' = crashed \union {s}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<leaseHolder, leaseTicksLeft, dispensed, timesDispensed>>

Next ==
  \/ \E s \in Stations, p \in Prescriptions : AcquireLease(s, p)
  \/ \E s \in Stations, p \in Prescriptions : Dispense(s, p)
  \/ Tick
  \/ \E s \in Stations : Crash(s)

  /\ \A s \in Stations, p \in Prescriptions : WF_vars(AcquireLease(s, p))
  /\ \A s \in Stations, p \in Prescriptions : SF_vars(Dispense(s, p))
  /\ WF_vars(Tick)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Fairness

AtMostOnceDispensed == \A p \in Prescriptions : timesDispensed[p] <= 1

EventuallyDispensed == \A p \in Prescriptions : <>(p \in dispensed)

====

A stock exchange runs an opening auction with a small number of fixed clearing slots, each of which can end up matched to at most one listed stock for that morning's open. A committee of matching-engine nodes decides which stock gets which slot by voting: the Propose action lets any node put forward a stock as the candidate for a still-unclaimed slot, as long as that slot has no candidate pending yet, and it casts the proposer's own vote in favor. The Finalize action lets the slot's candidate become the slot's actual, irreversible allocation once enough nodes (a quorum) have voted for it, clearing the pending vote so nothing further can attach to that slot. The AdminOverride action lets a privileged exchange administrator claim any still-unclaimed slot for a stock directly, skipping the vote entirely and wiping out any pending candidate and votes for that slot, but even the administrator cannot touch a slot that has already been claimed. The Audit action lets the committee perform a routine, no-op status check that changes nothing, so there is always something for the exchange to do even after every slot has already been claimed.   /\ votes \in [Slots -> SUBSET Nodes]
  /\ allocated \in [Slots -> Stocks \union {NoStock}]
  /\ allocCount \in [Slots -> 0..2]

  /\ votes = [s \in Slots |-> {}]
  /\ allocated = [s \in Slots |-> NoStock]
  /\ allocCount = [s \in Slots |-> 0]

\* Puts forward a candidate stock for a still-unclaimed, uncontested slot.
Propose(n, slot, stock) ==
  /\ allocated[slot] = NoStock
  /\ proposedStock[slot] = NoStock
  /\ proposedStock' = [proposedStock EXCEPT ![slot] = stock]
  /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![slot] = {n}]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<allocated, allocCount>>

  /\ proposedStock[slot] # NoStock
  /\ Cardinality(votes[slot]) >= Quorum

  /\ allocCount' = [allocCount EXCEPT ![slot] = @ + 1]
  /\ proposedStock' = [proposedStock EXCEPT ![slot] = NoStock]
  /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![slot] = {}]

  /\ allocated' = [allocated EXCEPT ![slot] = stock]
  /\ allocCount' = [allocCount EXCEPT ![slot] = @ + 1]
  /\ proposedStock' = [proposedStock EXCEPT ![slot] = NoStock]
  /\ votes' = [votes EXCEPT ![slot] = {}]

Patrons who want the book go through a lease-based hold system: the Reserve action lets an idle patron place a hold on a copy, provided the library is not already at full capacity for that title, and starts a countdown on how long the hold will be honored before it lapses. The ExpireHold action lets a patron's hold lapse once its countdown reaches zero, freeing up the copy it was holding for someone else. The Return action lets a patron who has checked out the book bring it back, likewise freeing up a copy. The AdminOverride action lets a privileged librarian check the book out directly to an idle patron, skipping the hold-and-countdown process entirely, but even the librarian is refused if the title is already at full capacity.   /\ checkedOut \in [Patrons -> BOOLEAN]

  /\ checkedOut = [p \in Patrons |-> FALSE]

  /\ activeHolds = 0

Reserve(p) ==

  /\ ~checkedOut[p]
  /\ activeHolds < TotalCopies
  /\ reserved' = [reserved EXCEPT ![p] = TRUE]
  /\ ticksLeft' = [ticksLeft EXCEPT ![p] = LeaseLen]
  /\ activeHolds' = activeHolds + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED checkedOut

  /\ activeHolds' = activeHolds - 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<checkedOut, ticksLeft>>

  \/ \E p \in Patrons : Return(p)
  \/ \E p \in Patrons : AdminOverride(p)

A subway signalling system keeps one shared occupancy record for the line: the set of track
blocks that have been claimed during the shift. Several interlocking cabins update that
record, and they do it through a compare-and-swap register: the record is stored together
with a version counter.

A cabin works in two steps. First it reads the register, taking a private snapshot of both
the version and the record contents. Later it writes back the snapshot with one extra block
added, but the write only lands if the register's version is still the version the cabin
read; on success the register takes the new contents, the version advances by one, and the
cabin is given an acknowledgement for that block. If the version has moved on since the read
-- because another cabin got there first -- the write is rejected and the cabin drops its
snapshot and starts over. A cabin only ever claims a block that is not already in the record
it can see, so the record only ever grows.

A cabin can crash silently: it stops with no announcement, and it keeps whatever snapshot it
was holding, so when it is brought back up it may still be carrying a snapshot from before
its outage. A crashed cabin cannot write. The version check is exactly what makes that
recovered, out-of-date snapshot harmless.

The actions are: a live cabin reads the register into its snapshot, a live cabin's
compare-and-swap succeeds and its block is acknowledged, a cabin whose snapshot version is
out of date has its write rejected and discards the snapshot, a cabin crashes silently while
keeping its snapshot, and a crashed cabin comes back up.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every block a cabin has been acknowledged for is still present in the
shared occupancy record, so no acknowledged update is ever overwritten and lost.

A bank's interbank settlement runs in batches. The clearing cycle has a small number of
settlement slots, and each batch that settles must occupy its own slot: two batches may
never settle into the same slot.

reserves a free slot for the batch and writes the reservation into two places -- the batch

member bank has voted, the coordinator commits the batch into its slot. If the coordinator
times out while any bank's vote is still missing, it aborts the batch and hands the slot
back, clearing both the batch's slot field and the slot register entry.

coordinator learns nothing and simply times out. A crashed bank may come back up later and
resume voting on batches still in the prepare phase.

bank votes for a batch in prepare, commit a batch whose votes are all in, abort a batch that
is still missing a vote and release its slot, a bank crashes silently, and a crashed bank
comes back up.

holder of the slot the batch settled into, so no slot is ever allocated to two batches.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A warehouse robot fleet feeds totes into the staging lanes of a pick station. Each lane holds
a limited number of totes and must never be overfilled -- an overfilled lane jams the station
and stops the whole aisle.

There is no lane lock. Robots work optimistically: a robot carrying a tote reads a lane,
taking a private note of the lane's identity and its current revision number, and later
tries to commit its deposit against that note. The commit only goes through if the lane's
revision is still the one the robot noted and the lane still has room; a successful deposit
adds the tote and advances the lane's revision. If another robot got there first the
revision has moved on, the commit is refused, and the robot throws its note away and retries
from scratch. The pick station also draws totes off a lane, which likewise advances that
lane's revision. Lane revisions advance only up to a bounded number of times in the window
modelled here.

Robots can be slow but they never fail. A slow robot is still running its path planner: it
neither reads a lane nor commits while it is slow, so its outstanding note simply ages and
is very likely to be refused when it finally tries. Slow robots resume at any time.

The actions are: a free robot picks up a tote, a running robot reads a lane and notes its
revision, a running robot commits its deposit when the revision still matches and the lane
has room, a robot whose noted revision is out of date discards the note and retries, the
pick station draws a tote off a lane, a robot becomes slow, and a slow robot resumes.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No staging lane ever holds more totes than its capacity.

\* not even by a deposit committed from an out-of-date read.

A desk is a critical resource: while one member bank is posting its batch at a desk, no
other bank may be posting at that same desk, or the two batches would interleave on the

desk, the register entry is cleared, and the bank's tally is wiped. Each member posts one

desk out of service for reconciliation and brings desks back later, but it never takes the
last desk in service out, so there is always at least one desk available.

request, the clearing house grants an in-service free desk to a request that has reached
quorum, a posting bank finishes and releases its desk, take an idle desk out of service, and
return a desk to service.

\* bank the desk's register names, and a register names one bank.

A warehouse robot fleet guards a high-bay aisle fitted with a one-shot foam suppression
canister. Firing the canister is irreversible: the foam is gone, the aisle is out of use
until it is re-charged by hand, and the fleet must never be able to fire it a second time.

The fleet controller runs the discharge as a two-phase commit with the robots working the
aisle. It opens a numbered round and asks every robot to prepare, which means clearing the
aisle and acknowledging. Each robot acknowledges the open round on its own. If the
controller gives up while an acknowledgement is still missing, the round is abandoned and
the controller returns to idle, free to open a later, higher-numbered round -- but only a
bounded number of rounds fit in the window modelled here. When every robot has acknowledged
the open round, the controller commits: the canister fires, the firing is stamped with the
number of the round that authorised it, and the protocol is frozen there. No new round can
be opened once the canister has fired.

Robots can be slow but never fail. A slow robot is still driving out of the aisle and will
not acknowledge; it resumes later and then acknowledges normally. Slowness is what makes the
controller abandon a round.

The actions are: open a new numbered round and ask for prepares, a running robot
acknowledges the open round, commit and fire the canister once every robot has acknowledged,
abandon a round that is still missing an acknowledgement, a robot becomes slow, and a slow
robot resumes.

round can ever be opened and no second discharge can occur.

  /\ acked \subseteq Robots
  /\ fired \in BOOLEAN
  /\ firedRound \in 0..MaxRound
  /\ slow \in [Robots -> BOOLEAN]

\* The irreversible discharge freezes the protocol on the round that authorised
\* it: no later round exists, so there is no path to a second discharge.
FrozenAfterFiring ==

  /\ phase = "idle"
  /\ acked = {}
  /\ fired = FALSE
  /\ firedRound = 0
  /\ slow = [r \in Robots |-> FALSE]

AbandonRound ==

A library branch keeps a hold shelf behind the desk for reserved books. The shelf has a hard
physical limit: the number of books either already sitting on it or promised to it by an
in-flight reservation must never exceed the number of slots it has.

asks for a title, the desk takes a shelf slot into escrow and puts the reservation into the
prepared phase, recording which patron it is for; the escrowed slot counts against the
shelf's limit from that moment, before the book has physically arrived. Each branch then
votes on the prepared reservation. Once every branch has voted, the reservation commits and
the book goes onto the shelf. If a vote is still outstanding, the desk may abort the
reservation instead, which gives the escrowed slot back.

The head librarian has a privileged override and may push a prepared reservation through to
the shelf without waiting for the branch votes; the override budget for the day is limited
and each use spends one. The override skips the consensus, never the shelf limit -- the slot
was already escrowed when the reservation was prepared. When the patron collects the book,
the slot is freed and the title can be reserved again.

The actions are: a patron requests a title, which escrows a shelf slot and prepares the
reservation; a branch votes on a prepared reservation; commit a reservation whose votes are
all in; the head librarian spends one override to push a prepared reservation onto the shelf;
abort a prepared reservation that is still missing a vote and release its slot; and a patron
collects a book from the shelf, freeing the slot.

prepared reservation never exceeds the shelf's slot count.

A subway line is divided into signalling blocks. A block is a critical resource: at most one
train may be inside a given block at a time, or the two trains are on a collision course.

Each block has a compare-and-swap occupancy register holding the current occupant, or Free,
together with a serial number. A train enters a block by swapping Free for its own identity;
the same swap advances the block's serial and hands the train a movement authority stamped
with that new serial. A train inside a block leaves it by putting the register back to Free
and surrendering its authority. Each train in this window makes one trip: it waits, occupies
one block, and then has arrived.

The number of blocks in service changes during operation. Control may take an empty block
out of service for track work and put it back later, but it never takes out the last block
in service, so a waiting train always has somewhere to go.

The actions are: a waiting train swaps itself into a free in-service block and takes the
stamped authority, an occupying train releases its block back to Free and has arrived, take
an empty in-service block out of service, and return a block to service.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every train that is inside a block is the occupant named in that block's
register and holds an authority whose stamp equals the register's current serial, so two
trains can never be inside the same block.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every waiting train eventually occupies a block.

Free == "free"
NoBlock == "noblock"
MaxSerial == Cardinality(Trains)

VARIABLES owner, serial, authority, inBlock, inService, arrived

vars == <<owner, serial, authority, inBlock, inService, arrived>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ owner \in [Blocks -> Trains \cup {Free}]
  /\ serial \in [Blocks -> 0..MaxSerial]
  /\ authority \in [Trains -> 0..MaxSerial]
  /\ inBlock \in [Trains -> Blocks \cup {NoBlock}]
  /\ inService \subseteq Blocks
  /\ arrived \subseteq Trains

\* Exclusion rests on the register: an occupant must be the named owner and its
\* authority stamp must still match the block's serial.
ExclusiveOccupancy ==
  \A t \in Trains :
    inBlock[t] # NoBlock =>
      /\ owner[inBlock[t]] = t
      /\ authority[t] = serial[inBlock[t]]

Init ==
  /\ owner = [b \in Blocks |-> Free]
  /\ serial = [b \in Blocks |-> 0]
  /\ authority = [t \in Trains |-> 0]
  /\ inBlock = [t \in Trains |-> NoBlock]
  /\ inService = Blocks
  /\ arrived = {}

\* The compare-and-swap: Free is exchanged for the train, serial advances.
SwapIn(t, b) ==
  /\ t \notin arrived
  /\ inBlock[t] = NoBlock
  /\ b \in inService
  /\ owner[b] = Free
  /\ serial[b] < MaxSerial
  /\ owner' = [owner EXCEPT ![b] = t]
  /\ serial' = [serial EXCEPT ![b] = @ + 1]
  /\ authority' = [authority EXCEPT ![t] = serial[b] + 1]
  /\ inBlock' = [inBlock EXCEPT ![t] = b]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<inService, arrived>>

Release(t) ==
  /\ inBlock[t] # NoBlock
  /\ owner' = [owner EXCEPT ![inBlock[t]] = Free]
  /\ inBlock' = [inBlock EXCEPT ![t] = NoBlock]
  /\ authority' = [authority EXCEPT ![t] = 0]
  /\ arrived' = arrived \cup {t}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<serial, inService>>

TakeOut(b) ==
  /\ b \in inService
  /\ owner[b] = Free
  /\ Cardinality(inService) > 1
  /\ inService' = inService \ {b}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<owner, serial, authority, inBlock, arrived>>

PutBack(b) ==
  /\ b \notin inService
  /\ inService' = inService \cup {b}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<owner, serial, authority, inBlock, arrived>>

ReleaseStep == \E t \in Trains : Release(t)

Next ==

  \/ \E b \in Blocks : TakeOut(b) \/ PutBack(b)

Spec ==

  /\ SF_vars(SwapStep) /\ SF_vars(ReleaseStep)

TrainsGetIn == \A t \in Trains : Waiting(t) ~> (inBlock[t] # NoBlock \/ t \in arrived)

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An air-traffic runway allocator is driven by two independent console instances that share one
pool of runway assignments. The pool sits behind a compare-and-swap register that carries a
generation number, and each console holds its own handle on that generation.

The supervisor bumps the generation whenever the airport configuration changes -- a runway
direction flip, a new noise regime. A bump immediately marks every existing assignment in the
shared pool as needing re-affirmation, because an assignment made under the old configuration
means nothing under the new one. A console picks up the new generation by re-reading the
register into its handle.

A console writes to the pool by stamping the assignment with the generation its own handle
carries. It may take a free runway and assign it, re-affirm an assignment of its own that is
waiting for re-affirmation, or withdraw one of its own assignments and return the runway to
the pool. Every one of those writes is only accepted while the console's handle equals the
register's generation; a console that has not picked up the latest generation is stale and
its writes are refused. That refusal is the entire safety mechanism, since either console can
touch any runway in the shared pool.

The actions are: the supervisor bumps the generation and flags every assignment for
re-affirmation, a console re-reads the register into its handle, a console with a current
handle assigns a free runway, a console with a current handle re-affirms its own flagged
assignment, and a console with a current handle withdraws its own assignment.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every assignment in the shared pool that is not flagged for re-affirmation
carries the register's current generation stamp, so no stale console's write is ever standing
in the pool as valid.

Nobody == "nobody"

VARIABLES gen, handle, assignedBy, stamp, flagged

vars == <<gen, handle, assignedBy, stamp, flagged>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ gen \in 0..MaxGen
  /\ handle \in [Consoles -> 0..MaxGen]
  /\ assignedBy \in [Runways -> Consoles \cup {Nobody}]
  /\ stamp \in [Runways -> 0..MaxGen]
  /\ flagged \subseteq Runways

\* Writes are stamped with the writer's own handle, so a stale write would sit
\* in the pool carrying an out-of-date generation.
NoStaleWriteStanding ==
  \A r \in Runways :
    (assignedBy[r] # Nobody /\ r \notin flagged) => stamp[r] = gen

Init ==
  /\ gen = 0
  /\ handle = [c \in Consoles |-> 0]
  /\ assignedBy = [r \in Runways |-> Nobody]
  /\ stamp = [r \in Runways |-> 0]
  /\ flagged = {}

BumpGeneration ==
  /\ gen < MaxGen
  /\ gen' = gen + 1
  /\ flagged' = {r \in Runways : assignedBy[r] # Nobody}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<handle, assignedBy, stamp>>

ReadRegister(c) ==
  /\ handle[c] # gen
  /\ handle' = [handle EXCEPT ![c] = gen]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<gen, assignedBy, stamp, flagged>>

Assign(c, r) ==
  /\ handle[c] = gen
  /\ assignedBy[r] = Nobody
  /\ assignedBy' = [assignedBy EXCEPT ![r] = c]
  /\ stamp' = [stamp EXCEPT ![r] = handle[c]]
  /\ flagged' = flagged \ {r}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<gen, handle>>

\* Re-affirmation clears the flag by re-stamping under the current generation.
Reaffirm(c, r) ==

  /\ r \in flagged
  /\ assignedBy[r] = c
  /\ stamp' = [stamp EXCEPT ![r] = handle[c]]
  /\ flagged' = flagged \ {r}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<gen, handle, assignedBy>>

Withdraw(c, r) ==
  /\ handle[c] = gen
  /\ assignedBy[r] = c
  /\ assignedBy' = [assignedBy EXCEPT ![r] = Nobody]
  /\ flagged' = flagged \ {r}

still the version in the snapshot. Acting means one of two things: releasing the batch, which
marks it released and advances its version, or amending it, which just advances its version.
Either way the version moves, which is precisely what makes every other outstanding snapshot
of that batch worthless. A gateway that notices its snapshot no longer matches the batch's
version throws it away and starts over. A batch's version can only be advanced a bounded
number of times in the window modelled here, and amendments stop early enough to leave room
for the release.

A gateway can crash silently: it stops with no notice and keeps whatever snapshot it was
holding, so it may come back up carrying a snapshot from before the outage. A crashed gateway
neither snapshots nor acts.

batch whose version still matches its snapshot, a live gateway amends a batch whose version
still matches its snapshot, a gateway discards a snapshot whose version no longer matches,

batch that has not been released, so no second release can ever be authorised.

successful write advances the version and clears the snapshot. There are two kinds of write:

A smart-home door lock network hands out a fixed stock of digital guest credentials. The
stock never grows and never shrinks: every credential is at all times either sitting unissued
in the hub's vault or provisioned into exactly one door's keypad. The hub also keeps a
running summary of how many credentials it has issued in total, and that summary must always
agree with what the doors actually hold added up.

Changing a door's credentials is done under two claims taken in order, coarse then fine: the
hub first takes the house-wide administration claim, and only while holding it may it take
the claim on an individual door. Provisioning moves one credential out of the vault into that
door's keypad and adds one to the hub summary; revoking moves one back out of the keypad into
the vault and takes one off the summary. The door claim is dropped when the work on that door
is finished, and the house-wide claim is only dropped once no door claim is outstanding.

A door's keypad capacity is re-provisioned at runtime while its door claim is held -- the
installer can set it to any value up to the model's maximum -- but it can never be set below
the number of credentials that door is already holding.

while holding the house-wide one, provision a credential from the vault into a claimed door,
revoke a credential from a claimed door back into the vault, set a claimed door's capacity to
a new value not below what it holds, drop a door's claim, and drop the house-wide claim once
no door claim is outstanding.

across all the doors, and that summary plus the vault always equals the fixed stock, so no
credential is ever conjured up or lost.

A subway signalling system allocates junction path slots to trains. A slot may belong to one
train at a time; handing the same slot to two trains routes them through the junction
together. The signalling centres keep two books for this: a free list of the slots currently
available, and an allocation table saying which train holds each slot. The two books are
supposed to be exact complements of one another, and a slot that is handed out while still
sitting on the free list is precisely how the same slot ends up allocated twice.

A train driver asks for a specific slot. The signalling centres then vote on the request, and
the allocation goes through once a quorum of distinct centres has voted for it: the slot
comes off the free list and the allocation table records the train. The duty controller holds
a privileged override and can push a pending request straight through without any votes, out
of a limited daily budget; the override skips the vote, not the books -- it still takes the
slot off the free list as it writes the allocation. When a train has cleared the junction it
releases its slot, which clears the table entry and puts the slot back on the free list.

The actions are: a train asks for a slot that is currently unallocated, a signalling centre
votes for a pending request, allocate a slot to a request that has reached quorum, the duty
controller spends one override to allocate a pending request without votes, and a train
releases a slot it holds.

outstanding quote is offered an in-service bin that is currently empty, and the

actually dropped into its quoted bin, but only if the stamped epoch is still

must be wired out, and a wire is irreversible: once the funds leave, there is
no way to take them back, so a payment must never be wired a second time.

fine claim on a payment that is still on the worklist. Wire: a bank holding the
fine claim on a worklist payment sends the funds, which moves the payment off

coarse claim. StandDown: the bank holding the coarse claim gives it up and

officer engages the override, takes the coarse claim, and strips every bank's
fine claim. AdminWire: with the override engaged, the duty officer wires a
worklist payment whose fine claim is free. AdminRelease: the duty officer
disengages the override and leaves the coarse claim free.

no participant holds the fine claim on a payment that has already been wired,
so no payment can be wired twice.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A clearing house settles an interbank batch by placing each payment into one of
a fixed number of settlement slots in the day's timetable. A slot carries at
most one payment, and the timetable is kept in two books that must mirror each
other: the slot book says which payment sits in each slot, and the payment book
says which slot each payment was given.

Only the elected settlement leader may write the books. Leadership is carried by
a term number: any live node may raise the term and take the leadership for
itself, and a node is the leader only while its own recorded term equals the
live term. A node can fail silently -- no announcement is made and the other
nodes are not told -- so the surviving nodes simply elect a successor under a
higher term, and the failed node's stale term locks it out if it ever comes
back.

Five things can happen. Elect: a live node that is not already the leader raises
the term by one and records that new term as its own. Fail: a node stops
silently. Restart: a stopped node comes back up, still carrying whatever term it
had. Allocate: the live leader places a payment that has no slot into a slot
that has no payment, writing both books. Recall: the live leader takes a payment
back out of its slot, clearing both books.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The slot book and the payment book are always exact inverses of
each other, so no settlement slot is ever allocated to two payments at once.

lease holder handles a student who has no decision yet when the seats already
taken have reached capacity, stamping a no-seat decision with itself and the
current generation. Resize: the registrar changes the seat capacity to a
different value.

the current one, every decision stamped with the current generation names the
worker that actually holds the lease right now, and every seated student has a

A network of vending machines draws from one central warehouse record for a
single product line. Cans are never created and never destroyed: every can is

commit is only accepted if the version has not moved since the read, and the
accepted commit bumps the version. If the version has moved, the machine throws
its read away and retries later. The operator also re-rates hopper capacity
while the network is running, so the per-machine hopper limit changes at
runtime.

current version number while the warehouse is non-empty. Commit: a machine
whose outstanding read still matches the live version, with the warehouse
non-empty and its hopper below the current limit, moves one can from the
warehouse into its hopper and bumps the version, clearing its read. Retry: a
machine whose outstanding read no longer matches the live version throws that
read away. Sell: a machine with at least one can in its hopper sells one can to
a customer. Rerate: the operator sets the hopper limit to a different value.

hoppers, and the cans already sold always add up to exactly the number of cans

of the lane while the lane is below its limit. ForcePush: the manager, with the
override still unused, forces a forecourt car onto the tail of a full lane and
burns the override. Pull: the conveyor takes the head car of the lane into the
empty wash bay. Finish: the car in the wash bay is washed and written into the
shared wash record, leaving the bay empty. NewCycle: once every car on site has
been written into the shared wash record, the whole cohort is cleared out of the
record and returned to the forecourt for another pass.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A clearing house settles an interbank batch in rounds, and each round is driven
by a two-phase commit across the member banks. The house runs against a bounded
liquidity window: the value already settled today plus the value provisionally
held for the round in progress can never exceed the window size.

A round opens by asking every member to vote. A member that votes to go ahead
takes one unit of the window and holds it provisionally; a member may only vote
to go ahead if that extra unit still fits inside the window. When every member
has voted to go ahead, the house commits the round and the provisional holds
become settled value. Otherwise the house aborts and every provisional hold is
released. A member can stop dead without telling anyone, in which case it never
votes and the round is aborted by the house.

Seven things can happen. OpenRound: with no round in progress and rounds left in
the day, the house clears all votes and opens the voting phase. VoteGo: a live
member that has not voted yet votes to go ahead and takes one unit of the
window, provided the unit fits. VoteStop: a live member that has not voted yet
votes to stop. Fail: a member stops dead silently. Recover: a stopped member
comes back up. CommitRound: with every member having voted to go ahead, the
house turns the provisional holds into settled value and closes the round.
AbortRound: with the round in progress and not every member having voted to go
ahead, the house releases every provisional hold, clears the votes and closes
the round.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The settled value plus the provisionally held value never
exceeds the liquidity window, and no value is left provisionally held once no
round is in progress.

TypeOK ==
  /\ round \in 0 .. MaxRounds
  /\ phase \in {"closed", "voting"}
  /\ ballot \in [Members -> {"blank", "go", "stop"}]
  /\ held \in 0 .. Window
  /\ settled \in 0 .. Window
  /\ stopped \subseteq Members

AllGo == \A m \in Members : ballot[m] = "go"

\* The bounded liquidity window covers settled value and provisional holds
\* together, and nothing stays held once the round is closed.
WindowNotExceeded ==
  /\ settled + held <= Window
  /\ phase = "closed" => held = 0

Init ==
  /\ round = 0
  /\ phase = "closed"
  /\ ballot = [m \in Members |-> "blank"]
  /\ held = 0
  /\ settled = 0
  /\ stopped = {}

OpenRound ==
  /\ phase = "closed"
  /\ round < MaxRounds
  /\ round' = round + 1
  /\ phase' = "voting"
  /\ ballot' = [m \in Members |-> "blank"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<held, settled, stopped>>

\* A member may only vote to go ahead if its unit still fits in the window.
VoteGo(m) ==
  /\ phase = "voting"
  /\ m \notin stopped
  /\ ballot[m] = "blank"
  /\ settled + held + 1 <= Window
  /\ ballot' = [ballot EXCEPT ![m] = "go"]
  /\ held' = held + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, phase, settled, stopped>>

VoteStop(m) ==
  /\ phase = "voting"
  /\ m \notin stopped
  /\ ballot[m] = "blank"
  /\ ballot' = [ballot EXCEPT ![m] = "stop"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, phase, held, settled, stopped>>

Fail(m) ==

  /\ stopped' = stopped \cup {m}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, phase, ballot, held, settled>>

Recover(m) ==
  /\ m \in stopped
  /\ stopped' = stopped \ {m}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<round, phase, ballot, held, settled>>

  /\ settled' = settled + held
  /\ held' = 0
  /\ phase' = "closed"

  /\ ~AllGo
  /\ held' = 0
  /\ phase' = "closed"
  /\ ballot' = [m \in Members |-> "blank"]

  \/ AbortRound

An airport baggage router keeps one shared routing record that says, for each
bag, which chute it has been committed to. Check-in desks post assignment
messages to the router over a fabric that gives no ordering guarantee: two
messages posted in one order can arrive in the other order, or a duplicate can
arrive long after the bag was already committed.

The router publishes its chute layout under an epoch number. A reconfiguration
bumps the epoch and takes some chutes out of service, but it is never allowed to
retire a chute that a confirmed bag is already committed to, and at least one
chute always stays in service. Every assignment message carries the epoch it was
posted under, so a message that survives a reconfiguration is no longer valid.

Five things can happen. Reconfigure: the router bumps the epoch and installs a
new out-of-service set that leaves at least one chute live and retires no chute
that a confirmed bag is committed to. Post: a desk posts an assignment message
naming an uncommitted bag and an in-service chute, stamped with the current
epoch. Apply: the router picks any in-flight message whose stamp is the current
epoch, whose chute is still in service, and whose bag is still uncommitted, and
commits that bag to that chute in the shared record, confirming it to the desk
and consuming the message. Discard: the router throws away any in-flight message
whose stamp is stale, or whose chute has been retired, or whose bag is already
committed. Unload: a confirmed bag is taken off its chute, clearing its entry in
the shared record and its confirmation.

record, and that entry never names a chute that has been taken out of service,
so no confirmed routing update is ever lost.

one bay to work. The plan is published under an epoch number, and each crane

yard office bumps the epoch and installs a different bay assignment. Refresh: a
crane whose copy is behind the published epoch picks up the current plan and its

container that is standing in the bay its current plan assigns it, so the
container is in the air under that crane. Land: a crane holding a container sets

yard truck drags a container that is standing on the ground from its bay to a
different bay.

ever holding a container, every held container is recorded as being in the air,
and every container recorded as being in the air is held by exactly the crane
that lifted it.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A car-wash conveyor line keeps one shared service record that says, for each
car, which attendant signed off its wash. Only the attendant currently holding
the site lease may write into that record. The lease has an expiry: when it
lapses the site's lease generation advances, which retires every write that was
issued under the old generation.

Attendants do not write the record directly. They post a sign-off message
stamped with themselves and the generation in force, and the record clerk picks
messages up over a link that gives no ordering guarantee, so messages may be
picked up in any order. Posting a sign-off also puts the car on the promised
list, and the site's rule is that a promised car is either already in the shared
record or still has its message in flight -- a promise must never evaporate.

Six things can happen. Grant: with the lease free, an attendant takes it.
Expire: the held lease lapses, leaving the lease free and advancing the
generation. Post: the lease holder puts a car that is neither promised nor
recorded on the promised list and posts a sign-off message stamped with itself
and the current generation, as long as the link is not already saturated.
Accept: the clerk picks up any in-flight message whose generation is still
current and whose attendant still holds the lease, and writes that car into the
shared record. Refuse: the clerk picks up any in-flight message whose generation
is stale or whose attendant no longer holds the lease, drops it, and takes the
car back off the promised list. Archive: a car already written into the shared
record is archived at the end of the shift, clearing its record entry and its
promise.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every promised car is either already written into the shared
service record or still has its sign-off message in flight, and every car in the
record is on the promised list, so no sign-off is ever lost.

An air-traffic runway allocator serves several tower positions, each of which
owns the inbound flights for its own sector. Only one position at a time may
issue clearances: a single token walks a fixed ring of positions, and a position
may only issue a clearance while it holds the token.

The runway complex has a hard occupancy bound. A clearance that has been issued
but not yet read back by the flight deck still counts against that bound,
because the clearance link gives no ordering guarantee: two clearances issued in
one order may be read back in the other order, so the allocator can never assume
an issued clearance has not landed yet.

Five things can happen. PassToken: the token moves one step around the ring of
positions. Issue: the position holding the token takes one of its own waiting
flights and issues a clearance for it, provided the outstanding clearances plus
the aircraft already on the runway are still below the occupancy bound. ReadBack:
any outstanding clearance, in any order, is read back by its flight deck and the
aircraft moves onto the runway. Vacate: an aircraft on the runway rolls clear of
the complex and is done. NewWave: once every flight in the wave is done, the
whole wave is reset and all flights go back to waiting at their own sector
positions.

outstanding never exceed the occupancy bound, and no flight is ever both on the
runway and holding an outstanding clearance.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every waiting flight is eventually cleared, lands, and rolls
clear of the runway complex.

  /\ onRunway \subseteq Flights
  /\ done \subseteq Flights

\* An issued-but-unread clearance still counts against the occupancy bound,
\* because the link may deliver clearances in any order.
RunwayBoundHeld ==
  /\ Cardinality(onRunway \cup outstanding) <= Occupancy
  /\ onRunway \cap outstanding = {}

  /\ outstanding = {}

several scheduler nodes. One node is elected to lead; only the leader may write
a new booking change, and it then pushes that change out to the other nodes. A
node can crash silently -- it simply stops answering, with no announcement --

A vending machine network is restocked by a fleet of vans. Before a van may
touch a machine it must take a restock lease on it, and the lease carries a
countdown: the lease ticks down and, when the countdown runs out, it lapses and
the machine goes back to being unleased whether or not the van got there.

The depot has a bounded crew: only so many machines may be under lease at the
same moment. That crew size is re-rated during the day, but the depot will only
re-rate down to a size that still covers the leases already out.

Five things can happen. Take: a van takes a lease on a machine that is running
low and is not already leased, provided the leases already out are below the
crew size; the countdown starts at full. Clock: while at least one lease is out,
the depot clock ticks every live lease down by one at once, and any lease that
was on its last tick lapses on the spot, going back to unleased with a zero
countdown. Fill: the van holding a live lease on a machine
restocks it, which clears the low-stock flag, releases the lease and zeroes the
countdown. Drain: a restocked machine sells out and goes back to running low.
Rerate: the depot changes the crew size to a different value that still covers
the leases currently out.

every leased machine has a countdown still running, and every unleased machine
has a zero countdown.

because the machine was restocked or because the countdown lapsed.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
An airport baggage router feeds bags from an input pier onto a sorter loop. The
loop has a hard bag capacity that must never be exceeded. The loop's bag count
is published in a single register that also carries a tag, and the tag is bumped
by every write, so the tag identifies the exact version of the count.

Loaders never write the register blind. A loader takes a snapshot of the count
and the tag, decides against its own snapshot whether another bag fits, and then
tries a compare-and-swap: the write only lands if the live tag is still the tag
it snapshotted. A loader is never out of service, but it can be slow, so a
snapshot may be very old by the time the loader gets round to using it; such a
compare-and-swap is rejected and the snapshot is thrown away.

Six things can happen. Arrive: another bag joins the input pier, up to the
pier's limit. Depart: a bag on the pier is taken away by hand. Snapshot: a
loader with no snapshot in hand records the current count and tag. Push: a
loader whose snapshot tag still matches the live tag, whose snapshotted count is
below the loop capacity, and which has a bag on the pier, writes the snapshotted
count plus one into the register, bumps the tag, takes the bag off the pier and
drops its snapshot. Reject: a loader whose snapshot tag no longer matches the
live tag throws the snapshot away. Unload: a bag leaves the loop down a chute,
which decrements the register and bumps the tag.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The published loop count never exceeds the loop capacity, and
any loader whose snapshot tag still matches the live tag has a snapshotted count
that still matches the live count.

VARIABLES count, tag, seenCount, seenTag, pier

vars == <<count, tag, seenCount, seenTag, pier>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ count \in 0 .. LoopCap
  /\ tag \in 0 .. MaxTag
  /\ seenCount \in [Loaders -> 0 .. LoopCap]
  /\ seenTag \in [Loaders -> (0 .. MaxTag) \cup {NoSnap}]
  /\ pier \in 0 .. PierCap

\* The tag is a true version stamp: a snapshot whose tag still matches must
\* still describe the live count, which is what keeps the loop under capacity.
LoopWithinCapacity ==
  /\ count <= LoopCap
  /\ \A l \in Loaders : seenTag[l] = tag => seenCount[l] = count

Init ==
  /\ count = 0
  /\ tag = 0
  /\ seenCount = [l \in Loaders |-> 0]
  /\ seenTag = [l \in Loaders |-> NoSnap]
  /\ pier = 0

Arrive ==
  /\ pier < PierCap
  /\ pier' = pier + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<count, tag, seenCount, seenTag>>

Depart ==
  /\ pier > 0
  /\ pier' = pier - 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<count, tag, seenCount, seenTag>>

Snapshot(l) ==
  /\ seenTag[l] = NoSnap
  /\ seenCount' = [seenCount EXCEPT ![l] = count]
  /\ seenTag' = [seenTag EXCEPT ![l] = tag]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<count, tag, pier>>

\* The compare-and-swap only lands while the snapshotted tag is still live.
Push(l) ==
  /\ seenTag[l] = tag
  /\ seenCount[l] < LoopCap
  /\ pier > 0
  /\ tag < MaxTag
  /\ count' = seenCount[l] + 1
  /\ tag' = tag + 1
  /\ pier' = pier - 1
  /\ seenTag' = [seenTag EXCEPT ![l] = NoSnap]

  /\ seenTag[l] # tag

  /\ tag' = tag + 1

  \/ Depart
  \/ Unload

A vending machine network shares one cash canister between all its machines.
The canister is the critical resource: at any moment at most one machine may
have its cash door open onto it, and the machine with its door open must be
exactly the machine the canister has been handed to.

A machine cannot open its own door. It puts a petition to the network's
controllers, and the controllers back it one at a time; the door only opens once
a quorum of controllers has backed the standing petition. The field technician
carries a master key that outranks the vote entirely.

Six things can happen. Petition: with no petition standing, the canister free
and the master key not in use, a machine puts up a petition and the backing list
starts empty. Back: a controller that has not yet backed the standing petition
backs it. Open: once the backing list has reached quorum and the canister is
free, the canister is handed to the petitioning machine, its cash door opens,
and the petition and backing list are cleared. Close: the machine whose door is
open closes it and the canister goes free. MasterOpen: with the master key not
in use and the canister free, the technician engages the master key, hands the
canister straight to a machine whose door opens, and tears up any standing
petition. MasterDrop: with the master key in use and the canister free, the
technician puts the master key away.

canister was handed to, the machine holding the canister always has its door
open, and no petition is ever standing while the canister is handed out -- so
two machines can never be on the canister at once.

taken off the table.

A multiplayer game lobby matchmaker is run as two independent matchmaker
instances that share one pool of lobby slots. A slot may only ever be filled by
one player, so an instance is not allowed to drop a player into a slot it has
not first taken out of the shared free pool.

To take a slot, an instance puts a lease on it, which removes the slot from the
free pool and starts a countdown. The lease only lasts while the countdown is
running; if the countdown runs out before the instance seats anybody, the lease
lapses and the slot goes straight back into the free pool for either instance to
try again.

Five things can happen. Lease: an instance takes a slot out of the shared free
pool, marks the slot as leased to itself and starts the countdown at full.
Tick: a leased slot whose countdown has more than one tick left drops by one.
Lapse: a leased slot whose countdown is on its last tick loses its lease, zeroes
its countdown and goes back into the free pool. Seat: the instance holding a
live lease on a slot drops an unseated player into it, which ends the lease,
zeroes the countdown and leaves the slot filled rather than back in the pool.
Leave: the player in a filled slot quits, emptying the slot and putting it back
into the free pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shared free pool is exactly the set of slots that are
neither leased nor filled, a slot under lease is always empty and always has its
countdown still running, an unleased slot always has a zero countdown, and the
seated players are exactly the players sitting in slots -- so the same slot can
never be allocated to two players.

A car-wash conveyor line has several wash bays, each with its own backlog of
cars waiting on it. A bay operator is not authorised to run the machinery on its
own say-so: a single duty token walks a fixed ring of bays, and only the bay the
token is currently parked at may pick up a run permit. A permit picked up by a
bay other than the token's bay, or a permit still held after the shift
supervisor has locked the line out, would be an unauthorised run.

The token only moves on once the bay it is parked at has no permit outstanding
and no cars left in its backlog. The shift supervisor can lock the whole line
out, but only while no bay is holding a permit, and can unlock it again.

Six things can happen. Grant: with the line not locked out and the token's bay
holding no permit, that bay picks up the run permit. Wash: the bay holding the
permit runs one car out of its own backlog through the machinery. Revoke: the
bay holding the permit hands it back. Pass: with the token's bay holding no
permit and its backlog empty, the token moves one step round the ring. Lockout:
with the line not already locked out and no bay holding a permit, the shift
supervisor locks the line out. Unlock: the shift supervisor unlocks the line.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The only bay that can be holding a run permit is the bay the
token is parked at, and no bay holds a run permit while the line is locked out,
so no unauthorised or superseded bay ever runs the machinery.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every bay's backlog is eventually washed down to nothing.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A stock exchange runs an opening auction. The sell interest sitting on the book
is split across price levels, and every share on the book has to end up in
exactly one of two places by the time the auction crosses: allocated to a buyer,
or returned to the seller unfilled. Shares are never created and never
destroyed.

Brokers work the book under a two-level discipline. A broker first takes the
coarse claim on the whole book, and only then may it take the fine claim on an
individual price level, and only a level that still has interest on it. Giving
up the coarse claim also gives up every fine claim the same broker was holding.
No broker ever drops out of the auction, but a broker can be slow: it may sit on
the coarse claim for a long time without doing anything with it.

Five things can happen. TakeBook: a broker takes the coarse claim on the book
while it is free. TakeLevel: the broker holding the coarse claim takes the free
fine claim on a price level that still has interest on it. Cross: the broker
holding the fine claim on a level with interest crosses one share off that
level and allocates it to a buyer. Pull: the broker holding the fine claim on a
level with interest takes one share off that level and returns it unfilled to
the seller. StandDown: the broker holding the coarse claim gives it up along
with every fine claim it holds.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The shares still on the book, the shares allocated to buyers
and the shares returned unfilled always add up to the auction's opening size,
and any fine claim on a price level is held by the very broker that holds the
coarse claim on the book.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every share still sitting on the book is eventually either
allocated to a buyer or returned unfilled.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home door lock network keeps one shared lock-policy record that every hub in the house can edit. Because any hub may go dark, the hubs run a coordinator election: exactly one hub holds the coordinator role at a time, and each election round is stamped with a monotonically increasing term number.

The shared record carries a version counter and the identity of the hub that last wrote it. A hub that wants to change the policy reads the record and emits an edit that quotes the term it believes is current and the version number it read. Edits travel over the home mesh network, which gives no ordering guarantee at all: the pending edits sit in an unordered buffer and may be delivered in any order, so an edit issued against an old version can easily arrive after a newer edit has already landed.

The system has four actions. Failover promotes some hub other than the incumbent to coordinator and increments the term, up to a fixed maximum number of terms. Propose lets any hub place a new edit into the pending buffer, quoting any term no later than the current one and any version no later than the current record version, provided the buffer still has room. An edit counts as installable when its term matches the current term, its author is the current coordinator, its quoted version equals the record's present version, and the record has not yet reached its final version. Apply takes any installable pending edit and installs it, bumps the version by one, records the author, and appends the edit to the accepted history. Reject removes any pending edit that is not installable, discarding it without touching the record.

The accepted history is the audit trail of the policy record. Each entry stores the author and the version that author was editing against.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The n-th entry of the accepted history always quotes base version n-1, so every accepted edit was computed against exactly the record state left by the previously accepted edit and no hub's write is ever silently overwritten.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

\* to the shared lock-policy record are accepted, and only when the writer
\* quoted the version it actually read.
CONSTANTS Hubs, MaxTerm, MaxVersion, MaxInflight

VARIABLES leader, term, record, inflight, history
vars == <<leader, term, record, inflight, history>>

Notes == [src: Hubs, term: 1..MaxTerm, base: 0..MaxVersion]
Entries == [writer: Hubs, base: 0..MaxVersion]
First == CHOOSE h \in Hubs : TRUE

TypeOK ==
  /\ leader \in Hubs
  /\ term \in 1..MaxTerm
  /\ record \in [version: 0..MaxVersion, writer: Hubs]
  /\ inflight \subseteq Notes
  /\ history \in Seq(Entries)

\* An edit is installable only while it is term-current, authored by the
\* incumbent coordinator, and quoting the version now on the record.
Installable(m) ==
  /\ m.term = term
  /\ m.src = leader
  /\ m.base = record.version
  /\ record.version < MaxVersion

Init ==
  /\ leader = First
  /\ term = 1
  /\ record = [version |-> 0, writer |-> First]
  /\ inflight = {}
  /\ history = <<>>

\* Failover promotes a different hub and bumps the coordination term.
Failover ==
  /\ term < MaxTerm
  /\ \E h \in Hubs :
       /\ h # leader
       /\ leader' = h
       /\ term' = term + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<record, inflight, history>>

\* A hub emits an edit quoting whatever term and version it last observed;
\* the network buffer is a set, so delivery order is unconstrained.
Propose ==
  /\ Cardinality(inflight) < MaxInflight
  /\ \E h \in Hubs, t \in 1..term, b \in 0..record.version :
       inflight' = inflight \cup {[src |-> h, term |-> t, base |-> b]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<leader, term, record, history>>

Apply ==
  /\ \E m \in inflight :
       /\ m.term = term
       /\ m.src = leader
       /\ m.base = record.version
       /\ record.version < MaxVersion
       /\ record' = [version |-> record.version + 1, writer |-> m.src]
       /\ history' = Append(history, [writer |-> m.src, base |-> m.base])
       /\ inflight' = inflight \ {m}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<leader, term>>

Reject ==
  /\ \E m \in inflight :
       /\ ~Installable(m)
       /\ inflight' = inflight \ {m}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<leader, term, record, history>>

Next == Failover \/ Propose \/ Apply \/ Reject

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* No edit is ever silently overwritten: the n-th accepted edit was computed
\* against exactly the record left behind by the (n-1)-th accepted edit.
NoLostUpdate == \A i \in 1..Len(history) : history[i].base = i - 1

A regional vending machine network runs a promotion in which exactly one promotional item exists across the whole fleet. Dispensing that item is irreversible: once a machine drops it into a customer's hands there is nothing to take back, so the network keeps a ledger naming the single machine that consumed it. The machines are wired in a ring and a circulating token travels around it; a machine only interacts with the shared promotion while it is holding the token.

There are five actions. Request models a customer walking up to a machine that has not yet taken a promo request in this campaign, adding that machine to the set of machines with a waiting customer and marking it as having asked. Circulate advances the token from its current machine to the next machine around the ring. Redeem fires when the token holder has a waiting customer and the ledger still shows the promotion unclaimed: the machine physically dispenses the item, writes itself into the ledger as the redeemer, and clears its waiting customer. Decline fires when the token holder has a waiting customer but the ledger already names a redeemer: the customer is told the promotion is over and the machine clears its waiting customer without dispensing anything. AdminRelocate is a privileged field-technician override that teleports the token to any other machine, bypassing ring order entirely; the master key has a fixed limited number of uses, after which the ring circulates on its own again.

Because the promotional item cannot be un-dispensed, the interesting question is not who holds the token but how many times stock actually leaves the fleet.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every machine recorded as having physically dispensed the promotional item is the one machine the network ledger names as the redeemer, so the irreversible dispense happens at most once across the entire fleet.
