A university runs two independent course-registration portals -- for example a web front end and a phone-in desk -- that both draw from a single shared pool of seats in one course. There is no lock on the pool. Instead the shared catalog carries a version number, and each portal works optimistically: it takes a snapshot and then tries to commit, discovering only at commit time whether the world moved underneath it.

The state consists of the free seat pool, a per-portal roster of seats that portal has placed students into, the catalog version counter, a per-portal draft record (a seat name and the catalog version snapshotted with it), the set of portals that currently have a draft open, and a per-portal retry counter that saturates at a fixed maximum.

There are four actions, each performed by one of the two portals. Snapshot fires when the portal has no draft open: the portal reads the current catalog version and names any seat it intends to fill, writes both into its draft record, and joins the set of portals with an open draft. A draft is committable when it is open, its recorded version still equals the live catalog version, the seat it names is still in the free pool, and the catalog has not reached its final version. Enrol fires on a committable draft: the named seat leaves the free pool, joins that portal's roster, the catalog version advances by one, and the portal's draft is closed. Restart fires on an open draft that is not committable: the portal closes the draft without effect, bumps its saturating retry counter, and will read the catalog again from scratch. Withdraw lets a portal return one seat from its own roster to the free pool, again advancing the catalog version.

Seats are physical capacity in a lecture hall. The registration system may hand a seat to a portal or take it back, but it must never conjure a seat that the hall does not have, and it must never lose one into a gap between the two portals.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The free pool together with the union of both portals' rosters always covers the entire seat set, and their sizes add up to exactly the number of seats, so every seat sits in exactly one place at every moment and none is created or destroyed.

A container-ship crane yard is divided into three areas: the apron, the gantry lane, and the ship's hold. A fixed fleet of boxes starts stacked on the apron. Several cranes work the yard concurrently. There is no reservation desk; instead the yard keeps a shared manifest with a revision number, and each crane works optimistically: it plans a move against the revision it read, and its commit succeeds only if that revision is still the live one.

Each crane carries an order record with a status of idle, open, or shut, plus the lane it wants to work (a source area and a distinct destination area) and the manifest revision it snapshotted. When an order is idle or shut its lane and revision fields are reset to a fixed parked default. Each crane also has a bounded re-read allowance, and the yard holds a bounded number of supervisor override uses.

There are six actions. Plan fires for an idle crane: it chooses any lane with distinct endpoints, stamps the current manifest revision onto its order, and marks the order open. Commit fires when the crane's stamped revision still equals the live revision, the source area actually has a box, and the manifest has not reached its final revision: exactly one box leaves the source area, exactly one box arrives in the destination area, the revision advances, and the order is reset to shut. Reread fires when an open order's stamped revision is stale and the crane still has re-read allowance left: the crane restamps the order with the live revision and spends one allowance. Force is a privileged yard-supervisor override: given remaining override uses, it pushes an open order through with no revision check at all, still moving exactly one box from source to destination, advancing the revision, consuming one override, and shutting the order. Settle fires only when every crane's order is already shut and simply leaves the yard exactly as it stands. Abandon shuts an open order that can no longer make progress -- either its revision is current but the source area is empty or the manifest is at its final revision, or its revision is stale and its re-read allowance is spent.

Boxes are physical cargo. Cranes relocate them between the three areas; nothing in the yard manufactures or scraps a box.

A smart-home door lock network has several hubs that all want to drive the same physical deadbolt motor on the front door. Commands are not applied directly. Instead each hub pushes a command into a shared command pipe of bounded depth, and a dispatcher hands the motor to one hub at a time. Because the pipe is bounded, a hub arriving at a full pipe is pushed back rather than buffered, and the network counts how many pushbacks it has issued up to a fixed ceiling.

The state is the command pipe (a sequence of hub names), a phase for each hub which is idle, queued, turning, or gone, the name of the hub the motor driver currently names (or none), the bolt position, and the pushback counter.

There are eight actions. Enqueue fires for an idle hub when the pipe still has room: the hub is appended to the pipe and moves to queued. Refuse is the backpressure path: an idle hub arriving at a full pipe is turned away, the pushback counter advances, and nothing else changes. Dispatch fires when the motor driver names nobody and the pipe is non-empty: the hub at the head of the pipe, provided it is still queued, becomes the named driver and moves to turning, and the pipe advances. Drain fires when the motor driver names nobody and the hub at the head of the pipe is no longer queued: that stale command is simply dropped from the pipe. Turn fires for the hub the driver names while that hub is turning: the bolt flips between locked and open, the driver is released back to none, and the hub returns to idle. Vanish models a hub dropping off the mesh without telling anyone: a queued or turning hub silently becomes gone. Reclaim lets the dispatcher release the motor when the hub it names has gone. Rejoin brings a gone hub that the motor no longer names back to idle.

The bolt motor is a single piece of hardware. Two hubs energising it at once would strip the mechanism, so the whole pipe-and-dispatcher arrangement exists to keep exactly one hub attached to the motor.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every hub whose phase says it is turning the bolt is the very hub that the motor driver names, so at no reachable state do two different hubs both hold the deadbolt motor.

  /\ driver \in Hubs \cup {NoDriver}

  /\ pushback \in 0..MaxPushback

  /\ phase = [h \in Hubs |-> "idle"]
  /\ driver = NoDriver
  /\ bolt = "locked"
  /\ pushback = 0

Enqueue(h) ==
  /\ phase[h] = "idle"
  /\ Len(pipe) < Depth
  /\ pipe' = Append(pipe, h)
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![h] = "queued"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<driver, bolt, pushback>>

\* Backpressure: a full pipe refuses the command outright.
Refuse(h) ==
  /\ phase[h] = "idle"
  /\ Len(pipe) = Depth
  /\ pushback < MaxPushback
  /\ pushback' = pushback + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pipe, phase, driver, bolt>>

       /\ phase[h] = "queued"
       /\ driver' = h
       /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![h] = "turning"]
  /\ pipe' = Tail(pipe)

  /\ pipe # <<>>
  /\ phase[Head(pipe)] # "queued"
  /\ pipe' = Tail(pipe)

  /\ phase[h] = "turning"
  /\ bolt' = IF bolt = "locked" THEN "open" ELSE "locked"
  /\ driver' = NoDriver
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![h] = "idle"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pipe, pushback>>

Vanish(h) ==

  /\ driver' = NoDriver

Only one hub at a time is entitled to cut them: the hubs run a failover election, and every election round opens a new epoch. The number of guest codes that may be live at once is not fixed. The householder can re-rate that allowance at any moment while the system runs, including to a number below the count of codes already cut.

CutCode fires for a hub that both reigns in the live epoch and whose own view equals the live epoch, provided the trail is shorter than the current allowance: an entry recording that hub and the live epoch is appended to the audit trail. ExpireCode drops the oldest entry off the front of the audit trail. Rerate is the householder changing the allowance to any different value between zero and the ceiling.

Nobody == "nobody"

  /\ reign \in [0..MaxEpoch -> Hubs \cup {Nobody}]

  /\ allowance \in 0..MaxCodes

The lease carries the name of the train that holds it and a wall-clock deadline after which it lapses. Some trains are simply slow: they take longer than a lease term to clear a block, but they have not failed and their track circuit still shows them present. The interlocking must never retire a lease out from under a train that is physically still there.

The state is each train's physical position (a block or outside), each train's outstanding grant (a block it has been given but not yet entered, or outside), the lease record for each block, and the clock.

There are six actions. Request fires for a train that is neither inside a block nor holding a grant: the signalling centre picks a block that is physically clear and whose lease is either unheld or already lapsed, writes a fresh lease naming that train with a deadline one term ahead (capped at the horizon), and records the grant. Enter moves a train into its granted block, provided the lease on that block still names the train and has not lapsed; the grant is then consumed. Forfeit fires when the train dawdled at the signal and its grant is no longer valid: the grant is dropped and, if the lease still names that train, the lease is handed back as unheld. Extend lets a train that is inside a block push that block's lease deadline forward by another term. Leave takes a train out of its block and hands the lease back as unheld. Tick advances the clock by one, but only while no occupied block's lease deadline is at or behind the new clock reading -- the track circuit veto that stops a slow train from being timed out.

Valid(t, b) == lease[b].holder = t /\ lease[b].until >= clock

A multiplayer game lobby matchmaker keeps one shared lobby roster. Several matchmaker nodes edit that roster, but never in place: a node first stages an edit -- a join or a leave naming some player -- stamped with the shard epoch that was live when it staged. Shard layout is periodically recut, which opens a new epoch; any edit still staged under an older epoch is stale and can no longer be committed. Alongside the roster the matchmaker keeps a journal of every edit it accepted, in acceptance order. The lobby's seat count is not fixed either: operators resize the lobby at runtime, including downward while players are already seated.

The state is the live roster, the journal, the epoch, the seat count, and one staging slot per node holding a kind (quiet, join, or leave), a player, and the epoch stamp.

There are five actions. Stage fires for a node with a quiet slot: it writes some join or leave for some player into its slot, stamped with the live epoch. A staged edit is ready when its kind is not quiet, its epoch stamp still equals the live epoch, the journal has room, and the edit actually applies -- a join needs the player absent from the roster and the roster below the current seat count, a leave needs the player present. Commit fires on a ready edit and performs the roster change and the journal append as one indivisible step, then blanks the node's slot. Drop fires on a staged edit that is not ready and simply blanks the slot. Recut advances the epoch, up to a ceiling, which strands every edit staged under the previous epoch. Resize sets the seat count to any different value between zero and the maximum, whether or not the roster currently fits.

The journal is the authority on what the matchmaker agreed to. If a node's edit changed the roster without landing in the journal, or landed in the journal without changing the roster, or clobbered another node's concurrent edit, the roster would drift away from its own history.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The live roster is always exactly the set you obtain by replaying the journal from the empty roster, applying each recorded join and leave in order, so no accepted edit is ever lost or overwritten.

A smart-home door lock network arbitrates the front-door bolt through a single compare-and-swap register. The register reads either free or the name of the hub that currently owns the bolt; a hub takes the bolt only by swapping the register from free to itself. Alongside the register the lock keeps an event tape: every time a hub takes the bolt an entry is appended, and every time the bolt is handed back another entry is appended naming the same hub.

The state is the register, a mode for each hub (idle, trying, driving, or dead), the event tape, a per-hub attempt allowance, and a fault budget.

There are eight actions. Attempt moves an idle hub with allowance left into trying and spends one attempt. A trying hub can take the bolt when the register reads free and the tape still has room for both a take and its matching give-back. Take performs the swap: the register is written with the hub's name, the hub becomes driving, and a take entry is appended. Yield fires for a trying hub that cannot take the bolt right now and simply returns it to idle. Give fires for a driving hub: the register goes back to free, a give-back entry naming that hub is appended, and the hub returns to idle. Fault models a hub dropping off the mesh with nothing announced -- a trying or driving hub silently becomes dead, spending one unit of the fault budget, and the register is left exactly as it was. Evict is the watchdog: when the register still names a dead hub, the watchdog swaps it back to free and appends the give-back entry on the dead hub's behalf. Rejoin brings a dead hub the register no longer names back to idle. Quiet applies only when every hub is idle with its attempt allowance spent, and leaves the network exactly as it stands.

The bolt is one motor. The event tape is the audit record of who had it and when, and it is only coherent if holds never overlap.

A smart-home door lock network keeps a single shared auto-lock profile: a set of rules together with a version number. Hubs do not lock the profile before editing it. Each hub reads the entire profile -- both the rule set it sees and the version stamped on it -- and then posts a write that carries that reading plus one new rule it wants added. The posts sit in an unordered radio buffer of bounded size, so a write may be delivered long after the profile has moved on under it.

The state is the profile, the buffer of posted writes, a record of the rule each hub last got accepted, a per-hub retry counter, and a counter of abandoned writes.

A posted write is current when the version it was built on still equals the profile's live version and the profile has not reached its final version.

There are four actions. Compose fires for a hub that has no post outstanding while the buffer has room: the hub snapshots the profile's rule set and version and posts a write adding some rule. Install takes any current post out of the buffer and writes the profile back as the rule set that post saw plus that post's own rule, with the version advanced by one, and records the added rule as that hub's accepted edit. That write-back is the whole point: a write installs the reading it was built on, so a write built on a stale reading would silently erase every rule accepted in between. Bounce takes a post that is no longer current out of the buffer while its author still has retry allowance and spends one retry. Abandon takes a non-current post out of the buffer when its author's retry allowance is spent and tallies an abandoned write, saturating at the ceiling.

The version check on Install is the only defence. Without it, two hubs that read the same profile would each install their own snapshot and the second would wipe out the first hub's rule.

A print shop spooler holds a fixed set of print jobs and distributes them across several printers. Jobs are not moved between printers ad hoc. The state is the set of jobs in each printer's tray, the migration crate, the discard bin, the epoch number, the stage, and the current per-tray limit.

Lift fires while draining: one job leaves some printer's tray and enters the crate; draining only ever moves jobs in that direction. Turn ends draining and begins filling. Drain fires while filling: one job leaves the crate and, if any tray is below the current limit, joins such a tray; if no tray has room under the current limit the job goes to the discard bin instead. CloseEpoch fires while filling once the crate is empty and returns the shop to spooling. Print fires while spooling: a job leaves a tray and goes to the discard bin as finished work. Retune sets the per-tray limit to any different value in range, whatever the trays currently hold.

A pharmacy prescription dispenser has several intake stations that all feed the same single dispensing head. Which station drives the head is decided by one compare-and-swap register holding either idle or a station name, together with a turn number. Swapping the register from idle to a station opens a new, higher-numbered turn for that station. Every dose the head cuts produces a slip recording the station that took it and the turn number that was open at the time.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A bank's interbank settlement batch moves money between member banks over a wire. Posting an instruction debits the payer's book immediately; the money then rides the wire until the instruction is credited to the payee. The wire is an unordered pool of bounded size: instructions are delivered in whatever order the network feels like, never in the order they were posted.

The batch is netted in numbered epochs. A cutover advances the epoch and puts the settlement into a cutover stage, in which every instruction still riding the wire is stale -- it belongs to the previous epoch -- and must be unwound back to the payer before the batch can reopen.

The state is each bank's book balance, the wire pool, the epoch number, the stage (open or cutover), and a tally of unwound instructions that saturates at a ceiling.

There are five actions. Post fires while the batch is open and some wire slot number is unused: a payer with sufficient funds is debited by an amount, and an instruction carrying that free slot number, the payer, the payee, the amount, and the current epoch joins the wire. The slot number is what keeps two otherwise-identical instructions distinct, and it bounds how many can ride the wire at once. Credit takes any instruction on the wire whose epoch matches the live epoch, credits the payee by that amount, and removes the instruction from the wire; because the wire is a pool rather than a queue, any pending instruction may be the one chosen. Cutover advances the epoch, up to a ceiling, and moves the batch into the cutover stage. Unwind takes any stale instruction off the wire during cutover and hands its full amount back to the payer, advancing the unwound tally. Reopen returns the batch to the open stage once no stale instruction remains on the wire.

Money is the conserved quantity. A debit that never becomes either a credit or an unwind would be money destroyed; a credit or unwind without a matching debit would be money created.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The sum of all the banks' book balances plus the total amount riding the wire always equals the day's float exactly, so settlement never creates or destroys money.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every cutover the settlement enters eventually finishes and returns the batch to the open stage.

Pot(S) ==
  IF S = {} THEN 0
  ELSE LET m == CHOOSE x \in S : TRUE IN m.amt + Pot(S \ {m})

Stale == {m \in wire : m.ep # epoch}

  /\ unwound \in 0..MaxUnwound

  /\ wire = {}
  /\ epoch = 0
  /\ stage = "open"

Post ==

  /\ \E i \in 1..WireCap : \E f \in Banks : \E t \in Banks : \E a \in 1..MaxAmt :

  /\ stage' = "cutover"

  /\ stage' = "open"

A blood-bank inventory tracker guards every labelled unit with its own compare-and-swap cell. The cell holds the unit's state -- in stock, held, or issued -- together with a stamp that ticks up on every successful swap. Issuing a unit is irreversible: it goes to a patient and never comes back. When a unit is issued the tracker writes an issue slip pinning the unit and the exact stamp the cell carried at that moment.

The state is the cell for each unit, the sequence of issue slips, the unit each technician is working on (or none), the stamp each technician saw when it reserved that unit, and whether each technician is up.

There are five actions. Reserve fires for an up technician with no current unit: some unit reading in stock has its cell swapped to held with the stamp ticked, the technician records the unit as its job and remembers the new stamp. Issue is the irreversible step and fires only when the technician is up, its unit's cell still reads held, and the cell's stamp is still exactly the stamp the technician remembered: the cell is swapped to issued with the stamp ticked, an issue slip is appended pinning the unit and that new stamp, and the technician's job clears. Collapse models a technician going down without telling anyone, still nominally holding its unit. Return brings a downed technician back up with its job cleared, so the unit it was holding is now orphaned. Sweep is the recovery path: a held unit that no live technician is working on is swapped back to stock with its stamp ticked, and that tick is precisely what locks out any technician still carrying the old stamp.

The stamp is the whole defence. A technician that came back from a crash and tried to finish an old reservation would be swapping against a stamp the cell has already moved past.

An air-traffic runway allocator records who is in charge of a runway in a single compare-and-swap strip holding the controller of record together with a fence token. Every time the runway changes hands the strip is swapped to the incoming controller and the fence token is burned and replaced with a higher one. Each controller desk also carries its own copy of the token, and some desks are slow: they are not broken and they will read the strip eventually, but they can lag behind the live fence for a while.

The state is the strip, each desk's copy of the token, the set of flights standing on the runway, the token each of those flights was cleared under, and a per-desk idling counter.

Handover swaps the strip to some controller and burns the fence token, advancing it by one; it is permitted only while the runway is physically empty and the fence has not reached its ceiling, and the incoming desk's own token copy is set to the new fence. Refresh is a lagging desk reading the current fence off the strip into its own copy. Clear puts a flight onto the runway: it fires only for the desk the strip names and only while that desk's own token copy equals the live fence, and it stamps the flight with the token the issuing desk was carrying -- not with the strip's value. Rollout takes some flight off the runway. Dawdle is a slow desk letting time pass, advancing its idling counter up to a ceiling and touching nothing else.

The stamping rule in Clear is deliberate. A desk operating on a lagging token would stamp its clearance with the old fence, and a handover performed while such a flight was still on the runway would leave an aircraft on the strip authorised by a controller who is no longer in charge.

\* It is only allowed with the runway physically empty.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A container-ship crane yard releases the twistlocks that hold containers down in a bay. Cutting a bay's gear is irreversible: the locks are cut away rather than unbolted, so a bay can be released exactly once and never re-secured within the operation. Because several deck crews have to agree before anything is cut, the release runs as a two-phase commit: a round is proposed over a set of bays, every crew votes, and only unanimous agreement cuts the gear. The deck officer also re-rates at runtime how many bays a single round is allowed to cover.

The state is the stage (idle or polling), the set of bays the live round covers, each crew's ballot (open, aye, or nay), the set of bays whose gear has already been cut, the current per-round bay allowance, and a round counter.

There are five actions. Propose fires while idle and below the round ceiling: it picks a non-empty set of bays that is disjoint from the already-cut set and no larger than the current allowance, makes that the round's sweep, moves to polling, and resets every crew's ballot to open. Vote lets a crew with an open ballot record aye or nay. Commit fires while polling once every crew has voted aye: every bay in the sweep has its gear cut and joins the already-cut set, the sweep empties, the round counter advances, and the yard returns to idle. Rollback fires while polling once any crew has voted nay: the sweep is abandoned with nothing cut, the round counter advances, and the yard returns to idle. Rerate sets the per-round bay allowance to any different value in range, whether or not a round is live.

The disjointness check inside Propose is the whole safeguard. A round that reached across a bay whose gear was already cut would commit a second cut on hardware that is no longer there.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a round is being polled, the set of bays it covers is disjoint from the set of bays whose twistlocks have already been cut, so the irreversible release is committed at most once for any bay.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

\* Releasing a bay's twistlocks is a two-phase commit across the deck crews,
\* and it is irreversible -- the gear is cut, not unbolted.  The number of
\* bays a single round may cover is re-rated by the deck officer at runtime.
CONSTANTS Bays, Crews, MaxSweep, MaxRounds

VARIABLES stage, sweep, ballot, freed, allowed, rounds
vars == <<stage, sweep, ballot, freed, allowed, rounds>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ stage \in {"idle", "polling"}
  /\ sweep \subseteq Bays
  /\ ballot \in [Crews -> {"open", "aye", "nay"}]
  /\ freed \subseteq Bays
  /\ allowed \in 1..MaxSweep
  /\ rounds \in 0..MaxRounds

Init ==
  /\ stage = "idle"
  /\ sweep = {}
  /\ ballot = [c \in Crews |-> "open"]
  /\ freed = {}
  /\ allowed = MaxSweep
  /\ rounds = 0

\* A round may only be opened over bays whose gear is still intact.
Propose ==
  /\ stage = "idle"
  /\ rounds < MaxRounds
  /\ \E S \in SUBSET Bays :
       /\ S # {}
       /\ S \cap freed = {}
       /\ Cardinality(S) =< allowed
       /\ sweep' = S
  /\ stage' = "polling"
  /\ ballot' = [c \in Crews |-> "open"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<freed, allowed, rounds>>

Vote(c) ==
  /\ stage = "polling"
  /\ ballot[c] = "open"
  /\ \E v \in {"aye", "nay"} : ballot' = [ballot EXCEPT ![c] = v]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<stage, sweep, freed, allowed, rounds>>

Commit ==
  /\ stage = "polling"
  /\ \A c \in Crews : ballot[c] = "aye"
  /\ freed' = freed \cup sweep
  /\ sweep' = {}
  /\ stage' = "idle"
  /\ rounds' = rounds + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<ballot, allowed>>

Rollback ==
  /\ stage = "polling"
  /\ \E c \in Crews : ballot[c] = "nay"
  /\ sweep' = {}
  /\ stage' = "idle"
  /\ rounds' = rounds + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<ballot, freed, allowed>>

\* The deck officer re-rates how wide a single round may be, at any time.
Rerate ==
  /\ \E n \in 1..MaxSweep : n # allowed /\ allowed' = n
  /\ UNCHANGED <<stage, sweep, ballot, freed, rounds>>

Next == Propose \/ Commit \/ Rollback \/ Rerate \/ \E c \in Crews : Vote(c)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* No live round ever overlaps a bay whose twistlocks have already been cut,
\* so the irreversible release happens at most once per bay.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A car-wash conveyor line has a fixed set of conveyor bays. Two independent booking channels -- the phone app and the drive-up kiosk -- send cars at the same bays; neither channel has bays of its own, they share one pool. There is no lock on the bay map. Instead the map carries a revision number, and a car books optimistically: it reads a bay that looks free together with the map's revision, then commits, and the commit succeeds only if the revision has not moved in the meantime.

The state is the bay each car has booked (or none), the map revision, each car's draft (the bay it read and the revision it read), a per-car retry allowance, and each car's standing: waiting, trying, parked, or gone.

There are seven actions. Read fires for a waiting car: it picks some bay that is not currently booked by anybody, writes that bay and the live revision into its draft, and becomes trying. A trying car is bookable when the revision in its draft still equals the live revision and the map has not reached its final revision. Park fires on a bookable car: its booking is set to the bay in its draft, the map revision advances by one, and the car becomes parked -- note that Park trusts the revision rather than taking a fresh look at the map, which is exactly what makes the revision check load-bearing. Reread fires on a trying car that is not bookable and still has retry allowance: it spends one retry and drops back to waiting. DriveOff fires on a trying car that is not bookable with its allowance spent, and the car leaves. Exit fires for a parked car while the map has room: its booking is released, the revision advances, and the car leaves. Balk fires for a waiting car when every bay is already booked, and the car leaves rather than idling. Closed applies once every car is either parked or gone and leaves the line exactly as it stands.

A conveyor bay holds one car. Two cars sent to the same bay by the two channels would collide on the track.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every car that starts trying to commit a booking eventually stops trying, whether by parking, by re-reading the map, or by driving off.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending machine network rolls out a fleet-wide price change as a two-phase commit. A coordinator opens a numbered round, machines vote, the coordinator closes the poll and sends a go-order to exactly the machines it tallied, and those machines install the new price. Everything travels over a shared radio pool of bounded size that provides no ordering whatsoever: a vote or a go-order transmitted during one round can still be floating in the pool when the next round has already opened.

The state is the round number, the phase (polling or closing), the quorum the coordinator has tallied for the current round, the set of machines that have installed the new price in the current round, and the radio pool.

A pooled message counts as stale when its round stamp differs from the live round, or it is a vote arriving outside the polling phase, or it is a go-order arriving outside the closing phase.

There are six actions. Open advances the round number, returns the phase to polling, and clears both the quorum and the installed set -- but deliberately leaves the radio pool untouched, so older traffic survives into the new round. Transmit fires whenever the pool has room: some machine puts a vote into the pool stamped with any round number up to the live one, which is how a machine running behind gets modelled. Tally takes a vote out of the pool that is stamped with the live round while the phase is polling and adds its sender to the quorum. Close fires while polling with a non-empty quorum and enough pool room: the phase becomes closing and one go-order stamped with the live round is placed in the pool for each machine in the quorum, and for nobody else. Install takes a go-order out of the pool that is stamped with the live round while the phase is closing and records its addressee as having installed the new price. Post -- an engine whose lease is still live applies the draft it carries, writing the draft's recorded base plus the instruction's amount into the ledger and marking that instruction posted. Discard -- an engine whose lease has lapsed throws away the draft it was carrying, releasing that instruction back into the shared pool. Tick -- the batch clock advances by one, up to a fixed cap; clock advance is the only thing that causes a lease to lapse.

An automated pharmacy prescription dispenser is organised into shelves, and each shelf is divided into slots; a bin is one slot on one shelf. Two robotic dispensing arms move over the cabinet. To avoid tearing a shelf's contents apart, the arms follow a strict two-level locking discipline: an arm must take the coarse lock on a whole shelf before it may take the fine lock on any individual bin of that shelf, an arm may hold at most one shelf at a time, and it must hand every bin of that shelf back before it hands the shelf back. Each shelf also carries a stock ceiling that a pharmacist can change while the machine is running.

The full action set is: TakeShelf -- an arm takes the coarse lock on a free shelf, provided it is not already holding some other shelf. TakeBin -- an arm that already holds the coarse lock on a shelf takes the fine lock on one free bin of that shelf. Dispense -- an arm holding both the shelf lock and the bin lock adds a number of units into that bin, provided the bin has room for them and the shelf's current stock stays within the shelf's stock ceiling. ReleaseBin -- an arm gives back a fine bin lock it holds. ReleaseShelf -- an arm gives back the coarse shelf lock, but only once every bin of that shelf is unlocked, which enforces the release order. Retune -- a pharmacist changes a shelf's stock ceiling while no arm holds that shelf, and only to a value that still covers the stock already standing in that shelf's bins. Collect -- a patient picks up everything in an unlocked bin, emptying it and freeing shelf stock.

The interesting failure is not that two arms collide: it is that the shelf's stock ceiling is a moving target. Stock can be pushed up to the ceiling by a dispense, and the ceiling itself can be pulled down by a retune, so either side can be the one that overruns the shelf if it does not check the other.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every shelf, the total number of units standing across that shelf's bins never exceeds that shelf's currently configured stock ceiling, even though the ceiling can be changed while stock is standing.

The blaster is the critical resource: exactly one car may be in the blast stage at a time, and the conveyor controller arbitrates it with a compare-and-swap register that names the current occupant, or reads clear when the blaster is empty. A car does not simply write itself into that register; it first copies the register into its own private view, and only then attempts the swap, which is accepted only if the register still holds the value the car copied. \* simply cannot hand in another ticket, which is the backpressure.
\* The single hoist motor is the critical resource, and a van that dies while
\* holding it stays silent -- only the depot supervisor takes the motor back.
TypeOK ==
  /\ backlog \in Seq(Tickets)
  /\ Len(backlog) <= QCap
  /\ motor \in Vans \cup {NoVan}
  /\ vanState \in [Vans -> {"parked", "hoisting", "dead"}]
  /\ carrying \in [Vans -> Tickets \cup {NoTicket}]
  /\ closed \subseteq Tickets

Waiting == Tickets \ (closed \cup {carrying[v] : v \in Vans})

Init ==
  /\ backlog = << >>
  /\ motor = NoVan
  /\ vanState = [v \in Vans |-> "parked"]
  /\ carrying = [v \in Vans |-> NoTicket]
  /\ closed = {}

HandIn(t) ==
  /\ t \in Waiting
  /\ \A i \in 1 .. Len(backlog) : backlog[i] # t
  /\ Len(backlog) < QCap
  /\ backlog' = Append(backlog, t)
  /\ UNCHANGED <<motor, vanState, carrying, closed>>

TakeHoist(v) ==
  /\ vanState[v] = "parked"
  /\ motor = NoVan
  /\ backlog # << >>
  /\ motor' = v
  /\ vanState' = [vanState EXCEPT ![v] = "hoisting"]
  /\ carrying' = [carrying EXCEPT ![v] = Head(backlog)]
  /\ backlog' = Tail(backlog)
  /\ UNCHANGED closed

Restock(v) ==
  /\ vanState[v] = "hoisting"
  /\ motor = v
  /\ closed' = closed \cup {carrying[v]}
  /\ carrying' = [carrying EXCEPT ![v] = NoTicket]
  /\ vanState' = [vanState EXCEPT ![v] = "parked"]
  /\ motor' = NoVan
  /\ UNCHANGED backlog

GoSilent(v) ==
  /\ vanState[v] = "hoisting"
  /\ vanState' = [vanState EXCEPT ![v] = "dead"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<backlog, motor, carrying, closed>>

TakeBack(v) ==
  /\ vanState[v] = "dead"
  /\ motor = v
  /\ Len(backlog) < QCap
  /\ backlog' = Append(backlog, carrying[v])
  /\ carrying' = [carrying EXCEPT ![v] = NoTicket]
  /\ motor' = NoVan
  /\ UNCHANGED <<vanState, closed>>

Revive(v) ==
  /\ vanState[v] = "dead"
  /\ motor # v
  /\ carrying[v] = NoTicket
  /\ vanState' = [vanState EXCEPT ![v] = "parked"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<backlog, motor, carrying, closed>>

Next ==
  \/ \E t \in Tickets : HandIn(t)
  \/ \E v \in Vans : TakeHoist(v) \/ Restock(v) \/ GoSilent(v)
                     \/ TakeBack(v) \/ Revive(v)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

\* Exclusion: any van actually turning the hoist must be the van the motor
\* grant names, and the grant is single-valued, so two vans cannot both hoist.
HoistExclusive == \A v \in Vans : vanState[v] = "hoisting" => motor = v
=======================================================================

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending machine network is restocked by two independent regional coordinators. They do not talk to each other, yet they draw from one shared pool of machine slots, and every allocation has to be agreed by every rack controller in the network. Each coordinator therefore runs its restock deals as a two-phase commit: first it pencils its chosen slot in on each rack, and only when every rack carries that pencil mark, and nobody else's, may it seal the deal and become the recorded holder of the slot.

The full action set is: Open -- a coordinator opens a fresh deal and names the slot it is going after, moving the deal into voting. Pencil -- a voting deal gets penciled in on one rack for its target slot, which is possible only if that rack has no other pencil mark on that slot and the slot has no recorded holder. Seal -- a voting deal that is penciled in on every rack, unanimously, commits: it becomes the recorded holder of its target slot. Erase -- the pencil marks belonging to a deal are rubbed out across all racks, which is the second-phase cleanup after sealing and also the way a voting deal can back off. Tear -- a voting deal that finds some rack already penciled for a different deal tears itself up, rubbing out its own marks. Vend -- a sealed deal whose pencil marks have all been rubbed out is dispensed, releasing the slot back to the pool with no recorded holder.

The hazard is double allocation. Because the two coordinators are independent, they can both be chasing the same slot at the same moment; only unanimity across the racks decides which one is entitled to it. A deal that sealed on partial agreement would leave two coordinators each convinced it owned the slot, and the slot's record could only name one of them.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every sealed deal is the slot record's own named holder for the slot it targeted, so no slot can ever be carrying two sealed deals at once.

\* commit once every rack has that deal, and no other, penciled in.

Name the module `W4Od13m4p6t1`.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending machine network is driven by a central dispatcher that cuts restock orders into a shared pouch of orders still in the air. The pouch holds only so many orders at once, and the dispatcher cannot cut another one while it is full -- that cap is the backpressure. The pouch is unordered: an order that was cut first is not necessarily the one a machine picks up first, so orders arrive at the machines in any order at all. Every order carries two things: the position it occupies in that machine's order stream, and the credential generation the dispatcher was holding for that machine when the order was cut. A machine that re-keys bumps its credential generation, which retires in one stroke every order for it that is still in the air, and starts its stream over from the first position.

The full action set is: Cut -- the dispatcher cuts the next order for a machine into the pouch, stamped with that machine's current credential generation and with the next unused position, allowed only while the pouch is below its cap and the machine's stream has not run out of positions. Rekey -- a machine bumps its own credential generation, clears its obeyed stream and tells the dispatcher to start numbering that machine's positions from the beginning again. Obey -- a machine picks any order out of the pouch addressed to it, and acts on it only if the order bears exactly the credential generation the machine is holding right now and sits in exactly the next open position of that machine's stream; the order is then appended to the stream and leaves the pouch. Refuse -- a machine picks an order out of the pouch whose credential generation no longer matches its own, and throws it away without acting on it.

The hazard is an order cut by a dispatcher that was working from a credential the machine has since retired: because the pouch is unordered, such an order can sit around and surface long after the re-key, looking perfectly well-formed. Acting on it would be a machine taking instruction from a stale authority, and it would also punch a hole in the machine's position numbering.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every machine, each order in the stream it has acted on sits in its own correct position with no gaps, is addressed to that machine, and bears exactly the credential generation the machine currently holds, so no retired or misaddressed order has ever been obeyed.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Whenever the pouch holds orders, every one of them is eventually either obeyed or refused, so the pouch always empties again.

VARIABLES inflight, cred, stream, nextSeq
vars == <<inflight, cred, stream, nextSeq>>

\* Orders sit in an unordered bounded pouch, so they can be picked up in any
\* order; the pouch cap is the backpressure on the dispatcher.
\* Each order carries the credential generation it was cut under, and a machine
\* re-keys by bumping its credential, which retires everything already in the air.
TypeOK ==

  /\ Cardinality(inflight) <= QCap
  /\ cred \in [Machines -> 0 .. MaxGen]
  /\ stream \in [Machines -> Seq(Orders)]
  /\ nextSeq \in [Machines -> 1 .. (MaxSeq + 1)]

Init ==
  /\ inflight = {}
  /\ cred = [m \in Machines |-> 0]
  /\ stream = [m \in Machines |-> << >>]
  /\ nextSeq = [m \in Machines |-> 1]

Cut(m) ==
  /\ Cardinality(inflight) < QCap
  /\ nextSeq[m] <= MaxSeq
  /\ inflight' = inflight \cup
       {[mach |-> m, gen |-> cred[m], seq |-> nextSeq[m]]}
  /\ nextSeq' = [nextSeq EXCEPT ![m] = @ + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<cred, stream>>

Rekey(m) ==
  /\ cred[m] < MaxGen
  /\ cred' = [cred EXCEPT ![m] = @ + 1]
  /\ stream' = [stream EXCEPT ![m] = << >>]
  /\ nextSeq' = [nextSeq EXCEPT ![m] = 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED inflight

Obey(o) ==

  /\ o.gen = cred[o.mach]
  /\ o.seq = Len(stream[o.mach]) + 1
  /\ stream' = [stream EXCEPT ![o.mach] = Append(@, o)]
  /\ inflight' = inflight \ {o}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<cred, nextSeq>>

Refuse(o) ==
  /\ o \in inflight
  /\ o.gen # cred[o.mach]
  /\ inflight' = inflight \ {o}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<cred, stream, nextSeq>>

RekeyStep  == \E m \in Machines : Rekey(m)
ObeyStep   == \E o \in Orders : Obey(o)
RefuseStep == \E o \in Orders : Refuse(o)

Next == CutStep \/ RekeyStep \/ ObeyStep \/ RefuseStep

      /\ stream[m][i].seq = i
      /\ stream[m][i].gen = cred[m]
      /\ stream[m][i].mach = m

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A library reservation system tracks the physical copies of every title it stocks. A title lives at a shelf mark inside a section, and each of its copies is, at any moment, in exactly one of three places: standing on the open shelf, waiting on the hold shelf for a reader who reserved it, or out with a borrower. Every move a clerk makes is a hand-off of one single copy from one of those places to another, which is the only way the counts are ever allowed to change. Clerks work under a two-level discipline: a clerk latches a whole section before latching any individual title inside that section, holds at most one section at a time, and gives every title back before giving the section back. The head librarian has an override that moves copies without latching anything at all.

The full action set is: LatchSection -- a clerk latches a free section, provided it holds no other section. LatchTitle -- a clerk holding a section latches a free title inside that section. Reserve -- a clerk holding both the section and the title takes one copy off the open shelf and stands it on the hold shelf. Lend -- a clerk holding both latches takes one copy off the hold shelf and gives it to a borrower. BookDrop -- a borrower returns a copy through the drop box, which puts it straight back on the open shelf and needs no latch at all. UnlatchTitle -- a clerk gives a title latch back. UnlatchSection -- a clerk gives the section latch back, which it may only do once every title in that section is unlatched. Override -- the head librarian pulls a copy off the hold shelf back onto the open shelf, ignoring every latch that may be held.

What matters here is not who is holding which latch; it is that each of these moves is a genuine relocation. The book drop and the head librarian's override both act outside the latching discipline, and either of them could quietly break the books if it added a copy in one place without taking it away from another.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every title, the number of copies on the open shelf plus those on the hold shelf plus those out with borrowers always equals the number of copies the library stocks of that title, so no copy is ever created or destroyed by any move.

A car-wash conveyor line ends at a single undercarriage rinse pit. The pit is the critical resource: exactly one user may be down in it at a time. ===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A power-grid load shedder decides which feeder gets to drop load in which shed window. No single operator can make that call: a feeder is awarded a window only when a strict majority of the relay controllers is backing it for that window. Each relay controller casts at most one ballot per window. The controllers are slow but never failed -- a controller copies a feeder's request onto its clipboard and then gets around to casting the ballot some time later, by which point the feeder may well have asked for a different window instead.

The full action set is: Ask -- a feeder that currently holds no window changes the window it is asking for. Copy -- a relay controller with an empty clipboard copies down one feeder's current request, feeder and window together. Cast -- a relay controller casts the ballot on its clipboard, marking that window with that feeder, provided it has not already balloted in that window; the clipboard is then empty again. Note that the request it copied may have moved on in the meantime, so the ballot can be for a window the feeder no longer wants. Tear -- a relay controller tears up a clipboard entry for a window it has already balloted in, without casting anything. Award -- a feeder holding no window is awarded the window it is currently asking for, but only if a strict majority of the relay controllers is backing it for that window right now. Shed -- a feeder that holds a window drops its load, gives the window back, and the ballots for that window are wiped so the window can be contested again.

The hazard is double allocation of one shed window. Two feeders contesting the same window will both accumulate ballots, and the slow controllers make it easy for the tallies to look tempting before they are decisive. Only the fact that no controller can back two different feeders in one window, and that awarding requires a strict majority, keeps two feeders from being handed the same window and shedding into each other.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Any feeder holding a shed window is backed for that window by a strict majority of the relay controllers, and since each controller ballots for at most one feeder per window, no window can ever be held by two feeders at once.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A print shop runs two spooler instances, a front-office one and a back-office one. They are independent programs and neither knows what the other is doing, but their spool nodes sit on one shared ring and they draw paper from one shared hopper. A baton travels around the ring, and only the node currently holding the baton may move paper into or out of its own reserve. Sheets in the shop live in exactly four kinds of place: the shared hopper, the private reserve of each spool node, the press, and the output bin.

The full action set is: PassBaton -- the baton moves from its current node to the next node downstream on the ring, wrapping around at the end. Draw -- the node holding the baton takes a batch of sheets out of the shared hopper and into its own reserve, which it can only do if the hopper actually has that many. Feed -- the node holding the baton pushes a batch of sheets out of its own reserve into the press. Impress -- the press prints a batch of sheets and moves them into the output bin. Pulp -- a batch of sheets is taken out of the output bin and put back into the shared hopper for reuse.

What matters about this shop is not who holds the baton. It is that the shop owns a fixed quantity of paper, and every single one of these moves is a hand-off: sheets leave one place exactly as many as arrive in another. Because two independent instances are drawing from one hopper, a move that took sheets out of the hopper without adding them to a reserve, or that added to the press without taking from a reserve, would quietly change the shop's paper count with nobody in a position to notice.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of sheets in the shared hopper, plus those in every spool node's reserve, plus those in the press, plus those in the output bin always equals the fixed quantity of paper the shop owns, so no sheet is ever created or destroyed.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: The baton always eventually comes back around the ring to the home node.

<|start|>user<|message|>Write a TLA+ specification that implements EXACTLY the system described below, and a TLC .cfg to model-check it. The system's safety property described in the NL text must be captured as a real, non-trivial INVARIANT (not `Inv == TRUE`) in the .cfg.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A bank's interbank settlement batch is divided into netting slots, and each slot has to be booked to exactly one member bank. No member decides this alone: settlement agents vote, and a slot is only bookable to a bank that a strict majority of the agents is backing for that slot. The agents do not talk to the batch controller directly. They post their votes as notes onto a wire, and the wire is unordered -- notes land in whatever order they happen to land in, so a note posted early can surface long after later notes have already been taken in. Each round of a slot closes when the slot settles, and notes carry the round they were posted under.

The full action set is: Post -- a settlement agent puts a note on the wire naming a slot and a bank, stamped with the round that slot is currently in, allowed only while the wire is under its capacity. Record -- the batch controller takes any note off the wire and enters it in the tally, but only if the note's round is still the slot's live round and that agent has not already been tallied in that slot; an agent's vote in a slot is therefore single-valued and first-entered wins. Bin -- the controller takes a note off the wire and throws it away, because its round has closed or that agent is already tallied in that slot. Book -- a slot is booked to a bank that a strict majority of the agents is currently backing for it. Settle -- a standing booking is settled: the booking is struck, the slot's tally is wiped clean, and the slot moves into its next round.

The hazard is double allocation of one netting slot. Because notes arrive in arbitrary order and can be stale by a whole round, the tally for a slot can look very different depending on which notes got taken in first. The only thing keeping two banks from both being booked into the same slot is that no agent's vote counts twice in a slot and that a booking needs a strict majority.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every booking standing in the batch is one whose bank is backed for that slot by a strict majority of the settlement agents at that moment, which rules out two banks holding the same netting slot.

===END NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===

CONSTANTS Banks, Slots, Agents, NoBank, WireCap, MaxRound

Notes == [agent : Agents, slot : Slots, bank : Banks, rnd : 0 .. MaxRound]

VARIABLES wire, tally, booked, round
vars == <<wire, tally, booked, round>>

\* Settlement agents post their votes as notes onto an unordered wire, so notes
\* land in any order and a note can surface long after its round has closed.
\* A slot is bookable only for a bank a strict majority of agents has voted for.
Backers(s, b) == Cardinality({a \in Agents : tally[s][a] = b})
Certified == {p \in Slots \X Banks : 2 * Backers(p[1], p[2]) > Cardinality(Agents)}

TypeOK ==
  /\ wire \subseteq Notes
  /\ Cardinality(wire) <= WireCap
  /\ tally \in [Slots -> [Agents -> Banks \cup {NoBank}]]
  /\ booked \subseteq Slots \X Banks
  /\ round \in [Slots -> 0 .. MaxRound]

Init ==
  /\ wire = {}
  /\ tally = [s \in Slots |-> [a \in Agents |-> NoBank]]
  /\ booked = {}
  /\ round = [s \in Slots |-> 0]

Post(a, s, b) ==
  /\ Cardinality(wire) < WireCap
  /\ wire' = wire \cup
       {[agent |-> a, slot |-> s, bank |-> b, rnd |-> round[s]]}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tally, booked, round>>

Record(n) ==
  /\ n \in wire
  /\ n.rnd = round[n.slot]
  /\ tally[n.slot][n.agent] = NoBank
  /\ tally' = [tally EXCEPT ![n.slot][n.agent] = n.bank]
  /\ wire' = wire \ {n}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<booked, round>>

Bin(n) ==
  /\ n \in wire
  /\ \/ n.rnd # round[n.slot]
     \/ tally[n.slot][n.agent] # NoBank
  /\ wire' = wire \ {n}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<tally, booked, round>>

Book(s, b) ==
  /\ <<s, b>> \notin booked
  /\ <<s, b>> \in Certified
  /\ booked' = booked \cup {<<s, b>>}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<wire, tally, round>>

Settle(s, b) ==
  /\ <<s, b>> \in booked
  /\ round[s] < MaxRound
  /\ booked' = booked \ {<<s, b>>}
  /\ tally' = [tally EXCEPT ![s] = [a \in Agents |-> NoBank]]
  /\ round' = [round EXCEPT ![s] = @ + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED wire

Next ==

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending machine network hands out restock slots to field runners. There is no lock on a slot; instead the network works optimistically. A runner peeks at a slot that currently has no owner and writes down, along with the slot, the version stamp the slot carried at the moment of the peek. Later it tries to claim the slot, and the claim is only accepted if the slot's version stamp has not moved since the peek. Every single change to who owns a slot moves that slot's stamp, which is exactly what makes a stale peek detectable. Runners are unreliable: one can go dark at any moment, without warning and without telling anybody, and if it was holding a slot the slot stays nominally owned until the depot sweeps it.

The full action set is: Peek -- a free runner picks a slot that currently has no owner and writes down the slot together with its current version stamp. Claim -- a runner that has peeked takes ownership of the slot it peeked at, but only if the slot's stamp is still exactly the one it wrote down; the claim bumps the stamp. Retry -- a runner that has peeked notices the slot's stamp has moved, throws the peek away and starts over as a free runner. Restock -- a runner holding a slot finishes restocking it and is done, keeping the slot recorded to it. GoDark -- a runner in any working state dies silently and stops acting for good, dropping whatever peek it was carrying. Sweep -- the depot notices a slot recorded to a runner that has gone dark, clears the owner and bumps the stamp so the slot can be handed out again.

The hazard is double allocation of a slot. Two runners can peek the very same free slot at the very same stamp, and a runner that goes dark can leave the network unsure whether a slot is really in use. What makes it safe is that a peek is only ever good while the stamp it recorded is still the live one: the instant anybody takes or releases the slot, the stamp moves and every outstanding peek on that slot is worthless.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A warehouse robot fleet keeps one shared count sheet for an aisle. The sheet is a plain record of which stock edits have been folded into it, and a bot does not patch the sheet in place -- it reads the whole sheet, keeps that reading, and later writes back the whole thing: exactly what it read, plus its own edit. Write access is granted by a lease with a fixed time to live. The lease is not handed back; it simply runs down, and once it has run out anybody may take a fresh one. That is deliberate, because a bot in this fleet can go quiet without warning and never say anything again, and the fleet has no other way of getting the sheet back from it.

The full action set is: Take -- a bot that is still responding and is carrying no draft takes the sheet lease, but only when no live lease is outstanding, and the fresh lease starts at its full time to live. Read -- the bot holding a live lease, and carrying no draft, picks an edit that is not on the sheet and that no bot is already drafting, and keeps a reading of the whole sheet as it stands together with that edit. Write -- the bot holding a live lease writes its draft back: the sheet becomes exactly the reading it kept plus its own edit, and the fleet is told that edit is applied. Countdown -- time passes and the outstanding lease's remaining life drops by one; when it reaches zero the lease is dead. GoQuiet -- a bot stops responding for good, without announcing it and without giving anything back. Bin -- a draft is thrown away by any bot that has gone quiet or whose lease is no longer live, releasing that edit to be drafted again.

The hazard is a lost update. A bot's reading is a snapshot of the whole sheet, and its write overwrites the whole sheet. If its lease has run out in between, another bot may have taken the lease, read, and written its own edit onto the sheet; a write from the first bot's old reading would then quietly erase that edit even though the fleet had already been told it was applied.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every edit the fleet has been told is applied is still present on the shared count sheet, so no acknowledged update is ever erased by a write built on an out-of-date reading.

A warehouse robot fleet shares one staging floor, and the floor holds only a fixed number of pallet places. Admission to the floor is by timed lease: a mover is promised a number of pallet places for a fixed span of ticks, and the promise simply runs out with the clock rather than being handed back. These movers are slow but never broken -- a mover can still be standing on the floor with its pallets down after its lease has already lapsed, and it will get around to rolling off eventually. That is precisely why the admission count charges for what is physically standing on the floor as well as for what is still under a live lease.

The full action set is: Promise -- a mover waiting in the yard whose lease has lapsed or was never granted is promised a number of pallet places, dated a fixed span ahead of the current clock, but only if those places fit inside the floor's capacity alongside everything already committed, meaning everything standing on the floor plus everything under a live lease. RollOn -- a mover in the yard that has been promised places and whose lease is still live rolls onto the floor. Extend -- a mover already standing on the floor whose lease has lapsed re-dates it a span ahead; it is already being charged for, so this changes nothing about the floor's occupancy. RollOff -- a mover standing on the floor rolls off for good, giving up its places and its lease. Tick -- the clock advances, up to a horizon; this is the only thing that makes a lease lapse.

The trap is to count only the live leases when deciding whether a new promise fits. A slow mover whose lease has lapsed is invisible to that count and yet its pallets are very much still on the floor, so a promise made on the strength of lease bookkeeping alone would put more pallets on the floor than the floor holds.

\* for live leases, not just for the leases.

Weigh(S) == IF S = {} THEN 0
            ELSE LET m == CHOOSE x \in S : TRUE IN load[m] + Weigh(S \ {m})

Committed == {m \in Movers : spot[m] = "floor" \/ expiry[m] > clock}

  /\ spot \in [Movers -> {"yard", "floor", "gone"}]
  /\ load \in [Movers -> 0 .. MaxLoad]

  /\ expiry = [m \in Movers |-> 0]
  /\ spot = [m \in Movers |-> "yard"]
  /\ load = [m \in Movers |-> 0]

The swap is accepted only if the write chain has not grown in the meantime, which is exactly the compare-and-swap test. Every accepted write is appended to the chain as a was/now pair, so the chain is the complete record of how the reading got to where it is. The line's throughput rating is also re-set while the shift is running.

The full action set is: Sample -- a bay with nothing in hand notes down the drum's current reading, the current chain length as its version tag, and how much it intends to add. Swap -- a bay swaps in its new reading, accepted only if the chain length still equals the tag it noted, if the chain has room, and if the resulting reading stays inside the line's current throughput rating; the was/now pair is appended to the chain. Bounce -- a bay whose noted tag no longer matches the chain length throws its note away without writing. Empty -- the drum is emptied at the tank, which is itself recorded on the chain as a was/now pair from the standing reading down to zero. Rerate -- the line's throughput rating is re-set to a different value while the shift runs, never below what is already standing in the drum.

A bay's note is a snapshot: between the sample and the swap, another bay may have topped the drum up, or the drum may have been emptied, and either way the reading the first bay is working from is no longer the one on the drum. A write built on that stale reading would silently wipe out whatever happened in between, and the write chain would show it: one link would not pick up where the last one left off.

Some time later it comes back and books the room, and the scheduler refuses the booking unless two things are still true: the room is still free, and the surgeon's badge has not been re-issued since the reading. Surgeons here are slow but never absent -- one can take an arbitrarily long time between reading the board and coming back to book, which is exactly when its badge can go out of date underneath it. Every booking standing on the board carries the badge issue that was presented when it was made.

The full action set is: Study -- a surgeon that has not yet operated and is holding no reading picks a room that is free right now and notes it down together with the issue number of its own badge. Book -- a surgeon books the room it noted, accepted only if the room is still free and its badge issue still matches what it noted; the booking is stamped with the badge issue the surgeon presented. Retry -- a surgeon whose noted room has been taken, or whose badge has been re-issued since the reading, throws the reading away and starts over. Operate -- a surgeon whose booking is stamped with the badge issue it is carrying now goes ahead with the surgery and releases the room. Reissue -- a surgeon's badge is re-issued with a new number, and every booking that badge is holding is struck from the board at the same moment.

The hazard is a room standing reserved to an authority nobody actually holds. Because a surgeon can be arbitrarily slow between reading and booking, a badge re-issue can land in that gap. A booking taken on the strength of the old issue number would leave the board showing a reservation backed by credentials that have already been withdrawn, and the surgeon would be operating on authority it no longer has.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every room standing booked on the board is stamped with exactly the badge issue its holding surgeon is carrying at that moment, so no booking or surgery ever rests on a badge that has since been re-issued.

NoRead == [rm |-> Vacant, ce |-> -1]
Reads  == {NoRead} \cup [rm : Rooms, ce : 0 .. MaxIssue]

vars == <<issue, booked, stamp, jotting, operated>>

\* issue number of the badge it is holding, then comes back and books, which
\* is refused unless the room is still free and the badge has not been
\* re-issued underneath it. A surgeon here is slow, never absent.
\* Each standing booking is stamped with the badge issue that was presented.

  /\ issue \in [Surgeons -> 0 .. MaxIssue]
  /\ booked \in [Rooms -> Surgeons \cup {Vacant}]
  /\ stamp \in [Rooms -> 0 .. MaxIssue]
  /\ jotting \in [Surgeons -> Reads]
  /\ operated \subseteq Surgeons

  /\ booked = [k \in Rooms |-> Vacant]
  /\ stamp = [k \in Rooms |-> 0]
  /\ jotting = [g \in Surgeons |-> NoRead]
  /\ operated = {}

Study(g, k) ==
  /\ g \notin operated
  /\ jotting[g] = NoRead
  /\ booked[k] = Vacant
  /\ jotting' = [jotting EXCEPT ![g] = [rm |-> k, ce |-> issue[g]]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<issue, booked, stamp, operated>>

Book(g) ==

  /\ booked[jotting[g].rm] = Vacant
  /\ issue[g] = jotting[g].ce
  /\ booked' = [booked EXCEPT ![jotting[g].rm] = g]
  /\ stamp' = [stamp EXCEPT ![jotting[g].rm] = jotting[g].ce]
  /\ jotting' = [jotting EXCEPT ![g] = NoRead]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<issue, operated>>

Retry(g) ==

  /\ \/ booked[jotting[g].rm] # Vacant
     \/ issue[g] # jotting[g].ce
  /\ jotting' = [jotting EXCEPT ![g] = NoRead]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<issue, booked, stamp, operated>>

Operate(g, k) ==
  /\ booked[k] = g
  /\ stamp[k] = issue[g]
  /\ booked' = [booked EXCEPT ![k] = Vacant]
  /\ operated' = operated \cup {g}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<issue, stamp, jotting>>

\* otherwise a room would be standing reserved to an authority nobody holds.
Reissue(g) ==

An air-traffic runway allocator works from a single strip-bay: a first-in, first-out queue of written clearances waiting to be read out to aircraft. The strip-bay has a working depth, and while it is at depth no further clearance may be written into it -- that is the backpressure on the writing desks. The depth is not fixed for the shift; it is re-set as weather and staffing change. Each runway strip is worked by exactly one desk at a time, and every clearance written carries the name of the desk that wrote it and the arrival window it grants.

The full action set is: Write -- the desk on duty for a strip writes a new clearance for one arrival window into the back of the strip-bay, allowed only while the strip-bay is under its current working depth. Read -- the clearance at the front of the strip-bay is read out and becomes the clearance in force on its runway, provided that runway has nothing in force already; it leaves the strip-bay. Roll -- the aircraft holding the clearance in force on a runway rolls and the clearance is spent, leaving that runway with nothing in force. Handover -- a strip is handed over to a different desk, and in the same motion every clearance for that strip is pulled: whatever was still queued in the strip-bay is removed, and whatever was in force on that runway is cancelled. Redepth -- the strip-bay's working depth is re-set to a different value during the shift.

The point of the handover pull is authority. A clearance is only as good as the desk that wrote it, and the moment a strip changes hands the outgoing desk's authority for that strip is gone. Paper written under it, whether it is still sitting in the strip-bay or has already been read out to an aircraft, is no longer backed by anybody, and reading out or acting on such a strip would be the allocator taking instruction from a desk that has been relieved.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every clearance still queued in the strip-bay, and every clearance actually in force on a runway, names the desk that is on duty for that strip at that moment, so no relieved desk's paper is ever left standing or acted upon.

\* nothing more may be written, which is the backpressure. The depth itself is
\* re-set during the shift as weather and staffing change.
\* A handover replaces the desk on duty for a strip and, in the same motion,

  /\ onDuty \in [Strips -> Desks]

  /\ onDuty = [s \in Strips |-> CHOOSE d \in Desks : TRUE]
  /\ depth = DepthHi
  /\ inForce = [s \in Strips |-> NoClr]

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A smart-home door lock network shares a fixed number of guest entry credits across its locks. The home owns exactly that many and no more: nothing in the system mints a credit and nothing burns one, so every operation is a hand-off of a credit from one place to another. Phone apps move credits around, and they do it without taking any lock: an app glances at a lock, noting the lock's revision number at that instant, and later tries to take a credit off it. The take is refused if the lock's revision has moved in the meantime, and every credit taken off or fitted onto a lock moves that lock's revision. The apps are slow but never dead: one can sit for an arbitrarily long time holding a stale glance, or holding a credit in hand, and will always eventually get around to fitting it somewhere.

The full action set is: Glance -- an app with empty hands and no reading takes a reading of one lock, noting the lock's current revision number. Fit -- an app carrying a credit fits it onto any lock, which moves that lock's revision; this is the only way a carried credit comes to rest. Take -- an app takes a credit off the lock it glanced at, accepted only if the lock's revision still equals what the app noted, if the lock actually has a credit, and if the home's transfer allowance for the day is not used up; the take moves the lock's revision. Stale -- an app whose noted revision no longer matches the lock's throws the reading away and starts over.

What matters here is not who is allowed to touch which lock. It is that the credits are a conserved quantity: at any instant, some of them are sitting on locks and some are in apps' hands on their way between locks, and those two amounts have to add up to what the home owns. A take that emptied a hand without debiting a lock, or a fit that credited a lock without emptying a hand, would silently change how many guest credits the home has.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The credits sitting on the locks plus the credits carried in apps' hands always add up to exactly the fixed number of guest entry credits the home owns, so no credit is ever created or destroyed in transit.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Whenever some app is carrying a credit, every carried credit is eventually fitted back onto a lock, leaving every app's hands empty again.

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A vending machine network is restocked from two regional desks. The two desks run as completely separate programs -- neither can see the other's plans -- but they do not have separate work queues: they push their restock chits into one shared spool of bounded depth, first in and first out. When the spool is at depth neither desk can push anything, and that shared cap is the backpressure on both of them at once. A central ledger records, for each machine, the one desk that machine currently answers to, and machines can be re-assigned from one desk to the other. Each machine also keeps a note of which desks it has actually run work from since it was last re-assigned.

The full action set is: Push -- a desk appends a chit naming a machine into the shared spool, allowed only while the spool is under its depth cap; a desk may push a chit for any machine, including one it does not currently own. Run -- the chit at the front of the spool is taken off and run, but only if the ledger says that machine answers to the desk that wrote the chit and the machine is not already busy; running it adds that desk to the machine's note. Refuse -- the chit at the front of the spool names a desk the machine no longer answers to, so it is discarded unrun. Finish -- a busy machine completes its restock and goes idle. Reassign -- a machine that is idle is re-assigned in the ledger to the other desk, and its note is wiped, because from that moment the previous desk has no standing at that machine at all.

The hazard comes from the shared spool. A chit written by one desk can be sitting in the spool while the ledger is re-assigned underneath it, and because neither desk can see the other, the desk that wrote it has no way of knowing its authority for that machine is gone. The only thing standing between a relieved desk and a machine acting on its instructions is the check made at the moment the chit reaches the front.

SAFETY PROPERTY: For every machine, every desk it has actually run work from since its last re-assignment is exactly the desk the ledger says it answers to, so no machine has ever acted on a chit from a desk that did not own it.

  /\ Len(spool) <= QCap

  /\ ledger = [m \in Machines |-> CHOOSE d \in Desks : TRUE]
  /\ ranFrom = [m \in Machines |-> {}]
  /\ busy = [m \in Machines |-> FALSE]

Push(d, m) ==

  /\ spool' = Append(spool, [mach |-> m, by |-> d])

     /\ ~busy[c.mach]

  /\ ranFrom' = [ranFrom EXCEPT ![m] = {}]

===BEGIN NATURAL LANGUAGE DESCRIPTION===
A bank's interbank settlement batch is rated to carry only so many instructions at once. The whole of that admission control lives in one compare-and-swap register holding two things: how full the batch currently is, and a tag that moves every time the register is written. A clerk who wants to add an instruction copies the pair -- the fill count and the tag -- onto a slip and posts the slip. Slips travel over an unordered wire and are picked up in whatever order they happen to be picked up in, so a slip can be acted on long after the pair it was copied from stopped being true.

The full action set is: Draft -- a clerk copies the register's current fill count and tag onto a slip for an instruction that is not in the batch and has no slip already out, and posts it onto the wire; the shift's drafting allowance limits how many slips can ever be posted. Swap -- a slip is picked off the wire and the register is written from it: this is accepted only if the tag on the slip still equals the register's tag, if one more instruction still fits inside the rating, and if the register has tag movements left; on acceptance the fill count becomes the slip's count plus one, the tag moves, and the instruction joins the batch. Bounce -- a slip that fails any part of that test is picked off the wire and torn up without touching the register. Pull -- an instruction is pulled back out of the batch, which drops the fill count by one and moves the tag.

The hazard is that a slip is a snapshot of the admission control, not the admission control itself. Several clerks can copy the very same fill count, and because the wire is unordered they can come back in any sequence. If the tag test were not there, each of them would write a fill count computed from the same starting point, the register would end up claiming the batch is far emptier than it is, and instruction after instruction would be admitted behind the batch's rating.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of instructions carried in the settlement batch never exceeds the rating the batch is admitted for.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Whenever slips are out on the wire, every one of them is eventually picked up and either swapped in or torn up, so the wire always clears.

A vending machine network keeps a planogram: which shelf face each product line occupies. Head office keeps two books that are meant to be exact mirrors of one another -- one says which face a product line sits in, the other says which product line fills a face. Placement orders are cut by the planners and travel to the machines in an unordered bag, so orders are picked out and acted on in whatever order they come to hand, not the order they were cut. Every order is stamped with the planogram number that was current when it was cut, and the whole planogram is periodically re-cut under a new number.

The full action set is: Cut -- the planners cut an order naming a product line and a shelf face, stamped with the current planogram number, and drop it in the bag, which they can only do while the bag is under its capacity. Post -- an order is picked out of the bag and posted into both books at once, but only if its planogram number is still current, the product line is not already placed, and the face is not already filled. Shred -- an order is picked out of the bag and shredded unposted, because its planogram number has been superseded, or because its line has already been placed, or because its face has already been filled. Strike -- a placed product line is struck from both books together, freeing its face. Replan -- a new planogram number is issued and both books are wiped clean at once, which makes every order still sitting in the bag worthless.

The hazard is double allocation of one shelf face. Because the bag is unordered, two orders naming the same face can be picked out at any distance apart in time, and an order cut under an old planogram can surface long after the machines have moved on. If a second line were ever posted into a face that was already filled, the two books would fall out of step with each other: the first line's entry would still name that face while the face's entry named the newcomer.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The two planogram books are exact inverses of each other -- every placed product line's face names that line back, and every filled face's line names that face back -- so no shelf face is ever allocated to two product lines.

\* Planogram orders travel in an unordered bag and are picked out in any order,
\* so an order stamped with a superseded plan number can surface at any time.

  /\ fills \in [Faces -> Lines \cup {NoLine}]

  /\ fills = [f \in Faces |-> NoLine]

  /\ sits[o.line] = NoFace
  /\ fills[o.face] = NoLine
